summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 2, who was the Food Inspector in the Food inspector, P W. 3, who had examined the sample of the food inspector, found that the article was "adulterated" and an article of food was said to be adulterated if it is insect infested. The Public Analyst found in the sample only nine living meal worms and he has neither stated that it is unfit for human consumption on account of the presence of seasonal worm. The Food Inspector also found in his report that the sample was "dried" but not that it was unfit for personal consumption. The High Court held that the Public Analyst had found in its report only nine live meal wortorms, and he had neither stated nor that it has been otherwise unfit for animal consumption. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The word 'otherwise ' in sub clause (f) of section 2 of the Act is wide enough to include all the adjectives used earlier refer to the quality of the article being unfit for Human consumption. [467G] 1.2 In order to bring a case within its purview, it must be shown that the articles were "adricated" or insect flled infested". The word "otherwise" in the same dictionary is defined as "to overrun or inhabit in large numbers, usually so as to be harmful or bother some swarm in or about." According to Webster 's New World Dictionary 'infest ' means "to abide by the human consumption". It relates to a distinct and separate article altogether. It is said that the word "worm" in section 2(1)(f) means "a substance of a large group of small invertebrate animals characterized, in the adult state, by division of the body into head, thorax, and abdomen, three pairs of membranous wings: bees, flies, wasps, mosquitoes, etc. are insects". [467C D] 1:3 The word is not to be read disjunctively but conjunctively. If the phrase is to be construed disjunctively, the more proof of the whole or any part of the articles being "filthy", putrid, disgusting, rotten. . or insects infested" would be conclu 473 sive to bring the case within the mischief of this sub clause, and it would not be necessary in such a case to prove further that thearticle was unfit or for human use. [468D E] 1 :4 The word used in section 3(1) (f), means "any substance which is capable of being used as food". It does not mean "to pass any test, but it does not include "any article which is intended to be used as a food." The word has been defined as including "a thing capable of use by human beings or persons. " The word may be read conjunctively and not disjunctively. [469E F] 1.:5 In the instant case, the prosecution had failed to prove that the lal mirchi powder was adulterated, for the Public analyst ha not expressed his opinion that the Lal mirchi Powder was either worm or insection infested or insible or that on account thereof it was fit for human food. The evidence of the Food Analyst does not support the case of the prosecution that theLal mirchi scorms were either wy. infested nor that the same was unfit to human consumption. It seems to us (1) that the Food Inspectors had found that there was no other evidence in support of the case that the 'later ' was adulterated.

The appellant was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The Sessions Judge rejected his evidence on the ground that he was an agriculturist and that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands he had taken on lease from various parties. He also held that as he had stored foodgrains above the permitted quantities for a wholesale dealer, he would be regarded as a wholesale trader within the order. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the presumption under para 3(2) could not be drawn; (2) the evidence of the witnesses on the basis of which they spoke orally were not concocted to set up a false defence; and (3) the onus of proving that he is an agriculturist stands upon him. HELD: The presumption under section 4 of the Act is that the person who stores any foodgrains in any quantity shall, unless the contrary is proved, be deemed to store the foodgrains for the purpose of sale. [901 B] In the present case, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were granted to him. He executed a number Of lease deeds and proved by oral evidence that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land on which Paddy and other foodgrains found in his pos session were grown, 901 The presumption was drawn under para 4 of order. [0902 D] In view of the clear language of section 4(2), it is obvious that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "carrying on the business" are not there, because storage has reference to 'business as a trader and that is the essence of the Order. The fiction in the second sub clause must be carried to its logical conclusion.

The defendant was a tenant of the suit premises. The plaintiff 's father, who had been in possession of the land as a trespasser, died in 1916 leaving behind him a will by which the entire estate was bequeathed to the present plain tiff. In 1943, the defendant executed a registered Kabuliyat in favour of the Receiver, by which he purported to take settlement of the property in suit for a period of 10 years at a rental of Rs. 250. The Receiver was dis charged and the plaintiff got possession of his entire estate in July 1927. The defendant continued to be a tenant and no fresh tenancy was created by holding over as is contemplated by section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. On 8th December, 1924, the plaintiff executed a Kabuliayat in favour othe defendant for purposes of cultivation. In 1947, the Receiver purported to took settlement of land in suit, but on the expiry of the second annual lease, which happened on 7th December 1926, the respondent ceased to be tenant and continued to remain a tenant. The appellant 's suit was decreed by the trial court and the decision was affirmed by the District Judge. In appeal before the High Court, it was contended that the plaintiff was in possession as a trespassers all along and thus acquired a good title by adverse possession. Held, that the defendant was in exclusive possession of land as trespasser all along. The question whether payment to the Receiver amounted to payment to him was not one from month to month under section 106, Transfer of property Act. The nature of the renewal clause contained therein is not seriously disputed by Mr. A similar view seems to have been taken also in Matilal vs Darjeeling Municipality (3). It would be pertinent to point out that in the Second Appeal preferred by the plaintiff against the dismissal of his earlier suit by the lower appellate court, the High Courts clearly held that the tenancy was one from the beginning a tenancy from month and that the only question left open was whether payment amounted to payments to the plaintiff himself.

The Income Tax officer, on the basis of a search conducted by him under section 132 of the Income tax Act, 1961, found that the production etc. would not be in the public interest and consequently rejected the claim for privilege as claimed by the Income Tax Officer. The assessee 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was dismissed by the High Court. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the assessment records of an assessee filed before the income tax authorities, even after April 1, 1964, were immune from production in a court of law on summons for their production being issued by the court and that the disclosure of any information from the record even to the courts is subject to the veto powers of the Commissioner of Income Tax under section 137(1) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The exercise of the jurisdiction to seek production of documents relating to assessment filed after April1, 1964 in assessment proceedings 1964 65 onwards, after the omission of Section 137 of the 1961 Act, was not put under a cloud in so far as the record of assessment is concerned. [642D] 2. The power of the courts to summon the production of the documents relating only to assessments filed after March 1,1964, was an independent power and it could not be said that the exercise of jurisdiction to obtain production of such documents had, thus, been put under cloud in a cloud so far the record is concerned.[642E] 3. The expression "any information relating to any assessee" in section 137 (1) (b) of Income tax was wide enough to include the power to seek the production or supply of any document relating to an assessee in respect of any assessment made either under the 1922 Act or under the 1961 Acts on or after April Ist, 1964. [542D E] 4. The provisions of section 138(1)(b) were not intended to cover cases where the record was summoned even by a court. [567B] 5. Section 137(2) of 1961 Act provided as follows: "137. (4) . Where the documents, records, etc., are filed by an assessee or a third party after April, 1, 1962, in respect o assessment year 1962 63 and 1963 64 in proceedings for the said assessment years taking place under the Income 'tax Act, 1922, and before April 1 1964, in proceedings relating to the recovery of a demand prepared for the purpose of this Act, in any proceeding for the same assessment year taking place after April.

The appellant was the guardian of a minor son. He had two sisters, Kunhamu and his two sisters. The gift deed provided that if there was no such person one can be chosen and appointed by the Civil Court. The appellant 's mother died on May 3, 1946 without an issue. On the death of Seinaba, the present suit was brought by Kunhamudram for partition and possession of a 6/16 share of the property which he claimed as an heir under the Muhammadan Law. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the gift was invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that when succession opened out on the deathof Mammotty, his widow Seinha was entitled to the enhanced share of 1/4 as there was a declaration and a tender by the donor Mammatty was sufficient to establish the transfer of possession. HELD : (1) The gift must be immediate and complete (tamlik ulain) for the most essential ingredient of Hiba is the declaration "I have given". In the instant case there is a declaration made by the husband followed by the handing over of the deed to the minor possessing discretion and accepted by her. [766 F] (2) The donor was not in charge of the gift but was in charge thereof. He was in possession of the gifted property as guardian of his minor wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him, for after the celebration of marriage a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father be living; [767 E] (3) The declaration made in the deed was sufficient for establishing the transfer. [761 G] (4) The document embodying the intention of the donor was sufficient and to establish that the donee had given. the gift actually made. [758 A] (5) The statement made by a person who has it is not necessary that possession must be given to a guardian specially to be appointed by him to whom possession can be made over to manifest the intention. In the present case there was only a declaration of gift and a certificate by the donee was sufficient. [759 B] (6) The appellant had no right to make a declaration as required by section 6 of the Act. The High Court rightly held that the declaration made was sufficient in establishing the gift.

The respondents were the trustees of a religious institution. The Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Madras, issued a notification under section 100(1) of the Act prescribing a graduated scale of rates of contribution under section 76(1). The respondents challenged the validity of the demand on the ground that no rules had been framed under section100 of the , but the High Court upheld the plea on the grounds (i) that no Rules had been made under section 101(2), and (ii) that the audit fee demanded by the Commissioner was without jurisdiction, because the rules were framed at a time when several different kinds of services were intended to be rendered and the Court later struck down certain provisions of the act. The High Court held that sections 21, 30(2) , 31, 63 to 69 and 89 as amended by Act 27 of 1954 were ultra vires, in that they infringed the guarantee of the fundamental rights in articles 19(1)(f), 25 and 26 of the Constitution of India. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i ) the High Courts erred in holding that sections 76(2)(a) and 89 were invalid as no rules have been framed, and (iii) that section 76 (1) and (3) of Act 19 of 1951 were ultravires. HELD : (i). The Commissioner may not under section 77(1), impose a flat rate on the religious institutions governed by the Act. But if services are provided, assuming that the Venkataramana temple either does not need the services, or does not obtain the same degree of service as others may. [245 D] (ii)(a). The High Courts were right in holding, that section 78(1 ) and (2) of 1951 are ultra vires. [246 C] (b) The Commissioner has to determine audit fee for meeting the costs of audit of accounts as a per 924 centage of the income of each religious institution for the relevant year preceding the year is Rs. In the present case, conditions (1), (2), (3), (4) and 924 are satisfied.

The appellant was the contemner under section 19(1) of the , from the order dated 2nd April, 1975 of the High Court. The High Court directed the issue of notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be proceeded against for committing contempt of the Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that no appeal lies to this court as a matter of right from any kind of order made by the High court in the proceeding for contempt, and that an appeal does lie to this Courts under section 20 of the Act from an order or decision of a bench of the Supreme Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The preliminary objection raised on behalf o the respondents is well founded and must be accepted as correct. [501 D] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra, ; , referred to. (2) An order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further, does not decide any question. It may be a different matter if the order does decide some bone of contention raised before the High Courts affecting the right of the party aggrieved. [525 E] Barabakanta Misra vs JusticeGatikrunna Mishra ; , distinguished. (3) An appeal would lie as a "a matter of law" from any order or decisions of the court; and (4) an appeal would be maintainable if it is in violation of section 20.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another, in the Court of the Magistrate, First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) of the Act for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the , and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) section 6 of the . was repealed, and (ii) if section 6 was not on the statute book there could be justification for this view as the words it wireless telegraphy apparatus " in section 6 A were comprehensive enough to take in " wireless telegraphs" this Court gave leave limited to the question of sentence only. HELD: (i)(a) The word " text ", in its dictionary meaning means " subject or theme". When an enactment amends the text of another, it amends the subject ormatter of it, though sometimes it may expunge unnecessary words without altering the subject. [267 F] (b) Section 6 A of the Indian Wireless Telegraphy (Amendment) Act, 1949, is not covered by the provisions in section 4 of the 1952 Act. The word ' text ", means " with a view to bringing about an end to the amending Act. It includes " subject" or "subject to the provisions contained in the later statute. [268 G H] (c) Section 20 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, is only applicable to cases where an earlier Act is amended by a later Act, and it cannot be said that section 6A was either covered by section 4 or a surplusage not serving any definite purpose. The words " subject to the provision contained in section 3" are comprehensive enough so as to take within its sweep all other enactments in which the repealed enactment has been applied, incorporated or referred to. [269 D] (d) Section 4 of 1952 Act does not apply to cases of a later amending Act incorporating new provisions in an earlier statute, for, where an previously Act is repealed by a subsequent Act it cannot also be said to have been included in the definition of " text ".

The appellant, a managing trustee of the respondent 's estate, was the real lender and the real decreeholder in both these suits was put into execution. The last entry in the Hatchita was made in March 1929 and the total amount borrowed up to that date came to Rs. 3,801. The instalments not having been paid in either of the cases both the decrees were put into executed. In Execution Cases Nos. 261 and 262 of 1932, the properties mentioned in Schedule Ka in each case were put up to sale and they were purchased ostensibly by the two decreeholders Aditya and Dhiren. Three years later, execution proceedings were initiated against Satish Chandra, the managing Shebait, some time in October 1931 and a sum of Rs. 5,068, having been found due to the 128 990 creditor, Satish Chandra gave him a renewed Hatchitita for that amount. The properties mentioned therein were put to sale by the three decreeholders, but the sale proceeds were set off against the decretal dues. In execution cases Nos. 262 and 263 of 1932 the properties described in ScheduleKa in each cases were put on sale and it was found due from the 128 creditor, who purchased Ka and Kha Schedule properties sold respectively by a registered Kobala to the appellant 's wife. The appellant filed an application under section 36 of the Bengal Money Lenders Act for reopening of the decrees and making of fresh decrees in their places in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Subordinate Judge dismissed the application holding that the properties were not benami but were merely benamidars for Aghore Nath Roy, who was the actual lender and that the sale was made by the decreeholder himself and his wife. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High Court had erred in treating the Chakrabortys alone as the decreeholders; (ii) even if Aghoria was proved to have advanced the money upon which the Chakraborty's obtained the decrees, in reopening the decrees under section 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court could treat the Chakraborty as the judgment debtor and not the decree holder. HELD: (i)(a) The power of reopening a transaction, as contemplated by the section, extends to reopening of decrees as well. A new decree is passed only for the purpose of substituting the method of accounting sanctioned by the Act for the calculations upon which a original decree was passed and to give an opportunity to the judgment creditor to pay the decretal amount thus ascertained by instalments. [128 D] (b) The language of section 36(2) of the Indian Money Lender Act, is quite obscure and somewhat clumsy, but it is clear that the power of reopen a transaction as contemplated under the section extends to the reopening of decree as well as for giving an opportunity, to the decree debtor to pay his decretal dues thus ascertained. [129 E] (c) The object of the section is to enable the court to pass a new decree in accordance therewith and clause (e) further imposes a duty on the court, to give a direction in such cases that if there is default in the payment of any one of the instalments, the property restored to the Judgment debtor under clause (d) would be put back into the possession of the decreedebtor. [130 F] (2)(a). The language used in section 36 is quite clear and unambiguous. It does not say that a new order should be passed only on the basis of the original decree. A fresh decree is made only for purposes of substituting it the method by which the original judgment was passed, and to giving an option to the court under clause(e) also imposes a obligation on the Court to give such direction in cases where there is delay in payment of the decretal amounts.

The respondent company was a registered partnership firm. The appellant company had been carrying on business in the name and style of Habib & Sons, Bombay. On the 11th December 1950 the Custodian of Evacuee Property passed an order for sale of the properties to the respondent company. Before him the respondent Company filed an application under Order XXI Rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure for execution of the decree. The Additional Custodian of evacuee Property informed the appellant that by an order made on the 2nd August 1950 the Additional Custodian had confirmed "the transaction of transfer" and that the appellant was entitled to execute the decree for herself and as the guardian of Wajed. The respondent company then filed a suit against the appellant company in the Court of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Bombay, claiming that the sale deed executed by it was not binding on the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the document in question was a completed deed of transfer and that it was perfectly clear that if one were to construe rule 16 strictly there is no assignment of the same in writing executed by the transferor but is brought about by the operation of law. On appeal, the Additional Commissioner held that the transaction of sale was not an actionable claim and that therefore the appellant could maintain the application for execution. The High Court also held that Abedoonissa was entitled only to execute a decree for himself and as such the appellant had no right to execute it. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) A transfer of property is not by any assignment in writing or by operation of statute. It postulates first, that a decree has been passed and secondly, that an assignment or transfer thereof need not be effected in the manner prescribed by section 130 of the Transfer of Property Act. [273 D] (2) The transferee has a mortgage security on existing chattels and also the benefit of what in form was an assignment of non existing chattells which might be afterwards brought on to the premises. The property so transferred included book debts. Under the Transfer Of Property Act there can be no transfer of immovable property which is not in existence at the date of the transfer.

The respondent carried on the business of fabricating steel doors, windows, sashes and other goods. The contract was for work in the execution of which some movable property passed : it was not a contract for sale of goods but a combination of two distinct and separate contracts, one for supply or the sale of materials used in the construction, glazing, fittings and finish of the windows. In the course of the execution, the respondent made no separate charge for that service. The Sales Tax Officer held that the contract was one of sale of motor tyres, luggage carriers, air conditioning units, refrigerators and fitting of the doors. The respondent appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who remanded the case with a direction to assess tax on the price for sale. The Board of Revenue then remanded the matter with a further direction to determine tax on sales of materials only. The following question was referred by the Board of revenue to the High Court: Whether on the proper interpretation of the contract between the applicant and the Executive Engineer, C.P.W.D., the contract of sale was one for work and labour. " HELD : (i) The contract is for work, in the executing of which the use of materials is 'accessory or incidental to the execution or of the work; or it may be a contract of work and Labour. [501 B] (ii) The object of the respondent was to enter into a works contract. It may be an essential term of the agreement, but a contract to work and for labour. The main object of work undertaken by the payee of the price is not the transfer of a chattel qua chattel, the contract is 'one for work or labour. [504 C D] (iii) The contractor was to prepare the window leaves according to the specifications with glass plain or ground glass as may be decided by the Engineer in Charge. He gave instances of sale and hire purchase of motor tyre, luggage carrier, air conditionsing units etc., at certain rates. The quotation is based on the current prices of mild steel billets fixed by the Government. Sales Tax or any other tax is applicable will be extra.

The appellant State is an accused in a case under section 420 and the Indian Penal Code. On November 8, 1967 Shankerlal was also informed that he would arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. On December 16, 1967 Shankar Lal and Raj Kumar Agarwalla came to the shop of Ram Avtar with washer plates in a taxi. Price of the said goods was then demanded from Ram Avtar. Shanker Lal and Saheb Jaman Khan were thereupon arrested by the police. The appellant 's case is that on November 8 1967 Shanker Lal handed over the said formal order to Ram Avtar and introduced Saheb Jamam Khan as agent of M/s. Ashoke Trading Corporation of Indore. Ram Avtar was also told that this transaction would fetch him a profit of Rs. 3200/ . On November 16, 1968 Shankar Lal brought one Saheb Jama Khan alongwith him to Ram Pal and introduced Sahib JamanKhan as agent. Shankerlal and Raj Kr. Agarwalla were thereupon apprehended by the Police. The police did not submit any charge sheet on the basis of the report which had been lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Aggarwalla respondent because it is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned, no case had been made out against him. Charges framed against the appellant were accordingly quashed. The State appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 In view of the fact that there is no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High Court as might induce us to interfere with the order of the Trial Court as may induce us in interfering with the same. [279D] 2.2 The report which was lodged by Shankar Lal in the course of things making no mention regarding the name or names of Raj Kr Kumar Agarwalola respondent because he is the party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar, would hardly warrant an inference that Raj Kr had been a party to the conspiracy to cheat or cheat. [280E] 3. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he was present along with Shanker Lal, when the latter brought washer plate in a Tax and demanded the price of the washer exhibited from RamAIL.

The petitioner, a resident of Sultanbattery area in the State of Kerala and describing himself as a commuter of the Indian Railways, has alleged violation of fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 19 and 21 and claims reliefs of mandamus to the Union of India for implementing the reports of the Kunzru, Wanchoo and Sikri Committees, appointing a fact finding Commission to inquire and report about the several accidents from 1970 onwards and for various other directions to the Ministry of Civil Aviation. The petitioner has also alleged that unmanned level crossings are gradually being replaced by manned ones and improved technical gadgets are being provided for efficient operation. Dealing with manpower, the counter affidavit asserts that direct recruits are given proper training required for the respective posts and only qualified people are entrusted with assignments. Drivers are subjected to periodical medical examination until the age of 45 at intervals of three years and thereafter until superannuation every year. Accidents involving loss of human life and properties estimated over one lakh are earmarked for enquiry by Commissioners of Railway Safety who as authorities appointed under section 4 of the Act function independently of the Railway Administration and are under the administrative control of Ministry of civil Aviation. It has also been alleged that there is almost 120000 bridges on the Railways out of which 195 are important bridges and nearly 9400 are major bridges. Most of the States have framed rules under the , making it obligatory for 713 drivers of motor vehicles to stop short of unmanning level crosses, observe and then proceed. The Joint Director (Safety) has filed a counter affidavit in answer to the Rule on behalf of the respondents. It was further pleaded that periodic review is undertaken about manning of unmenned level crossing crossings with a volume of traffic of more than 6000 train vehicle units or poor approach visibility are being manned in a phased manner at the cost of the Railways and control at the gate is also being improved. Most Of the States had framed rules for making it mandatory for 713 vehicles to avoid short of Unmanned Level crossings, observeand then proceed, and that until superannuation each year. Accident involving loss caused by loss of Human life and property estimated over a lakh are allocated for enquiry under section4 of the , and thereafter till superannuation everyyear. The Union of Indian Railways is a socialised public utility undertaking. It had also prescribed rules and issued instructions which were not being properly implemented. The joint Director (Western Railway) has also filed a Counter affidavit in reply to the rule on behalf o the respondents, contending that periodic Review is undertaken over manning level crossing of unmmanned levels crossings and opening of new level crossing in consultation with appropriate State Governments. It is further stated that there are nearly 120000 bridge on the railways out ofwhich 195 are vital bridges and almost 9400 were major bridges; and improved Technical gadgests are also being provided to efficient operation, and this control should not be an arbitrary right of interference but a regulated authority defined and declared by law which is not to be needlessly or vexatiously exacted but which, in my humble judgment, is necessary at once for the interests of the State and for the protection of the public interest. The Railway Protection Force is maintained to protect consignments booked for transport as also Railway property. It further provides that unmmenned levels crossing crosses with a mass of traffic are annually built. It would be difficult to say that the encounters are as just and as free from arbitrariness as are the familiar encounters of the rights. Everyone in the country must realise this and be told the great truth said by Lord Wright: "The safeguard of British liberty is in the good sense of the people". The safeguard of Indian citizens is in a good sense, of the inhabitants of the country.

The appellants, who were the holders of proprietary jagirs, applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953. The application was rejected by the Collector on the ground that they were barred under article 168 of the Limitation Act read with Regulation 55 and 0.41, rr. 55 and o. 41, rr., 55 and O.41 respectively. The appellants filed appeals before the Revenue Tribunal against the orders of dismissal passed by the authorities below. The Tribunal held that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, they were within 30 days from the date of receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications for restoration should have been allowed as they were prevented for sufficient cause from appearing at the hearing of the appeals. The Revenue Tribunal held against the appellants. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since they had applied for restoration, they could not be said to have made an application within 30 day from the receipt of order of the dismissal and therefore the applications were barred by article 168 Of the Limitation Code read with section 17(1) of the Jagirs Abolition Act. HELD: (i) The Tribunal has no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it is obligatory on its part to decide the appeal on merits and to record its decision even though there is default on the part of the appellant to appear in person or through his agent or lawyer when the appeal or application is called for hearing the Tribunal may decide the same on merits. [144 E] (ii) The order of this Court dismissing the restoration applications Nos. 28, 29 and 30 of 1960 are ultra vires and illegal and must be set aside and order that these four appeals should go back to the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal for being reheard and dealt with in accordance with law. [145 D] (iii) The orders of the Gujarat revenue Tribunal dismissing the appellants ' applications Nos 28,29 and 30 are ultra void and cannot be allowed as it is not obligatory on their part to determine the appeal.

The plaintiffs, who were the descendants of one Dinanath Sao, filed a suit for declaration that Telibandha village was held by the defendant in trust for Shri Ramchandra of the Dudhadhari Math and that he had committed breach of trust. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that it was superseded by the Award of Mr. To explain his possession of the village, the defendant referred to a partition in 1901 between Sarjoo Prashad 's four sons on the one hand and jamuna Prasad, on the other at which, it was said, that Tekibandha village fell to the share of Sarjoo Prasad Sao and that the dedication was confirmed by all the co sharers at the time of DinanathSao. The High Court also held that the defendant was the trustee of this public trust and had committed breaches of trust by transferring trust properties and appropriating its proceeds and finally by his express repudiation of this trust, and was therefore liable to be removed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the High court erred in holding that the suit was barred by limitation; (ii) the defendant had committed acts of breach of Trust by transferring title or interest to the plaintiff in his place; and (iii) the respondent had committed offences under section 409, 420, 467, 468, 471, 477A, 120B, 120 B, 420 read with section 34 I.P.C. HELD: (i ) The High court rightly pointed out that the award was a good and valid award. [419D] (ii)(a) It is not correct to say that these words as used in the original necessarily mean " from the profits and income of mouza Teli�". This plea was not taken by the respondent in his written statement nor did it appear to have been urged seriously before the courts below. [420B C] (b) The High Courts rightly pointed Out the course of conduct of the parties is of no relevance for the construction of a document which is itself unambiguous and clear. It has to be borne in mind that very many words are used in more than one sense and that sense differs in different circumstances. What is to be done where this happens ? Kamgar Shah vs Jagdish Chandra Deo Dhabal Deo. [416C] (c) The word "Malik" came up for consideration before the High Courts of judicature at Nagpur, in a series of cases, including the present one. It was not disputed that the respondent was the Manager of the public trust. He had been appointed as manager on behalf and by his descendants.

The appellants before this Court are the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Faizabad Bar Association. There were three charges against the appellants. They were that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar. The High Court discharged the notices. The appellants filed an appeal before this court. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Chairman of the Action Committee described as contemner No. 2 was actively associated with the passing of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Judge and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he is guilty of having committed contempt as contemner Nos. 1 & 2 were guilty of contumacious conduct, and the High Court gave the ground that they were responsible for the passing thereof. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The High court confused 'criminal contempt ' with 'contu macious conduct '. [604B] (2) The language used by them was unfortunate. It is a matter of regret that the indiscretion will not be repeated.[605C] (3) The Judges have to discharge their duty with dignity, decorum and discipline. [065D] (4) The words "in regard to the resolu tion" in clause 14 of the U.P. High Court 's Amalgamation Order, 1948 in a very partisan manner are unfortunate. They do not want to be over sensitive in the matter, keeping in mind the surrounding circumstances in which the contu mious act was committed by them. [ 065E] (5) The terms used by the appellants were unfortunate. The language of the Resolution clearly showed that the members of the Bar did not act with dignity in regard to their resolu ment.

The appellant, a sole proprietor of a joint family, entered into an agreement with the respondent No. 1 for partition of joint movable and immovable properties and the same was registered by which the abovenamed arbitrators were given the option to take assistance of one, two or more persons. The arbitrators gave their consent to take the assistance of three persons. On or about 2nd of July, 1977 the appellant No. l filed an application under section 14 of the , before the learned Sub Judge praying for a direction on the arbitrator to file the award in the court in Misc. Case No. 74 of 1977 and the interim injunction order was vacated. The respondent No 1 filed an objection before the Sub Judge stating that during the subsistence of the interim order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo till the disposal of Misc. 74, 1977 initiated by the appellant, the same agreement was re written on a fresh stamp paper and the said application was rejected. Thereafter the appellant filed an appeal under section 15 of the Act before the High Court which allowed the appeal holding that during subsistence of interim injunction orders on the parties including the arbitrators, to maintain Status quo till disposal of the Misc. case, namely, 28th January 1978, should be excluded in view of the principle laid down under section15 of the . The High Court also ordered return of the award to the arbitrators. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending, namely 28th of January, 1978 to 24th November, 1983 should be included in view the principle enunciated under section 18 of the ; and that the limitation for registration had already expired. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The limitation period for registration is four months from the date of its execution. [690G] 1.2 In this case admittedly during the period from 26th July, 1978 till 20th December, 1982 there was subsisting injunction preventing the arbitrators from taking any steps. It was not disputed that during this period there was existing injunction restraining the arbitratorsfrom taking any step. The limitation for filing an application for registration has already expired and as such was beyond time. [0690D] 1:3 In the instant case admittedly the award was in the Court of the learned Munsif from 28th July 1978 to 20th of December, 1983. Therefore the cumulative effect of sections 23 and 25 read together is that total period of eight months is available for registration if the conditions are fulfilled. [ 0690F] 1 :4 The law does not compel a man to do that which he cannot possibly perform. In the present case admittedly there was an injunction on 26th of July 1978 restraining the arbitrator from taking steps. Therefore, this period, that is to say from 28nd January,1978 to 24rd November, 1982 till 20st December,1982. [ 690G H] 1.:5 The law did not compel any man to perform that which him cannot possibly possibly perform; but no arbitrator could be compelled to disobey the order of the court and if in compliance or obedience with court of doubtful jurisdiction he could not take back the award from the custody of the Court to take any further steps for its registration then it cannot be said that he has failed to get the award registered as the law required.

The appellant was a tenant for about 20 years in the premises known as " Fida Ali Villa" in Kalyan. The respondent had four sub tenants, three of them also shifted to the new premises which were let to him by the respondent. There was some dispute as to the date when these new premises were let out to the appellant and the respondent filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground that they were let on July 1, 1948, and the sub tenants were not licensees of the respondent and in this Court no serious argument was addressed on those points. The trial court held that subletting was lawful in spite of section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act 1947 (Bom. LVII of 1944) and sections 13(1)(e), and 15 of that Act did not preclude an agreement between the landlord and tenant, nor was the prohibition limited to cases for which a penalty is exigible. The High Court affirmed the order of ejectment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises. HELD : (1) The respondent was only seeking to enforce his rights under the statute and the appellant cannot be permitted to assert in a court of justice any right founded upon or growing out of an illegal transaction. [1068 C] (2) The question is not merely whether waiver of statutory rights enacted for the benefit of an individual but whether the Court would aid the appellant in enforcing a term of the agreement which section 15 was applicable to contracts between the parties as to sub letting; and, therefore, section 15 could not be invoked. [ 1068 D] (3) The provisions of the Act do not preclude any person from relying upon a contract the making of which the law prohibits (section 23 of the Contract Act). [1069 E F] (4) The appellant cannot claim to have the right under section 13(2)(e) because he had no right to sublet the premises to a sub tenant.

The appellant was appointed as a District Judge on August 31, 1990. He was promoted to the post of District Judge by an order dated October 26, 1985. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court which held that the Samiti was vested with power to grant licence to hold the fair under section 23(1) of the Act and that the decision of the Divisional Board in turn was on behalf of the State Board. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Society was vested in power to appoint a District judge and dismiss the appeal. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the finding of the High court that the institution was vested only with power of appointment including initial posting and promotion of the District Judge and dismissal, removal and reduction in rank of the district Judges within the exercise of the control vested in the High Courts is erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The examination committee if relies upon such evidence to come to the conclusion that the examinee has used unfair means in answering questions then it is not open to the High ourt to interfere with that decision merely because the High 'Court may take a different view on re assessment of those circumstances. [782G] 1.2 In civil cases the standard of proof is satisfied on a balance of probabilities. The examination Committee if relies on such evidence, to come tout justice then academic standards require that the authority 's appreciation of the problem must be respected. If there is sufficient material on which it could be demonstrated that the Authority was right in its conclusion that it was right. [788B] 1:3 In civil proceedings the standard required that the authorities ' appreciation of evidence should be respected.[782A] 1 :4 The test of probability, and the degrees of it, cannot obviously be expressed in terms of units to be mathematically enumerated as to how many of such units constitute proof beyond reasonable doubt. [789B] 2.1 In civil suits the standard requires that the author 's evaluation must be fair and reasonable. If the authority concerned acted fairly and reasonably to meet out justice then it was not open for the HighCourt to interfere in that decision, merely because it may take another view on the re assessment o f those circumstances.] [785C] 2:2 The test is not beyond all reasonable doubt but the degrees or of it cannot obviouslybe expressed in term of units. But the reasons may be precise. The need for recording reasons is greater in a case where the order is passed at the original stage. It also aids the appellate or revisional authority or the supervisory jurisdiction of this Court under article 226 or the Appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136 to see whether the authority charged acted fairly or justly to meetout justice to the aggrieved person. [783D E] 2 :3 The test for determining whether a particular function is quasi judicial or quasi judicial, depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is not necessary that the body concerned must be given an opportunity to lead evidence on its behalf and if the authority is right in his conclusion that he has used such unfair means then academic standard require that it should be avoided. [784E F] 2(a) The test laid down by this Court in Union of India vs H.C. Sharma, ; , referred to. (b) The principles governing the exercise and discharge of functions under section 22(1)(e) of Act are not exhaustive. It may be that the power of appointing a District Judges is exercised with great care and caution and it is open to him to examine them. [779D E; 878A] 2.(a) In civil matters the standard for proof is not a high degree akin to trial in a criminal case.

The appellants were charged with having committed offences under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special Judge convicted them and sentenced them to three months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 500. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the offence as defined in section 161 of the Indian Penal Code, if it is habitual, falls within clause (d) of section 5 of the Act and therefore, the conviction could not be sustained. HELD: The words "corrupt or illegal means" are used in the sense of making more effective provision for the prevention of bribery and corruption. It is not necessary that an offence under clause (c) to prove all these ingredients should be proved by a public servant. [184 D] In the present case, the offence was committed with the object of inducing the public servant to give an acceptance of bribe by a person who knows to be inadequate or to be likely to be concerned in any proceeding or business transacted or about to be transacted by him or for any other person. The offence as contemplated in section 5 (2) is not confined only to the purpose of proving all these ingredient. [185 E F] In view of the clear language employed in section162, it cannot be said that the Act seeks to create and create an independent offence distinct from simple bribery. It can come into play only when there is no offer to give a acceptance of a bribe by public servant or for some other person, any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage.

The appellant was the surety for a sum of Rs. 81 in favour of the Bank. The principal debtor executed a bond Ext. P 4 in favour, agreeing to give personal guarantee on the specific understanding and with full knowledge of the bank that the principal debtor had offered security by way of pledge of goods and the goods were to be kept under the lock and key of the respondent Bank. On the same day the principal creditor also executed a demand promissory note, Ext. 76 in favour and the Bank issued a letter of continuity of the bond and the promissory note Ext. 77,368.04 P in this account to the Bank on September 16, 1957. The appellant filed an application under section 141 of the Indian Contract Act for permission of the General Manager of the appellant bank to extend the facility. The High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal amount and he should not be exposed to second round of litigation for restitution of the amount and that this Court should give a direction to the respondent to pay the balance amount with interest at current rate to the appellant. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The surety has made an application that in compliance with the decree made by the trial court he had paid the entire amount and the surety gave personal guarantee to the satisfaction of the Court. [923D] 2. In view of clause 5 of the letter of guarantee, Ext Should the customer be a limited company, corporate or an incorporate body, committee, firm, partnership, trustees or debtors on a joint account, the provisions hereinbefore contained shall be construed and take effect where necessary as if the words importing the singular number included also the plural number. [969B] 3. The respondent surety has not taken more than one security on the basis of which advance was made and the sureties gave personal guarantees on the good faith of other security being offered by the principal borrower which itself may be a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee and the creditor by its own negligence lost one of the securities. [970F] 4. The bond Ext, should be properly construed as "any security other than the pledge of property mentioned in the primary agreement, exhibit P 1 between the Bank and the firm. [971G] 5. In the instant case, the surety has given an undertaking that he will not be liable to any further loss or damage if the goods are kept under lock and keys of the godown in the compound of Vijay oil Mills under the custody of the creditor Bank. It is not a case of granting time or indulgence to the principal offender or variation of the credit or taking one set of security in substitution of some other security or release of any security. In an almost identical situation with regard to an identical clauses in Amrit Lal Goverdhan Lalan vs State Bank of Travancore and Ors, this Court after referring to clause 5 in the letter OF guarantee, held as under: "On behalf of the respondents Bank it is not necessary that the words bringing the singular numbers included also plural number included along the plural.

The appellant was the local representative of the then sovereign authority, and the State of Bombay was respondent No. 1. The lands in suit were comprised in six survey numbers stated in paragraph one of the plaint. In 1923 there was a partition between the appellant and respondent No, and in 1904 there was no satisfactory proof) in perpetuity subject to a quit rent of Rs. 500 for each netan; it was also stated that this was supported by old judicial usage. The Inam Commissioner held that the appellant was not entitled to hold the "patelki inam" lands which were given as emoluments of his office to the working patel from the Rokade family. On appeal, the High Court held that in view of the provisions of section 192 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879, the suit was not maintainable and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the suit filed by respondent No was barred by limitation; (ii) the order of resumption was not a valid order; (iii) the High court had erred in holding that the suit for possession was barred under section 192 and (iv) the appellant 's claim to title by adverse possession could be disposed of in a few words. HELD : (i)(a) The claim of title by way of adverse possession can be disposed off in a certain manner as the revenue authorities are empowered under the Law to determine, and among the matters mentioned in the section is any claim against the State relating to any property or emoluments appertaining to the office of any hereditary officer or servant. [727 C] (b) The appellant was entitled as of right to a share in the emoluments of the patel 's office and that Government had no right to resume " patelki Inam lands and regrant the same to the officrancer; it is enough to state that no decision has been brought to our notice in which it has been held that a member of the family is entitled as Of right to share in emoluments of an office. [761 G] (c) The order of resumed will have to be modified so as to exclude it. [758 D] (d) Rule V of the said Law states that the emoluments appertaining thereto shall be enjoyed solely by the person for the time being holding the office; even a substitute shall receive the whole of the emoluments relating to the Office, unless the Deputy Commissioner otherwise directs.

The respondents, who were the sons of one late Shri G.B. Bucker, filed a suit for partition of their properties and for possession of certain properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the Khojas were governed by the Hindu law of survivorship, and that the custom put forward before him as proved was not binding on the parties to the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the custom which followed by one, particular family would not "convert" the family into a coparcenary governed by Hindu Law; (ii) the Khoja was governed by his personal law unless he renounces the old law and accepts the new one, except where a statutory provision is made. HELD : (1) The custom in question was not based on any custom followed by another, particular, family would be governed by their personal law, unless they renounces it; (iii) the customary law did Halai Memons follow in regard to succession to their properties; and (iv) the right of a son by birth in such pro perty and its devolution by survivorship was not affected. [234 D] (2) The High Court had rightly held that the customary laws were governed under the Hindu Law, and the Bombay view as expressed in section Haji Aboo Buckers ' case(1) was correct. [236 E F] (3) The question whether a Khoja of the Shia Ishna Ashari sect could dispose of the whole of his property by testamentary disposition is not a matter of custom but it is a matter which must be determined on the facts and circumstances of each case. [237 D] Haji Aboor Sait vs Mongbibai, A.I.R. 1939 Mad. 235, referred to. (4) The customary law in question did Hala Memons appear to have been followed by some other family members. It was not disputed that the family emigrate to another country was governed under Hindu Law and it would not be just to interfere with those rights on account of this recent change of opinion. [238 E F]. (5) The Bombay view in Haji Abee Buckel vs Mendbibai (2), followed. (6) The decision of the High Court that the succession was governed only by the customary Law, was correct and must be set aside. [239 G] (7) The Hindu law did not Halai memons follow the customary custom prevailing among the Khoias and Cutchi Memons alike, as if they were on precisely the same footing and urged the necessity of deciding the cases of Cutchi memors in respect of them rather than the customs prevalent among the khoias. [240 G] Haji Mohammad AbooBucker Sait, ; , referred to (8) The rule was that the Hindu laws governed them. It is not necessary for a Hindu family to have a customary law which has to be traversed for a proper determination of the case. It would be open to a Hindu widow to make a claim in respect thereof.

The appellants are manufacturers of yarn which is also removed from the factory. The appellants were manufacturing yarn which was also removed by them on payment of excise duty. The Central Excise authorities issued a show cause notice to the appellants for removal of the goods. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the show cause notices and the High court allowed the writ petition holding that there was removal of calcium carbide for the 708 purpose of levy and collection of excise duties. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the expression "factory" under section 2(e) of the Act has to be construed in the light of the definition contained in section 2 (e) and that the words used therein are capable of comprehending them. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The word "factory ' under section 3(4) of Central Excise Act is a wide enough to include within it demand for more than six months from the date of the amendment. It contemplates physical movement of goods from one place to another It is well settled that a deeming provision is an admission of the non existence of the fact deemed. [707B] 1.2 The words "any premises appurtenant thereto" occurring in rule 9(1) of Excise Rules do not qualify the words " any premises appurtenant to such premises". This contention finds support from the decision of this Court in Jawaharmal vs State of Rajasthan and others, [19661 I S.C. Explanation. But such demand, though it may include within them demand for less than six month, must be made within a period of six months form the date when the law was made and, unless a contrary intention appears, an interpretation should be given to the words use to take in new facts and situations, if the words are capable, of comprehendings them. [758C D] 1:3 The word 'factory ' used in rule 8(1)(b) is wide enough and comprehensive enough to cover all excisable goods produced or manufactured by a manufacturer. It is not possible to accept that the definition of "factory " under section 4(4), is wide in its amplitude. [759D F] 1 :4 The words 'any premises belonging thereto" used in Rule 9(2) are capable to comprehend them. They relate to or qualify the word 'premises appurtenant thereto. It does not mean any place where they are produced, cured or manufactured. [761G H] 1.:5 In order to appreciate the ground of such challenge, we may once again refer to section 51 of the Finance Act, 1982. The definition of expression " factory" under Section 2(d) is made in the licence and in the declaration that has to he furnished by the manufacturer in Form D 2. The words used in clause (b) of rule 9 are capable only of comprehendating them. It may include outside it demand of more than 6 months, but relate to goods which are produced or processed. [752E F] 2:6 The word `factory ' is a comprehensive enough and wide enough. It connotes physical movement and not merely physical movement. It has been held that the word `premises appurtenant to a factory is used in the sense of physical movement, as provided in the Explanation to rule 9. [754F G] 1;707A B] 2.8 The words `any premises ' which are required to be given by a licensee for the manufacture of excisable goods, are not capable of comprehendeding them or qualify them. The word used in section 4 (4) is wider enough to comprehend all excisable products manufactured or produced by a person who is engaged in the manufacture or production of any other commodity whether in a continuous process or otherwise, in such place or premises appurtenant thereof.

The petitioner, a holder of a permit issued under Chapter IVA of the Act to ply a stage carriage on Bulandshahr Siana Garh Bugrasi Brijghat Bhasians Shambhaoli Babugarh Jadol Jahangirabad route in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The petitioner filed his objections to the said scheme along with several others. After a number of adjournments the Hearing Authority empowered under section 68 C of the , was able to conclude the proceedings by April 26, 1979 and it was published on April 5, 1975. The State Transport Undertaking, i.e., the Regional Transport Authority, Meerut, filed its objections to that scheme along wit n several others and also some others. Thereafter, the petitioner filed an application before the Civil Judge for staying the hearing of the suit till the disposal of a special leave petition before this Court since the question relating to maintainability of suits of similar nature was involved in the said special leave Petition. The Civil Judge refused to grant the request of the petitioner and fixed the suit for arguments on November 8, 1985. Against the order of Additional District Judge, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed the same. Hence this appeal by Special Leave. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The jurisdiction of the civil courts is impliedly barred from entertaining suits of the present nature. Whenever statute uses the expression that a decision of an authority shall be final, the jurisdiction of a civil court to go into the correctness or otherwise of the decision is taken away. All the contentions urged in the plaint relate to the merits of the scheme and the desirability of bringing the scheme into force. [145E F] 1.2 The jurisdiction conferred on the civil Courts is impliedly bar from entertaining cases of similar kind excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred. In cases of the nature where invariably reliance is placed by the private operators on Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, a writ Petition lies before the high court. Such attempts should be curbed at the earliest opportunity. This is a suit which should have been rejected at the threshold under order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that it did not disclose a cause of action. [146F G] 1:3 The jurisdiction to entertain suits of civil nature excepting suitsof which their Cognizance is either specifically or impliedly excluded. Where invariably reliance was placed by private operators, on Article 14(1) (g), a writ of certiorari lies before a High Court. Such attempt should be discouraged at the first instance. [147B C] 1 :4 The jurisdiction under Order 7 Rule 11 of Code of civil Procedure is expressly barred from entertain suits or proceedings of civil character excepting suits which theirisance is either express or impliedly prohibited. In case of the instant nature where normally reliance is laid by privateopera tion on Article19(1), a Writ Petition lies against the orders of a Special Tribunal, the civil court jurisdiction must be held to be excluded insofar as the merits to the case is concerned. [148C D] 1 5. The jurisdiction vested in the civil Court is impliedly ousted from entertaining any suits of a nature excepting suit of which its cognizance is neither expressly nor impliedly barred by law. [149D E] H. C.

The appellant was charged under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on August 29, 1963 at about 9.30 or 10 P.m. the appellant went to Ambala to his maternal aunt, who was employed as a sister in the Ambala Air Force Hospital and gave birth to a son there in July 1963. On August 25, 1963 the child was handed over to Roshan Lal and he took the currency notes from the pocket of the appellant. The appellant asked Russel Nathaniel and his wife to make arrangement for bringing up the child. But on September 4, 185 1963 Russel C. I. R. 82/C.I 68 13 186 also referred the matter to the anti corruption department. Mukatdhari Singh turned up and recovered the currency note from the appellant and handed over the currency to Roshanlal. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant of the charged framed against him and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ . In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian penal Code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from Russel P.W. 2 for doing or procuring an official act, he would be guilty of the offence charged. Held: (i) The order also recites that Mr. P. C. Singh who was the sanctioning authority. was expected to maintain a high standard of integrity and to uphold the maintenance of law. [187 D E] Mahesh Prasad vs The State of Uttar Pradesh, A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 827; (ii) The appellant had not obtained money for doing nor prevented Russel from sending the currency currency notes to the police station and therefore the appellant was guilty of an offence charged under the Prevention Of Corruption Act. [188 D E F] Mahesh Kumar Prasad vs State of U.P., A. I R. 1966 All. 829; and (iii) The concealment of a birth of illegitimate child is not an act which is punishable under the Code or other criminal statutes.

The appellant was charged with the offence of criminal misconduct under section 161 I.P.C. and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1), clause (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special Judge acquitted him on the ground that he had not applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and was satisfied that in the interests of justice, the appellant should be put on trial in a Court of competent jurisdiction for offences under section 5 of the Act. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the sanction given by the Special Judge was not valid; (ii) the evidence of the witnesses showed that he did not investigate the truth of the matter presented against him and that in view of the fact that the appellant had applied his minds to the fact of the settlement, it was not necessary for him to examine the witnesses on behalf or to find out as to how they stood. HELD: (i)(a) The sanction given under section 6(2), read with Section 5(1), is a valid sanction and must be satisfied that the facts disclosed in the sanction were such as would justify the granting of a certificate; (b) the sanctioning authority had applied its mind to all relevant papers and was of the opinion that in order to secure the ends of justice the appellant must be put to trial in an appropriate Court of Competent jurisdiction for offence under section 165 I. P.C., and section 6 (2), clause(d) readwith section 5, clause (c). [1005 D] (ii)(a). The sanction is marked exhibit 6. It does not call for the connected claim cases nor did it call for any record in connection with the matter from his office nor did he call for a connected claim case or find out whether they stood or found out as a result of passing final orders himself or by making recommendations. [1006 E] (b)(i) The sanctioning authority has to consider all relevant documents and was not satisfied that there was a proper sanction in the case. It is inconceivable that an officer of the rank of Mr. It may be assumed that he does not require any record from his Office nor did the appellant call for such connected claim Cases or findout as to what they stood, but he did so. [1015 F] (2) The fact that he was not called for any records in connection therewith is a relevant circumstance and cannot be said to have been overlooked by the sanctioning Authority.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenants under section 14(1) (b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The tenant resisted the suit on the ground that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and for reconstruction. The trial court held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the tenants against the orders of eviction and set aside the orders passed by the appellate authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the landlord had only a life interest in the premises and that it is inherent in such a life estate that it was not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1) proviso (b). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The right between section M. G. 276 Ramachandra and others (1). is outside the ken of this Act. [275 D] 2. The rights between section H. 276 Ramchandra and others vs Narayanaswami Naidu, A.I.R. 1973 Madras, referred to. 3. Section M. Gopalakrishna is issueless. It win also not affect the efficacy of the nature of the plea of bona fide on the part of the landlord, if otherwise so. [276 E] 4. The Rent Controller and the High Court were right in holding that the tenant had no right to ask for eviction on the grounds of demolition and reconstruction. [278 F G] 5. Section H. 277 is issueableless. [277 C] 6. The provisions of section M, K. & P. Act are not applicable to the present case.

The appellant decree holder filed a suit for recovery of possession of the land in dispute. He claimed that he was entitled to the right in trees of groves as these minors were not part of a grove, and that the respondent decree holder had no right to the trees of the groves. The trial court decreed the suit holding that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6(h) of the Act in the State of Uttar Pradesh, new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 18 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal by certificate it was contended on behalf of the appellant decree holders that after the coming into force of the , Act in its State, new regidhari rights come into existence Under section 18 Of the Act read with section 73 of the . It was further contended that after such clear words of the enactment, there is a distinction between, trees and grove land, which are parts of bhumidhari right. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The definition of intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of U. P. Zamindari Act 1950 does not include trees, before they are cut, form parts of 'land '. [34B] 2.1 In view of the clear legal position, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut trees, which were parts of grove and grove lands. The proposition is well settled that trees before they were cut, formed part parts of the 'land'. [34C] 2:2. In view Of this very clear legal principle, it was not necessary to consider earlier definitions or make out a specious distinction between standing un uncut tree, which is parts of land and grove and grove property. The contention is well established that trees after they were cutting form parts are equated and groves are on ly collections of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them.

The appellants were charged for an offence under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC. The trial court found accused Nos. 1 to 4 guilty of the offences and sentenced them to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year. All the accused were also convicted for an offences under Sections 143, 341, 323, 324 read with section 149 IPC but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. In appeal before this Court it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that clear evidence of the eye witnesses was only against accused Nos 1 to 3 and that the injuries could have been caused by beating him with weapons, knife, iron rod etc. The appellants contended that there was no direct evidence against them and that they were not guilty of any offence under section 302 readwith Section 149 I.P.C. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A combined reading of Section 141 and Section 149, IPC show that an assembly of less than five members is not an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 142 and cannot, therefore form the basis for conviction for an accused with the aid of Section 149. [94D E] 1.2 The intention to cause death of Suku deceased, could not be attributed to him and the medical evidence also shows that the injury on the deceased had been caused due to multiple injuries. It is, therefore, necessary in a case like this to determine as to which of the accused is guilty of an offence of murder under Section 304 Part I read with Sec. 149 IPC since the injuries inflicted by him were not sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause the death of the deceased. [95E F] 1:3 The intention of causing murder of Suka was not proved, and the Medical evidence also showed that the accused had caused injuries with a weapon which he was armed and the nature number and seat of injuries inflicted on him were also not sufficient. [96F G] 1 :4 In the instant case, the prosecution has failed to prove that the appellants had committed any offence punishable under Section 307 read with 149 IPC or that they had been guilty of murder. The High Court was right in holding against accused No. 1 and convicting him for the said offence without a specific charge having been framed against them as envisaged by law. [97F G; 98A B] 2.1 In view of the limited notice issued by this Court on 4th September, 1991, it stands established that an unlawful unlawful assembly had to be an assembly within five or more persons, where the common object of the persons comprising that assembly is to commit any of the acts enumerated in the five clauses of that section. [98F G]. 2.2 In a case under Section 326 IPC read with Sections 149 and 149 IPC (supra) there can be no doubt that an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life cannot be committed unless it is proved that the assembly consisted of five or less persons, but if the existence of such an unlawful intention is not proved the conviction with the help of Section 34 IPC cannot be recorded or sustained. [99F G H] 2:3 In a given case where the existence or absence of such a unlawful intention may not amount to murder, it would be necessary for the prosecution to prove by direct evidence that the common intention was to cause such death of any person and that such knowledge was likely that death of such person may be caused. [100F G, 101A B]. 2:4 In a particular case where there is no specific charge being framed against an accused as envisaged under law, it cannot form the foundation for conviction of an accused of an alleged offence of which he is guilty.

The assessee company, a non resident, receiving its income outside India could be assessed to tax only under section 5(2) (b) of the Income Tax Act on accrual basis. The Indian Company had credited to the assessee 's account books for the relevant years (accounting year for the Indian Company was stated to be the calendar year). For the assessment years 1969 70 and 1968 69, it took the same stand. For the next assessment year 1970 71, however, he refused to accept the assessee "s plea that it was maintaining its accounts on cash basis. In these returns, it disclosed a royalty income of Rs. 4,57,311 respectively. For this assessment year, the assessee did not actually receive the amount nor did it take credit for the said amounts in its books at Coventry. The Income Tax Officer refused to allow the assessee to accept it 's plea. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the royalty amounts should be assessed on cash income basis and since it did rot actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax was payable by it. On reference, the High Court answered the question of method of accounting adopted by the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 In regard to the assessment year 1969 70, it did not say anything regarding the method of valuation adopted by it in respect of the royalty amount and that the alleged statement in the returns relating to the assessments years 1967 68 and 196869 were based upon the said premise. [71C] 1.2 The assessee was maintaining accounts at Courtry in the United Kingdom on receipt basis. It confined the said plea to its Indian income alone. His contention was that mere entry in the books of the assessee cannot amount to receipt and that it had been maintaining its account on cash grounds in respect thereof. [72D] 1:3 The agreement, from which we have quoted the relevant term, provided that the Japanese company desired that the assessee firm should open an account in the name of the Japanee company in their books of account, credit the amounts in that account, and deal with those amounts according to the instructions of the Indian Japanese Company. [73E] 1 :4 The agreement from which the Tribunal has referred to is an incorrect statement made by the Indian company which was not aware of the true state of affairs relating to its accounts. It cannot be said in such a situation that he has not received the income in India. [74D] 2.1 The assessee did file its return for the assessment period 1969 70 on correct basis showing that it is maintaining its books and balance sheets on cash account basis in respect whereof were concerned, because that income will have to be remitted to the nonresident by obtaining an irrevocable letter of credit and will thus be received only outside India. The assessee company did dispose of a part of amounts by instructing the assesseefirm that they be applied in a particular way. It was not the basis put forward by the Income tax Officer nor did he take credit of the amount in its Books at Coptry. [75F] 2:2 In the instant case, the royalty income is concerned, the asses see see see to have received the royalty in India and that, therefore, no question of any tax being payable on receipt outside India would arise in regard to this royalty amount. The agreement also provided that if it was found that the company was maintaining their accounts and balance sheet on cash credit basis in the Indian Bank, the income should be remitted only outside country. [76G] 2 :3 In the present case, there is no evidence to show that the said royalty amount had been paid by the appellant at any point of time till it to the filing of return for assessment year 1968 70.

The appellant was convicted under section 302, Indian Penal Code read with section 34 for the murder of one Lahu Vithu Patil on the night between May 23 and 24, 1960 at village Pasarde. The third accused who was a wrestler and his brother used to sleep in the fields and they also had donegs and for that reason the murder could not be committed for sometime. On June 25, 1960, Rama Krishna Patil accused No. 1, Bhiva Doulu Patil accused no. 2 (now appellant before us), Lahu Santu Patil accused NO. 3 and Deoba were unarmed. Two blows were given by accused No 1 to one on the throat and the second one on his left side of the chest. Both these articles have been found to belong to accused No, 1 Rama Krishna Pawar. The fourth accused who had a liaison with the deceased, was also seen by him in the company of the appellant. On the night of the murder the deceased was killed with the knife which was used by Rama Krishna Pandey accused No.. 2 and Deba Santu. The appellant 's brother used the weapon of offence on March 17, 1960. After the murder he was arrested on information received by police Sub Inspector Nandke. On July 25, 1961, the appellant was arrested under section 27 of the Evidence Act. He was convicted for an offence under section 307 read with sections 34 and 302 read with s 34.
