The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the evidence of the approver is not corroborated in material particulars; (2) the testimony of the witness is not reliable; (3) the statement of the third accused has been corroborated in evidence and qua the appellant, the conviction is unsustainable. HELD : (i) The conviction of an accused on the testimony Of an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal yet the Courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence Of such a witness without corroboration in material details; but the judge should point out to the jury that it is within their legal province to convict upon such unconfirmed evidence (R. v Stubbs, Dears 555) and in the discre tion of the Judge, to advise them not to convict Upon such evidence, but the Judge should point Out to the verdict that it was within his legal province. [835 F G] R. vs Baskerville, ; , referred to. (ii) The High Courts were right in holding that there could be corroboration of the accomplice 's story which would be sufficient to connect the appellant with the murder, under section 34 of the Indian Penal code.

The appellant was a peon attached to the office of the Superintendent of Salt Department in the district of Mozafferpur. He was prosecuted under section 161 Indian Penal Code and section 21 of the Indian Penal code. The trial court convicted him under section 7(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years under section 5 (2) of that Act. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant was not a "public servant" within the meaning of section 5(2) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act and that he was not an "public Servant" within section 2(1) of Prevention of corruption Act, as the definition of "public servants" in section 2 (d) is wide enough to include every person who is in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Government. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant was an officer and he was the servant of the State Electricity Board constituted under the provisions of the , and pay of the Government and he is attached to his office as Superintendent of the Salt Department. [782 H] 2.1 In view of Explanation 4 to section 21, Indian Penal Act, it is not necessary that a person who has been convicted as a public servant is acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions Of the . The appellant while taking the bribe, cannot be deemed to be a "Public Servant" under section 2 1, el. (d), of the . [785 A] State of Maharashtra vs Jagatsing Charansingh, ; , followed.

The appellant was tried and convicted under r. 125(9) Defence of India Rules, 1962 for contravening cl. 4(b) of the Maharashtra Declaration of Stock Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ , in default further rigorous imprisonment. The sentences were directed to run concurrently. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that r. 141(2) of Defence ofIndia Rules, 1963 is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to. the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: (1) The rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. [273E] (2) Section 114 of Evidence Act does not enable the Court to order forfeiture of a juar seized from the house of the accused because, he says, the Maharashtra Jowar (Restrictions on Purchase 'and Sale and Control of Movement) Order, 1965, does not empower the Court. [274B] (3) The rule is contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the Defence of Indian India Act provides that "the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act". Section 43 gives very wide powers. It seems to us that r, 141(1) of The Defence of Indue (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order 1964, is ultra constitutional because it provides a rule for publication of order made under section 3(1).

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 109 and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction of the appellant but reduced the sentence to one year rigorous imprisonment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the State that the evidence of a witness should be corroborated in material particulars and that the testimony of such a witness must be accepted as true unless it is corroborated in any material particular. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The statement of a person who is not an accused is at best a relevant circumstance and he does not, without more, necessarily justify the inference that he was a party to the murderous design. It says "In case of Smt. Sheolet who was working as a Nurse with a doctor was friendly with Sia Ram who was his compounder but that may rather explain why, if at all, she agreed to do as directed. That is not the only point in favour of Shri Ram. The evidence leaves much to be desired and, at the least, it shows that it would be unsafe to reply on his capacity or ability to identify Shri Ram, [638 B] 2. The words of Violet are at best in the nature, of a circumstance and they do not, with more, normally justify the conclusion that he is a party thereto. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate the commission of the murder, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. [639 C] 3. The word "Whoever" in section 107 means something which is done by or on behalf or on his own and it does not mean that the person who has been convicted is not necessarily required to inform him so that he might accomplish their aim. It is true that the words of the section are at least in the character, of an offence but they do no, without less, necessarily indicate that the intention was to facilitate commission of that act. [613 D] 4. The fact that a person has been acquitted by the trial court does not make him liable for any subsequent proof. It would be safe to rely on the testimony given by a witness in the case or in the evidence adduced by him in the course of the trial and if he is found guilty, it may be unsafe for him to explain his presence. [539 F] 5. The burden was on the prosecution to establish its case and no adverse inference could be raised against Violets for her failure to explain her utterance. [625 G H] 6. The circumstances that Shri Ram had voluntarily accepted the risk of being identified, in a parade but was denied that opportunity was an important point in his favour. It shows that he did not remember or that he had not seen the accused persons were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplishes their aim." [640 C] 7. The prosecution has failed to establish the case against Vialet for her absence from duty as a witness. It was not the case of the prosecution that the appellant had voluntarily made the offer or that she did not know that the accused were lying on the spot along with him or who appeared the case along with them or who used to instruct them in the Case.

The appellant was charged with committing the murder of Vishwanath. The prosecution examined eye witnesses, who deposed that the four accused were not identified but more than one had taken part in the assault. The trial court acquitted all the accused. On appeal by the State to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the High Court erred in holding that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not reliable; (2) the evidence was directed to establish that the said four persons had taken parts in the murder and that the prosecution witnesses named only accused 1, 3 and 4; (3) the conviction of accused 2 under section 302 read with section 34, IPC was bad as it did not consider the evidence on record in its proper perspective; (4) the judgment of the High court was erroneous. HELD : (1)(a) The High Court was right in holding against the appellant under section 304 Part I, I.P.C., and sentencing him to imprisonment for life. [682 C] (b) In the present case on a fair reading of the entire judgment it would be clear that the High 'Court had not considered the evidence in its correct perspective. The evidence was direct to prove that the accused persons were not known or unknown, who took part in committing the offence. [683 G H] (c) The evidence is directed to prove hat A, B, C and D along with 3 others have jointly committed the offence and that accused No. 2 along with three others had jointly committed an offence under section 307 read with Section 34, as well as section 323, read with s 149, of the Indian Penal Code. [684 G] (d) The prosecution witnesses mentioned only the said accused persons but not more than five. It is not possible to say that they did not take part in any the assault and that they were not so identified. [686 C D] (e) The conviction of the appellants under section 324 read with sections 34, 323 read with 149, I P.C. was bad because it did no considerate the evidence as a whole. It was not possible for the High Courts to hold that the witnesses named in the charge did not have part in their assault.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of MSCR defective sheets or coils, filed bills of entry for ex bond clearance. The goods were bounded on 7th August, 1984. It was endorsed on 24th August 1984. The clearing agent of the petitioner filed six bills of Entry for ex post bond clearance and the duty as leviable on 21st August,1984. The Customs Department issued a notice to the petitioner for the import of MSC defective sheets and coils on 30th July, 1984 for warehousing under section 59 of the . The petitioner filed four bills of entries for ex pany clearance. This was endorsed by the clearing agent on 24 th August, 1985. The petitioner 's clearing agent filed six Bills of Entry. On 30th March, 1988, the Income Tax Department issued the necessary no objection certificate, thus lifting the ban. The duty as is prevalent now is Rs.5,000 per M.T. + addl. duty 45% and CVD. at Rs.325 per M..T. and 10% C.V.D. At Rs. 325 per M.,T. & 10% E.V., D.V.; D.L.D., Rs.650 per M,T. (Erstwhile) will be released forthwith on petitioner 'S paying customs and other duties as leviable under the . Section 16(1)(b) of the , on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse. The demand, according to the peti tioner, was arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional. The respondents filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the levy of customs duty on the ground that the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods should be determined according to law prevalent on the dates they were actually removed therefrom from the warehouses after the amending Ordinance had come into force. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the customs authorities and the Central Govern ment were right in taking the view that the rates of duty prevailing on the day when these were actually removal from the warehousing premises should be taken as correct according to Law prevalent on that date. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The clear ance can only be made on payment of duty as enjoined by the . [638G H] 1.2 In the instant case, such clear ances can only been made on payments of duty and tariff valuation of imported goods. [639C] 1:3 It is not permissible to move this Court on the theoretical basis that there is breach of fundamental rights, but relates only to the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part 111 of the Constitution. The reve nue has proceeded on that basis. This is not impermissible and should never be 628 entertained. It has further to be reiterated that for enforce ment of fundamental right which is dependent upon adjudica tion or determination of questions of law as well as ques tion of fact without taking any resort to the provisions of the Act, it is not possible to move the Court on theoretical basis. [625D E] 1 :4. The pre existing rate of customs and tariff value, if any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force (a) in the case of goods entered for export under section 68, on thedate of payment of the duty; (b) in case of any other goods, on date of payment, on that day; (c) in cases where goods are cleared from a warehouse under section68 on the basis of an invoice issued by the importer, the bill of entry shall be deemed to have been presented on the said date. [ 625E F] 1.:5. The provisions of this section shall not apply to baggage and goods exported by post.

The appellant was the Managing Director of Dharwar Urban Co operative Bank Limited which went into liquidation. In that capacity he received a monthly remuneration of Rs. 15,100 and made an application to the Deputy Registrar of Co operative Societies for registration of the sale deed. The Deputy Registrar held misfeasance and ordered a contribution of Rs, 15,000 to be made by the Deputy Registrars of Cooperative Societies on April 21, 1942. On appeal the High Court held that the debt was not avyavaharika as there was no evidence to support the finding of the trial court that the suit was collusive; that the liability which defendant No. 1 was under section N. 1387 could not be termed avyvaharika and that the decree was not binding on the sons but a civil debt arising on account of the receipt of monies by the father which were not accounted for could not therefore be termed as avyVavahaedia. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The liability of the Hindu son based on his pious obligation again received the approval of this Court in Sudheshwar Mukherji vs Bhubneshwar Prasad Narain Singh (1923) L.R. 17 I.A. 1. [457 F] 2.1 In the instant case, the right of the father to alienate for payment of personal debt is ended by the partition, but as he was grossly negligent in the discharge of his duties and responsibilities as managing director and that after a thorough enquiry the DeputyRegistrar held misfeasance proved and ordered an contribution of RS. 15. The question whether the debt of the mother was avyaviaharika or not could be called avyavahirika. [414 G] 2:2 In the modern age with its complex institutions of banks and Joint Stock Companies governed by many technicalities and complex system of laws the liability such as has arisen in the present case could be termed agyavahus. The right of a father to sell for payment personal debt was ended by partition but as there were no proper arrangements for the payment of such debts at the time when the partition was effected, though the father could have no longer any right of alienation in regard to the separated share of the sons. [416 G H] 2 :3 The liability to discharge the debt is founded on the pious obligation of the members to discharge their debt of their father. A. It is settled law that even after partition the sons could be made liable for the pre partition debts of the parents if there was proper arrangement for the payments of such dues at the date when the sale had taken place, though they might have no more right of alienations in regard thereto. [413 F G] 4. The debt of a son based upon his pious duty again received approval of the Supreme Court in Sandheshwar Mukarji vs Kantoo Lal (1924) L R. 17 1.A., referred to.

The petitioners who are both guardians of law and who constitute two important segments of society on whom the stability of the country depends. It is hoped that cordiality between the two sections will be restored soon. In order to avoid any further delay in the proceedings before the Committee consisting of Goswamy and Wadhwa, JJ., constituted by Order dated 23rd February, 1988 to enquire into certain incidents which took place on the 15th January, 1988 and 17th February,1988 respectively. The Delhi Administration has to examine first all its witnesses as required by Rule 5(5)(a) of the Commissions of Inquiry (Central) Rules 1972 framed under the (hereinafter referred to as 'the Rules '). Even those witnesses who may have filed affidavits already may first be examined in chief before they are cross examined, since it is stated that when the affidavits were filed the deponents did not know what the other parties who had also filed affidavits had stated in their affidavits. The Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8 B of the Act before asking them to get into the witness box for being cross examined. The committee would have then asked them to give PG NO 523 evidence along with others who were similarly placed at the end of the inquiry. This is not a case where the circumstances in which the several incidents that had taken place were not known to anybody else. Taking into consideration all the aspects of the case we feel that the Committee should not have in the circumstances of the cases directed the filing of a complaint against either of the petitioners for an offence punishable under section 178 I.P.C. before asking the petitioners to get in the witness examined at the conclusion of the enquiry. The petitioners who were in the same position as those three persons, are persons who fall under section 8B of the . The Committee would have thereafter asked them not to make any difference if they otherwise satisfy the conditions mentioned in section 8 C. The matter should be decided by the Committee in accordance with section 8C of the , and the petitioners should give PGNO 523 evidence on their side.

The petitioners were carrying passengers and goods carried by road in motor vehicles. The State Government issued a notification under R. F. Public carriers (Goods Vehicles) Act, 1959, for levying tax on passengers and Goods carried by Road in motor vehicle. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification before the High Court which upheld the validity. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the tax was borne by the operators because of competition with the Railways. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: (1) The levy of tax cannot be said to offend articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. [515 F] (2) The tax is for purposes of State, and falls upon passengers and property carried by motor vehicles within the State. It may be directory but it cannot be denied by the Rules. These arguments are not accepted. There are good reasons for upholding the fixation of lump sums. [ 523 A B] (3) The Act creates an option, it cannot, be negatived by the rules. These submissions cannot be accepted. [525 C D] (4) The incidence of the tax is upon passengers & goods carried within the state. It includes a proviso that in the case of passengers the tax becomes chargeable only on entry in the State, if the journey commenced outside the State and having jurisdiction over that area: Provided that where the journey began outside the state, a proportionate decrease in the amount due for that quarter may be made, (c) if the owner ceases to ply his vehicle for a continuous period of not less than three months and produces a certificate from the authority competent under the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act, 1951 or the rules made thereunder to the effect that he has been refunded the tax for that period under section 7 of the Act no amount by way of tax under the Act shall be payable for such period. [415 F G] (5) The word "accept" shows that the incidence of tax is on passengers & property, though the amount of fare or freight. It does not mean that the levy of the taxes cannot be sustained. [616 C D; 525 A B].

The appellant was a private limited company having set up an industrial unit in engineering industry. The appellant served notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen alleging non availability or raw material to utilise the full installed capacity, power shedding limiting the 566 working of the Unit to 5 days a week and the mounting loss. The Labour Court held that the reasons stated in the notice dated 1st July, 1974, Ext. 'the Labour Court by its award directed reinstatement of five out of seven workmen and directing reinstatement of all the workmen with full back wages permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the appellant. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Labour Court had erred in holding that the reason stated in Ext. "the Labour" Court by itself was not sufficient for the purpose of awarding reinstatement and that the non availability of raw material or recurrent power shedded and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or a ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the Appellant consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to be raised(l. The contention was that the reasoning given in Ext 'the 'the High Court was erroneous and that it was motivated and the relief of reinstatement must follow, has become final. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Labour court had rightly held that retrenchment was not bona fide and that there was no justification for interfering with the award. [682B] 2.1 In breach of the statutory obligation the services were terminated and the termination is found to be invalid. [613C D] 2:2 The workmen have already been reinstated and therefore, they have started earning their wages. Therefore, they had started earning the wages. They have started earn their livelihood. They are kept away therefrom. Therefore they have stopped earning their wage. [582D] 3.1 It is no more open to debate that in the field of industrial jurisprudence a declaration can be given that the termination of service is bad and the workman continues to be in service. The relief of reinstated with continuity of service can be granted where termination of services is found invalid, reinstatement as a matter of course should be awarded or compensation would be an adequate relief. [561E] 3:2 In the field, industrial jurisprudence is intended to be an self contained one and it seeks to achieve social justice on the basis of collective bargaining, collaboration and arbitration. A free and 568 liberal exercise of the power under Article 136 may materially affect the fundamental basis of such decisions, viz., quick solution of such disputes to achieve industrial peace. [565A B] 3 :3 The relief for reinstatement with continuity in service can also be granted when termination of employment is found not to be valid; reinstatement as an matter of right should be granted wherever termination of the service is found. [567C D]. 4:4 In breach Of the statutory obligations the services are terminated and termination is held to be illegal. The workmen though willing to do the assigned work and earn their living livelihood, were kept away from therefrom. A Statement of Account certified by the Chartered Accountants of the company dated 25th July, 1978 shows that the appellant has been making profit since 1976 77. 74,587.26 was paid to these 36 workmen for the work rendered by them since the date of retrenchment. The workman though willing, to do so, were keep away therefrom and therefore they have been kept away with.

The accused was charged under section 302 Indian Penal Code for committing murder of his wife Churl. The Sessions Judge accepted the confessional statement and convicted him under section 304 Part I read with section 34 IPC. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the confession recorded by Shri Mahajan during investigation of the case could not be used as a substantive piece of evidence and that the confessional statements were inadmissible in evidence. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The statement given by Shri Thakur during investigation cannot be used for corroboration of his confession. [446C] (2) It is not necessary to dilate upon this aspect because it was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [427B] (3) The question whether a confessional statement recorded by an officer during investigation or before the commencement of the investigation cannot, therefore, be used against the accused has to be decided on its own facts and circumstances. [413D E] (4) It was not necessary for the prosecution to prove that the accused had killed his wife. If someone other than the accused murdered his wife it would have attracted to the spot his neighbours like Poshu Ram PW. So far as the sentence is concerned, the same is admissible in evidence and the confession made by him must be held inadmissible. [414E] (5) The fact that a person who was not a witness to the occurrence or had been examined during investigation could not have attracted the provisions of section 164 Cr. P.C.

The plaintiff, a minor son of the deceased, filed a suit for partition of his properties and for a sum of Rs. 1,144 8 6 in resisting Mst. 40,253 11 4. The defendants resisted the suit contending that the mortgage was exe cuted on the 12th June, 1936, in favour of one Mst. 42,253 10. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff had failed to prove his case and that the defendants were shut out from relying on section 82 of the Transfer of Property Act read with the Civil Procedure Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the mortgage deed was ex facie a mortgage; (2) the mortgagee had no right to redeem the whole of the balance of the property, and (3) the plaintiff was entitled to receive the balance amount of Rs 1,145 4. 53,481 11 4 as the balance due on it under section 82. HELD : (1)(a) The entire law of mortgage in India including the law of contribution arising out of a transaction of mort gage, is now statutory and is embodied in the Transfer Of Property Act, read with section 83, except where there is a contract to the contrary. It is not for judges to consider whether that is the best possible solution but the rule at any rate obviates the necessity of roving enquiries into the objects of a borrow ing and the application of the funds. [10 C D] (b) The whole law of trust in India includes the law relating to contribution arising from a transaction which is the subject matter of a suit or mortgage. But when these figures are ascertained, I would direct that a mortgage decree for sale be drawn up in the usual way affording either defendant the right to redemption the whole balance of property 193 (excluding the plaintiff 's) for the aggregate sum due as above and, in default of payment, limiting the liabilities of each item of property to the sum rateably due on them under section 83. [11 E F] (c) The question is whether the entire law relating t o a loanee who has borrowed money from a creditor or other person for the performance of the promise unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. If the defendants deliberately withheld from the Court that assist ance which is its due I can only conclude that their case was too shaky to stand further proving. [12 E F G] (d) The doctrine of the (1 ) Pat. J So far as section 43 is concerned, it is now statutorily statutory and embodied in Transfer of property Act readwith the Civil procedure Code. [13 C D].

The State of Karnataka vs M. Veerappa, S.A candidate No. 1 secured 69.96% marks in the qualifying examination thus in all 99.46 marks out of 150.23 marks out Of 150.24 marks out from 150.25 marks out. Both the appellants were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants in the competitive examina tion but had secured very high marks in viva voce out of 50 marks kept for this purpose. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3 was excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court. The Tribunal by its order dated 24th May, 1990 dismissed the petitions and the appellants aggrieved against the aforesaid decision have approached this Court by grant of special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of the fact that the result of the impugned selections was declared in 1987 and the selected candidates had already joined the posts, they before us were bound to be selected on the basis of marks secured by them in interview calculated on the base of converting the same to 15% of the total marks. [418C] 1.2 In view Of the fact the result was declared according to the Rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the appellants before us, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [519D] 1:3 In view the fact situation that the results of the selection were declared in 1988 and the selectees have already joined t the posts and, therefore, both the appellants are bound to get selected and a large number of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appellant. [619D E] 1 :4 In view thereof it is an admitted position that if the marks for interview were kept even at 15% and merit list is prepared according ly then both the appel lants are bound t to be selection on the principle of 'last 17 years, and there was no allegation or any malafides against the matter o f the impugned selection. [719G] 1.:5 In view o the fact in the case the marks secured for vivavoce would have been kept say at 15%. The appellants before this Court were found suitable in all other respects according to rules. They had approached the Tribunal for relief, the cases of other selected candidates cannot also be considered on the same ground. [765D] 2.6 In view Rule 5(1) of the Rules it is clear that a large percentage of candidates have been selected though they had secured much higher marks in interview, calculated on conversion of the same into 15% or 15% for the purpose of selection. The selections were made according to these rules and this practices is being regularly followed for last 17 year and there has been no allegation that any malafides are in the mater of the said impugned selections. [764A B] 2:7 In view, the fact tha that the marks awarded to the selected candidate have already been kept at 15%, the appellants after approaching the Tribunal seek relief only to the present appellants who were vigilant in making griev ance and approaching the Tribu nal in time. The case of others cannot be treated as a precedent for the purposes of applying the principle laid down by this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C.R., 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Punjab & Ors, J .T. On a direction given by this court on 4th September, 1991 the record of the 496 Selection Committee was produced before this court at the time of hearing.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to ten years ' rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to one year rigorous imprisonment, which was affirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the confession made by the accused persons before the Magistrate was not admissible in evidence; (2) the confessional statement made by them before the police officer was inadmissible in evidence and could not be relied upon as a substantive piece of evidence; and (3) the High court committed an error in placing reliance on the confessional statements made by him before the Police Officer. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The confession is admissible in law to prove that it is voluntary or not. [440C] 2. In the instant case, the confession was made after the arrival of Sadanand at the jail and enforcement of rules became slack and there was a regular flow of food from outside. There were two confessions a judicial confession before a Magistrate, being Exhibit 44 and the other is extra judi cial confession. From the confession I find that it was in the nature of the cross examination which was not permissible under the law and has been depricated by the Supreme Court and different courts of the country. The prosecution has further led evidence to show that after the departure of Sadananda at the Jail, enforcement of Rules became s black and there were a regular movement of food between outside and outside. [411D] 3. In Hari Charan Kurmi & Anr. vs State of Bihar, ; , this Court observed: "Thus, the confessional confession may be regarded as evidence in that generic sense because of the provisions of section 30, the fact remains that it being not evidence as defined by section 3 of the Act. The chain has to be completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [413E F] 4. In this case, there is no direct evidence that Yadav was very close to Sadanand. The confessional statement has to he kept out of consideration. There are two confessions in the same trend about Yadav confession before them. They are P.Ws. 3 and 4. The police officer who had recorded the confession stated: "He was assaulted with slaps, fists and asked as to why he did so. " Several other witnesses were examined to show, turned into a den of criminals. There is no evidence that Sadanand was very near to Sadananda. [414B C] 5. The judicial confession has to remain out of considerations. Several prosecution witnesses have spoken about Yadav having been assaulted by the angry mob soon after his apprehension. They were P.W.4 on that day. They have spoken regarding Yadav being assaulted by angry. There was a direct evidence of his involvement and he had also confessed to his guilt but gave out that he had committed the ghastly murder at the behest of appellant Tripathi. The defence sought to place reliance upon circumstantial evidence, which if accept ed, could provide some link between the two for the commis sion of the offence. [416D E] 6. In view of the fact that it has been established that Yadav had been called in his jail on 10th July, 1982 Sadanand had continuously been detained in jail till the Collector 's murder on 11.4.1983. There have two confessions one judicial confession, a judicial confessions before a magistrate, being Exhibits 44 and 44 cannot be rejected as when on 10.7.1982 Sadanand is taken into custody following the raid on the Ashram, Yadav was not found there.

The appellants were employed in the appellant company. The workmen of the appellant Company were employed by the appellant companies and they were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 365 per month. The appellant company was a subsidiary of the respondent company. There were two references each with respect to Ruston and Hornsby Private Limited, and three references with respect thereto were included in the award. The Tribunal gave the same dearness allowance to the factory workmen as to the clerical and subordinate staff and directed adjustments also on the same basis. It gave the dearness allowance at the same rate to the Factory workmen as was to the supervisory staff and other employees including factory workmen. In appeal to this Court it was contended that in flying 366 scales of wages the Tribunal increased the maximum and the annual rate of increment and decreased the span of years in which the maximum would be reached. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal was not justified in creating a new category of higher unskilled. It overlooked the financial stability of the appellants, emoluments needed upgrading. [367 C] (2) There is force in the contention of the respondents that the Tribunal should have taken into account comparable concerns in the same industry and provided wage scales on the basis of the comparable industries which it took into account. The entire matter is left to the Tribunal and it may follow such method as it thinks best so long as it arrives at a fair conclusion after making the necessary comparison. [368 D] (3) There was force in this contention inasmuch as the Tribunal had not taken into consideration comparable concerns of the employees in different industries. It was not possible for the Tribunal to rely on the comparable concerns. The whole matter is still left to it and it might follow such methods as it think best so far as manufacturing concerns in that region carrying on the similar industry are concerned.

The appellants, who were the registered occupant of the mortgaged property, executed a usufructuary mortgage (Ex.D 51) in favour of one Lalchand Gujar and Tuljaram Bhavanchand Gujar for Rs. 1,100 due under a previous mortgage and Rs. 2,000 as the judi and incur the expenses of the Nand Deep and that on failure of the mortgagors to meet the out goings, the mortgagees would incur the said expenses and add the same to their claim on the mortgage. The mortgagees, defendants 1 to 4, appealed to the District Court, Belgaum, in Regular Civil Appeal No. 16 of 1945 which was filed by defendants 1 and 2. The High Court having refused to grant leave to appeal against the decision of the Division Bench in so far as it upheld the rejection of their claims to Annappa 's half share in the mortgaged properties, dismissed the appeals. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) A relinquishment may be in favour or of more persons than one. [799 C] (2) The right is given to all occupants, if there are more than one, for the singular includes the plural. [700 G] (3) It is not necessary that a relinquishment should be in respect of more than two persons. [699 D] (4) A transfer may be made in favour either of more person than one and it is not possible to hold that the relinquishment was in respect only of the co mortgagor.

The respondent, a company incor pated under the Indian Companies Act dealing in carbon paper, typewriter, ribbon and stepler pins, despatches the said goods from its head office at Kanpur to its branch office at Delhi. During the course of assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the respondent claimed that carbon paper not being paper falling within the ambit of Entry No. 2 of the Schedule to the aforesaid Notification but a specialised article used for copying purposes, its turnover had to be assessed at the rate of 6 paise per rupee i.e. 6% prescribed in the aforesaid notification. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the claim and held that carbon papers not being Paper falling within Entry No, 2 of Schedule to Notification No. 1/66 dated July 1, 1966 were liable to tax under Entry No,. 2 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that carbonpaper was not paper falling under Entry 18 of the First Schedule to tile aforesaid Notification and therefore a specialised item used for printing purposes, their turnover had been assessed at 6% and ribbon at 10%. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The word 'paper ' has not been defined in the Act or the Rules. [840C] (2) In popular parlance, the word ' paper ' is understood as meaning a sub stance which is used for bearing, writing, or printing, or for drawing on or for decorating, or cover ing the walls. It is, therefore, necessary to know what is paper as commonly or generally understood. [ 840D] (3) In our opinion, Carbon paper is not paper as envisaged by Entry 2 of Notification No 1/ 66 dated July 21, 1966. [884C D] (4) The High Court was in error in holding that carbon sheets were not paper within the meaning of Entry 18. [874A B] (5) In the instant case, Carbonpaper is not a part of the type writer though it may not be possible to type out any matter without it. Typewriters are being sold in the market without the typewriter ribbons and therefore typewriter poc fice is not an essen tial part of a car in the same way, rib bon is not one of the types writer though they may not have been able to type up any matter with it.

The appellant Mills purchased the building machinery and other equipment of another sugar mill at Amroha. The new factory was named Pannijee Sugar & General Mills, Bulandshahr. The respondents through their representative, the fifth respondent, protested to the General Manager against the transfer. But the Government of U.P. by its notification dated November 7, 1955, referred the following question for decision to the State Industrial Tribunal for U. P., at Allahabad: " Whether the employers have wrongfully and/or unjustifiably terminated the services of Sarva Shri Zia Uddin, Raisuddin, Shafiquddin and Ahmed Bux for refusal to obey the orders of tranfer to M/s. If so, to what relief are the workmen entitled. The State Industrial tribunal held that both the concerns, i.e., the mills at Amroha and the mills in Bulandshahr formed one unit, the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside that finding under section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1950. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondents were not proprietors of the Sugar Mills at Amroha, and that the workmen were not entitled to any of these amenities. Held: (i) The respondents were employees in a business or a concern and the question whether they had been employed in a trade or concern is one of fact which must be decided on the facts of each case; (ii) The question whether the transfer from one branch to another was valid or amounted to victimization cannot be said to be an alteration of any service condition within the meaning of section 33 of the Act. It would be enough to point out that in all the aforesaid decisions the workers had been working in a concern, and the fact that they were employed in business or concern and their duty to join the concerns to which they may be transferred was not in contemplation. The question as to whether the respondents had wrongfully and /or unjustically terminated the service of Sarava Shri Zi Uddin was one of law and it would be sufficient to point Out that in each case the transfer was one under the appellant 's contract of service or under any statutory provisions.

The appellant company was formed in 1965 and went into production the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the by stages. The scheme could not be implemented straight away throught out the country but could only be implemented by stages; and that could only mean implemented by stage. The appellant company challenged its liability to pay special contribution under Chapter V B of the Act by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the contribution payable under Chapter VI A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the amount of contribution which may be varied from time to time is a fee, and its imposition is illegal as it does not contemplate rendering of service or conferment of a benefit to an employee as quidpro quo for payment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act provides for certain benefits to industrial employees in case of sickness maternity and employment injury injury. The payment of contribution by an employer towards the premium (what else is it ?) of an employee 's compulsory insurance under the falls directly within entries 23 and 24 of List II of the Constitution. [1096G] 2. The amount of contributions which may not be varied in time totime is a tax, fee or neither it has sufficient constitutional protection. [1197C D] 3. The contribution payable by an employee towards the premiums (what otherwise is it?) of any employee towards premium (What else is the same ?) and is bound to be conferred on the employees and through them on the employer, in due course, when the scheme becomes fully operative in all areas. [1106G] 4. The levy of special contribution by a employer towards premium is illegal because the Act does not envisage the rendering or conferment or conferment thereof any benefit or advantage to the employee or its workmen as quid pra quo for it. [109F G] 5. The question whether such questions and facets of such questions arose for consideration or not in that case. [111G] 6. The very approach of the respondent company to the problem at issue suffers from a basic defect. It is in pursuance of these Directive Principles that we find entries 23, 24 and 24 in list III of the VlIth Schedule of the constitution. List lIth schedule of the Union is for meeting the needs of the transitory period. The rate of contribution payable in respect of an employees shall comprise contribution payable and contribution payable to the premium(what else was it ?). [1107C D].

The plaintiffs claimed their title to the property on the basis of various purchases from the heirs of this Azam Ali. The defendants contended that the grant of the lease created a new title in the grantee since the original lease in 1928 was due to expireon March 31, 1929 and that the plaintiffs were precluded by 0. r. 1 of O. No. 9 of 1928. Held, that the suit was substantially barred by O. 1, r. I of O., No. 10 of 1928 and not by O., 9 of 1929. The plaintiff set up his purchases as the source of his title to sue, but if he had been granted the full title to it, he could not succeed in proving that he had consented to put him forward as the ostensible owner of the property with the result that he was ' estopped from impeaching the mortgage and the sale of the properties. The plaintiffs were entitled to a decree for possession of the land on the footing that they had agreed to put them forward as his ostensible owners. The mere fact that the original tenancy in 1928 did not subsist, would not make it a case of estoppel by the purchaser. In the present case, the plaintiffs had no right to the full 16 as. share in the property under the lease granted in 1928 and the plaintiffs could not rely on O. I, r., 1, O. 9, O., C. P.C. The suit was therefore rightly dismissed. The High Court was wrong in holding that the plaintiff set out his purchases of title to a part of the estate in addition to the 8 pies share decreed to them by the High Court.

The appellant was convicted under section 302, read with sections 34 and 109 of the Indian Penal Code. The conviction and sentence were affirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the omission complained of in the first information report should not have a more farreaching effect than the omission to carry out the provisions of section 162 or section 360 of the Code; (2) the failure complained of should not be fatal to the prosecution case, and (3) the defect should not vitiate the trial. HELD: (1)(a) The omission complained Of in the second information report must not have any more serious effect than that prescribed by the Code. [646 B] (b) The omissions complained of were not material and could not be ignored. [613 A] (c) The failure complained was not fatal to it, because the omission alleged was not material. [547 C] (d) The defect complained of was not a sufficient ground for interference with the conclusions of the courts below on the merits of the case. [625 B] In the instant case, the omission made in the third information report was not relevant and had not been done much harm to the accused persons, but certainly the provisions Of section 162 and section 360 were not observed. [643 C] The omission alleged in the fourth information report could not have been ignored by the courts on the ground that it was not necessary for the prosecution to prove that the omission was material. It was a matter of common knowledge that the accused had committed the offence charged against him, but that he did not do so.

The appellant was the owner of a well situated in the area known as Harijanvas and Kolivas close to the vicinity of the channel. The respondent Municipality had carried out similar tests for analyzing the water of various wells and that if such analysis had been made it might be allowed to inspect and survey the reports and other relevant papers connected therewith. The appellant was asked to arrange the discharge of the effluent through a covered pucca drain for pumping it over a distance of about 8 miles as shown in the plan would involve an expenditure of nearly 8 to 9 lakhs of rupees which, having regard to the prevailing conditions, would involve a capital outlay of such an enormous amount as to cripple the appellant 's activities. The Municipality by its order dated the 17th May, 1958 appointed Mr. Justice A. K. Sen and Justice A N. Sen to hold an enquiry into the matter and make his report both as to the manner in which the effluent should be discharged. The Special Officer recorded the order which was the subject matter of the present appeal by special leave. The High Court held that the question whether the discharge was polluting water and adversely affected the fertility of the soil was a question of subjective satisfaction of the Municipality and that this question was beyond the scope of the enquiry before him. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the enquiry must necessarily relate to the entire dispute and the words " to hold any enquiry" are wide enough to suggest this; (2) where the existence of a nuisance is assumed because that was a matter for the subjective satisfaction, then it would not require a judicial officer of the rank of a District Judge to enquire and report only as to whether the effluent could be discharged; and (3) where he consents to it subject to modification. HELD: The enquiry must obviously relate to a whole dispute and not to the whole dispute. [398C] In the instant case, the existence or absence of a notice under section 153A of the Act is implicitly admitted at id need not be enquired into. If the existence was assumed because the existence had been assumed because there was a thing for the satisfaction of a Municipality, then the fact in question is not relevant. [399D] In such a case, it would be open to the Municipality to proceed further and to do something more, then, the fact that the Legislature has conferred on the Municipality jurisdiction to determine whether a particular state of fact exists and on finding that it does exist to proceed again and do something 397 more, than the words ' to hold enquiry into' the matter " are wide sufficient to suggest that this. question is beyond the purview of the inquiry before him and as such was beyond his scope of enquiry before he had exercised jurisdiction.

The appellant was found in possession of railway stores which by the definition of section does not include all articles which are 'the property of a railway administration but only those which are used or intended to be used for the construction, operation or maintenance of a Railway. The prosecution examined three witnesses and the manager of the transport company examined the goods said to be unauctionable a third party could not satisfactorily account how they came by the same. The Magistrate found him guilty and sentenced him to imprisonment for two years. On appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the prosecution must first adduce evidence to show that there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully; and (2) the onus shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his possession of the same, and that the burden in respect of this is discharged by the prosecution that the onus shifted to the appellant to account satisfactory explanation of his actual possession of goods. HELD: (1)(a) The mere description of the goods as new would not fulfil the requirements of section 2(b). In order to prove that the articles were railway stores it must be shown that they had been manufactured for such us,. [189 B] (b) The prosecution must also prove that there were no cause for reasonably suspicion of their stores being theft or obtained fraudulently. It is only when the burden shifts to a person in unlawful possession thereof that the prosecution can be successfully launched against a person who has bought them from someone fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the The facts in this case are as follows: (i) The appellant was not found in any way connected with the railway administration. [189 C] (ii)The mere description or the goods mentioned in his report were used or meant to be use for the purpose of construction, operations or maintenance or of a railways. It was only when he had examined the articles that satisfy the definition that the accused had been in possession thereof. He may for instance show that he had bought themfrom someone bona fide in belief that they have been manufactured from somebody bonafide in the faith that the purchaser had lawfully procured the goods from someone bonafidely in the sense that the purchasers had bought it from someone bona fides in the expectation that the purchase was made by him to a bona fide purchaser. [190 C D] (iii)The prosecution must further prove that he has purchased the property in open market where goods of this 189 kind are usually sold or that he have bought them therefrom. The mere fact that some stolen railway property had been kept in the shop of the owner would not have to be taken into account for determining whether the articles in question were railway Stores within the meaning of section 3(b) of the Act and as such the question of punishment under section 3 did not arise.

The appellants were tenants of the demised premises. The respondent accepted the rent after determination of the lease. Therein the definition of 'Tenant ' was amended by Section 3(ii) of the Amendment Act introducing to Section 3 Clause (vii), thus: "(vii) "tenant" means any person by whom or on whose account or behalf rent is, or but for a contract express or implied, would be payable for any premises to his landlord including the person who is continuing in its possession after the termi nation of his tenancy otherwise than by a decree for evic tion passed under the provisions of this Act; and 10 (b) In the event of death of the tenant as is referred to in sub clause (a), his surviving spouse, son, daughter and other heir in accordance with the personal law applica ble to him who had been, in the case of premises leased out for residential purposes, ordinarily residing and in the cases of premises let out for commercial or business purposes, normally carrying on business with him in such premises as member of his family upto his death. The appellants were inducted into the demised shop by the respondent on the basis of a lease deed dated July 5, 1985. In the meanwhile, the definition was amended with retrospective effect from August 1, 1965 and Section 3 (vii) of Act provided that where a tenant continues to remain in possession even after the termination of a tenancy, his surviving wife, son and other heirs in accordance With the personal Law applicable thereto shall be deemed to have an estate or inter est in the tenanted premises and tenancy rights in respect of commercial tenancies on the death of such tenant. The amended definition of "Tenant" was amended w.e.f. August 1 1965 by Section 4(1) of Amendment Act, introducing to Sections 3 and 13 (1) a new definition of tenant. In other words to avail of the statutory right under section 3(viii)(b), there must continue to subsist the unity of action and continuity of membership of the family between the deceased tenant and the spouse etc. The amendment was made with retrospective operation. The Amendment Act introduced by Section 5(1)(a) of Rajasthan Act No. 1 of 1965 introducing the definition clause in Section 3, which reads thus: "tenant means any persons holding or occupying the prem ises and includes any person holding or occupy the prem arees as a sub tenant, or any person continuing in possession after termination of the tenancy." The amended provision was brought into force with retrospective retrospective effect. The definition of landlord under section 2(i) of The Rajasthan Act was amended on August 1 1966 by Section 6 of Amendment Rules, which came into force w. e.f., September 1, 1966 introducing to section 3 Clause(vii), thereby bringing about an end of the relationship between the tenant and his heirs. In view of the amendment made in Section 5 (1)(b) of amended Act, the appellants became trespassers. The respondents filed a suit for ejectment against the appellants on the premise that on the date of the death, the tenancy had not been terminated by the appellants. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that the appellants had no right to continue in occupation of the premises and that the respondent landlord after termination had no locus standi to continue as tenant. On appeal, the High Court held that since the appellants were jointly carrying on the business with the tenant during her life time as family business they were not entitled to the benefit of amended definition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the Amending Act did not apply to all tenants as defined in Section 2(vii)(a), and that, therefore, the Amending act did not affect the rights of the appellants under the unamended Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The amended provisions were brought into effect with retrospective amendment.

The appellant Board was willing to extend that scheme to all the workers except the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The appellant Board is willing to provide that the employees contributing equally shall be entitled to receive from one establishment to another both which may not he covered by the same scheme under the Act and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. The workmen also contended that the services of the workmen of the Board are liable to be transferred from one employer to another, both which might not he governed by the Act, and such anomaly will be removal by making it the benefit under both these schemes similar . Held, that the Tribunal had dealt with the matter in a perfunctory manner. The Tribunal has treated the whole matter in an unsatisfactory manner. It has made no effort to work out the financial implications of its order. The Board is not bound to make it clear what exactly are the total wages. In considering the question of provident fund and gratuity which stands more or less on the same footing as provident fund which is also a retiral benefit, the Tribunal has to look at the profits made without considering provision for taxation in the shape of income tax and for reserves. The provisions for income tax, for reserves must take second place as compared to provision for wage structure and gratuity, which stands on the Same footing as Provident Fund which isalso a retiral benefits. It will certainly result in some reduction in profits; but if the industry is in a stable condition and the burden of provident funds and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer that burden will have to be borne by the employer like the burden would have to bear by the employers like the onus of wage structure in the interest of social justice. The burden of Provident Fund and gratuity is on the employer, like the State Government, which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4 per cent per annum. The employees also contended, that if the interests realised by the State were excluded from consideration, there would be surplus in favour of the appellant Board.

The respondent wife was married to the appellant on July 11, 1978. Both the parties lived together in a house of her husband and both the parties were living separately. The respondent alleged that she was maltreated and ultimately driven out of the house by her husband on July 12, 1978, and that both the appellant and the respondent were physically incapable of having sexual relations with the respondent. The Magistrate held that the husband had been found to be impotent and hence she was entitled to the grant of maintenance. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Magistrate and directed the appellant to pay a sum of Rs. 1,000/ as maintenance to her. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the husband having been found guilty of cruelty to her, she was not entitled to grant of any maintenance; (2) the wife having been subjected to mental cruelty and harassment, the question of refusal of maintenance did not arise at all. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object of section 488 is to provide an effective and summary remedy to provide for appropriate food, clothing and lodging for a wife. [939F] 2.1 In order to establish legal cruelty it is necessary that physical violence should be used. [1040B] 2(a) the question whether the husband has contracted marriage with another wife or keeps a mistress before the amendment made in section 488 does not arise. [1141C D] 3.2 The object and purpose of section 125 is to providing an effective remedy to providing for appropriate protection, clothing, lodging and lodging and for a woman. In order that the wife should live away from the husband, it is essential that physical intercourse should be resorted to. [1240D] 4.3 In the instant case, the husband was forced or compelled to live a life of celibacy while staying with her husband who is unable to have sexual relations between them. The plaintiffs, the Union of India and the State of Gujarat, were the owners of certain lands in Bhavnagar Municipality. The second part of the land was owned by the Government of India. The first part of it was covered by Survey Nos. 37 dated 19th January, 1948 fixed the boundary marks and that the Government had decided to sell the land in question to the State Public Works Department of the State. The plaintiffs ' case was that by Resolution No. 37, the Municipality was constituted and the buildings known as infantry lines and Lancer 's lines were taken over on 7th June, 195 1 by the State Government of Gujarat. The defendants claimed to be the owner of the Parade Ground in or about June, 1961 fixed the boundaries and that they were in possession in the suit property till 7th July, 1952 when physical posses sion was handed over by the military engineers of the Gov ernment of India to the state Public Works Depart ment of India, and that on the ground that in respect of Rasala Lines the plaintiff had admitted that they did not own the buildings thereon, they were not entitled to recover possession of the lands covered by the Survey numbers de scribed in the second part. The Trial Court held that the plaintiffs had proved its title to the suit land and that there was nothing on record to show that the Municipality had been formally handed over the land to the Government, that its right over the lands was never recognised by the Union Of India or the State Govern ment and that, therefore, the various documents filed in this case would go to show whether the Municipality is formally handedover the land for use. The High Court dismissed the cross objections filed by the Municipal ity holding that Resolution No 37 dated 18th January 1948, the title to possession of 'Parade Ground ' was never recognized by the union of India or State Government and that in view of the provisions contained in section 37 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949, the suit was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The right of the Municipality to sell land and to give it on rent lease and to get the out come there from shall apply to the land of the Government coming within the limit to the Municipality decided fixed on the date of the Order of the state of Bhavnagar i.e. dt. 18th Jan., 1948, that is to say if the locality is fixed in the development scheme for industrial or residential purpose the land shall be given for that particular purpose. [224F G] 2. The suit lands do not vest to the Govern ment of Saurashtra. It amounts conferring an authority or authorising the Municipalities to execute the sale deeds in respect thereof. It is also in evidence that these buildings were there long before 1948 and that therefore, possession was handedover by the Defence Ministry of the Union oi the State Govt. on 7rd July,1952 for use, and remained under the control of the Defence Minister of India as well as the recommendations of the Board of Officers consisting of six members including Executive Engineer, Public Works department as representative of the Central Government. The claim will now have to be veri fied. 1951 which are communications from the Government oi tiated it is only stated that suit lands did not vest in the Municipality. It was also in eviden ce that these properties were there much before 1948 or that, thereafter, the land alone could not have been vested in the Municipali ty without buildings. [225F G; 226A B] 3. The plaintiff had proved his title to this property and that he did not possess any right of ownership with the plaintiff as the title was not vested in them. [226C D] 4.

The appellant was a Class III servant employed as a metal examiner, also called Chaser. He was charged under section 5(1)(d) of the Indian Penal Code for having induced the said Nanak Singh to deliver to him currency notes of the value of Rs. 150 by dishonest representation that he could secure a job for Kallu and it was held that no case under section 420, Indian Penal code was made out against him. The Judicial Commissioner acquitted the appellant but on appeal the Judicial Commissioner granted certificate of fitness for appeal on two main grounds viz., (1) whether the appellant was an "officer" within the meaning of section 21(9), Indian Penal Act; and (2) whether he was rightly convicted of the offense under section 161, Indian penal Code. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) that the appellant could not be held guilty of the offence under section 3(1) (d) read with section 21 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. (ii)that the provisions of law in regard to the first question may be conveniently set out at this stage. The duties which he performed were contractual dutiesrementers deception in the discharge of which might subject him to punishment for cheating but not duties attached to any office conferred on him or his predecessor in title, failure to perform which with integrity could make him liable as an officer, to the special penalties prescribed for delinquent public servants. (iii)that he did not fall within the terms of the last portion of clause (9) of section 2 of the Act and therefore a public servant within the definition of a public Servant contained in section 21, Indian Police Penal Code and being such public servant be fell within the ambit of that term as used in section 2.

The Respondent, a licensee for the year 1968 69, was granted a liquor vending licence for the period 1967 69. The licences paid a sum of Rs. 86,450 leaving the balance unpaid in spite of repeated reminders. Ultimately recovery proceedings under the said Act were started by the department and the Collector cum Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner, Patiala Division, issued a proclamation prohibiting the transfer or creation of a charge by the Respondent of his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga, with a building constructed thereon. The auction in respect of the said share was notified for June 14,1977. Just a day prior to the holding of the aforesaid auction sale the Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala C. for a permanent injunction restraining the State and the Excise Department from auctioning his said half share. The Trial Court dismissed the suit with costs. The High Court allowed the second appeal holding that the portion of the building used for residence was exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (l) of Section 60, while that portion in which the liquor shop was situated was liable to be attached and accordingly issued a permanent order restraining the Respondent from auctionising his said share. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The attachment levied on and the auction sale notified in respect Of, the Respondent 's half share was not in execution of any decree of a civil court but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorized to adopt proceedings under that Act for recovery of revenue due to the State. [848B] 2. The properties, if my, which are exempt from attached and sale in revenue recovery proceedings Under the said law would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said provisions. So far as the said section is concerned, it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery and recovery of arrears of revenue. [884C] 3. The property, if I my, the same are exempt under clause(ccc). [849E] 4. The attached properties, therefore, would be liable to attachment and sale under clause.(ccc), while that part in which liquor shop is situated was not liable to such attachment or sale.

The respondent, a widow of the deceased, acquired agricultural land in Moosapet village belonging to one Rashid Shapoor Chenai. The Government did not accept the decisions of the Civil Court and filed appeals to the High Court challenging the enhancement. The High Court held that having regard to the enhanced compensation granted by the Civil court for the lands such property had been undervalued in the original assessment and as such it had escaped assessment to duty. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 Under section 61 of the , the only record that the assessing authority can look into is the record relating to the assessment of estate duty and not any other record such as the be cord in the probate proceedings which are not relevant. [429C] 1.2 The Civil Court 's evaluation of this right done subsequently would be its valuation as at the relevant date either under the Estate Duty Act or the Wealth Tax Act. [427B C] 1:3 In the instant case, the wards made by the Special Deputy Collector were not accepted by the heirs of the appellant and the Land References were sought by them and the same were pending in Civil Court at the time when the assessment was made. The respondent 's failure to disclose full particulars regarding the land acquisition proceedings, lead to the conclusion that the acquired lands still formed part of the estate of the erstwhile deceased and as a result thereof the assessments were being initiated. [544D] 1 :4. Under section 11 of the Act, the only records that the assessment authority can looked into is ' record relating 'the assessment of the estates duty and also not anyother record such like the beem cord in probate proceedings. The Revenue will pay the costs of the appeal to the appellant Turning to Civil Appeal No. 44 of 1966, the respondent as well as the High court had proceeded on the wrong assumption that the said fact was a primary and material fact and not an inferential fact and its non disclosure amounted to omission or failure which could lead the assessing authorities to a reasonable belief that property chargeable to estate duty had escaped Assessment and as Such the respondent had jurisdiction to issue the notice. [529G] 1.:4. The Civil Courts decrees in Land References had escaped assessments in the earlier assessment proceedings and since such escapement was due to the respondent ' s failure to disclosed full particulars about the land acquired proceedings, the reassessment proceedings were being started.

The appellant was elected as Director of the Bank. The appellant 's election was challenged by the respondent on the ground that he had repaid the entire loan before the impugned notice under section 78(1) of the Act and that the question of giving retrospective effect to the section did not arise because the appellant was a defaulter when he contested the election and though he paid all the debts on 21.10.1986 yet he could not be "absolved of the disqualification on the day he contested election". The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the dues calculated on 31.1.86 became recurring dues every following day and on 12.5.1986 when section 73FF came into force the outstanding dues continued even on 18.8.1986, when the appellant contested the elections. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The disqualification as defaulter continues after the election of the appellant and section 78 envisaged such a default and the appellant having continued to be a defaulter was lawfully removed and the fact that he repaid the loan before his notice was issued would not be material for the purpose of taking action under section 79. [680B C] 2.1 The disqualification on account of default is common both for election and for continuation as a Director in the Committee, the special provision for setting aside an election must prevail over section 78 as there would be apparent conflict between the two and the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, would apply. [679C D] 2:2 The disqualification under section 73(1), as a defaulter continued after the elections of the appellants and section 79 envisaged such an default and section 144E deals with disqualification for membership. Section 144E provides that notwithstanding anything contained in section 91 or any other provisions of this Act, any dispute relating to an election shall be referred to the Commissioner of the Division in which such election is held or to an officer not below the rank of Additional Commissioner of division authorised by the State Government in this behalf. [681D] 2 :3 The disqualification that was imposed on the appellant ' s election as a director of the bank and section 80 envisaged such default and, therefore, the disqualification as arrear continued after 18.08.1986 would not apply because the Act prescribes a separate procedure for calling in question the appellant's election as Director or creasing to be Director on account his having committed default. [683E] 2:-4 The disqualification imposed by section 78 is not common both with election and the special provisions for settingaside an election are not derogate with special, will apply, if there would have been apparent conflict in the two. [684D] 3:1 In the instant case, the appellant had repaid his entire loan after the impugned order was passed. The question of repugnancy involved in Zaverbhai Amaidas. vs The State of Bombay, [1955] 1 SCR 799 does not arise in this case. [685F] 2):5 The disqualification which was imposed by Section 78 is a common one and the principle generalia Specialibus non vacant general word do not conflict with special., would apply, [684G] 3 :6 In the present case, there was no room for holding that he paid the entire amount before the notice was given. It is only when the disqualification was set aside by the impugned orders that the appellant could be said to have made default on the first day of his directorship and on every subsequent day till the instalment or instalments were paid. The fact that the loan was repaid before the issuance of the impugned notices under section 80(1)(e) would not make any difference in the matter of disqualification as a partner in the committee.

The respondent was in the service of the State as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. After his retirement the respondent was served with a charge sheet containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. On the conclusion of the enquiry the State Government issued orders reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. A Division Bench of that Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State 's orders dated December 4, 1982 on the ground that the State had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from Service. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The Government has power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. [189G] 2. Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part of the pension payable in respect of misconduct which he may have committed while in service, provided that before any order to this effect is issued, the procedure referred to in Note I to Rule 33 of Bombay Civil Service Conduct, Discipline and Appeal Rules shall be followed. [190H] 3. The State Government has powers to reduce the amount by taking action against a government servant even though after his retired from services on attaining that age he may had committed while service or after the completion of his service. [191B C] 4. Rule 188 expressly confers powers on the State Govt to withhold pension payable under the rules to Government servants who is borne on its establishment. The power to reduced or withholding pension by way of taking proceedings for determining the respondent 's pension is preserved by these Rules. Rule 187 expressly confers Power on the government to reduce, withholding or withdrawing any part or of it if the pensioner be convicted of grave misconduct while he was In service or during the period of his services. The validity of Rule 189 does not depend upon the good conduct of the respondent. [192D E] 5. The question whether the State is competent to take action against the Respondent by reducing his pension by 50% would seriously affect his living.

The appellants were the tenants of certain premises in which the Act applied. The respondents resisted the claim made by them on various grounds. On the question whether the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 3(3) was valid or not, HELD : (1) The order passed by the appropriate authority under the relevant provisions of the Act is final under sub section (4), subject to any order passed in that behalf by the State Government under section 7 F.
