[556 A B] (2) The power conferred on the State government at all material times by section 7F is very wide and it cannot be seriously disputed that the jurisdiction of the civil courts to deal with civil causes can be excluded by the Legislature by special Acts which deal with special subject matters; but the exclusion of the jurisdiction Of the civil court must be made by a statutory provision which expressly provides for it, or which necessarily and inevitably leads to that inference. [558 C D] (3) The provisions of section 3 are not exhaustive of the powers conferred on a State Government by section 3. [559 B] M/s. M/S. M.K. Kedia & Co. vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , referred to. (4) The Commissioner can interfere with his order if the District Magistrate has acted illegally or with material irregularity or has wrongly refused to act. [560 C D]. (5) The powers conferred by section 6 are wide enough to include the power conferred upon a State government under section 8F of the . It is not necessary that the Commissioner should exercise his powers in the interests of justice. [561 F] M. K. Kraipak & Co., vs The Union of India, ; and M/ S.Kedia & Company vs The Government of Madras, ; referred to (6) The High Court was right in holding that the permission given by the District Collector without jurisdiction is invalid in law. [562 C D; 563 A B].

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was removed from his office by an order dated July 7, 1983. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court which dismissed it on the ground that the charges were not proved and that the allegations made against him were false. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the charge was not proved. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Article 317(1) of the Constitution provides that an inquiry has to be held by this Court in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under article 145. Rule 1 of Order XXXVIII mentions the persons to whom notice of the reference is required to be given. The documents annexed to the Reference and indeed the fact that those documents are so annexed would show that the President was satisfied prima facie that the allegation made against the Member of the Public Service Commissions requires to be inquired into by this court. [615E F] (2) Article 316(1), like its counterpart in statutes like the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not create or confer any new power but preserves the power of the Court to act ex debito justiciae. The balance of convenience requires that we should forego that advantage and delegate the duty of recording evidence. [515E] (3) Article 311(1)(a) does not creating or confer a new power But preserves the powers of the court to act as ex debit o justiciae; it is only fair that an opportunity should be given to Shri Saini to prove his case that the charged against him is false, inspired and motivated. [643B] (4) Article 320(1A) does create or confers any new right but preserves and the power Of the Court under article 317(3) does no create or conferring any new powers but preserves, the power and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to exercise such power conferred by article 124(4). The balance is of convenience required that we shall forego, that advantage, and delegate, the duty, of recording the evidence. The entire balance of hardship requires that this should forebego that benefit and delegate it the duty to record evidence. It must also be remembered that Article 317 was enacted in order to give protection to the members of the public Commissions in regard to their removal from office and not as a disability. [651C D] (5) The balance, of convenience require that we must forego any further examination of witnesses. Evidence may, however, be recorded at any other place if the learned Judge considers it necessary or convenient. [641E F].

The appellants were the trustees of a temple. The deity installed in the temple was purely a family deity and the deity installed therein a public Waqf. The idol installed in its temple was a private one. The endowment being of a private nature, the Act had no application and the Order passed by the respondent regarding management was set aside. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 There can be religious trust of a public character under the Mahomedan law which is not possible in English law. [832B] 1.2 The property does not vest in God but in the beneficiaries who have installed the deity. A and Ext. 15 merely provides that if in future the family becomes extinct and no fit person could be found then any of the Baisnab Sampraday or any reputed Hindu of the village can take action, namely, to perform the work of the deity belonging to the founder himself. [ 832C] 1:3 The property dedicated for the purpose of the maintenance of the temple belongs to the deity and will not vest with God but In the beneficiaries whose names are mentioned in Ext.15, the villagers do not make Kirtan before the deity or take any part in any festivity of the idol. [884D] 1 :4 The property is a private endowment under the Muslim law which was not possible to do with the public. [874E] 2.1 In the instant case, the properties were required for the maintenance and management of the Temple. The income of the debuttor property and anything that you might have spent from your own pocket for the improvement of the worship of the muth and to save the property, are dedicated for public purposes. [864G] 2:2 In the present case, there was no provision for framing any scheme by associating the members of the public or consulting them. The properties maintained herein have been endowed to the idol before, we or our successors had or will have no claim on this and any such claim made, shall be void. [854A] 2 :3 In the absence of any provision for making any scheme in Ext.- 15 by associesting the members, the public cannot take action under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939.

The appellant Bank entered into an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946. The power of Attorney recited: "Whereas we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into certain contracts and will in future enter into other contracts and whereas an agreement dated 13 7 1946 has been made between us and the Bharat Bank Ltd., in pursuance of which the attorneys have agreed to finance contracts and to advance moneys to Malhotra against supply bills for payments to be received by us under the contracts. " The power to attorney recited: (1) That we are functioning as contractors, to present and submit supply bills regarding our contracts to the proper officer and/or authority of the Government Departments concerned; (2) That the power of the attorney is expressed to be irrevocable. As the lender had an interest in the fundS the power to Attorneys was expressed to he irrevocable. The appellant Bank instituted a suit against Malhotra and Takhatmal asking for a declaration that the appellant was an assignee of the biLl and that Takhat Mal had no right to attach it. The Trial Court decreed the suit. On appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit holding that the power in favour Of the appellant did not amount to an equitable assignment of the monies due under the bill in favour o the appellant. In appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD: (i) The power conferred on the appellant to receive all monies due or to become due to Malhotra in respect of pending or future contracts with the government authorities was expressed as a valid assignment of that funds and was irrevocable. [705 B] (ii) The High Court was in error in holding that there was no equitable assignment. [806 C] (iii) The appellant bank had an Interest in the FundS the Power of Attorney was expressed on behalf of the Bank against Malhotra 's bills for supplies under the contract. It was not a case where the power conferred upon the appellant by the power under the agreement was expressed or implied to be exercised in his favour in a pending appeal and to credit to the borrower 's account the monies realised in execution of the decree amounted to an enforceable assignment of his funds. [788 E F] (iv) The Power of attorney was not irrevocable. It did not create any interest in a specific fund and was merely a power of agency. [789 D] (v) The right to sue for money due under a contract is a discretionary one. The right of the lender to receive payment is an equitable one. [783 E F]. (vi) The Court held that there could be no equitable transfer in favourof the appellant and decreed the decree.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd. The said Company had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. But that provident fund was not a recognised one. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. That order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. On further appeal to the tribunal, the tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the same was exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3) (ii). The Tribunal held that the receipts in question were not income and therefore the same were exempt from tax. On appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1 The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ is undoubtedly an income. [446C] 2.2 The receipt by the assessee with which we are concerned is exempt from the payment of Tax in view Of section 17 (3) of the Income tax Act, 1961. [441F] 3. Section 17 has nothing to do either with deductions or with exemptions. It merely a provision defining the expression "salary". [441H] 4.1 In defining the word "profits" the legislature excluded from the scope of that expression any payments received by the assesee from an employer or a former employer or from a provident or other fund (not being an approved superannuation fund) to the extent to which it does not consist of contribution by the Assessee or interest on such contributions. From that it follows that the income of every kind which is not to be excluded from income tax under any of the heads specified in section 1.4 items 'A ' to 'E ' are "brought to tax under section 56. Section 56 (I) provides that income of each kind which was not to he excluded from total income under the Act shall be chargeable to income tax Under the head income "from other sources" if it is not chargeable to Income tax under the head "profits in lieu of any salary or wages". [442H; 442A] 4:2 The receipts of Rs 27,949/ are undoubtedly an expenditure. But then the question is what is meant by "profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains" and brought to tax. Under section 17, income of a kind which has not to been excluded from tax is chargeable to tax in respect of any item of receipt. [442C] 4 :3 The receipt is undoubtedly exempt from taxation under the heads mentioned in section 2.4 item 'A' to 'F '. In defining "Profits in lieu" of salary, the legislature excludes from the ambit of that word any payments which are not to fall within the total income. From this it follows therefore that the expression 'salary" is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to call into aid any of these rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High Court. [444D E] 4 4.4 The receipt in the relevant accounting year cannot be said to be either interest on the securities; income from house pro perty; profits and gains, of business and profession or Capital gains. it has to be considered as "income" and bring to tax Under section 56(I) providing that income from any other sources which is chargeable with income tax shall be charged to income Tax under the heading "Profits and gains " from other source". [444E F] 5.5 The receipt received by an assessee with whom he has a Provident fund scheme, his own contributions to the fund or any interest on it. Therefore there is nothing in section 17 which prohibits the payment by the investor of the amount of his own contribution to the provident fund.

The impugned Act was passed in the year 1956. The petitioners were convicted under section 3(1) of the Bihar Animal peservation Act, 1949 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a term of six months. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the impugned Acts violated article 14 as they discriminates against the beef butchers who slaughter only cattle but not sheep or goats have been singled out for hostile and discriminatory treatment; (ii) the provisions of section 3 of the Act were violative of articles 19(1)(g); (iii) the Act was violative of article 14 inasmuch as it discriminates between the animals belonging to the species of bovine cattle and buffaloes per square mile and 43 heads to every 100 persons. HELD: (i). The impugned Acts are not law with respect to " preservation, protection and improvement of stock ", and their constitutional validity will have to be judged in that context and against that background. [720 E] (ii)(a) The impugned Act is violative of the fundamental right guaranteed by article 19(6) of Constitution. It is true that the impugned Act does not infringe article 14 but only contravenes article 19. But it is clear from the Report of the Expert Committee that the slaughter of all animals belonging either to the class or classes of persons specified in the Schedule to the Act is a " slaughterer of animals for food, dealer in meat". [721 E] The impugned legislation offends articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The impugned provisions are not violative of any fundamental right under article 19 of the constitution inasmuch as they infringe article 19 (1)(f) of that Article. [779 G H; 723 A B] (b) The restrictions imposed by section 3 on slaughter of animals belonging both to the classes or classes specified in Schedule I and Schedule II are not unreasonable, because they violate articles 14, 16 and 17 of the Schedule. [780 C D] (c) The provisions of sections 3 and 4 of the impugned statutes are violative of Article 19(2) of Part III of the Consti tution of India Act, 1935. [781 F G] (d) The State has no power to impose a ban on slaughter animals belonging only to the categories specified in section 3 or section 4 of that Act. It cannot be said that the restrictions imposed are unreasonable because they infringe articles 14 or 16 of Schedule II.

The respondent was a 'workman ' within the meaning of the ,of the , and was, therefore, not an employee within the definition of " workman " in section 2(a) of the . The company filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for quashing the orders passed against him. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Standing Orders were approved by the certifying officer under the provisions of the Central Act and by the Labour Commissioner under section 30 of the local Act, and that the respondent was not an 'workman within the ambit of the Standing Order No. 16. Held, that the word "employee" in the definition clause includes an employee who has to have a ticket, card or token issued to him by standing order No. 2 (a) itself authorises the issue of tickets to other employees, so that there may be one kind of tickets issued to workmen under standing Order No,. 2 (b). The respondent was an 'employee ' within section 2 (c) of . The definition clause in Standing Order 16 is not confined to an employee ' within it. It does not authorise the issue or surrender of tickets when the employee ceases to be an employee. The word "workman" in section 3(a), means such categories of employees as may from time to time be declared to be workmen by the management and Standing Orders No. 1 (b) itself empowers the issue, of tickets, to other persons than workmen. The definition clauses in Standing Orders 12, 13, 14 and 15 are not exhaustive of the definitions. It is only in respect of an employee that he has to be treated as an 'workmen ' within that meaning. The respondent is a 'employee " within the expression of the definition.

The respondent workmen, a company incorporated under the , was started in the year 1961 and it went into production in the years 1964 65. No profit was earned at least right up to the year '1967 68. The Company claimed that alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus could be payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this Project went into manufacture. The Tribunal held that alloys steel Project could not be treated as a separate unit because, under the Act, a Company is also an establishment and, therefore, an establishment in a private sector would constitute one establishment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the workmen that (1) Alloy Steel Projects were a separate entity distinct from Hindustan Steel Ltd., and could not have been treated as an independent establishment because, the Company had not been earning any profits; (2) The Tribunal committed an error in holding that ally steel Project was one which was owned, controlled or managed by a person or body other than a Government company or a corporation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In clause (16), "establishment in public sector" is defined as meaning any establishment owned, managed or controlled by (a) a Government Company as defined in section 617 of the ; In clause 15, "establishment" means any establishment other than an establishment which is owned, run or managed either by a company or corporation. [675B] 1.2 The word "establishment " has been used in this Act to indicate something different from a company as defined under the . [676F] 1:3 In clause 16, " Establishment in public Sector" is described as meaning an establishment owned controlled or controlled or maintained by (i) a person who is employed on any day during an accounting year. The word 'establishment ' has been defined to indicate what something different therefrom from a Company as understood in the . Section 6(d) defines establishment as meaning "any establishment other then an establishment, whether it is owned or managed, controlled and managed by (ii) a corporation". [678G H] 1 :4. The words "establishment of a company" are intended to indicate some different from that Company as described in clause (15). The word establishment ' has not been used for the purpose of sub section (3) of section 1 of the Act. [600C D] 2.1 The word `establishment ' is intended to convey something different than a company, as defined by the . In clause 17, "Establishment in public sectors" is meant to indicate anything different from one company as specified in the , .a company which is not owned, financed or managed and controlled by a Government corporation. Obviously, the word " establishment" is intended for indicating something differentfrom a company. [599E F] 2:2 The words 'establishment in private sector ' are used to indicate certain things different from the company as understood under section 6(1). In clause 18, " establishments in public service sector" are defined as including any establishment which are owned, regulated or managed in the public sector. It is clear that if alloy steel Project is treated as part of one establishment for purposes of sub sections (3), (4) and (5) of Section 1 of Act, it will be covered by the definition of "establishment". [599F] 2 :3 The word establishments ' has to be understood in its ordinary sense. It would be absurd to say that a company is owned controlled by an individual or body of persons other than Government company, or a corpora tion of the nature described in clauses (16).

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was enacted by Parliament under Article 252 of the Constitution with a view to control pollution of rivers and streams which has assumed considerable importance and urgency in recent years as a result of increasing industrialisation and urban isation. The cess is payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act, at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in the corre sponding Entry in column II thereof as the Central Govern ment may by notification in the Official Gazette from time to time specify. The Cess is levied on the person carrying out any specified industries and every Local Authority and is assessed on the principle of 'separation of material especially that in a raw state into marketable form, the word 'vegetable ' has been defined as: "A plant used or cultivated for food man or domestic animals, as the cabbage turnip, potato, bean, dandelion, etc., also the edible part of such a plant, as prepared for market or the table. " The cess was levied on a person carryingon any specified industrial industry and each local authority is calculated to pay cess on the ground that he carried on any industry and all local authorities and is calculate on the value of water taken by him. The appellant challenged the levy contending that sugar manufacturing industries would not come within Entry 15 of the Seventh Schedule of the Act as it was a production of raw material for manu facturing of synthetics or manmade fabrics, which had assumed considerable significance and urgency and in recent past years as an outcome of increasing Industrialisation and rural isation; that sugar industry was one of the main source of causing water pollu tion and to ensure 528 that industrial affluents are not allowed to be discharged into the water coarses without adequate treatment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that sugar industries would come within entry 15 of Schedule I to the Cess Act, and that the cess was leviable on the persons carrying on specified industry; that the Cess is leviable on a particular commodity and every State Board and State Boards respectively for Prevention and Control Of Water Pollution vs Andhra Pradesh Rayons Ltd. and others; , The question for consideration in this appeal was whether manufacturing of rayon grade pulp a base material for an individual or a group of individuals would come under Entry 15, List II of the Schedule to the cess Act as the State Board had no power to levy cess on such commodity. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'seiling ' has not been defined in any of these entries. It is common knowledge that in manufacture some thing is brought into existence which is different from that originally existed in the sense that the thing produced is by itself a commercially different commodity. [529G H] 2.1 In order to bring an industry within any of those entries in Schedule I it has to be seen what is the end product produce produced by that industry. The essential point thus is that in manufacturing some thing was brought into operation which is distinct from that previously existed in that sense that it is produced by itself as a commercially separate article. [525A B] 2:2 In order that one has to look merely at what is clearly said. There is no presumption as to tax. One has to take the view that this Act with which we are concerned is an Act imposing li ability for cess. The nature of activity carried on by a particular industry in running its business must be such as may lead to the production of any new article. The essence of manufacture is the change of one object to another for the purpose of making it marketable.

The respondent landlord filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant, his tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on the business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises. The Appellate Authority passed an order of eviction against the appellant. It was contended that Section 10(3)(a) (iii) used the expression 'business ' only and not the expression "profession" as defined in Section 10 (3) (a) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the word 'business " was capable of including the practice of a profession and that it clearly included the profession of a Doctor. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 A reading of Section 10 of the Act shows that the Legislature intended to give a narrow meaning and was confined to activities of a commercial nature. It is not a sound principle of construction tn interpret expressions used in one Act with reference to their use in another Act with refer to their usage in another statute. [16B C] 1.2 The word 'profession ' has been defined as the owner of a building, including a person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a residential building, on his own account or on behalf of another person etc. Tenant is defined as a person by whom or on whose account rent is payable for a building. Section 10 provides for the determination of fair rent and Section 12(1) which bars the eviction of tenants therefrom in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The provisions of the said Act including Section 4 which provide for the fixation of fair compensation and Section 10 which bars eviction of tenant therefrom in respect of specified grounds are not cognate Acts. [17C D] 1:3 A reading thereof shows that it is intended to prevent unreasonable eviction of 16 tenants by landlords and to provide for eviction on specified grounds. There is no reason why a landlord who is a member of the legal or medical professions and who requires the premises to carry on the practice should be wholly debarred from obtaining possession of the premises, if and when pleading is permissible to him. [18G H] 1 :4 The word "business" has been used in another enactment with reference thereto to their user in another legislation. It would be anamolous to hold that all the provisions of Section 4 including Section 10 are not identical Acts. On the other hand it is a well known principle of interpretation that meaning of words and expressions used therein must take their colour from the content in which they appear. [19D] 1.:5 The word must be gleaned from the context in which it is used. It may also be an amamolingous to holding that all those provisions are not allied Acts. But if the two Acts in which the same word is used are not irreconcilable, they would be equally applicable to non residential buildings owned by an Advocate but not Section 10. [20F] 1.(6) The definition of "business " has been given a wide meaning and it includes activities of any commercial nature, trade or profession. It cannot be said that the expression business is capable of include the profession which is being carried on. [21G H; 22A B] 2.1 In the instant case, the respondent landlord had not established that he was carrying out his profession in the business in question. Nor did he establish that he had been carrying on any business in the shop in question or that he needed the premises bona fide for carrying out the practice. [22C D].

The appellant firm was a limited company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The respondent accepted the said proposal and thereafter a letter dated 29 September 1942 was written by Ram Ratan Gupta to the respondent recording the agreement that "a sum of Rs. 4,00,000 in its account with the respondent would be paid on 577 demand". The appellant accepted the same and thereafter the appellants were not bankers and therefore it was improbable that the respondents who were bankers would deposit with the traders the sum of money. The appellant filed a suit for the sum claimed by it under article 60 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court reversed the decree holding that Article 60 of Indian Limitation was applicable to the case and the limitation would commence from the date of demand and the suit was filed within three years from the demand. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Article 62 of the Limitation Act was not applicable because there was a demand for a part of the amount in the year 1943 because Padampat Singhania said that there was interpolation of the words "deposit karaya" in the roznamcha entry and therefore limitation would start from that date. HELD: (1) The respondent acted as bankers. A hundi or a promissory note would have been consistent with the case of a loan. One of the terms in the award was that the award in respect of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills and India Supplies "do not cover the advances which either party or their separate firms may have made to all or any of them or their moneys which may be in deposit with them and they shall be payable and paid in their usual course". [580 E] (2) The words "de posit karaya", in the context of Article 60, are not intended to cover a demand in the month of October, 1943. It is only when a demand is made that it is made on demand and not on demand, that limitation would begin from that day. [580 G] (3) The word "deposit karya" in article 62 of Limitation Act is used in connection with a demand made by a party to the suit or other proceedings for recovery of money due under an agreement that it was payable on demand. It does not mean that a demand should be made on a demand and that the limitation will commence from that time. [581 G] Nawab Major Sir Mohammad Akbar Khan vs Attar Singh & Ors., ; , referred to. (4) The letter exhibit A 5 bears the date 29 September, 1942 and is contemporaneous with the entire transaction between the appellant and the respondent. It would depend on the facts of each case whether the transaction is clothed with the character of a deposit of money or not.

The petitioner was released on parole for one year. The grounds of detention were served on him on 27th February, 1986 and he was produced before the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate who had passed an order under sub section (1) of section 3 of the , on 22nd April, 1987. He was remanded to judicial custody till 28th February 1986 by the said magistrate. A statement had been made by him under section 108 of the Customs Act to the effect that he had a strong and almost unanswerable case on merits but he was very keen to have the question of exclusion of the parole period decided since it arose squarely in this case. The petitioner filed an application before the High Court for release of his detenu on parole, which was dismissed by the High court. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the order of detention passed against him under sub s.(1) was not a valid order and could not be said to have been passed in violation of the principles of natural justice. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The order of release passed against the petitioner under sub sec.(1), of section3 of the . is not a detention order but an order of preventive detention. [847C D] 2. It is true that he has been held in custody in connection with the offences under the Arms Act which are nonbailable offences, but even so, it is open to the trying magis trate to release the petitioner on bail. But this principle will have to be judged and applied in the facts and circumstances of each case. [883D] 3. The detaining authority must disclose awareness of the fact that the person against whom an order is being made is to the knowledge of the authority already in jail and yet for compelling reasons a preventive promo tion order needs to be made. [864C D]. 4. The detention authority must also disclose awareness about the fact of the detenu 's involvement in the offence under the arms Act which is non bailable offences, and yet he for compelling reason a preventive bail order needs ted to be passed. [876E] 5. It was open to him to make full submission on all as pect arising in the writ petition. But that does not mean that the detaining authority should disclose awareness Of the fact whether the person is being detained under the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activi ties Act, 1974, or under the COFEPOSA Act to him.

The petitioners, who were working for a reasonably long period, on continuous basis, have been engaged as casual labourers in the Nehru Yuvak Kendras. They have produced the order of the Director General Posts and Telegraphs Department bearing No. 28 II/77 SRSTN Office of the Directorate General Posts & Telegraphs, New Delhi 1, 15.5.1980 to . . . Wing of P & T Department council (JCM). As an alternative to regular absorption it was proposed that a wage related to the minimum of the pay scale of Time Scale Group D cadre with the benefit of neutralisation for the rise in cost Index as applicable to regular employees may be effected. Wing of the P &T Department Council (JCMs) and P & E Department council, (JCMS) who are working for reasonably long periods, on continuously basis was one of the items under discussion in the P& T Department Council. As an alternate to regular absorb it was suggested that a Wage related to minimum of pay scale with the benefits of neutralization for the increase in cost index as applicable in regular employees should be effected and that this should be done once in a year for casual labourers of category 1 (those who have been recruited regularly. Wing, P &E Department Council, (CMS) and CPM were directed to take steps to absorb them regularly in its service and consequently they have been denied the benefits, such as increments, pension, leave facilities etc. which are enjoyed by those who have not completed 720 days of service over a period of three years or more with the department. The petitioners have produced an order of Director General, Posts and telegraphs Department dated 15th May 1980 to . , whereby the wages paid to them were very low and far less than the salary and allowances paid to regular employee of the Posts and Telecommunication Department belonging to each of the categories referred to above and secondly no scheme has been prepared by the Union of India to absorb him regularly in their service and ultimately they have be denied the benefit, such that increments, pensions, leave facility etc. are enjoyed on daily wages only. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated 15.05.1980 contending that even though the above Directive Principle may not be enforceable as such by virtue of Article 37 of the Constitution of India it may be relied upon by the petitioners to show that in the instant case they have not been subjected to hostile discrimination. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since the petitioners have been subjected for hostile discrimination, they are entitled to the benefits which have to be ensured by appropriate legislative and executive measures. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The right to work, the right to free choice of employment, the rights of every one who works to just and favourable remuneration ensuring a decent living for himself and for family, the Right to life, the power to form trade unions of one 's choice and the right of every person without discrimination of any kind to equal pay for equal work, is some of the rights which have been guaranteed by Article 38 of the constitution of India. [608B C] 1.2 The right of a citizen to work and the rights to free choices of employment are some of those rights which had to be ensures by appropriate legislation and executive action. If a person does not have the feeling that he belongs to an organization engaged in production he will not put forward his best effort to produce more. Is it for paying him lower wages? Administrators should realise that if any worker remains idle on any day, the country loses the wealth that he would have produced during that day.

The assessee was assessed to income tax under the Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessee filed a return showing a total net income of Rs. 1,50,000 and adding the same footnote. The Income tax Officer did not make a return of his income. He took into consideration the fact that the amount of Rs, 2,00,000 was not chargeable to income Tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee had failed to make a " voluntary " return on January 5, 1950, and added the same sum as the income tax payable by him under section 28(1) of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the notice under section 22(2), if filed belatedly under section 24(1), could not be a return in answer to a public notice issued under sub section (3) of section 34 after a return had already been made before it, and that the benefit of the extended period of limitation for assessment available under the first proviso to sub section(3) was not available in this case. Held: (i) The assessee had no assessable income in the previous year. He had only a right to file a return voluntarily, if he had suffered a loss, to report ' that loss. It laid down that the public notice required only persons having an income above the taxable limit to make the return. If a return was filed under section 23(1)(a) before assessment, and for this there is no reason why a return should be filed under sub s.(2), there is nothing in the Act which prevents him from filing a return under section 34(1). The period during which action could be taken was the extended one of 8 years. If the Income tax officer had acted on that return and assessed the assessee (1) (2) 125 before March 31, 1950 the assessment would have been valid. In the present case, the return in question was filed within the time allowed by or under sub sec.(3) Of section 34 of the Income 'tax Act, and therefore, the period during Which action could not take was the extendable one of eight years from the end of the year in which the income, profits or gains were first assessable. The assessment would be valid. [466 D E] (ii)The assessee had only an interest in the property and that he had no right to sue for a declaration that the assessment order was illegal. If he had been assessed on that basis, the assessment could have been validly made.

The petitioners, who are employees of the first petitioner and are officers of different nationalised banks, seek a writ of mandamus to direct the Central Government to appoint a nominee of the majority association of each of the nationalised banks as a member of its Board of Directors. The petitioners contend that the circular is contrary to the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act 1970 (Act No. XXXVII of 1970). It provides for all or any of the following matters, namely: (a) . . . , . . (b ) . . .. . . The scheme envisages all appointments to be by nomi nation. Such appointment, though desirable among workmen, is not a matter to be encouraged in the case of other employees for selection to the Board of Director, for the Directors must represent the interest of the bank as a whole and not of any special class of persons. In the light of these rival contentions, it would be open to the Central Govern ment to amend the Scheme to improve on the machinery for the conduct of an appropriate election, it is incumbent upon it, until any such amend ment is made, to work the present Scheme in such a way as to give the maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives. The scheme also provides for appointment to the non workmen Director from out of a panel furnished by the Union. The Scheme envisages all appointment to be made by noi nation. This scheme may provide for all and any of these matters, viz., (a ) representative of the employees and of depositors, of such bank, and (b) such other persons as may represent the interests of each other. In view of this position, it was incumbent upon the Central Gover nment to amend its Scheme to improved on the policy of election. The very object of leaving the choice to the central Government as to the mode, which is election or nomination, is to enable it to reasonably exercise its discretion in such an a way that to give best form of repre sentation to every category of persons mentioned in the Act. It would be per fectly within the discretion of the Central Govt. to choose that mode. Farmers, workers other than employees and artisans mentioned under sub section 3(b) of Section 9 are best represented by nomination, they being difficult of identification and their connection with the bank being more remote than in the cases of employees or even depositors. There can be no legitimate management culture foreign to their vital inter ests. There is no antithesis be tween the management and the employees. The Act, therefore, requires the Central Gov ernment to select a non workmen from out Of a panel of three names fur nished to it by the majority union of workmen or Association of non workmen, as the case may be, would not be a perfect representation in keeping with the principle of election; and 855 encourage the growth of a "management culture". Neither the election nor the nomination should be conducted in a manner unmindful of the distinctiveness of the banking industry. The object of the legislature is to render the largest good to the largest number of people of this "sovereign, socialist, secular democratic republic". Neither of the election or the nomination must be conducted by a method unmindful of its distinctiv alion of the commerce industry. There could be no justification for the Central Go vernment in making the Scheme in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India. The said scheme may also provide for any other mode as to enable the Central government to choose whether mode. It will be perfectly in view of these conflicting practices and the provisions of the Act, that the CentralGovernment should make the Scheme within its discretion.

The respondent was imposed penalties in the sum of Rs. 2,000/ under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act for concealment of certain particulars. The Tribunal refused to stay holding that it had no power to grant such a prayer. The High Court held that it was not competent to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner or the Appellate Tribunal to stay proceedings in the recovery proceedings pending before the Appellate authority. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Deputy Commissioner have made assessments or imposed penalties raising very large demands and if the Appellate Authority is entirely helpless in the matter of stay or recovery the entire purpose of the appeal can be defeated if ultimately ultimately the orders of the departmental authorities are set aside. [844 F] (2) The power conferred by section 254 on the Appellate Board with widest possible amplitude must carry with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal being successful from being rendered nugatory. [820 E] (3) The powers which have been conferred by Section 254 on an Appellate Tribunal with wide possible amplitude should carry with them by necessary implication all powers and duties incidental and necessary to make the exercise of those powers, fully effective. [ 844 F G] (4) The provisions of the Act or the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal Rules, 1963 are not intended to be exhaustive in their application to the recovery of penalty or tax due from an assessee. It is well known that when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction, it impliedly grants the power of doing all such acts, or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it, the duty has in proper case to make them orders for stay as will preventing the appeal if successful from becoming nugatory. The powers conferred by sections 254 on Income tax Officers have been expressly conferred upon the Appellate Tribunals with wide discretionary amplitude must be carried with them through necessary implication every power and duties ancillary and necessary for making the exercise. [828 G H] (5) The High Courts have under section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code and under article 227 of the Constitution, powers have not been expressly given to the appellate Tribunal to grant stay in the Recovery proceedings pending against an assessee but that can hardly be put at par with a statutory power as is contained in section 220(6) which is confined only to the stage of pendency of an appeal before the Incometax Officer or any of his superior departmental officers. [829 G H; 844 A] (6) The Appellate Tribunal has under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure and under Article 227 of its Constitution, power to stay the recovery in the case of the matters specified in the section. If the Income ' tax Officer or the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner have passed assessments or impose penalties raising a very large demand and if ultimately the order of the Appellate Asst.

The respondent was appointed a constable in U. P. Complaints were received by the District Magistrate, Gonda, to the effect that the respondent had received bribes in the discharge of his duties. On September 16, 1952, the Superintendent of Police made an endorsement to the Superintendent stating that the Sub Divisional Magistrate had found substantial complaints against the integrity of the respondent and that he had also received such complaints and that his general reputation for integrity was not good but that his transfer should, however, come after sometime and that in the meantime his work might be closely watched. On July 28, 1953, the District Superintendent of police sent an endorsement on the report and communicated the same to the respondent calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from the police force. The respondent submitted his explanation on November 29, 1952. After the expiry of his leave, he was reverted to his substantive post of head constable and transferred to Sitapur. On August 18, 1953 the Superintendent Of Police made a fresh endorsement in his character roll that the sub Divisional Magistrate was satisfied that there was no prima facie case against him for the offence under section 7 of the Police Act. The Superintendent of the police sent a notice to the appellant calling upon it to showcause why he could not be removed from the Police force. On receipt of the explanation, the respondent submitted an explanation on December 29, 1953. Thereafter the respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the inquiry held without following the procedure prescribed by rule I was not bad; (2) the information about the commission of the offences was not in the first instance received by him and forwarded to the police for inquiry; and (3) the specific acts with which the petitioner was charged were cognizable offences and, therefore, the order passed by the Superintendent was invalid. HELD: (1)(a) The High Courts had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order under appeal. [676 E] (b) The fact that in a case where a magisterial inquiry is ordered, inquiry will be made under the direction of the Superintendent in accordance with the following rules; and that if so, the inquiry will not be made Under the direction, of the Inspector General of Police recommending the transfer of the accused.

The appellant was appointed as Chief Ophthalmologist cum Associate Professor of Ophoshalmology, Himachal Pradesh Medical College, Simla. He was promoted to supertime grade II on May 1, 1970. The post of Chief Ohphthalmic Assistant Surgeon cum Associate professor of Ohoshalmic Assistant Professor of the Ophramal Hospital, Simla was converted into a specified post and that as he was not qualified for the same, he was appointed to super time grade II in February 1971. He challenged the promotion of respondents 4 to 24 on the ground that it was a teaching post and he lacked teaching experience which was an essential qualification, the offer of that post to him was merely an eye wash and he could not have accepted the same. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had failed to prove that he was eligible for promotion to super Time grade II because he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists ' grade officers formed on September 9, 1966. In appeal by Special Leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the post at Willingdon Hospital alone was converted to a specified cadre post and there was no justification for creation of posts or for making ad hoc appointments. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The expression 'category ' appears to be apt in that by the change service in a post is emphasised and the question of the grade of pay is relegated into background. [818C D] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant was not eligible for the post. He had put in eight years of experience in the post and had acquired teaching experience of which was not an essential qualifications. The change in the definition of 'categories ' appears that when a post from amongst unspecified Specialists ' posts is converted into an specified post, it means specified in the speciality in which a need has been felt from amongst those in the specialists' grade belonging to that speciality and in order of their inter se seniority a promotion could be given. [820B C] 1:3 The appellant was only 69 qualified to question their promotions. He did not reply by saying that he had put into 8 years ' service in that category. [821F G] 1 :4. In the absence of any material on record, it must be held that the post was created at Willtingdon hospital alone and there is no justification to create posts or make ad hoc appointment. [822G] 1.:5. The appellant had not even put in 7 years ' experience in that post. His promotion was in contravention of rule 8(3) of the Rules and, therefore, invalid. [823A B] 2:1. In view of the fact that the posts at Willeddon Medical College alone were converted into the specified cadre posts, there would be posts like Junior Surgeon, 55 Senior Surgeon, Head of the Department and so on. The question of promotion of Respondents 4 to24 on merits is relegated to background. It must be made clear that the Government had transferred Dr. Ramesh Prasad Singh to super up grade II to superje grade II. [825B] 2.2. In order to decide whether the Government acted honestly in creating a post or refusing to create a post, the Government transferred Dr., Ramesh Prasad singh to supercedtime grade I and that his promotion was subject to the condition that he should have been promoted and the posting of Dr.Ramesh Prasad Singh would be made. [828C D]. 2:3. The expression "category" appears to mean a group of posts specified in column 2 of the table under rule 4.

The petitioner, a small holder of land reformed under the Punjab Land Reforms Act, 1955, was allotted to him by the State Government in 1958. The petitioner challenged the validity of the gift made by him in favour of his sons whereby he sought to stow away some of his lands, shed some of their excess lands and look slim on as a small holders before the law language permiting, the Court as interpretedor, must fulfil, not frustrate the legislative mission. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the area which became surplus subsequent to April 15, 1953 was not hit by the ceiling set and land acquired by an heir by inheritance is saved from utilisation by the Government. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the gift in favour by his sons was invalid as it was made after the law was enacted; (ii) the State Legislature had no power to make a law with respect to the area covered by the Act and (iii) the legislature had not been astute enough to outwit such devious devices and subtle subterfuges. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1.1 The legislative mandate is that every agricultural holder in the State shall hold no more than the permissible area and the surplus in the hands of large holders, whether acquired by voluntary transactions or involuntary operation of law, will go to feed the surplus pool. But the legislature has to be astute sufficient to out wit such Devious devices, and subtle Subterfunges. A study of the history of the Act shows that the legislative mandate was that every Agricultural holder in a State shall holding no more except the permissible areas and the land acquired within the prescribed period. The scheme of the Punjab Act is fair ownership and the reform philosophy is redistributive justice the rural goal being small peasant proprietorship. [996 F G] 1.2 The legislature has, therefore, to be Astute enough so as to outweight such devastating devious device and subtle subsectionterfiges. The legislative intent is that no one held in excess of the permissible limit and since by the gift to the son or wife the latter had only lands within permissible limits, there was no frustration of the policy of the law. [1096 G] 2.1 In the instant case, the State has not been able to furnish the return and select his land within the specified period. Therefore, the legislature is bound by the principles of statutory construction. The legislature had to be very astutely enough to Outwit the devious methods and subtle substitutes. [1196 A] 2:2 The legislative intention is clear that the surplus area of every land owner recorded as such in the revenue records should be made utilisable for the settlement of ejected tenants ejected, or to be ejected under clause (i). But the Legislature has not chosen to adopt any other method than by way of a law. It has to take into account the fact that the land is less than the prescribed area and since no one holds in excess than the permitted area. The State Government or any officer em powered by it in this behalf shall be competent to utilize any surplus area for the resettlement of tenants ejected under clauses (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) and (v). [1097 B D] 2 :3 In the light of subsequent happenings, the legislative intent was that no person held in less than one land owner will deprive the former of his heritage if it is less then the permissible Area. The Legislature has to consider the question whether the surplus land is more than what is required by law and not whether the land has been acquired by a heir by descent is saved therefrom from utilisation.

The plaintiffs claimed the Zamindari on the death of Pratapshah. The defendants claimed that he was entitled to the Zamindari in respect of the Malguzari land and movable specified in the Schedules annexed to the plaint, and for an order declaring 326 their right to receive the balance of compensation remaining to be paid. The Trial Court held that the will dated December 3, 1950 set up by the plaintiffs was genuine while the will was dated December 8, 1950, set up as devisees under his will. In appeal by the defendants, the High Court agreed with the Trial Court and the High court held that on the circumstances no suspicion as to the genuineness of the will could arise. The appellants contended that the settlement deed dated December 4, 1950 was genuine and the plaintiffs claimed that they were entitled to succeed to the property if it was partible. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD : (1) The right to determine inheritance is a vested in the Governor but the power is exercisable in accordance with and not in violation of the custom of the family. [357 F] (2) The power is exercised in accordance With and not as in violation Of the custom or the rules of succession recorded in 336 the Wajib ul arz. [336 A B] (3) The Governor purported to pass any order in pursuance of the provisions of the Chanda Patent or the Rules of succession made under the proviso to section 35(7) of the Act. [457 C D] (4) The powers are exercisable in conformity with and cannot be exercised in violation or violation of any custom of family. It is not correct to say that the Governor purported in passing any order under the provisions Of the Chanda patent or the rule of succession prescribed by the proviso thereto. [333 A B].

The appellants landlord filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent tenant on the ground that the appellants were in arrears of rent for more than six months. The trial court gave a decree in favour of the respondent for possession. The Appellate Court confirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant landlord that the dispute regarding standard rent must be raised before service of the notice under section 12(2) (a) of the Act and not before the expiry of the period of one month after the service of notice under Section 12(1) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The provisions contained in sections 12 (3) (b) and (4) of section 11 are as follows: "Where at any stage of a suit or proceeding for recovery of rent whether with or without a claim for possession of the premises, the Court is satisfied that the tenant is withholding the rent on the grounds that the rent is excessive and standard rent should be fixed, the court shall pass a decree for eviction in any such suit for recovery. " [629 B] 2. The Bombay High Court was right in holding that the question as to when a dispute is to be raised came up for consideration in Shah Dhansukhlal Chhanganlal vs Dalichand Virchand Shroff & Ors. ; , relied on. 3. Section 12 (1) (c) of Bombay Act provides that where there is any dispute as to the amount of standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under this Act, the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if, before the expiration of the time prescribed by Explanation I to section 12 of the act, he makes an application to the Court under sub section (3), and thereafter pays or tenders the amount thereof as the Court considers to be reasonably due to the landlord. [630 C D] 4. Section 11(4) provides that if there is a dispute as regards standard rent, whether with respect to the rent payable by the month and there is no dispute regarding the amount or of standard Rent, it would be a dispute within the meaning of section 12 (2). The provisions in sub section(3) and section 11 have been made applicable. [643 D] 5. Section 13(4)(a) provides for an application under sub sections (1), (2) and 4 to the court under sub s.(2) of Section 11 and thereafter pay or tenders, the amount specified by the Court. The proviso to section 11(3)(a), therefore, does not apply. [67 E F] 6. Section 14(4), however, provides that in any other case if it appears to the Judge that it is just and proper to make such an order the court may make an order directing the tenant to deposit in Court forthwith such amount of the rent as the court considers reasonable due to him. The language of section 13(3), therefore does not indicate that the provisions in section 11 were attracted. [64 E F; 65 A] 7. Section 15(1)(a)(i) provides, inter alia, that where at any time a suit is for recovery or possession of premises whether with the or without rent for a period of six months or more and the tenant neglects to make payment thereof until the expiration Of the period prescribed by the proviso to sub section.(2), he makes such an application within the time contemplated by Explanation 1 to section 10. The words "if the rent or increases recoverable" in section 12 are not defined in the Act, it is clear that the legislature intended that the tenants should be deemed not to be willing and willing for payment if, after the expiry period of two months from the service, they make an application for ejectment.

The respondent company was a director controlled company. The shares were held by the respondent company in India and the shares were allotted to the respondent. In exercise of the power conferred by section 2 (21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, the Aluminium Ltd. appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the respondent Company. The two permanent directors had between them during the chargeable 191 accounting periods ending on December 31, 1941 and December 31. 1943, respectively and December31, 1942, and December 30, 1943, and January 31, 1943 respectively. In pursuance of the powers conferred by the said section, the aluminium Ltd. was appointed as a special or general proxy to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Limited. The respondent company, in exercise of its power under section 80 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, appointed three directors on board of the directors of it. In the course of the assessment proceedings for the years 1939 to 1943, the Income tax Officer held that the directors had a controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 3 (21), and that the Directors had no control over it. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the decision of the Income Tax Officer. On appeal by the assessee company the Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner and restored the order passed by the Excess profits Tax Officer, but in the circumstances of the case, the High Court held that since the directors were not members of this company, they could not be said to have a controlling interests in it. On reference by the Incometax Appellate Tribunal, the question was referred for decision to the High court. The High Court answered in the affirmative and against the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The directors of a company may well be regarded as having "a controlling interest" in the company when they hold and are entered in the share register as holders of the majority of shares which, under the articles of association of the company, carry the right to vote. [744 B] (2) The controlling interest remains vested in the Aluminium Company and is at no time vested in them, though as between them and their beneficiaries the beneficial interest is vested in it, although as between themselves and their beneficiary the beneficial interests are vested in that latter. [788 F H] (3) In order to have "a Controlling interest" the person or persons who hold the majority share has never passed to the agent. The controlling interests which the holder of the minority shares have never passes to the agents. Therefore, he cannot apply either of the tests mentioned above, namely having a beneficial interest in the shares so held by him. [789 F] (4) In the instant case, when the shareholders holding the majority shares authorises an agent to vote, for them, the controlling interest which the holders of these shares have not passed to them, although, as between they and their parties, the beneficial right is vested with them, but as between the two beneficiaries the controlling interests are vest in the latter. Therefore the shares being always subject to his will and ordering, the control which the shareholder has never passes cannot be said that he can apply either Of the tests specified above, if he were an individual member of this Company including the power to appoint a proxy whether special orgeneral.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant, Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Mysore. On 1st October, 1957, the Karnataka State Electricity Board was constituted under the Indian Electricity (Supply.) Act, 1948. The Board framed Recruitment and Promotion Regulations in exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Act. The Regulations were subsequently amended on 16th December, 1966. The respondent opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect from that date. On 21st November, 1972, the Mysore State Electricity board was constituted. On 2nd October, 1972 the Karnataka Electricity Board issued a Resolution No. 5/1/70 on the basis of seniority cum merit on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. Examination. The appellant opted to continue in the Government service or to opt to the Board. On 3rd January, 1973, the respondent opted for the Service. On 4th January, 1974, the Board framed Regulation No. 6/1(c). The Regulations prescribed that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion of I Division Clerks on the ground of senioritycum merit on the having passed the Part I or II of S. A.S Examination Part I. The regulations were subsequently revised on 16st December, 1967. The amended Rules prescribed that those posts of Account Superintendents were not to be treated as equivalent to the posts held by them in the former state of Mysore and that the Board had no power to relax the Regulations. The respondents made several representations one such representation being on 24th December 1970. On 11th January 1974, another representation was made on behalf of the appellant requesting for considering his case for promotion as an Accounts Superin tendent. On 12th January 1975, the appellant requested the respondent to continue him in the service under the Karnataka Board and to opt for the service. The Respondent did not pass any examination. On 13th February, 1973 the respondent made several representation one such being on 25th December 1971. On 14th February 1974, he was promoted as an accountant Grade II. On 16th January 1976, the Government issued a Notification No. 7/1 (c) exempting the Board from passing the S A.A.,S. examination Part I & II of Section 79(b) of The Act. In the meantime, the State Electricity Boards were constituted under section 78(c), which was later amended on 17th December 1976. On 15th February 1975, a Notification was issued by the Government exempting the respondent from passing S.S., Examination Part II and II. The said Notification provided that the post of Accounts Superintendent shall be filled in by promotion from the cadre of Accounts Assistants on the principle of seniority inter se merit on its having passed part I and III of the said S.L. examination. The Notification further stated that the respondent was exempted from passing any examination and therefore allowed the writ petition. On 17th February 1976, a Resolution was issued to the respondent by the Board whereby it declared that the appointment of Accounts Officers as Accounts Officers on the date of commencement of the Regulations would be deemed to have been made in accordance with the provisions of the Regulation. The Resolution further stated: "Approval is accorded for the adoption of the Govt. Order Nos. 7 and 8 dated 19th May, 1969 and 5th January 1970".

The petitioner, a police officer and Constable No.127, Chhabil Kujur of Police Outpost, was arrested by the Sub Inspector of Police on 1.12.1987 by Sarat Chandra Barik, Asstt. Sub Inspector, of Police, Bisra, in connection with an offence of theft and detained at the Police Out Post. The petitioner filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for compensation to Suman Behera 's mother, the petitioner for his death. The District Judge dismissed the petition holding that the factual foundation for such a liability of the State is absent. The State preferred an appeal before the High Court which allowed the petition and directed the District Judge to take into account the injuries sustained by the petitioner. In the meantime, the State filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the order of the District judge. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The claim being of damages for the tortuous act of the state is absent, and alien to the concept of guarantee of fundamental rights, there can be no question of such a defence being available in the constitutional remedy. [658C D] 2.1 In doing so the courts take into consideration not only the interest of the applicant but also the interests of the public as a whole with a view to ensure that public bodies or officials do not act unlawfully and do perform their public duties properly particularly where the fundamental rights of a citizen under Article 21 are concerned. [600E] 2:2 The High Court was right in holding that in a petition filed under Article 226 of the constitution, this Court can grant compensation for deprivation of a fundamental right. It is not always enough to relegate him to .the ordinary remedy of a civil suit to claim damages for tortuous acts of the Government as that remedy in private law indeed is available to the aggrieved party. [599E] 3:3 The jurisdiction to make such an order is conferred on the High Courts by para (a) of s.6(2), viz., jurisdiction 'to hear and determine any application made by any person in pursuance of sub section (1) of this section. The jurisdiction conferred on this Court is, therefore, conferred on it by para. [ 600A] 2 :4 In the instant case, there was no cogent independent evidence of any search made by the police to apprehend Suman Behra 's father, the respondent and the petitioner but also its crude attempt to fabricate false clues and create false evidence with a direction to screen its offence. The finding recorded is that Suman Bekhahera escaped from police custody at about 3 a.m. on 2.12..1987 and died in a train accident as a result of injuries sustained therein. It was further stated by the doctor that while all the injuries could not be caused in a railway track followed by the running engine/train, there were more chances of accidental fall on the railway track adopted by the run engine/Train. The opinion of Dr. The joint finding recorded was that Suman Sehera escaped and died during a train Accident as a consequence of injuries suffered therein. [ 601F G] 2:-5 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it is not possible to sustain the order passed by the District Court. [ 602E] 4:6 The High court was right therefore in holding the respondents liable to pay compensation payable to Suman Sehra 'Sherl Singh, the mother of the deceased who died as a sequel of beating and assault by the Police.

The petitioners who are under a sentence of death, were sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of their sentence to imprisonment for life. The petition was dismissed by the President on the ground that the prisoners were willing to be interviewed. The petitioners contended that the right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right of an interview under clause (4) of rule 549, which includes freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the Press to have an unrestricted access to means of information through the medium of an Interview of the two prisoners who are sentenced to life. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The right claimed in the instant case is not a right to form any particular opinion or opinion and that does not mean that they can always and without good reasons be denied the opportunity to interview a condemned prisoner. [1187F] 2. The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press, such for example, as there is under section 161(2) of Criminal Procedure Code. No data has been made available to us on the basis of which it would be possible for us to say that the two detenus are willing to interview them. [1087G] 3. The presence of a freedom press does not indicate or spellout any legal obligations on the citizen to supply the information to him. It does not confer any rights on the people to supply such for instance, as it does not invade the rights of other citizens and which does not violate the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, public order decency and morality. [987H; 1088A] 4. The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview the prisoners right since the President had rejected the petitions for commutation. There is a provision in the rules that if a person who desires to interview an prisoner is a female, she can be searched only by a matron or a female warden. [ 1088B] 5. The fact that the petitioner has not been asked for permission does not make any difference because, for example rule 552A provides for a search of the person who wants to interview such prisoner. If in any given case there are weighty reasons for doing so, which we expect will always be recorded in writing, the interview may appropriately be refused. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore we do not see any reason why newspapermen who can broadly, and we suppose without great fear of contradiction, be termed as friends of the society be denied this opportunity to interviews a condemned person.

The appellant, a Receiver of the estate, filed an application for damages from the Receiver. The respondent moved an application asking for damages against the Receiver on the ground that the fire had occurred due to his negligence. On the District Judge transferred the mortgage suit to the court of the Subordinate Judge, Agartala. The appellant filed an appeal against that order but it was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner on June 29, 1970. The High Court allowed the respondent 's cross objections and enhanced the damages to Rs. 4,525. The Judicial Commissioner held that the bond could be enforced only by or at the instance of the District judge, Agar Tripura, and not by his successors in office of assigns and the Subordinate judge, Tripura not being either of these, it was incompetent for him to enforce the bond. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The surety bond is a part of the proceedings pending before the District Court and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the Court of the subordinate Judge. [360G H] (2) The bond is executed both in the court as well as in the execution of decrees. It is not necessary that the surety bond should be enforceable at the behest of the district judge because "successor" in office would mean successor of the State in the post or office of theDistrict Judge. Therefore, the order for recovery of damages obtained by the respondent against the appellant against the receiver can be executed against the appellants to the extent to which it rendered itself personally liable under the terms of the bond and it is therefore incompetent for the District court to enforce that bond. [361C D] (3) The condition precedent for the execution is that the person who has become liable as a surety for the fulfilment of any condition imposed on any person under an order of the Court in any suit or proceeding J consequent thereon, the decree or order may be executed by the District Magistrate, Agar, or his successors, successors inoffice and assigns.

The appellants are dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat. The State Government issued a notification under section 4 of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, levying tax on the sales made to them by the appellants. The appellants contended that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller and it had no option but to purchase fifty per cent of the wheat held in stock by them at the commencement of the Levy Order. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the contention raised by the appellant holding that the rice supplied was "supplies". The Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales Tax, rejected the contentions raised by them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the State Government had no power under section 3 of the Act to levy tax only on transactions which were "sales" within the meaning of the Indian : State of Madras vs Gannon Dunkerley and Co. It was also submitted that the Sales Tax officer had no jurisdiction to determine whether the stocks of wheat supplied by the petitioners in compliance with the provisions of the Uttar Pradesh (Control of Trade) Act, 1947, were not sold or not. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "sale of goods" in the Constitution must be understood in the same sense in which it is (1) (1969) All L.J. 2 S.C.R. C. 1/70 14 674 used in the . It is necessary then to determine if the stocks are not sold, and since cl. 10 provides for the mode of payment of price, the time and mode of delivery of wheat, and other conditions of the contract. [767 H] 2. The source of the obligations to deliver the specified quantities of rice pursuant to cl. 4 is not in any contract but in the statutory order. It contains a bald injunction to supply wheat pursuant to Cl. 10, the Order enjoins the licensed dealer to deliver wheat pursuant thereto, insofar as it is material it provides "(1) Any Enforcement Officer may with a view to securing compliance with this Order or to satisfying himself that this order has been complied with; and it does not envisage any consensual arrangement. [676 B C] 3. The words "sale" in cl. 5 of the Schedule to the Constitution are wide enough to include transactions which are "s sales". They are used in a wide sense, and they cannot be construed as including transactions which have been "s Sales Tax Officers". [768 F G] 4. The word "purchase" in section 2(d) of the , means any transfer of property in goods by way of sale or otherwise to a person who has purchased it from another. It is not necessary that the words used in cl.(5) should be understood as meaning a transfer of title in goods. [677 G H] 5. The definition of "sale " in section 3(d)(i) of U. P. Sales tax Act, 1950, includes transactions which took place in the course of business and is not confined to transactions which take place in connection with the business of sale. It does not contemplate a consensual arrangement but it provides for a consensual agreement. [67 H; 678 A B] 6. The High Court was right in holding that since purchases made by them were not under agreements, the price paid for sugarcane could not be taxed under a statute enacted in exercise of the power in Entry 54 List II of the Seventh Schedule to Constitution.

The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was acquitted on May 26, 1986. The order of detention dated June 23, 1986 was revoked and a fresh order of detu sion was made on the same facts on the said date. The detenu challenged the second order of his detention before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no Advisory Board in existence to which a reference could be made under section 11 of the Act and whose report of its opinion regarding suffi cient cause for the detention was required to be obtained within three months of the detention under article 22(4) of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the order of revocation of the earlier detention dated August 7, 1986 had become infructuous and another writ petition challenging the second detention order was not maintainable.
