In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the detaining authority did not apply his mind to the question as to whether there was sufficient cause for detention of the person concerned; (2) the report of such an Advisory Board had to be obtain ed before the expiry of three months from the date of detention and therefore, the detention should be upheld. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Court was not confronted with the present situation at all. [796B] 2. The observation of the court to the extent that there were no sufficient cause is not a sufficient answer to say that the procedural requirements of the constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date on which its report could be obtained as required by the Constitution, but it is no answer to saying that the procedure of the Advisory Board was not followed before the commencement of the hearing. [765D] 3. The observations of the Court to the effect that an order of preventive detention should have been made, knowing full well that there had been no Advisory board in existence were complied with after the date when the detention order dated June 22, 1986 were revoked and fresh orders of detention were passed on the basis of such report cannot be sustained. [769E] 4. The decision of this Court in Shibapada Mukher jee vs State of West Bengal, , relied upon by the learned counsel for the appellant is not applicable to the facts of the present case. [771G] 5. The fact that there has been no report of the Board within three weeks of the date fixed for hearing of the case does not mean that the reference, though not made within three days, was made before the hearing of a case. It is only when the report could have been obtained as contemplated by section 15 of the National Security Act that the report had to contain the opinion of the advisory Board which has to be submitted within three week from the day of detention. [773G] 6. The law relating to preventive detention in the instant case, does not require that a reference should have be made within 3 weeks, it is not necessary for the Court or the Advisory board to specify its opinion as to what the reference is to be made. If a reference to an Advisory board is to contain a clear statement of the facts on which the order has been passed, it would be open to the Court and the Advisory Boards to give their opinion thereon. [777A] 7. The Constitution does not contemplate that a referee should have a fresh report of his opinion regarding the sufficiency of cause for his detention. If the reference to any Advisory Board is to make within three month, it was no answer at all to say whether the reference though not making within three calendar months, was given before the pronouncement of the judgment. [779D] 8.

The respondent, a father of the respondent, was awarded a contract for carrying on business in the name and style of Vaidyas. The petitioner 's father had intervened between them with good intention to bring their disputes to an end. The respondent filed his objections to the application but did not file any application within the prescribed limitation of 30 days. The trial Judge rejected the objections filed beyond the period of limitation and for the reasons that (1) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the award, (2) the time for making an application to set aside the award had expired and no such application was made (3) the award was not remitted under section 16(5) of the Act. The High Court found that the petitioner and the respondent had referred their disputes with one Kantibhai Vaidya who had intervened in between them, with good intent to bring his dispute to an effect amicably; and (4) the entire responsibility of solving the dispute was entrusted to him and the petitioner had taken the responsibility. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was right in dismissing the application in the manner it did. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The award was signed by both the parties as well as their respective advocates. It was signed at twice, firstly by signing an endorsement below the award and secondly by entering into an agreement in the form of a letter dated 14th August, 1978 (Exhibit 40). In that view of the matter, it could certainly be construed to be a proper arbitration agreement in terms of section 2(a) of The Act. 1988 S.C. 205 where all the relevant authorities on this point have been discussed. [501B] 2.1 The High court was right, in doing so. It is not necessary that the Court should decide the case; and even if it decided wrongly, they did not exercise their jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity. Section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code provides that the Courts shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred. [601C] 2:2. The Court has no power to decide the matter; and in the instant case, the High court had rightly dismissed the application. [643E F] 3:3 In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, it cannot be said that the previous proceedings were without jurisdiction. [401F] 4.1 In the instant cases, the petitioner is not entitled to challenge the award. The question whether the earlier proceedings were with respect to which there was no factual dispute, reiterated the fact that the parties had agreed to refer the disputes to arbitration has been decided against him, and even though they decided wrongly they did so, they chose not to exercise their powers illegally or without material irregularity, and that the award is not remitted within 30 days of the date on which the application was filed. [525G] 4:4 In the present case, there was a written agreement signed by all the parties about the passing of the Award and secondly, by entering an agreement with the petitioner in the Form of a Letter dated 14 th August,1978 (Exhibit 43). The said letter of 14th September, 1978 was replied in the forms of a letters dated 4th September 1978 addressed to the respondent by the arbitrator, that is Exhibit 137. In that light of this evidence, it can certainly be safely construed to mean that on this aspect the petitioner was not entitled for challenge the Award. [500A B] 5:5. The letter of 15th August 1978 was also replied in a form of an endorsement dated 14st August, 1979 (Exhibit 39).

The appellants were the sub mortgagee of certain properties. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the Searsole Raj Estate in which he claimed that the properties belonged to him and his two sons, namely, the appellant and the respondent. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the decree put into execution was adjusted after remission of a large amount of interest by the out sale of certain property by a registered Kobala dated 4th January 1939. The High Court held that the order of January 30, 1937, was in form and substance a final order of dismissal of the execution case and as such it could not be taken to have any wider operation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the decree was not a final decree for the balance remained unsatisfied on January 1, 1939; (ii) the execution proceedings were pending after January 1 1939; and (iii) the order dated June 2, 1939, did not amount to an order of discharge of the mortgage debt. HELD : (1) The order of December 30, 1938, was a final one and could not have been taken to be a dismissal of a suit in execution. [118 E F] (2) The decree was a preliminary one and it was not open to the Court to interfere with it on the ground that it did not contain an assignment of that debt or of all the rights of the parties. [119 G H] (3) The execution proceedings, in the circumstances, need no execution proceeding to support it.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The appellant was his concubine since 1945 until his death on February 22, 1949. By two registered deeds purporting to be sale deeds, the appellant transferred certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1947 he transferred to the appellant certain properties which belonged to the Joint Family. He also executed a severance of the joint status between Venkatacharyulu and his sons. In 1954 his widow and sons instituted O.S. No. 62 of 1954 against one of his sons and another person asking for damages and mesne profits for wrongful trespass on the properties. The trial court dis missed O. S. No, 63/54 and decreed O. P. No., 62 of 1953. From these decrees appeals were preferred in the High Court of Andhra Pradesh. The High Court confirmed the decree in O.P. No,. 62/54, and decreed the two other appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transfers under exhibit A 1 and exhibit A 2 were not supported by any consideration by way of cash or delivery of jewels. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The transfers were made in pursuance of a conspiracy between Venkatagharyulu, his wife and sons. It was not necessary to prove that the transactions were made with the intention of compensate the concubines for her past services. [45H] (2) The gifts were not hit by sec. 6(h). [46B] Balo vs Parbati, ; , referred to. (3) The alienations were without consideration and were invalid. Properly speaking, the past cohabitation was the motive and not the consideration for the transfers. [47C D] (4) The transactions were in reality gift deeds. Under section 6(g), the gifts were made by way Of gifts and not in consideration of past cohabitations. In lieu of her services, she promised to give his services only and not his properties. She did not make any such gift. A 1 was and is not competent to alienate for value his undivided interest in the coparcenary properties to his concordine. [48D] Balosati vs Parbatati, (1923) All.

The appellant, a widow of the deceased employee, was served with a notice under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on the ground that she took steps to get the notice vacated in order to safeguard her interest in the policies. The ITO did not revoke the order of attachment in spite of the LIC making the requisite state ment on oath under section 227(3)(vi). The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notice and also the consequential civil appeal in this Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not liable to pay any interest for the period during which it was restrained from making the payment on account of the I.T.O. Rao, learned counsel for the appellant advanced several arguments. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A perusal of section 226 (3) shows that the benefit claimed by the L.I.C. is not available to it in the facts of the present case. [113F] 2.2 The High court was right in holding that there was no suppression of any fact or misapplication of law. [114G] 3.1 In the first place, such a statement was in fact made without hesitation by the 113 L. I.C., on 5.12.75 after the assignee was compelled to obtain such a direction in a writ Petition filed by her. The appellant 's own stand which in fact was so made on 5 12.75 did not involve even remotely the possibility of any risk of personal liability. It is obvious that the inordinate delay in making the statement on oath by the appellant on oath was the result of misconstruction of the provision and misappreciation of its liability thereunder. [115G] 4.2 In the second place, it was so done on 5th December, 1975 after the assignment was made. The very fact that such a declaration was in reality made without belief by the Income tax Officer under section 132(3), did not make any difference to the position of law and the appellant could not be said to have been prejudiced by the non compliance with the provisions of section 132 (3)(vii). [114A B] 4:4 In the instant case, the appellant had made a declaration in her letter dated 28.8.72 that she would take steps to obtain the notice vacating in order that she will get the benefit of the policies on account Of the I.'T.o. Rao. The Income tax officer did not cancel the said declaration and the consequent civil appeal filed by the respondent was dismissed as withdrawn. [116C] 5:5 In the third place, the High court had assumed that the money payable on maturity of these policies belonged to the in sured/assessee/defaulter G.V. Ranade. The inordinate delay was the results of misconstruction and mis appreciation of its Liability under section 281 of the Act.

The respondent filed a suit for recovery of possession of certain properties in the District of Burdwan. The appellant contended that section 29(2)(a) applies to an appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure and that the expression "appeal under the Indian Limitation Act" in article 156 of the Limitation Act means an appeal governed by the Code Of Civil Procedure. Held, that the word "appeal" in section 29 (2) of the Indian . is not confined merely to a suit or proceeding in the civil court but also to a decree or order made by a Court under the , Code of Criminal Procedure. The expression "appellate under the Act" means an order made under section 98 or section 99 to the High Court in which the Tribunal is situated. It may combine two sentences dealing with the same subject without one depending upon the other. R. [1956] 2 All. C. R., and Daropadi vs Hira Lal, (1923) L.R. 51 I.A. 67, referred to. The word "appeal" in the section is not restricted merely to an order passed by a civil court under section 99 or section 100 of the Code. It does not mean an appeal filed under the . Civil Procedure Code but also includes an appeal preferred under the provisions of the ,Code of Civil procedure. The words "appeal " in section 30(2) are wide enough to include an appeal against an order of a civil Court under section 96 or section 97 of the Act. It is not intended that article 156 would furnish the period of limitation for such appeals but the special law by limiting it provides for a different period. The fact that the words "appeals" in sub section (1) of section 29 are wide and comprehensive enough to cover all cases where an appeal lies under the Civil Procedure code, is not decisive of the question whether the expression 'appeal under this Act means a suit, appeal or application by any special or local law. The distinction between the period prescribed for an appeal and the time prescribed for it can be said that under the First Schedule of the . Limitation Act an appeal can lie only at any time but the general law by restricting it provides a different time limit to it. In other words, the expression is equated with an appeal ' which has been filed under section 116 A(2). The word 'appeal ' in section29(2), therefore, means an application made under the, Code of civil Procedure and not an appeal " within the meaning of article 156 Of the Limitation.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, was carrying on business in the State of Uttar Pradesh. He challenged the validity of the Order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate declaring Plot Nos. 501 of 1986 filed before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magis trate to fix the places for the bus stand/halting place '. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the District magistrate fixed the area as a bus stand and hence the order made under section 76 was unassailable. It was further submitted that the High court was in error in holding that the Town Area Committee had been authorised by the State Government under section 78 of the U.P. Municipalities Act, 1961 to pass an order fixing the Municipal Bus Stand as a Bus stand for purposes of the said chapter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The District Magistrate fixed the Municipal bus stand as a stage carriage stand and the Dis trict Magistrate could not be equated with the Regional Trans port Authority constituted under the Act. [723B] 2.1 In view of the decision in T.P., at page 297 of the Re ports this Court has observed that the town area Committee had made bye laws under the provisions of section 358(7)(f) and (m) read with section 349(ii) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act 1961. [783D] 2:2 The District Magistrate had been authorized by the Regional Transport Author ity to exercise the powers under section76 of the act which is confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the Transport Authorit y. [784E] 2 :3. The Town Area Committees had been empowered by the Government under Section 76 of U. P. Municipalities (Amendment) Act, 1976 to pass a resolution fixing the limits of the area and not in the district Magistrate 's jurisdiction. The Municipal Council of Bhopal had made Bye laws under section 358 (7)(a) and Section 349(i) of that Act which empowered the District Magistrates to fix any area as bus stand for the purpose of the aforesaid chapter. [789F] 2 4.1 The High court erred in holding, that the order passed by it under section 75 was not valid because it was passed by a Regional Transport Authority constituted unders ection 76 of that act and hence no order had been passed by any Regional Transport authority, Mathura to determine the area in question as a vehicle stand which can alone be notified under the said Chapter. [823F] 3:2. The expression 'duly notified ' is not defined in the Act but it is reasonable to presume that a duly notified stand must be one which is notified by a Transport Authori ty and by none other. [825C] 3 :3 In the instant case, no order has been passed under section 77 of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities ( Amendment) Act 1976 to determine whether or not the said area is a bus Stand or a bus stands for purposes o f the Act and it is not disputed that in the instant cases no order was passed on by the competent authority to determine parking places. [829G] 4:4. The appellant had obtained an order of stay restraining the Town Areas Committee from collecting the fees. Immediately after the Writ Petition was dismissed, the Executive Officer of the Town area Committee, Baldev to the President of the Union requiring the bus operators to stop their buses at the bus Stand and to start from there and to permit the passengers to get out of their buses.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 3(1) of the . The trial court convicted all the accused persons but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction and sentence. In revision, the High Court dismissed the revision petition. Held: (i) There was no export of paddy within the meaning of Para 2(a) of Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence. It follows therefore that the appellants should not have been convicted under section 7 of the , and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt. Nor can he be convicted of this offence if he approaches the stack with matches in his pocket, but, if he bends down near the stacks and lights a match which he extinguishes on perceiving that he is being watched, he may be guilty of an attempt to burn it. The point at which such a series of acts begins cannot be defined, but depends upon the circumstances of each particular case. Section 8 of the states that "any person who attempts to contravene or abets a contravention of any order made under section 4 shall be deemed to have contravened that order". It follows accordingly that the appellant should not be convicted under s 7 of . P.N.U. and the two appellants should also not have committed an attempt which constitutes an offence if they approach the studdack with the matches in their pocket, and secondly, to have carried an act on which constitutes that actus disgraced.

The assessee company was incorporated in the year 1943. Under clause 6 of the Sassooris, their successors and assigns were to be at liberty to retain, reimburse and pay themselves out of the moneys of the Company inter alia all sums due to them for commission and otherwise. The managing agents were to remain at liberty during the period of the year during which they might have served the company in their capacity as Managing Agents, and thereafter until they resigned or were removed from their office by a special resolution of the company and the appointment of the firm of E. D. Sassoon United Mills Ltd., was one entity and no severance of I such periods of service during the course of a particular year was ever contemplated under the Agreement. The assessee company claimed that the remuneration for the broken period was paid to Chidambaram Mulraj and Company Ltd., who became the Managing Agents in place and stead of the Sasssoons in the years 1944, and that it was remuneration for work done and completely done in the particular year though it was ascertained and paid to them at the end of every calendar year. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim holding that the income, profits or gains accrued to the assessee and in order that the same may accrue to him it was necessary that he must have acquired a right to receive the same or that a right had become vested in him though its valuation might be postponed or though its materialisation. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the orders of the Income tax officer. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that the commission paid was remuneration and not remuneration for services wholly performed in the specific year and that the receipt of the commission therefor as remuneration did not amount to a receipt of income. In reference to the High Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the managing agents had been referred to as service and the commission thereof as remuneration could not be said to have accrued to them when their capacity was changed by the transfer of the shares in question. Held, that the Managing Agency Agreement between the Sassoons and the S Asssoons which were relevant only in the appeal relating to the Agarwals, did not create a right in favour of the assessee company to receive any part of the income for the year. It was a case of property whose ownership itself, in the ordinary course and by lapse of time, gives rise to income and is analogous to head No. Income of the kind with which we are concerned in this case does not arise by virtue of any mere ownership of an asset. The remuneration was for the purpose of convenience, that it could be said that the assessee had at the date of the transfer a right or a right of property in the goods and that he had acquired a vested right to the income from the business. The receipt of commission therefor was not a payment of income but a consideration for services rendered by the Managing Agent.

The appellant was a resident of Pachperwa in the District of Gonda. He had two sons, Badri and Kirpa Shanker. The deceased was residing with his father. On August 12, 1963, at about 6 p.m., he was found with serious injuries in the room of their house where she was sleeping and the appellant was not in the house. On the morning of August 13, 1963 when he was alive, he came out of the house and saw the accused going out of his house. The appellant brought her buck, and after some wordy altercation between them they slept in the only room of his residence. On hearing the cries of the deceased, the appellant brought his buck and after sometime went back to the house of the appellant. The prosecution case was that on August 12. 1963, when he had gone out of their houses, he woke up and saw that the appellant had murdered Sunderpatti. The trial court convicted the accused under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to death. On appeal by the State, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the accused that the evidence in the case was circumstantial and that the circumstances established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the respondent and the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency and that they should be such as to exclude other hypotheses but the one proposed to be proved. HELD: (1) The statement made by an accused admitting his guilt can certainly be offered only by witnesses who heard the admission or confession, as the case may be. [446 D] (2) The evidence in a case of oral admission or confessions cannot be used as corroboration of any other evidence except that of circumstantial evidence. It is implicit in the concept of confession, whether it is extra judicial or judicial, that it shall be communicated to another. Admissions and confessions are exceptions to the hearsay rule. [449 E] (3) The Evidence Act places them in the category of relevant evidence, presumably on the ground that, as they are declarations against the interest of the person making them, they are probably true.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi. The general insurance business was nationalised and its management was taken over by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972. The appellant was kept under suspension pending investigation into the embezzlement, Explanation was called for on October 16, 1973. In response thereto, the appellant submitted his reply on december 7, 1974. While dropping the 223 proceeding, the respondent was served with termination order dated April 17,1975 issued by the respondent. Section 7 of the Act provides that every whole time officer or other employee of an existing insurer employed in connection with his General Insurance business immediately before the appointed day shall become an officer/employee of the Indian Insurance Co. Ltd., Merger Scheme, 1973 and vested in the custodian of the New India Assurance Co.Ltd., the management of Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Ltd. The management of the appellant society was taken under General insurance (Energency Provisions), Ordinance,1971 replaced by the Act 57 Of 1972. By operation of s.7 of the said Act, the services of the employee stood transferred and vested with the custodian. The Central Govt. framed the New Insurance Scheme, 1976 with effect from December 31, 1973 with effectfrom December 31. 1973. The employees were kept under suspended pending investigation in the embezzlement. The charges were dropped. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated May 17, 1975 issued by it and for quashing the same on the ground that the service of the respondent had been terminated in terms of the existing rule 5 of the Rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondent 's services stood transferred to the custodian and could hold his office on the same terms and conditions as would have been admissible to him if there had been no such vesting and shall continue to do so unless and until his appointment is terminated. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The rule is valid. But Rule 8 is available for taking action for misconduct but was not availed. [223D] 2.1 In the event of the Society not having any further need of the employees ' service, whether permanent or temporary which shall be decided by the Board, the Principal Officer shall give 30 days ' notice in writing for termination of his services or in lieu thereof pay such employee a sum equivalent to his one month's salary including allowances upto the period of termination. [224F] 2:2 The rule does not provide that the services are terminated on giving one month 's notice in terms thereof. It is settled law that there is a presumption of constitutionality of the rule. If the provisions of law or the rule are construed in such a way as would make it consistent with the constitution and another interpretation would render the provision or the Rule unconstitutional, the court would lean in favour of the former construction. [225H; 226A] 2 :3 The words "in the event" occurring in Rule 5 of Rules of Delhi Transport Corporation Service Regulation gives naked power to terminate the services by giving one months ' notice or pay in lieu of notice. It does not mean that the rule is void. If so read, the rule would be invalid. But if so read it would make the provision and the rule unconstitutional, it would lean In favour of former construction.[226B] 2 4.1 Rule 8 was available for take action for offence etc. but was never availed. It was not avail. The compensation awarded would be staggered between the year 1973 till date for the purpose of income tax and given the appropriate relief. [227C D] 2 5.2 In the instant case, though action was initiated against the appellant for the charges of embezzlement etc., which were misconduct, the charges were dropping.

The appellants, who were the unsuccessful bidders, felt aggrieved and filed an appeal before the Excise Commissioner against the notice issued by the Collector for reauction on May 1, 1970. The Collector issued a notice for re auction on May 2, 1970 and Ajodhya Prasad amended his petition for quashing the notice also. The appellant challenged the validity of the notice on the ground that it was ultra vires the Act as the State Government had not been specified, the Government had "appropriated for itself absolute and naked power" to accept any tender or reject any tender for any reason whatsoever or without rhyme or reason; and that the Collector committed an illegality in ordering a reauction under the directions of the State Govt. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions and that of the appellant before it, was also dismissed. In appeal by special leave, the appellants contended: (1) that the amendment to the Act was ultra virus the Constitution; (2) that section 29(2)(b) did not authorise the exercise of "such absolute and unfettered power" in determining the sum of money as was sought to be done by the order dated August 19, 1970; (3) that since the Collector had committed an error in ordering reauction, it could not be said that the State had no right to collect a tax under the garb of a fee "under the garb Of a fee" and the "auction price for a license is not duty within the meaning of Entry 51 of List 11 of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. HELD: (i) The High Courts were wrong in taking a contrary view. [785C] (ii) The collection was in the nature of a tax and section 29 was therefore ultra vires. [769D] (iii) The expression "or otherwise" used in Entry 51 is wide enough to include all kinds of taxes which are levied by the State or any local authority, but which are not levied by it. [771E] (iv) The levy of a duty under section 29 is not a fee or tax. It is only a mode or medium for ascertaining the best price obtainable therefor. [773G] (v) The amount realised by the auction is illegal. No. 1185 1190, 1223, 1224 and 1226 of 1970. Nos. A writ petition (O.J.Cs. No, 1185 of 1970) was dismissed.

The prosecution case was that on the day of occurrence, accused No. 2 was at the time of the judgment of High Court of 17 years of age. Accused No. 3 was at his house regularly and he had gone to his native place leaving his grandson Narendra 's wife on 4 January, 1968. He was a registered medical practitioner. The head office was at Bombay. The owner of bungalow No. Narsanna was a person of unsound mind and accused No, 17. There were civil and criminal proceedings out of that transaction. Accused Nos. 2 and 3 were charged under sections 201, 454, 380 and 411 of the Indian Penal Code. Dalichand Nanavati, the grand father of deceased Naren drakumar who met unnatural and unfortunate end at the hands of accused No., 17. The prosecution case is as follows: Accused No, 3 was a resident of Bombay. He had been residing in the house of his grand father with his wife on the date of occurrence. Accused 1 Hiralal Jamnadas Joshi, accused 2 was also at the relevant time staying in the bungalow. Accused 2 and 4 were also staying in that bungalow. The deceased Narendra was seen alive by Kewal Ram, owner of the betel shop on 26th December, 1967. Accused 3 told accused No,. 2 that he would take them out from the house and then go to his village regularly. On 25th January,1968 accused No 1 gave a sum to the tailor. The police came to the conclusion that there was corroboration in regard to the crime. The High Court found that there is corroboration of the evidence which connected accused No; 3 with murder. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution case as against accused No 2 was not supported by any independent witness and that the only evidence against him was that he had given Rs. 3 to the deceased. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The conviction of accused Nos. 1 and 2 is set aside. Accused no. 3 is acquitted of all the charges. He is convicted under section 302 read with section 120B as well as under section 201 I.P.C. [638F G] 2. The name of accused no. 2 in the charge sheet was that those articles were given by accused No 17 to a person called Takalkar. The evidence of the tailors was that that those items were given to a, person called cheaper and that those article were given on 16 January, 1967 and that they were handed over to him. At this stage it is to be noticed as to whether there was sufficient corroboration in material particulars to connect accused with the time. [643G H] 3. The identification of accused 2 by the prosecution witnesses was not challenged by the appellant. It was for the first time during the trial that the identification parade was held and the identification of the accused by the police was not questioned by the accused. The identity of the person who gave the articles to a witness was not disputed by the defence. The fact that the clothes were given in the custody of the police, did not make any difference as regards the time at which they were recovered. [539G H; 540A B] 4. The presence of accused 1 and 3 at the place of occurrence was not established by the evidence on record. It is also not proved that the deceased had been seen alive with the accused No in the company of the deceased or that he used to wash the clothes of accused NO. 2 sold a cycle carrier to Rupvate on 16th January 1968. The recovery of the dead body from the place where it was recovered was not proved by the medical evidence. [525A B, D] 5.

The appellant, a Town Planning Officer, was awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. Not satisfied with the decision of the Town Planning officer determining the amount of compensation payable to him, preferred an appeal before the Board of Appeal. The Board of Revenue dismissed the appeal and confirmed the order of the town planning authority. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the scheme was not a scheme within the meaning of Art 31 (2) of the Constitution and that the Town planning Officer had no power to determine compensation payable under section 32(1). HELD: The expression "person interested" as defined in section 3 of the Land Acquisition Act means all persons claiming an interest in compensation to be made on account of the acquisition of land under that Act. [92D] State of Karnataka vs Shri Ranganatha Reddy, ; , followed. (i) The expression 'person interested ' as defined by section 3(2) means all person claiming an interests in compensation for the land taken on account or acquired by the local authority under that act. It is a principle applicable to all cases in which by virtue of the operation of the Act a person is deprived of his land whether in whole or in part. [93E] (ii)The expression "Person interested" in section 2(9) means persons claiming interest in the compensation to which the owner was entitled to compensation under that section. The expression `person interested' as defined under section 3 includes all persons who claim an interest therein. It does not mean any person who is entitled to a compensation for such injurious affection. [94D] (iii)The word 'person ' as used in section 32 of the Bombay Town Planning Act means every person claiming interest therein, and all persons are claiming an Interest in compensation. The property or right affected remains with the owner who is not provided with a plot in the final scheme gets his right to compensation from section 71 of the act which says that the net amount of loss shall be payable to the owner if he has been deprived by the 92 scheme estimated on the date of declaration of the intention to make a scheme amounted to specification of a principle of compensation within the ambit of Art, 31 (1).

The testator made a will on October 4, 1927. He left the management of his properties to his brother and provided that as soon as his minor daughters attained majority Seetharama should give to them per head one veli of nanja land and one vela of punja land in vattam No. 978/8. The testator had made bequests to his sons, grandsons and great grandsons for the benefit of their daughters. He also executed a will by which he devised one kani of paddy and Rs. 1,000 each of nba land in favour of the appellant. The appellant did not accept this right of selection and contended that the daughters were entitled to their lands taking into account lands of good and bad quality. Held, that the testator intended his daughters to select. the object of his bounty meant for the legatee and once the selection is made by the legatee the will takes effect. In the present case there was no evidence to show that the legatees had a right to make a selection in a case of this kind. The bequest was not void for uncertainty and that the heir would be entitled to six acres on partition but was not entitled to selection. The fact that there were ways of partition available to parties in England also did not affect the application of the rule, for it was only one instance that the legatee intended his daughter to select a third person who may select the object Of his bounty intended for the legateee. In such cases where the uncertainty is of a less degree and the intention of the testator to gift certain property is clear, though there may be some difficulty because there might be some difficulties because there was more property of that kind than actually bequeathed, that (1) (1860) 5 N.C.R. 325. (2) (1920) 6 Ch. D. 426, followed.

The appellant was the widow of Syed Laek Husain and defendants No. 2 to 8. The plaintiff 's case was that she was living with her sons at Lucknow and her husband 's cousins were looking after the lands which consisted of agricultural land and groves and she was given her share by her cousins from time to time. In her statement before the trial court, she has clearly stated that the defendants had committed fraud on the consolidation authorities. The appellant 's name was wrongly deleted after 1359 Fasli and there was no order of any authority or Court to show the circumstances under which the plaintiff 'S name was suddenly deleted nor were there any judicial proceedings under which her name was changed nor were they there any Judicial proceedings under that Act. The trial court accepted the allegations of the defendants and dismissed the suit. The High Court, however, reversed the decision of the District Judge and held that the appellant had no concern with them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the plaintiff was not entitled to any share in the land or plots in dispute and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern therewith. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit was contested by the respondents mainly on the ground that the defendant 's names were wrongly deleted from the revenue records and full advantage was taken of the consolidation operations in the village by the defendants. [868G] 2. The plea of the bar of the civil courts ' jurisdiction to investigate and adjudicate upon the title to the land and sonship of the plaintiff has no substance. It is well settled that unless there is an express provision barring a suit on the basis of title, the courts will not readily infer a bar of suit to establish the title of the parties. [889B] 3. The result is that the plea of bar of civil courts jurisdiction to enquire and adjudicate on the title in the property or sonshipof the plaintiff have no substance.[868C] 4. In these circumstances, therefore, the finding of the High Court regarding fraud having been committed in the consolidation proceedings was not legally sound. [879D] 5. The judgment of the trial Court cannot be allowed to stand. [869E] 6. The view taken by the District judge and the High court that the suit was barred by limitation is not correct. It was never the case of the respondent that any fraud was committed on the Consolidation authorities. In this connection, the learned District Judge found as follows: "The appellant 'S names were suddenly deleted after completing 1359 Fasli, and there is no evidence to prove that the respondent was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950. The respondents did obtain the plots through litigation, even then it cannot be said that the respondents did obtained the plots exclusively through litigation. Even if this fact be admitted, then the legal position would be that Mohd. Basir and Mohd. Rasheed were co sharers with the plaintiff in the khewat and had also sirdari tenants under them, how could the sirdri tenants occupy the land of one of the co sharer leaving the defendants alone so that the plots were re allotted to them.

In view of the fact that Respondent No. 1 is just as Deputy Prime Minister while being sworn into office, he described himself as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He maintained that yet in view of his fact that the Constitution describes him as the Prime Minister, while being oath into office he describe himself as the Chief Minister and this practice is in vogue eversince 1950. The oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime minister and all others ministers signas Ministers. Respondent No 1 further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Chief Prime Minister was descriptive only and for all purposes he is a Minister and there is no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Minis ter as such. Relying on a bench decision of this Court in the case of Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., , learned Attorney General further contends that the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. And according to him, as long as the substantial part is properly followed, a mere mistake or error in the descriptive part would not vitiate the oath. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of Article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. [319D] 2.1 In view Of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney Gen er, that Respondent 1 is not just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Leader but the description of him as Deputy Cabinet Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Ministry, along with his other submis sions, we think the first contention raised by the petitioner himself does not press it. [340E F] 2:2 The words which precede this portion are merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. [341G] 3.3 In view o the clear statements made by Respondent No1 that describing him as Prime Ministers is descriptive only, and for All purposes he was a Minister, it would be open to the petitioner to raise such contention in appropriate proceedings. [342F G] 4.4 The words "which precede this part are merely suggestive of the persons and of their nomination as candidate. " In view thereof, the essential requirement of article 173 readwith Form VIIA is only for a Minister of the Union and there was no 3 Constitutional sanction for post ofDeputy Prime Mini ter assuch. [343G H] 5.5 The words 'which precede the portion are mere descriptive of his person and the description thereof does not conferring on him anyone powers of any other member of the council of Ministers although he has not been described in the particulars of him.

The appellant, a carding and spinning department of the Carnatic Mills stopped work on the night of 1st November, 1948. The strike ended completely. On the 3rd November, 1949, the management put up a notice that the stoppage of work on a day was illegal and a break in service within the meaning of the Factories Act (XXV of 1934) and that the management had decided that the workers who had participated in the said strike would not be entitled to holidays with pay as provided by the Act. The appellant contended that the termination of service amounted to an illegal strike and that it was not necessary for the workmen to go up on work even for 2 hours in the course of a working day, and that no substantial question of law arose in this case because the workers had been denied the right to terminate their services by reason of the strike. Held, that the appellant 's failure to turn up for work was not an illegal act but a case of an individual worker 's refusal to work even after the attempt made by the officers and their own Madras Labour Union representatives indicated that they were not as a body prepared to resume work unless their demand was conceded. The action of the management in awarding punishment, reduced the punishment by 50 per cent and held that the workmen would be deprived of only half their holidays with wages under the Act inasmuch as they would have otherwise got under the rules of the Mills which prevailed prior to the coming into force of the Act and the provisions of sections 49 A and 49 B were not therefore attracted to it.

The appellant, a film producer, was convicted under section 292 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three years and to pay fine of Rs.5 lakhs. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by him. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to establish that the fascinating title was misleadingly foul and beguiled into degeneracy. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A certificate granted under section 5A(1) of the Act by expert authority can be stultified by a simple prosecution of a shower of prosecutions for an offence under section 293 I. P.C., driving the producer to satisfy a 'lay ' magistrate that the certificate of the Board of Censors notwithstanding, the film was offensive ? [501F] 1.2 The cinema is one of the major mass media with millions of viewers and many millions in investment. It is an antinomy to say that under section 79 I.A. of the , the Board certifies a film as suitable for public exhibition and for section 292, I.L.R. [502F] 2.1 The resolution of the problem raised in this case thus becomes simplified. [525C] 2:2 In the instant case, the prosecution is unsustainable because section 79 is exculpatory when read with section 5 A of the . It is a antinetic to say "that under section 65 I.T.A., driving a producer to satisfying a ' Layer" magistrate that he has the certificate granted by it by expert body can be straightaway stultified. [500D] 2 :3 The cinema being one of its major mass mediumes, it is not possible for the Board to hold that the film having been duly certified for public show by the Board was offensive. [601F G] 2:-4 In the present case, there is no evidence to establish the fact that the appellant had a certificate under section 70 I.D. and the certificate issued thereunder. The prosecution has failed to prove that the films were not obscene or objectionable in any department more so in cinema pictures. The Board, alive to its public duty, shall not play to the gallery; nor shall it restrain aesthetic expression and progressive art through obsolete norms when the world is wheeling forward to glimpse the beauty of Creation in its myriad manifestations and liberal horizons. [511F] 3:5 The film having already been duly verified for public shows that the picture was great or the audience may lose lucre and culture in the bargain. What with the art of the cameraman with trick photography, vistavision and three dimensional representation, the celluloid art has greater capabilities of stirring up emotions and making powerful mental impact so much so the treatment of this form of art on a different footing with pre censorship may well be regarded as a valid classification, as was held in K. Abbas. Maybe, art cannot be imprisoned by the bureaucrat and aesthetics can be robbed of the glory and grace and free expression of the human spirit if governmental palate is to prescribe the permit for exhibition of artistic production in any Department, more so, in cinemaiqj pictures. [401F H] 3.1 In the facts and circumstances of this case, it cannot be said that the offence under Section 292 I P. C. was not made out against the appellant. The conviction of the accused is set aside. He shall be released forthwith unless he has been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause why his sentence should not be enhanced.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader for the Patna District, was given short shrift by the High Court in a laconic order. The petitioner was asked to make over those briefs to the new nominee. He went to the extent of writing to Government: "I am, therefore unable to comply with your instruction in allowing any Assistant Government Pleader to work in this case." Chagrined by this loss of income and mayhem to his monopoly he rushed to the High court for the universal panacea of a writ. The State of Bihar, like many other States in the country, has an enormous volume of litigation. It vests no sole control on one Government Pleader over others and Government is perfectly free to put a particular Government Pleader in charge of particular cases. "The petitioner was also requested to make available the briefs for his personal use. The Government Pleader, Madras, was requested to give him a short shraft by way of fees and more fees if they are contested 763 cases and this secret is perhaps at the back of this lawyer 's litigation. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Government Pleader had no legal right to appoint more than one Government pleader in charge. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The petitioner has been rightly impleaded as a party to the writ petition. [763C] 2.1 In the instant case, the legal position is plain. They are purely administrative prescriptions and serve as guidelines and cannot found a legal right, apart from the fact that they do not contradict Government 's power to appoint less than one private Pleader. [758E F] 3.2 The legal position in this regard is clear. They have fought innovations even in their own profession. Each one is a Public Prosecutor under Sec. Public offices and Government Pleadership is one shall not succumb to Tammany Hall or subtler spoils system, if purity in public office is a desideratum. Adjournment to suit advocates ' convenience becomes a bane when it is used only for augmentation of counsel 's income, resisting democratisation and distributial justice within the profession. [759F G] 3:3 The legal status of Government Pleader is an integral part of the rule of law for a groaning people. It vested no sole authority on one government pleader over others but Government Pleaders in charge and the Government is fully free to appoint a more than two private Pleader in Charge of particular case. [761F] 4.1 There is no legal or statutory right, except that Government Pleader has been impleaded as party to a writ petition under Article 136. The observations of Tabachnik, in 'Professions for the People ', about English professions of the eighteenth century smell fresh: "One could carry on commerce by sleight of hand while donning, the vestments of professional altruism. Adjournments to suit advocate ' convenience become a bale when it was used only as a fitting honorarium (1966 p 37). The remarks of Tabachanik are in no worse position that an ordinary litigant and is not bound to encourage monopoly within the service.

The appellants held a total issue of 800 shares of the Mills. The shareholders had to pay Rs. 100 for each new share. The shares were quoted in the market at more than Rs. 50. The appellants agreed to the allotment of these shares and ultimately transferred them to a private company Jesinghbai Investment Co. Ltd., Kalol, a public limited company. The Mills as holder of 5,000 ordinary shares offered by 'the Bank of India Ltd. had to make a payment of Rs. 1,6662 shares of this company at the rate of Rs 100 per share. On receiving the circular letter, the Directors passed the following resolution: "Resolved that the company having a holding of 5.,000 ordinary share in the capital of the Bank of Indian India Ltd., having now received an intimation from the said Bank that this company is entitled to get 1,6762 more ordinary shares on payment of a premium of Rs 50 for each additional share. This last option could be exercised by nominating the persons who were to take over the shares and that is what the Mills did. By its resolution, the Mills had decided that the right to apply for the shares of 'the Company of India shall be distributed among its 800 share holders. The Board of Directors passed a resolution increasing the share capital of ' the Bank and for that purpose offering new shares to the existing shareholders in the proportion of their right to the remaining 1,600 shares offered and resolved that the rights of this Company to apply to the shares be distributed amongst its 800 shares holders. This resolution was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and by the Income Tax Officer reassessing the income of the seven appellants was confirmed. The Tribunal held that the distribution of the right of the shareholders amounted to a distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 in enlarging the scope of the question and in answering it in the light of its ordinary meaning. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the distributed of the rights to apply under section 66(1) of Income Tax Act amounted to distribution of "dividend" within the ambit of section2(6 A). [775 D] (2) The distribution of a right which had a monetary value, is not a distribution or distribution of any dividend. It takes the form of distribution of an interest in the shares. By the definition in section 2 (6A), "dewividend", means dividend as normally understood and includes in its connotation various other receipts set out in the definition. [776 E] (3) The right to takeover only 66 shares of a company given to its shareholders is still dividend.

The appellant was declared elected. The election petition filed by the returned candidate was dismissed on the ground that he had not been given permission to examine. his 54 witnesses who were kept present in the Court and therefore, the election petitioner could not be permitted to examine such witnesses. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the purpose for which the witnesses were offered is not mentioned in the list but it was only a procedural requirement. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 1A of order XVI Rules 1 and 2A of Order XVI Rules l and 2 of Order XVII Rules l, would clearly bring out the underlying scheme under order XVI Rule 1 and Rule 22 of the High Court Rules would not derogate from such scheme. But if on the date fixed for recording the evidence, the party is able to keep his witnesses present despite the fact that the names of the witnesses are not shown in the List filed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1, the parties would be entitled to examine these witnesses and to produce documents through the witnesses who are called to produce them. [529G H] 2. The scheme clearly emerges from the various provisions herein discussed. It is only a ground on which the learned Judge declined to permit the appellant to examine his witnesses who have been kept present during the Court, and this ought to be so because the Court wants to be satisfied about the necessity and relevance of the evidence of such witness whose presence will be procured with the assistance of the Court. [630G H; 528A] 3. Rule 2A is subject to sub rule(3) of rule 1 and therefore the Court must ascertain how far sub rule.(3) would carve out an exception to the enabling provision contained in Rule 1 A. The analysis of the relevant provisions would clearly reveal that the obligation to supply the list as well as the gist of the statement of each witness whose name is entered in the lists has to be carried out in respect of those witnesses for procuring whose attendance the party needs the assistance. [ 528A B] 4. Rule 22 is subject only to sub Rule (3) and therefore it is not possible to derogate from that scheme. The Court must determine how far Sub rule(1) would come into play. But where on the day fixed for the recording of evidence, a party is unable to keep their witnesses present inspite of the fact fact that he has been kept in the court and this ground is utterly unsustainable, it necessarily follows that the party can produce such witness on the dates fixed for his attendance in Court. The court may, in its discretion, issue a warrant either with or without bail, for the arrest of such person, and may make an order for the attachment of his property for such amount as it thinks fit.

The appellant, a teacher of the respondent college, applied for appointment to the post of Principal on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay alongwith DA admissible under the rules. On receipt of this letter of appointment the appellant presented himself at the College on May 1, 1981 and requested the Manager to hand over charge to him. The Manager refused to handover charge to the appellant. A notice was sent to the District Inspector of Schools, Ballia and the Committee of Management of the college, after considering the objections raised by the appellant, passed an order dated April 27, 1981 directing that the appointment of the appellant be cancelled. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of cancellation of his appointment on the ground that he was not qualified to be appointed as Principal of the institution and that the Selection Committee had no power to make the appointment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the day i.e. May 1 1981 and the message of the G.O. have been sent to them by telegram, the appellant was selected as a Principal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The State Government had power to sanction or not to sanction the regulation proposed by the Board. [978G] (2) The power of appointment conferred by regulation on Committee of management to make appointments and withdrawal and/or suspending power of appointments of Principal and teachers is being regulated by the regulations, 979 Thus it becomes clear that the power of appointing authority conferred by Regulation on Committee constituted under section 16 A of the Act is an administrative power. [969B] (3) The appointment was in contravention of any provision of the statute. [970C] (4) The order conveyed by the radiogram would be to rescind the regulation conferring power on the Committee to make appointment and withdraw or suspending power. The effect of this order is that the selection committee had no right to select the appellant nor the Committee has any power to appoint the appellant or the Committee on behalf of the Committee. [971D] (5) The provisions of the U.P. Intermediate Education Act, 1921 are a pre Constitution Act enacted in 1921 with a view to acquiring power to establish a Board to take the place of the Allahabad University in regulating and supervising the system of High School and Intermediate Education of the United Provinces. But there was a comprehensive amendment of the provisions of section 7 prescribing the power to frame regulations conferring power upon the Committee, which would also imply duties and functions of the Board, [970F] (6) The scheme of Administration was to inter alia provide for constitution of a Committee of Selection Committee of the Management of all non government aided schools to make an appointment and withdrawal or suspension power of appoint Principal and teacher. The power to issue appointment order is conferred by the regulation.

The petitioners, a textile mill, sold by the Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd., to the respondents, who were manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and weave it into a fabric in the same way as is being done by the first petitioner". The respondents contended that the goods now sought to be taxed are not the "end product" but the "tyre cord fabric" is an integral part of the whole fabric. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected the petitioners ' objections, and confirmed the assessment on the ground that the sales of these goods had wrongly escaped assessment. The petitioners challenged the order and provisional assessment dated 21 st November 1 972. Civil Appeals Nos. 886/72 and 888/72 were filed by the respondents against the orders and provisional assessments dated 21st November 1, 972 passed by the Commercial Tax officer rejecting their objections to Sales tax on "rayon tyre cord fabric". The petitioners contended that, from year 1966 to 1969, the respondent Commercial Tax officers was not subjecting the goods of this description to sales tax and accepted the case of the petitioners that they were exempt from taxation. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The word "textile" has a wide meaning. It is more than that. In any case it is a question on which two views seem possible on apparent facts. [501B] 2.1 A perusal of item 22 in the first schedule to the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 clearly shows that we are dealing here with "textiles fabrics". The residuary entry and the descriptions in preceding entries seem to us to make it abundantly clear that we were dealing only with "Textile fabrics" which ultimately emerges by subjecting the cotton fabric to a process of impregnating with rubber. There fore, the essential question to determine is the stage at which the goods under consideration become a 'textiles fabric". [502C] 2:2 The essential question for determination is whether the product for which the Delhi Textile Mills claims exemption Is a textile fabric and not any other kind of fabric. It must acquire a body and a texture. If the "lyre cord" is so well established a category of rayon "fabric", it could have found mention specifically in item 19. 22 does not enumerate specifically in items 19.22 do not enumerate separately in preceding entry seem to me to make them abundantly clear. [525A B] 2 :3 The word 'textile fabric" has been used in the context of the definition of "t Textile fabrics". It is a well established principle that, when goods are sought to tax, they must be regarded as a textile fabrics just because it requires some skill to make the same. In other words, if the "dry fabric" was so well known and capable of being used merely for tying the warp threads together for the purpose of convenient transport or storage but form an integral whole fabric, it could not be said that the product was intended to be used only for turing the warps. [500D] 2(a) The word `textile fabrics ' has a wider meaning. The term fabric has a very wide connotation. It means that the tyre cord fabrics serves as raw material for another fabric which ultimately emerged by subjecting it to a processing of impabricating with Rubber. [511B C] 3:1 In any event, it is more or less that. [550E] 2.(b) The term 't Textile fabric ' has been defined in the Act. It has a long connotation. The word fabric has an wide meaning and its definition has a broad meaning. Its dictionary meaning has a limited meaning. [549C D] 3 :2(a).

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal washeries on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied work. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. The Labour Court registered the case as refer ence case No. 1/1988 under section 33 B of the , but transferred the said proceeding to the Labour Court, Patna for speedy disposal from the stage at which the case was transferred. The High Court dismissed the writ petition with an observation that no prejudice is being caused to the appellant and no allegation of mala fide has been made against the presiding officer, Patna, regu larly due to his residence at Hajipur is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure 'A ' pending before Labour Court. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the High Court did not agree and summarily dismissed the Writ Petition with an observations: "Since no prejudice has been caused to any of the parties, the courts may be able in suitable cases (perhaps always) to imply an obligation to act with fair ness. It extends to both the fields of judicial and administrative. Good administration demands fair play in action and this simple desideratum is the fount of natural justice. Good governance demands fairplay in action, and this Court does not interfere with the order under challenge. " The validity of the reasons given by the Government for transferring the case is another question to be considered. In the present case, the State has withdrawn the pending refe 301 rence from the Labour court, Dhanbad and transferred it to another Labour Court at the distant District of Patna on the representation of the workman, without getting it veri fied from the management. The validity and legality of the reason given by Government for transfer was challenged inter alia on the ground that no reasons were stated for passing the order. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have not agreed and summarily rejected the writ peti tion. [319D] 2.1 In the instant case, there is no right to any party to have any question decided by a partic ular court. Both the authorities laid down that for application of rules of natural Justice, the classification of functions as 'judi cial ' or 'administrative ' is not necessary. [519D E] 2:2 The concept of rule of law would lose its vitality if the instrumentalities of the State are not charged with the duty of discharging their functions in a fair and just manner. That is, however, not the same thing to state that they must act judicially or quasijudicially. [620E F] 3.1 There is no provision in the Act which empowers the Government to transfer a pending case from one tribu nal to another. The concept that justice must not only be done but be seen to be done is basic to our system and it is concerned not with a case of actual injustice but with the appearance of injustice or possible injustice. [613B C] 3:3 In the facts and circumstances of this case, it would be difficult to appreciate how under such circumstances, the Government could be called upon to give a notice to the parties before making an order under section33 B. The question whether such reasons in fact exist and whether those reasons have any relevance for a transfer could be tested only if the other party has notice of the same. [720G H] 4.2 In the case, no prejudice was being caused by the Presiding Officer, Patna to the management, the High Courts were not inclined to interfere with such order under Article 226 of the Constitution.

The appellant, a hotel operator, was the manager of a Hotel Imperial, New Delhi. The main contesting respondent is the Hotel Imperial and its workmen as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi. On a consideration of the report submitted by the Director of Industries and Labour, Delhi under section 12 (4) of the as amended, it appears that an industrial dispute exists between the management of the hotel and its employees as represented in the Hotel Employees ' Union. The appellant was the Manager of the Hotel and its workers as represented through the Hotel Worker ' Union Katra Shahahi,Chandni Chowk Delhi. In October 1955, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of reference on the ground that it did not indicate how many of the 480 workers of thirty different categories working in the hotel were involved in the dispute. The High Court dismissed the writ application holding that there was no force in these grounds of attack. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) There is no force for the contention that there is a dispute between the appellant and its management as represented under section 36 of the Act. [283 D] (2) The reference which is otherwise valid does not become incompetent merely because it is mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by such and such union in the disputes. [284 E F] (3) There was no substance in the contention of the appellant that there could be a dispute with respect to the terms of employment Qr conditions of labour of the workmen. The reference was in these terms: " WHEREAS an industrial Dispute has arisen between the workers and managements of the cinema talkies in the Madras City in respect of certain matters; R 334. The question is whether the reference which was otherwise valid did not become competent merely because there was a dispute referred to it by the Union that it relates to retrenchment or reinstatement. [285 G H] (4)(a) The words "as represented by" in section 36 are wide enough to include the words " as represented". The word "as representing" is used in the sense of including the words 'as represented '.

The appellant, a manufacturer of motor vehicles, imported by the appellant, was granted exemption from payment of Customs duty in respect of the rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by it. The goods were assessed to customs duty under Heading No. 84.06. The appellant claimed that they had been imported by them as parts of the engines referred to in Heading No, 84.63 Transmission shafts, (a) 60% cranks, bearing housings, plan shaft bearings, gears and gearing (including friction gear and gear boxes), flywheels, pulleys and pulley blocks, clutches and shaft couplings; (b) 60%, cranks and cameras, flywhes and pulleyk blocks, whereas Heading No 84.6406 did not refer to the parts of internal combustion piston engines, but also to 'parts thereof '. The Appellate Tribunal held that the bushings and bearings are the same and as the bearings come under the Heading No 85.06, they were not entitled to the benefit of exemption under the said Notification. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Notification is inapplicable to the part of the engine or engines mentioned in Heading 84.6. 8406. [226B] 2.2 The Notification does not mention 'the parts of any of the parts ', the Notification is applicable to the Parts, will be to amend the Notification, which the court will not do. [227C D] 3.1 In other words, as soon as it is proved that the parts are parts of such engines, mentioned under Heading 8406, are excluded from the benefit Of the Notification. The intention of the Notification was clear enough to provide that the Parts of the vehicles mentioned under heading No.84.06 are excluded therefrom from the benefits of the notification. [228D E] 3:2 In the instant case, the intention is clear enough and manifest, it will be unreasonable to take a narrow view of the Notifications and not to extend its benefit to the components of the Engine referred to therein. [229E F] 3 :3 The Notification has been inartistically drafted. When, therefore, the intent is clear and manifest it will not be unreasonable for taking a narrow interpretation of the exemption Notification. 8405.06 does not include parts of engines mentioned under headings 84.04. [225F] 4.2 In other word, as the functions of 226 bushors are the different functions but, nonetheless, they are distinct and separate. But, nevertheless, they have been called bearings and, therefore they are separate. It merely provides 'parting thereof ''. Therefore, they cannot be said that the bushes, which have been imported, are parts or parts thereof. [224F G] 4:4 The Notification, therefore is inapplicable only to the motor vehicles mentioned in heading 84.05.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for declar ment of right and management in the Dargah. The defendants contended that they were entitled to be in enjoyment and pos session of Saint Syed Moosa Shah Khadiri Dargah in Madras for a period of 27 days in all in the months of February, March, June, July, October & November. According to Muslim Law females were excluded from performing the duties of the offices of Peshimam Khatib and Mujawar. It was further alleged that as Fathima Bee ever made a demand or asked for share of the Hundial collections as such it should be held that her rights had become barred by limi tation. The Trial Court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs were entitled only to the right in the management and not to any right in respect of the offerings in the wakf. In appeal, the High Court held that Fathiman Bee was a co sharer in the right of management and possession of the Dargah as well as the offerings made by her father in the mosque and on that account she was also a Mujawar along with his brother associated himself in the Management of the Wakf. The High Court further held that there was no evidence whatsoever to show at any point of time till her death in 1957 that Fatima Bee had no right or claim of share in the offerings. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A great capital has been raised on the basis of the above decree by the learned counsel for the defendant respondents that no share was given to the female members in the above said decree, namely, to Wazir Bi and Mohideen Bi and from this it was clear that neither in the written statement nor in reply to the notice of the plain tiffs any stand was taken that Fayima Bee or plaintiffs were specifically denied on any particular occa sion so as to put them on notice that from that date the possession of Fathimiya Bee ever make a demand and asked for a share of their Hundal collections as aforesaid it should he held that she had become entitled to any rights in the administration or offerings in respect thereof. [529D] 1.2 The High court was right in holding that Fatsima Bee was not a co spec sharer within Muslim Personal Law and that the females were totally excluded from discharging the duties as the offices were being looked after by her broth ers and she was in fact being paid portions of the income from the Dargah and on this account she had been satisfied in allowing the brothers to enjoy the office of Mujawar on her behalf also. [525E] 1:3 The High Courts were right in taking the view that Falsima Bee 's title at the time of the judgment of the High court in 1909 did not care to make a demanded or asked a share in his offerings in any point o f time. [500F] 2.1 In so far as there was absolutely no evidence whatever to show that Fatesima Bee and others were totally exclusion from performing their duties, the plaintiffs who were claiming through Fathyam Bee were also not entitled to the same. The possession of one co heir is considered in law, as possession of all the co heirs. Thus it is clear that none in the Written Statement or in reply thereto any stand had been taken that the right to management and custody was denied on a particular occu sion. [511F] 1 :3 In the instant case there has been expressed denial of Fatiman Bee 'S title at that time till she died in 1957.

The appellant, a railway employee stationed at specified headquarters were eligible for the allowance of Rs. 290 as part of his wages. The 1st respondent was the authority responsible under section 4 of the , for payment of house rent allowance to him from the 19th August 1948 when he was offered by the Government quarters suitable to his post, but he refused to occupy the same. On his refusal to occupy it, the house rent allowances were stopped with effect from the 20th August 1949. The appellant filed a claim before the Authority for Rs. 291,840. The Authority condoned the delay and that part of the order condoning the delay was not in controversy before us. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The rules clearly provide that the allowance will not be ad raissible to those who occupy Government quarters or to those to whom such quarters have been offered but who have refused to take advantage of the offer. [1353C] (2) The statutory rules framed by the Railway Board governing the grant of house Rent Allowance do not make it unconditional and absolute in terms. [1254D] (3) The Rules clearly provide for the payment of House rent allowance being admissible, namely, that the employee should be posted at one of those places, like Bombay, Calcutta, 1350 Madras ' etc., before the claim for house rent Allowance could arise and that there is a condition subsequent, namely that the employees posted at any one of these places will cease to be so entitled. [1054E] (4) The rule which must be included in the terms of contract between the employer and the employee contemplates that an employee posted at some one of them will cease not to be entitled to the allowance if either the Government provides accommodation to the employee in question or the employee refuses to occupy such quarters so offered to him. [ 1054F] (5) The provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the Act are inconsistent with the provisions of section 7 and cannot be said to create any absolute right in the employee to the house Rent allowance.

The detenu, who was a Customs Officer at Bombay raided the premises of the said firm and in the course of raid, seized diamonds and pearls worth about Rs. 1,40,000 in Indian currency and two gold sovereign coins. The detenu claimed that the gems and other articles seized were not smuggled goods but were local materials, locally acquired. Both the father and the son were arrested and were produced before a Magistrate. The detaining authority, however, called upon the detenu to furnish the detenus with the material relied upon by the detaining authority in the grounds of detention. The representation was rejected by the State Government on March 24, 1980. The petitioner challenged the order of detention mainly on the ground that the supply of copies of the statements and documents at this stage would have adversely affected the investigation and harmed public interest. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The detaining authorities were right in rejecting the representation made by the detenu.
