[348B] 1.2 The supply of the copies of statements and papers to the detenus was not only on March 25, 1980 but also on March 27, 1980, i.e., after more than one month thereof. The very fact that soon after the directions of the Central Government copies were ready and despatched to the detenu within three days thereof, shows that there was no physical difficulty in preparing and supplying the copies to the detained persons with due promptitude. [349C D] 1:3 The supply was made by a person who had either deposed against the detenus or provided clues. It is well settled that "the constitutional imperatives enacted in Article 22(5) of the Constitution are two fold: (i) the detaining authorities must, as soon as practicable after the detention communicate to the detenue the grounds on which the order has been made; and (ii) the detenu earliest opportunity of making a representation against the detention order. This principle was enunciated after an exhaustive survey of the authorities by Bhagwati J. who delivered the opinion of the Court. It was held after an elaborate survey of all the authorities that the supplies of the earlier statements which were entirely in favour of the detenus and the full texts of which had been with held, could not, by any reckoning, expose those persons to any alarm or danger at the hands of the agents or partisans of the detenu, [348F G] 1 :4. The supply, according to the grounds, of the earliest statements which had already been disclosed to the petitioners, could be detrimental to the investigation in progress from prosecution point of view and might even endanger the life of such witnesses who have either deposedagainst the detenus nor provided clurs. [347G H] Khudiram vs State of Maharashtra, ; , referred to. 1:5. The supplies of copies were made by persons who had not either deposed before the Magistrate or furnished any evidence against them. It could not be said that the supplied copies would have exposed the informants to bodily harm at the hand of the agent or partities of the petitioners. [ 348D] Khudram vs Union of India, ; and Khudi Ramchand Bharvani vs State, ; referred to; 1:6. The fact that immediately after the direction of the Government copies had been ready and dispatched to the Petitioners within three months thereof, showed that there were no physical difficulties in preparing or supplying the copy to the detaining persons with proper prompacity. [ 349D] 1.:7. In the peculiar facts of the instant case, it is clear from the police records that the representation, dated March 24 was considered by the Adviser to the Governor of Maharashtra and the State then being under President 's rule. The letter clearly suggested that copies should not be given Annexure "A".

The appellant was tried jointly by two accused persons. The trial court acquitted the respondent but convicted him under section 419 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year. In appeal, the High Court set aside the acquittal of the respondent on the ground that the Full Bench decision holding a joint appeal to be maintainable in law was not binding on it. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The Full Bench judgment of the Gujarat High Court correctly distinguished and explained the principle that a joint appeals against an order acquitting (1 ) A.I.R. 1962 Guj. 125; (2) A. I. R. 1962 Bom. 125, referred to. (3) The decision of this Court in Rabari Ghela Jadav was not applicable to the proceedings in Gujarat High court. [746 B] (4) The view taken by the Full bench of the Bombay High Court on the construction of section 419(2)(c) Cr. P.C. is clearly unacceptable. [750 C D] (5) The High Court rightly distinguished and applied the principle of res judicata in a case where the decision of two judges of the same High Court was wrong. [751 E F] (6) The appeal against acquittal by several accused persons was competent. [752 A] (746) In the instant case, the Full Court had not considered the question whether the earlier decision was wrong or not. It was only in a limited jurisdiction that the High court could decide whether the decision was correct.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family carrying on business in India and in the former Federated Malaya States and it was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The income tax Officer accepted the fact of partition amongst the members of the family, but rejected the contention that the assessee was entitled to exemption under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act except for the income received from the house properties in Malaya. The Appellate Tribunal held that the foreign business of the assessee could not be deemed to have been charged under the provisions of the 1918 Act because the assessee had only taxed on remittances received from a business in a foreign territory such assessment was an assessment of the business and there was no tax on the foreign income. In appeal by certificate, HELD: (i) The foreign business was charged upon the assessee in respect of his activity styled ,foreign business ' and in relation to it and it must hence be taken upon the facts found by the Appellate Tribunal in this case, that the Indian income tax Act was not charged upon it under the 1918 act. [908 B] (ii) The assessee was not entitled to any exemption under s 25(2) of 1922 Act in respect Of interest on securities as well, and there could be no discontinuance but only succession by the firm of the businesses of the company. [098 C D] (iii) The income received by the assessee on the profits rec eived from a foreign business and in connection with it and was therefore liable to tax under the head "Profits and gains of business, profession or vocation" within the meaning of section 25 (3). [910 E F] Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City vs Chugandas and Company, , distinguished.

The assessee entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Govern (1) 14 S.T.C. 766 for the manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said Department and the supply of bricks to it in terms of their running Bill No. 1/69 dated 6th September, 1965 for the purpose of manufacturing and supplying kiln burnt brick bricks to that Department. The assessee received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. The Deputy Commissioner held the supplied of bricks by the assessee as sales. The Tribunal held that the transaction was a works contract. In coming to this conclusion the High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the transactions envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department were works contracts. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court was right in distinguishing the present case in view of certain distinguishing features of the contract with which we are concerned. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contract with a contractor for work and labour is often a fine one. [163H] 2. The contracts with which the contracts were entered into have been transferred as a chattel for consideration and we are clearly of opinion that this has taken place in this case. [164B C] 3. The essence of the contracts was, therefore, the delivery of the bricks after manufacture. The delivery of bricks after manufacturing is not transfer to third parties without permission of the company. [165H; 166A] 4. The materials described in the undermentioned memorandum are inclusive of sales tax and the contractor will pay the same himself, Clause 24:ALL rates quoted by the contractors arc inclusive of sale tax and The contractor will be strictly in accordance With the specifications and particulars contained in the Schedule and accompaniments hereof and the contract hereby guarantees that the said articles would continue to conform to the description and quality aforesaid for the period shown in the schedule from the data of delivery of such articles to the purchaser and that notwithstanding that fact that 163 the purchaser may have inspected and approved, the said article be discovered not to conform with the specification and quality thereof or has deteriorated and the decision of the purchaser in that behalf shall be final and conclusive. Or such portion thereof as is rejected by the purchaser otherwise the contractor shall pay to the Government such damages as may arise by any of the breach of the condition herein contained, nothing herein contained shall prejudice any other right of the purchasers in that respect under this contract or otherwise. [166B C; 166D] 5. The fact that the goods were sold after manufacture was not transferable to third party without permission is not a ground for holding that it was a work contract. [167F G] 6. The facts and circumstances of the present cases are similar to those in the case of State of Gujarat vs Variety Body Builders, ; , followed.

The petitioner, a member of the Legislative Assembly of India, was elected to the Lok Sabha on March 3, 1971. The Proclamation of Emergency issued by the President on March 27, 1977 was revoked by the Proclamation dated June 25th, 1975. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Proclamation on various grounds: (i) that the proclamation of emergency had been duly issued by both Houses of Parliament as required by law and that actually the proclamation had been revoked by him by the proclamation dated July 23, 1977; (ii) that since the proclamation was revoked, the second proclamation must be deemed not to have been in existence on 4.2.1972; (iii) that even assuming that the Proclamation was issued mala fide, it could not be said that the second Proclamation had ceased to operate on 4th February, 1972 and the Proclamation of emergency dated June 21, 1975 were revoked by a Proclamation dated July 25th , 1977. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the two Proclamations of Emergency had been validly issued by two Houses of the Parliament as set out earlier in the course of this judgment; (iv) that it was not possible for the petitioner to accept the submission of the petitioner that for the various reasons assigned by them, the first proclamation must have been deemed not in existence and that the third proclamation must also be held to have ceased to exist on 4rd February, 1973. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The two Procts of Emergency have been duly approved by both the Houses of Legislature as set forth earlier in this judgment. [448C] 2.1 The Proclamation dated March 27th, 1977 is not a valid law. It is not possible to accept that the resolutions of both the houses of Parliament approving a Proclamation of Proclamation should be given due publicity. [453D] 3.2 The resolution of the Council without further publication or promulgation of the law was not sufficient to make the law operative and the Jaipur opium Act was not therefore a valid Law. [454E F] 2:3 The two proclamments of Emergency having been approved by the resolutions passed by both of them as setout earlier in their course of the judgment are not invalid merely because they were not published in the official Gazette. [449C D] 3:4 The resolution dated March 28, 1977 approving a proclamation of Emergency should be deemed to have become effective on 4st February, 1978 and on that date the Proclamation shall cease to operate at the expiration of two months unless before the expiration thereof a resolution approving the Proclamation has been passed by the House of the People. [450E] 3 :5 The fact that the Proclams had been approved in the second course of their judgment is not disputed by the petitioner. It was not necessary for us to accept this submission of Mr. Gupta that for various reasons mentioned by them the first Proclamation must be held invalid merely on the ground that they were published in a official Gazette and that it did not have effect on 4 th February, 1971 when the proclamation under Article 352 of the Constitution had been issued. [444F G] 3(a) The resolution passed by two House of Parliament was not valid law as it was issued by a competent authority. It could not therefore be said to have affected the validity or invalidity of the second order dated March 29, 1977. [443C D; 454A B] 4:1 The resolution approving a Proclomations of emergency should be made due publicity and that must be done forthwith.

The appellant 's case was that the property in dispute belonged to the Thoguluva Thirumalayyan and certain other idols were located constituted a temple within the meaning of the said Act, the appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The District Judge dismissed the application on the ground that the subject matter of dispute was the private property of the family and that it was alienable property of that family. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court and held that the premises in question did not constitute a temple and set aside the decision of the District Judge. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The appellant ' s case was one of the grounds on which leave was granted under article 133(1)(a) and (b). [156B] (2) The High Court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to the respondents the property was inalienable and was a public temple. [156C D] (3) The question whether the property belonged to or was not a public religious trust could have no market value and therefore was incapable of valuation as it could have in either case no market Value. [157D E] (4) The suit in the first instance was filed by him in the form of an application, being O.P. No. 37 of 1950 under section 84(2) of Madras Act 11 of 1927. That being so, the property belongs to and was an alienable private property capable of alienation, the question whether it was a private or a public endowment could have been determined with reference to the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to him the property is the private properties of the same family capable of alienated, the Court ought not to have valuation the property.

The appellant, who was a clerk in the appellant 's concern, claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of their tiffin arrangements. The Tribunal held that the practice started by the appellant of re employing retired persons should be discontinued. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal had erred in law in making an award in respect of the cash allowance for tiffins, because he argues that it is not obligatory on the part of the employer to provide any further facility to the employees by way of giving them a cash allowance. HELD: The Tribunal has overlooked the fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the respondent in re employing the retired personnel. It does appear that when the respondents had raised a dispute on this point in 1960, the State Government had refused to make a reference on the ground that only 4 cases of reemployment had been brought to its notice, and so, the problem did not call for any consideration at that stage. [571 C] The fact that they felt that the policy adopted by them was not based solely on humanitarian grounds cannot be ignored. It is true that some of the re employments may have been actuated by humanitarian considerations but the appellant cannot, therefore, be blamed on that account; but there are certain other factors in relation to this problem which cannot be overlooked. [572 D] In the instant case, the evidence shows that in the region as many as 31 comparable concerns were supplying free tiffine to their employees (Ext. 10). The correspondence between the parties on this subject shows that the respondents felt that they were not bound to support the appellant. It also does appear from the correspondence between them that the respondent felt that it was not obligatory for the appellant to make any provision for the tiff in addition to the wages and dearness allowance, because the said formula takes care substantially of the rise in cost of living from time to time.

The respondent, a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund, was governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules whereunder payment of provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. The appellant who was an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber under the State Government, claimed immunity from attachment. The execution application filed by him was struck off on December 7, 1956. On August 26, 1947, Browne addressed a letter to the Chief Accounts Officer communicating the sanction of the General Manager for payment of the special contribution to provident fund to Browne in sterling and to transmit the fund in sterling to the bankers of Browne. The respondent Radha Kissen Agarwalla filed an application under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, praying that the amount standing to his credit in the Provident Funds be remitted to him by Bank Draft on the District Bank, Water Street, Liverpool. The executing court overruled the objection holding that the attachment issued by the Court on December 8, 1956, was perfectly in order and it was not immune from attachment as claimed by the objector. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Union of India had no interest in maintaining an application for removal of attachment. When the amount lying with the Reserve Bank as the agent of the Railway Administration was attached the Union had clearly an interest to maintain the application for removing attachment. [32 D] (2) The Railway Administration had undertaken to discharge its obligation by arranging to have the amount converted into sterling and sent it to the Reserve bank for conversion of the amount to Brownee in sterling, if the country in which it was to be paid, the rupee is not legal tender. [33 E F] (3) The Bank had clearly a interest to maintaining an Application for removal from attachment, as soon as B put into the post a letter containing the note duly addressed to A. The illustration only covers cases in which a creditor has directed the debtor to send him the amount owed by the, debtor in a certain manner. Only after the direction of Brownee regarding transmission of the fund was complied with, the obligation of the railway Administration could be discharged and not till then. [34 F G] (4) The letter dated July 27, 1955, issued by Browne to the Railway administration, was clearly an intimation of the sanction prescribed by the General Secretary to the Government of India for payment at the place at which payment was required, and the payment was necessary either under the first intimation at Liver by bank draft or under the later intimation by payment to the Bank. [35 F G; 36 A] (5) The amount lying in the custody of the Reserve Railway as the Agent of the Railways Administration was not exempt from attachment because it had been specifically mentioned in the letter dated August 26. 1947, that the money remained under the control of the Government as provident fund money, and it had undertaken by arranging a suitable note duly signed to A for Rs. 100, to enable him to send the amount through a bank for payment. [36 F G].

The appellant was a workman of the respondent company. He had been dismissed from service by the management on the ground that he had lost confidence in the employee. The management claimed that the alleged annoyance with the workman for union activity was a concoction in self defence, as the Management had not even knowledge of the formation of the Union. The Labour Court held that the action being a simple one termination without a sting, the process and consequence of a disciplinary action were not attracted. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the order of termination was not bona fide; (2) the management had failed to prove the mala fides of the 'firing ' as contrasted with the colourable exercise of power hiding a not so innocuous purpose; and (3) the action was a mere camouflage to cover up what really was an order (1 ) 496 of dismissal. HELD: (i) The Industrial Court has misled itself on the law land, and has acted within the jurisdiction under article 226 when it set aside the order. [446 D] (ii) The Tribunal had misdirected itself in its approach to the question whether the termination was a colourable exercise or an unfair labour practice. It is manifest that the management could have divulged in writing to the Conciliation Officer their legitimate fears about the worker 's integrity and their considerate action of simple termination. [493 E] (iii) The Labour court had misled itself upon the law law land and set aside its order. The High Court has acted beyond the jurisdiction conferred on it by article 226. [48 H] (iv) The management could not have divulted in writing the reasons which led to the order and then consider for itself whether the action of the management was a sham exercise of unfair labour practices or mala fides recorded, against the management.

The appellant, a doctor of the Government, was charged with having committed breach of duty in sanctioning permission for the conduct of the 'eye camp ' without ensuring a strict compliance with the conditions prescribed by the Government in that behalf and in not effectively dis charging the duties enjoined upon them to over see the satisfactory and safe functioning of the camp. The appellant, who was a doctor in the Government Hospital, Jaipur, was prosecuted under section 3(1)(a) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for having committed offences punishable under sections 120B, 121, 121A, 121B, 122A, 123 and 124A IPC. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that he had been convicted by a criminal Court for an offence under section 161 IPC and section 5 (2) readwith section 5 of the Act. On appeal, the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to any benefit of pension under the existing schemes now in force in the State. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the findings recorded by the trial court were perverse and that the High Courts had erred in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The doctor may not be justified in this description of the large scale and calamitous effects the operation has on the hapless victims. But the picture is entirely different. A cataract affected eye when properly operated is expected to become normal. In White vs Board of Governors of Westminister Hospital, a surgeon accidentally cut the retina during an operation on the plaintiff 's right eye. [250G H] 1.2 The doctor might not be unjustified in this sense of the term as used in the guidelines prescribed by Government in the revised Guidelines of 9th February 1988. But, for the sake of special emphasis keeping their importance in view the above aspects stressed in the Report of the Sub Committee of the Indian Medical Council may be considered for incorporation in the Revised Guidelines of9th February, 1988. [251B C] 1:3 The doctor must not be a justified person in this case in view of the noble objective of this kind litigation, it would not in any manner be prejudicial to the answering re spondent. [252D] 1 :4 In White ; , Dr. R.M. Sahay and his team of doctors to offer the surgical services, both oral and local for the infection. Similar mishap, but on lesser scale affecting some 15 patients, repeated itself at Moradabad. But on lesser scales affecting some of the patients, continued again at Moradabad and administered anti biotic medication, both written and local, for, the infection, and sent Dr. All this was done in the same room in which the earlier operations were performed. The very large number of cases of impairment of visual acuity in the country needs the purposeful involve ment of voluntary social organisations so as to provide an augmented broad based participatory medi care for the general improvement of the tone of ophthalmic health in the Country. [253E F] 1.:5 In White, Dr. Sahay expressed the confidence: " . that cannot be allowed to pass without comment.

The petitioners were the members of a society registered under the Assam Rashtrabha sha Prachar Samiti. The petitioners, who were then) of Mizoram and also production and publica tion of prescribed text books in Hindi for Primary Schools, High School Higher Secondary schools and the Colleges upto the degree standard, were appointed as the Adhyaksha of the Samiti. They challenged the validity of the said resolution on various grounds including that they had been wrongly dropped by the amendment of the Constitution. The petition was contested by the petitioners contending that the amendment was passed in 1983 and therefore the Chief Minister ceased to be the Ex officio President and since then according to the petitioner he had nothing to do with the Samiti, and that as this heading shows that a temporary arrangement was made because the management of the Society was not in proper hands and the temporary arrangement could only improve the functioning after holding elec tion in accordance with the constitution of the society regis tered under the Bidhan (constitution of the Societies) Act, 1984. The respondents contended that the petitioners had been rightly dropped by this amendment and that the Chief Minis ter was annoyed but attempted to suggest that there was some mismanagement of the affairs which could not be said to be not ideal and which had started working on some ideals which could never be said 'not for public good '. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners were rightly dropped from the office of the Chief Secretary and therefore they are entitled to succeed in this petition. [174G] 1.2 In view of the fact that the State has no desire to restore it back to its elected authorities and office bearers despite the fact, that there is some mismanagement or the society was not willing to restore the Society back to their elected bodies and officebearers, inspite of the clear direction by this Court in Damyanti Naranga 's case goes a long way. Any law, by which members are introduced in the voluntary Association without any option being given to the members to keep them out, or any law which takes away the membership of those who have voluntarily joined it, will be a law violating the right to form an association. It is not only that but it is also apparent that since 1984 when this Act was passed and a notification appointing a Board was issued, the Government has not chosen to take any steps to restore its society back to the Society but rather attempted to suggested that there should be some mismanagement in the affairs of the societies registered discharging functions which could have been said 'Not for public purpose '. [175G H] 1:3 The petitioners are entitled for a declaration that the order dated 7.7.84 passed by Respondent No. 2, the Chief Executive Officer, the State Government and the Union Territory of Mizoram was illegal and void. [176H; 174A B] 1 :4 In view the observations of this Court, it is not necessary to decide whether the petitioners were wrongly dropped from their office or bearers. The mere perusal of Entry 25 will reveal as to how difficult it will be to stretch Entry 25 to mean the authority to deprive an association of its right under Article 19(1)(c) of the Consti tution without any options being given by the members, to keep it out or any Law which takes over away the Membership of those persons who have voluntary joined it. [177A B C] 1.:5 The mere fact that there has been some mismanagement and the society is not intending to restore itself back to it will not be a proper law violating Article 19 (1)(a) of t he Constitution of India. [178C D] 2:6 In view, the observation of 174 the Constitution Bench in Damayanti Nargaanga 'S case goes on a long line.

The appellants were the tenants of a house in which a large number of houses were situated. The respondent No. 1, who was the husband of the appellant, filed a suit for partition of his property and for a declaration that he had no right to make a gift as marriage dowry of her daughter, but the trial court decreed the suit on the ground that there was no " sankalpa" or promise of a gift of four houses at Asansol. The High Court affirmed the decree of the trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (1) the gift was void and inoperative against the plaintiffs beyond the lifetime of defendant No. 2 with the alleged collusive and fraudulent allegations binding on the plaintiffs on her death; (2) the gifts were made at the time when the deed was executed and registered; (3) the gowns ceremony were a ceremony of importance, closely connected with the marriage, though it was not a ceremony necessary to complete the marriage. HELD: (1)(a) The gift was valid and binding on all persons including the husband and son in law. [467 D] (b) The gifts were valid and enforceable at the date when the document was executed; and (c) the payment of the consideration for the gift made at a time later, was not sufficient to constitute a gift. [468 E F] (2)(a). In the instant case, the gift had been made at an earlier stage and it was held that the ghars ceremony was a ceremony which took place some two years after the marriage and it could be said that the gift when made fulfils that moral or religious obligation. The gift did not have any absolute right or interest in the share allotted to her on partition. [469 E] (3)(b) In the present case, there were no compelling reasons for the High Court which was the appellate court to differ from the appreciation of oral evidence by the learned Subordinate Judge, who had the advantage of seeing the witnesses with regard to the question of the ante nuptial agreement said to have been made. [470 G] (4) The authorities should be understood to empower a qualified owner like Thaiyyu Ammal to do all acts proper and incidental to the marriage of a female according to the general practice of the community to which she belongs. [472 E F].

The appellant, a candidate for the post of Sarpanch, filed an election petition in the Punjab & Haryana High Court against Tej Singh alleging that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices. The polling took place on May 31, 1980 and the counting was done on June 1, 1980. The margin between the votes secured by Tej Singh and Avtar Singh was only 123. It appears that the margin between votes secured in favour of section Tej Singh had been very small viz. 123 votes, if such a misrepresentation was not made, in all probability the votes would have gone to the appellant (Avtar Singh) and, therefore, the result of the election would have been materially altered. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practices were clearly proved. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 In the end r submission that every vote cast in favour o Tej Singh will be deemed to have been cast in his favour', it is imperative to defeat the dictatorial Congress in these elections. [421B] 2.1 The effect of the posters was that all the voters who would have voted for Ruplal would now cast their votes in favour, and elect Shri Tej Singh Singh, the joint front candidate of Akali Dal, because Shri Tej singh is the only candidate who can defeat the Congress. In other words, the effect of these posters was to mislead the voters so as to make them believe that one of the candidates, viz.; Ruplals would now casting their votes. [409D] 2:2 The effect and operation of the poster was that every voter who would not have voted in favour for Ru Plal would then cast his vote in favour. In these circumstances, therefore the irresistible inference and inescapable conclusion that can be arrived at is that Tej Singh has actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the corrigendum. [416E] 2 :3 The effect or operation of this poster would have materially altered if the votes were very small, viz.123 votes, If such a false misrepresentation was made, it would have resulted in materially altered votes. Therefore, the irresistible conclusion and inescapable inference that can been arrived at by is that the appellant had actually paid the posters.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was elected as a Forest Secretary in the Legislative Assembly. The said Devinder Sharma was defeated in the legislative assembly election held in 1982. He filed an application for contempt against the respondent, Bhajan Lal and others alleging that after having failed to threaten and demoralise the appellant through indirect means the respondent had withdrawn from the petition. The further allegation of the appellant was that after failure to threaten, demoralisation and threat of the writ petitioners to withdraw the writ petition, the respondent threatened the writ petitioner to withdraw his writ petition and, pursuant thereto, eleven officers withdrew from the writ petitions. The application for Contempt was admitted and a rule nisi was issued upon the respondent. The appellant filed an appeal before the Division Bench of the High Court challenging the order of discharge. The Single Judge dismissed the application and discharged the rule ni sion. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that as no punishment was imposed on the respondent by the High Courts in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 215 of the Constitution, such appeal could not be entertained. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has exercised its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215. When an order or decision is that of a single judge, to a Bench of not less than two Judges of the Court, such Appeal shall lie to the Supreme Court. [894C D] 2.1 In other words, the High court derives its jurisdiction only by punishing for contempt. The jurisdiction of the Supreme court is to punish for contempt from Article 215 and it is difficult to say that the High ' Court has exercise its jurisdic tion as conferred by Article 216 of the constitution. [820C D; 894A] 2:2 In the instant case, the Sales Tax Officer disallowed the claim of the petitioner to exemption from payment of sales tax under a certain notification. The High court did not exercise its jurisdiction nor power to punish him for contempt, for such exercise will mean that the Supreme ' Court should act in a particular manner, that is to say by imposing punishment for contempt; and the High courts do not exercise their jurisdication as conferred under Article 227 of the Consti tution. [821C D]. 2:3 The view which we take finds support from a decision of this Court in Paradakanta Mishra vs Mr. It is for the first time that under section 19(1) of the Act, a right of appeal has been provided for. Any person who moves the machinery of the court for contempt only brings to the notice of the courts certain facts constituting contempt of court. The aggrieved party under section19(1), can only be the contemnor who has been punished for contempt of Court. Even though no appeal is maintainable under section 18(1)(a) of Act, the petitioner in such a case can move this Court under Article 136 of the ^ [820D E] 2 :4 The High Courts do not have any jurisdiction to punish the alleged contemnor, the appellant in such an event can only move this court under Article 226. [822C D F] 2(a) In the present case, there is no order as to costs. The question whether the High Curt had exercised its power or power under Article 142 of the Constitu tion was not a matter for the High Cou rt to decide in exercise Of its jurisdiction as conferred upon it by article 215 of t he Constitution.

The appellant was the lessee of a suit land. He leased out his lands to one Ladha Ibrahim Sheth for Rs. 982 of 1938 in the court of the I Class Sub Judge at Poona. The rent note provided for payment of the agreed rent in the month of Pousb every year and stated that in case of default the tenant or his heirs would have no right over the land. The appellant filed a suit against Ladha for possession on the ground of forfeiture. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court granted relief against forfeiture. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts should have interfered with the discretion of the lower courts in refusing relief against forfeited forfeiture in the circumstances of this case. HELD: (1) The rule applicable for the exercise of the discretion in such cases is that a tenant cannot by his unilateral act and by his own wrong determine the lease unless the lessor gives an indication by some unequivocal expression of intention on his part of taking advantage of the breach. [682 F] (2) The requirement as to written notice provided in the section therefore cannot be said to be based on any general rule of equity. It is one thing to decide what is the true meaning of the language contained in an Act of Parliament. No rule of Equity can be invoked in the case of a tenant of this description. [864 D] (3) The rules of justice, equity and good conscience also govern those transfers. It has to be seen in every case whether the particular provisions of the Act relied upon restates a known rule of law prevailing at the time and the only rule applicable seems to be that a lessee cannot by unilateral act or by his wrong determine a lease unless he gives an express indication by any unequivocal expression Of intention on the part of the lessor. [874 E] (4) The mere fact that the lessor gave notice of his intention so to do does not mean that the lessee should have given notice of its intention so as to do.

The respondents were called upon to submit their explanation in respect of the charges levelled against them. The Enquiry Report was forwarded to the General Manager who after considering the entire evidence led before him came to the conclusion that the first three charges were fully proved and the fourth charge was partly proved against all the respondents while the additional charges against Emmanual and Mohd. Rauf were further charged with threatening the gheraoed staff with dire consequences, if they moved out; and Mohd., Rauff, the then General Manager of the appellant company withdrew from the enquiry on 24th October 1968 on the ground that while fomenting the strike the conduct of Emmanulual andMohd. Rahaf was not done, whereafter the enquiry proceeded ex parte and on a consideration of the entire evidences led before it the Enquiry Officer came to conclusion that all the four charges were partly proved and fourth charge against each of them was partly established against all of them while the fifth charge was partially proved against both the respondents. The appellant challenged the Award in the High Court by means of a Writ Petition (Misc. 129 of 1970) contending that assuming that the enquiry was vitiated for the reason mentioned by the Arbitrator even then once serious mis conduct was proved by leading evidence before the learned Arbitrator it was not open to him to interfere with the punishment of dismissal unless the punishment was so harsh as to smack of victimisation. The High Court dismissed both the writ petitions holding that though before him the Management had by leading evidences proved their mis conduct by establishing the first two charges against all, the fifth charges againstEmmanual, Mohd.Rauf could be confirmed but set aside the dismissal in respect Of Rama Shanker and Barmapradhan on the grounds that while conducting the enquiry the Enquiry Report did not contain any opportunity to meet the charge framed against each one of them. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The only ground on which inquiry was held to be invalid by the arbitrator and by the High court must disappear. [209E] 2.1 In the instant case, the enquiry got vitiated the entire field of determining the mis conduct as also the punishment therefor became open and the Arbitrator had directed their reinstatement. It is thus clear neither under the ordinary law of the land nor under industrial law a second opportunity to show cause against the proposed punishment was necessary. [210F] 2:2 The only reason on which enquiry was held was that while passing the order dated 14th September, 1968 the Enquiry Committee had not considered the entire record of determining whether the first four charges against the Emmanianual and Md. Ruf were fully established and the fifth one was partly found guilty of misconduct defined in Standing Order No. 365 of 1970. [211F] 3:3 The only question on which the inquiry was vitiated by leading testimony before the Arbitrator was whether the enquiry held to have been vitiated for any reason mentioned in the relevant sentence of para 3 of the Standing Order. [212E] 4.1 The Arbitrator had misconstrued Standing Order Nos. 365 and 368 of 1970, which speaks of awarding lighter punishment like dismissal and since specific mention of opportunity as made in cases of graver punishment in the various sentences of para 2 it must have a meaning and the words cannot be considered a surpulsage and, therefore, the opportunity mentioned in para 3 refers to the second opportunity being given to the delinquent at the stage of inflicting the punishment. [214F] 4:4 The Arbitrator has held that though after he had taken into account the previous service record of the Respondents by his order dated 31st December, 1968, the Enquiry report was forwarded and it was found that the fourth charges against Shri Raufef could not be confirmed because while fo feeding the strike, the conduct was not proved.

The appellants were occupying private forests or unsur 111 veyed lands to be deemed tenants ejected from the land. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended by Act 35 of 1969. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the benefit of the above section would apply only to persons whose posses sion had a lawful origin and not to persons m unlawful occupation based on trespass or forcible and unlawful entry. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the expression "in lawful occupation" occurring in Section 7D must be construed as meaning "in actual occupation". Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to those persons whose possess ed lands had a valid origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to he Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had come into posses tion with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. [114D] 1.2 The expression "In occupation" occurs in Section 2(b) of the Act. It is not within the contemplation of the section that the occupation by such person was on the ground of an oral permission or an unregistered deed purporting to be a lease deed granted by a person who had no right over the land or who was not competent to lease the land, [114E] 1:3 The expression 'in lawful possession ' occurring in section 7 D must be interpreted as meaning 'in actual posses ment. " In the present case the finding of fact entered by the High court is that the appellant had come in possession of the lands by trespass. Therefore the benefit under Section 7 D would apply to persons who had wilfully trespassed upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin. [115F] 1 :4 The expression in occupation" appearing in Section 6D must, therefore, be construed in as meaning (in lawful posses tions) 'in possession '. In the instant case the findings of fact recorded by the courts are perfectly correct. For a proper understanding of the scope and intendment of Section 7A it is necessary to examine the setting and the context in which the said section occurs in the Act, [115G] 1.:5 The expression used in Section 8D must have been construed as including 'in due occupation '. It was not within that contemplation to confer the benefit on persons who were cultivating land on varam arrangement. [116H] 2.1 In the facts and circumstances of the case the High Courts were in error in holding that section 7A would apply even to persons possessing lawful origin in a sense that it did not have any lawful origin. The finding of facts entered by them is perfectly correct.[114G] 2:2 The appellant was not entitled to the protection of Section7D.

The appellant was convicted under section 135(b) (ii) of the , and sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. Goods in respect of which this offence was found to have been committed were also confiscated. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's simple imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the presumption contained in section 123(1) of , could not be applied when the case came up for trial before the Presidency Magistrate who actually decided it on 15 7 1969, and that even if the appellant was deemed to be in possession with full knowledge of what the goods actually were. the Court could not go further and assume them to be smuggled or imported into the country from another country of their assumed origin after a time when the restrictions on their import had been imposed. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The presumption contained under section 123 (1) is a procedural rule and they could be applied whenever the case comes up for trail before the Magistrate who finally decided it. [542A] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant had not produced evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there, or that there was any reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. He had not given any evidence to prove that his goods were smuggled or brought into the Country without payment of customs duty at a time before the restrictions imposed on their importation had been impose. The admissibility and sufficiency of (1 ) [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 364, referred to. 2.2 In the absence of any evidence in support of the presumption under section123(1), the burden of proving that they are smuggled goods shall be on the person from whose possession the goods were seized. [543B C] 3. The onus of proving innocent possession of these goods upon the appellant is not discharged by the prosecution. It is immaterial that the appellant has not produced any evidence or that he should permit them to have use the portions reserved by them for himself, and, (2) that, the goods in question were actually smuggled or bring into the India without payment thereof at a later date when payment of such duty had become obligatory. [544C] 3:3 In the present case, there is no evidence to establish that the goods are smuggled or not imported into India. The appellant was dealing with them knowing them to he be smuggled goods. He was dealing in them knowing it to be foreign goods. It was immaterial that he was dealing dealing with these goods knowing them about them to being smuggled or import into the territory of India without paying customs duty. [546D] 4:4 In the circumstances, the presumption is not attracted when the appellant himself was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. The burden of proof that the consignment was smuggled or was brought into India is on the appellant. Burden of proof in certain cases. [547E F] 5. Section 123(I) of . cannot be applied where the case coming up for investigation before the magistrate who actually decide it on merits, and the Court can take a different view of the matter.

The appellants were members of the Association at Budhar. The Association was formed in contravention of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The association functioned through a President and a pioneer worker; they kept accounts and distributed the profits. The Society functioned by a president and a Pioneer workers. They kept accounts, distributed the profit. The appellants were joined as proforma defendants. The suit was decreed in favour of the plaintiff appellants. The preliminary objection raised on behalf of respondent no. 1 was that the suit was not maintainable because the provisions of section 69(3)(a) of Indian Companies Act were not applicable to the case and the appeal filed by the plaintiffs must fail. Held, that the provisions Of section 4 of the Vindhya State Companies (Transfer of Property) Act, 1947, are in these terms: " 4(1). The members of a firm have no remedy against each other for contribution or apportionment in respect of the partnership dealings and transactions. The members have no right to bring a suit for accounts of the association which was dissolved in February 1948. The partners have no option but to keep them in their pocket. Such a claim is clearly negatived. [775 D] (2) It is not confined to affording a party a protection, of which he may avail himself or not as he pleases ". The appellants had not asked for a return or refund of their subscriptions; on the contrary they have asked for rendition of accounts in enforcement of an illegal contract of partnership. [771 E] (3) It was not confined only to affording an opportunity to be heard before the preliminary objection could be raised at this late stage. The question whether the suit is maintainable must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The object of section 5(2)(a), therefore, is to give a party an option of taking over the consignment. [773 G] (4) It has been held by this Court in U. Phyu vs Sardar 774 Bahadur that where there was no direct compulsion that a partnership firm must be registered, though the disabilities consequent on non registration may be extremely inconvenient. The right to sue is not absolute but conditional and it is subject to the conditions prescribed under section 5 of the Partnership Act.

The petitioner was prosecuted for the offence of murder under section 302 IPC read with sec. 54 and 39 of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972 on the allegation that he had committed the murder of a elephant. The prosecution case was that the petitioner was the owner of a large number of elephants in the State of Bihar and that the matter was under investigation by the police. The petitioner contended that the Magistrate acted beyond jurisdiction in taking cognizance against him when for the same allegations the investigation was proceeding and pending. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Judicial Magistrate acted without jurisdiction in passing the order of taking cognizance. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the judicial Magistrate acted outside jurisdiction in issuing process under section 190(1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 when for an offence under sec. 258 of the Act the investigation is proceeding and that therefore the Magistrate acting beyond jurisdiction could not take cognisance more than once and, accordingly, section 210 had no role to play. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Judicial Magistrate acting without jurisdiction committed a serious offence apart from the fact that cognizance of such an offence can only be taken on the complaint of the Chief wild Warden or such other officer as the State Government may authorise in this behalf. [929G] 1.2 In exercising that jurisdiction the High Court would not embark upon and enquiry whether the allegations in the two complaints are likely to be established by evidence or not. It is, therefore, necessary to analyse and compare not the allegations but the ingredients of the two offences and see whether their identity is made out . [930C] 1:3 The Judicial magistrate acted beyond the jurisdiction in initiating proceedings for taking cognisance of the offence under section 258 of 1987(R) and Crl. Misc. Jha, J. [Sundaram vs State of Maharashtra ; , referred to. 2.1 In exercising the powers under section 156(2) of Cr. P.C., 1973 the High court would not be attracted having regard to the position that cognizance can only take in one way and that on the complaints of a particular statutory functionary there is no scope or occasion for taking congnizance more than twice once and the Magistrate takes cognisance less than once. [1030D] 2.2 The Judicial Magistrates acted beyond their jurisdiction in entertaining the complaint when for some reason the investigation had not been proceeded with. They were therefore, justified in taking cogn cognizance against the petitioner when for a different allegation the investigation could not be proceeded with and that there was no scope of interference by the High Courts in exercise of its powers under Article 226 of the Constitution. [1130C D] 2:3 In exercising jurisdiction the Supreme Court would ordinarily not embark on and enquiry Whether the allegations are likely or not, but, if they do not constitute a part of the same offence, they cannot be said to have been established by the evidence or is not made out. [1231D] 4.1 There can be no doubt that the power under section 154(2), Cr.P.C. is discretionary and it is not necessary for the Magistrate to take cogn cognizance more than thrice once and then, he has to consider whether there are sufficient grounds for taking cognizance of an offence. [1330F] 4:3 It is a well settled principle that in exercising jurisdiction under section 200(1) Cr. PC., the High 'Court would not ordinarily embark upon or enquiry whether there is sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused. [1431C D]. 4.2 There can also be no dispute that the investigating officer acted beyond his jurisdiction in filing a complaint and issuing summons to the petitioner. The Magistrate acting under section 202(1), Cr P.

The petitioner was released on bail by the Magistrate under section 167(2) Cr. P.C., and he moved this Court again to modify the original order "to the extent that petitioner be released on furnishing surety to the tune of Rs. (2) If the court decides to grant bail with sureties, what criteria should guide it in quantifying the amount of bail, and (3) Is it within the power of The court to reject a surety because he or his estate is situate in a different district or State ? Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 A liberal policy of conditional re lease without monetary sureties or financial security and release on one 's own recognizance with punishment provided for violation will go a long way to reform the bail system and help the weaker and poorer sections of the community to get equal justice under law. [327C D] 2.1 The Supreme Court exercises wider powers with grater circumspection. It has been repeatedly held that a liberal policy is necessary. The court of appeal may release a convict on his own bond without sureties. Such a strange anomaly could not be, even though it is true that the Supreme Court exercising wider powers in respect of pre trial release which has now been developed in socially advanced countries and particularly the United State should now inform the decisions of the Magistrates in regard to pre trial releasing. [428D E] 2:2 The Supreme court exercises wider power with grue circumspection. The experience of enlightened Bail Projects in the United States such as Manhattan Bail Project and D. In one case the poor accused is fleeced of his moneys by touts and professional sureties and sometimes has even to incur debts to make payment to them for securing their release; in the other he is deprived of his liberty without trial and conviction and this leads to grave consequences, namely: (1) though presumed innocent he is subjected to 343 the psychological and physical deprivations of jail life, usually under more onerous conditions than are imposed on convicted defendants. [427F G] 3:3 The Supreme Courts exercise wider powers With grater caution. It would be appropriate if the court is powerless to dispense with surety or to receive an Indian bailor across the district borders as good or the sum is so excessive that to procure a wealthy surety may be both exasperating and expensive. [416F G; 428A] 4:4 The Supreme courts exercise wider power in respect to pre trials release which have now been established in socially and advanced countries, particularly the National Bail Research Commission, held in 1964 that bail reform was necessary. [414C D]. 5:5 In the instant case, the petitioner is entitled to bail on his executing bond without surety or financialsecurity and release from jail because any sentence has been passed.

The assessee, a newly established undertaking, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1951 52. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee on the ground that no question of law arose out of the order of the Tribunal refusing to state the case and refer it to the High Court under section 66(2) for an order directing the Tribunal to state a case and to refer it, if the Appellate Tribunal had refused to state it. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the assessee 's claim on the view that no questions of law arise out of such order. The Tribunal however modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to 'Castle ' in the computation of capital invested for the purpose of 429 section 15C. The High Court, however, held that the finding of the Appellate Assistant commissioner was one of fact as it was based on a presumption arising from the non inclusion by the Income tax officer in the assessment in question of the income of 'Costle ' and that "the factor taken into consideration by the Appellate tribunal in coming to the conclusion, it did," was a relevant factor. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Courts were in error in law in arriving at its finding on a question of fact. [446 B] (2) The Tribunal had considered evidence covering all the essential matters before arriving at the conclusion. It could not be regarded as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court.

In view of the order made by this Court, the appeal is against the order of the High Court dated November 18, 1974. The Minister concerned heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The writ petition was thereafter amended and 97 in the amended petition Duggal respondent also challenged the validity of .the later order of February 18.75. At the resumed hearing of the appeal before this Court it was contended that looking to the facts of the case if the High court came to the conclusion that the Minister was a necessary or proper party, this Court should not interfere in the matter. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The direction for impleading the Minister as a party is given by the High Courts with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. [97D] 2. The other part of the Order whereby the Minister concerned was directed to file his personal affidavit is set aside. The appeal shall stand disposed of accordingly. [98F G] 3. The High Court was in error in directing that the Secretary be impleaded as a respondent. [991B] 4. The order whereby the Secretary of the Department was directed not to file an affidavit. It is essentially for the Minister, concerned to decide in the light of the allegation made in petition as to whether he should or should not file an Affidavit.

The respondent was the owner of a house and buildings mentioned in the section. The appellant filed an application under article 227 of the Constitution for realisation of a sum of Rs. 1,000 as rent on land and buildings. The magistrate held that he had jurisdiction and issued warrants for attachment of the movable property of the respondent on June 13, 1961. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to entertain the application under section 259 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court could not interfere with the order or the magistrate if it came to the conclusion that the magistrate had no power and issued warrant for attachment. HELD: (1) The section provides for recovery by suit also and as such it wilI not be possible for the Board to recover rent of land and building let out by it even by suit if the rent in the case was not claimedable by the Board under the Act or the Rules. [347 C] (2) The High court could not have interfered with the orders or the Magistrate if it had come to the conclusions that the section did not apply to the facts of this case. [349 D] (3) The provisions of the lease in favour of the respondents were not intended to be included in the expression "claimable by a committee under this Act" in section 259. It was not possible for him to contend that this was what the Legislature had intended. [348 E F] (4) The words "rent on land" and "under the rules" did not appear in section 260. But if the expression 'rent" is confined to money due under some express provision of the statute it will lead to a strange result.

The appellant was appointed as a section salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. The various correspondence and other evidence produced before the Labour Court showed that the appellant was employed for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sales of the company. The Tribunal also found and in fact it has referred to as an admitted case of both the parties that the respondent company sells its product i.e. cigarettes manu factured by it directly through their wholesalers who in turn sell the product to various dealers appointed by the company in the area. The Labour Court held that the appel lant was not a "workman" and that, therefore, the reference was incompetent. It also found that the reference had been incompetent. In appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the finding of the Tribunal that the termination itself was illegal was erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question whether an employee is a workman is a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before it. [401B] 2.1 In the instant case, the finding on the nature of the work is a finding on a question which could not be termed as either manual, skilled or unskilled in nature. Such a person cannot be termed a workman. The duties involve the suggesting of ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a studyof the market condition. These duties do require the imaginative and creative mind which could Not be termed either manual or clerical in nature.[401C] Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distribution Company vs Burmah Foreman Management and Staff; , D.S. (42) P. 440, J.J. Dechane vs State 476 of Kerala and others ; ; D. S. (43) P, 440, Burmah Birdi ties & Horticultural Co. Ltd. vs Burma Shell Management and staff; , E.C. (4) P., 440, referred to. 2.2 The appellant was not an "workman". He was employed to do canvassing and promot ing sales for the company and to collect the amount of sale proceeds and depositing the same with the company, but it was only incidental to his main function of canvassing and promoting sale of the product of the Company in the four districts allotted to him. The appellant cannot be regarded as a workman under the Industrial Dis putes Act. [467C D] Burmahu Shell Oil storage and Distribution Co. vs 1959 11 LLJ 9; Burmah Halsbury Oil Storage & Distribution Co., Ltd. and others, ; , D S. J. Decane Distributor vs State 480 of Kerala & Ors., ; , referred to and relied on.

The appellant company entered into a contract of lease with the Gwalior State Government (Sanitary Engineering Department) for a period of one year in Samvat 1999. When proceedings were initiated on 16.7.1952 to eject the Company, the Company filed suit No. 14 of 1960 for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The Company filed an application under section 182(2)(i) of the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1959 for eviction of the Company. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the land admeasuring 495.05 acres was held by the Company in terms of the lease granted by the State and the Company was not a `pakka ' tenant and did not enjoy the status of a " Gair Maurusi" tenant. The High Court, however, reversed the judgement of the trial court holding that since the land was neither zamindari nor ryotwari land, the provisions of the Zamindari Abolition Act did not apply, since they were already held by a State when that came into force or who may in future be duly recognised as such by a competent authority. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The Additional Collector had rightly taken note of the fact that the Company had been holding the land from the State Government when that coming into force of the Act No. 66 of 1950 and that appeal was pending in this Court. [299D] 2.1 In either event, the company has been holding a land from its State. Land revenue Code, 1958 as "a person holding land from a State Government under section 181", Section 182(4) of that Code reads: "182. (2) Every person who at the coming into operation of this Code (a) hold any land in the Madhya Bharat region as an ordinary tenant as defined in the M P. LandRevenue Code, 1949; or (b) hold such land as an Ordinary tenant as define in the Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007 (66 of 1950); or (c ) . . . " [299E] 2:2 The Additional District Collector was well justified in having recourse to the proceeding prescribed under section 183 of the Code. [300B] 3.1 Section 182 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue & Tenancy Act does not apply to lands which were already holding by the Government when the coming in force of this code (a person holds land from State Government, under section 61(2) of this Act; or . . [299C D] 4. The provisions of section 182 of that Act do not apply in respect of lands which are acquired by the Gwalior Government under the lease deed dated 9.2.1971.

The appellant, a raiyat of land in the State of Orissa, was granted exemption from the operation of the ceiling on certain lands vested in the Government under section 45 of the principal Act. The appellant challenged the validity of the provisions of the Act by way of writ petitions in the High Court which were dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the provisions contained in Ch. IV of the Orissa Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1965, were inconsistent with or take away or abridges any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III Constitution; (2) the proviso to article 31 A of the Constitution was not applicable to the landholders who challenged the vires of section 45 and (3) the right of the appellant to resume land for personal cultivation, the extent of that right and the proceedings for resumption of land. HELD : (1)(a) The provisions contained therein were inconsistent in or take off or abridges the fundamental right conferred by article 31A of the constitution. [ 595 A] (b) The proviso to section 47 of the amending Act was not attracted to the appellant 's case because the subsequent legislation sought to restrict the ceiling limit and to vest the surplus land in Government under Section 45 as amended, there was compulsory acquisition of land which may be laid only if the law provides for payment to the landholder for extinction of his interest, the market value of that part of the surplus lands which is within the ceiling limits applicable to him under a law for the time being in force. [595 D] (c) The right of an owner to resume possession of land for his personal cultivation was not affected by the amendment made in the Constitution by the 17th Amendment Act, 1955. [599 E F] (d) The appellant ' s case fell within the ambit of section 47 and therefore the provisions were void. [659 G] (e) The High Court was right in holding that section 47 was not a law in force, but it was not necessary to consider whether the provisions in Ch., IV of Act 13 of 1965 were inconsistent or take out or abridge any fundamental rights. [557 E F; 596 A B] (f) The contention that the proviso was not retrospective because the amending statute provided for payment of compensation at a rate which is less than the market price of the land falling within the maximum limit under the principal, Act was also not correct.

The widow of Bai Kashi, who was the adopted son of Bai Ramavindra Nath, filed a suit for partition of her properties on the allegation that, by adoption, Sivabhai became a co owner to the extent of half share in them. The trial court recorded its findings on both these issues after taking additional evidence and its finding were in favour of the plaintiffs. On appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal and gave a declaration in favour Of the appellants to the effect that there was disruption of the joint family in the year, 1913. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that (1) the widow by suffering the trespassers to remain in possession of her husband 's estate for more than the statutory period had placed it ab solutely beyond her power to deal with it any further; and (2) the right of the adopted daughter to challenge the alienations during her lifetime was not prejudiced by the unauthorised transfer. HELD: The widow by making a surrender of her deceased husband 'S, who got the property by way of gift from her, could not be defeated by the surrenderee who gets the property through the widow so as to allow the transfers to remain valid for her lifetime. [349 E] (2)(a) In the case before us no equitable considerations at all arise in the present case. The right of a widow to challenge it is no part of the widow 's death. It is not correct to say that the transferee acquires necessarily and in law an interest commensurate with the period of natural life of the deceased, but such adopted son is given the rights of a posthumous son and the fiction is that he was in existence from before (1 ) Vide Vaidyanatha vs Savithri, I.L.R. , referred to. (b) The widow 'S 's right to challenge an alienation made by her after surrendering her husband's estate cannot be defeated merely because it would not work any hardship if the reversioner, in whose favour the surrender has taken place, had succeeded to the estate of the last male owner and derived title from him, he is nevertheless 1stiously from challenging any alienations made by the widow during her life as if he were a grantee from her. [350 G H] (3)(a). The right to recover possession of the property during the widow "s lifetime" on grounds of equity, justice and good conscience in proper cases, it is not possible to say, by voluntary act operate her own death.

The appellants were the Directors of a company. The Company was dissolved by an order dated November 15, 1977 under section 169 of the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order and also the validity thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the requisitionists were not entitled to requisition the meeting. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had erred in holding that there was no provision in the Code for charging orders, but on the Original Side of the High Courts, which had inherited the older jurisdiction of the Court of Chancery, it was urged that the Cotton Mills Company could not, therefore, join the other requisitionists in issuing the notice under section169 of the Act calling upon them to call the extraordinary general meeting and without the support of the shares held by the Cotton Mill Company. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding on the facts that none of the provisions referred to above has any bearing on the question before it. [878G] 1.2 In view of the fact that none were opposed of the removal of the sitting Directors also filed an application for being impleaded as a party, the High 'Court was justified in holding the requisitionist to be a shareholder of the company. [889A B] 1:3 The High ' Court was right therefore in holding against the appellants. [878C] 1 :4 In view Of the fact, that none was opposed of any removal of a sitting Directors, it is not possible to hold that the Company could be joined as a shareholder in issuing notice under Section 169 of Act calling for the extraordinary General meeting and after the receipt of the requisition from the shareholders, the remaining requisitionists would not have been eligible to requisition. [899D] 1.:5 The High `Court was right, therefore in setting aside the order of the Board of Directors. [868G] Hawks vs Mc. II at page 1510 is instructive and it reads thus: "There is no provision for charging any orders but on Original Side. On the Original side of the Allahabad High Court, which has inherited the younger jurisdiction of this Court of Calcery, there is no mention in the order that it enables the Court on the one hand to gain time and on the other hand to protect the decree holder. The shares belong to the company and the orders referred to therein cannot have any effect on them.

The petitioners were plaintiffs. The Panchayat in the course of its written statement inter alia pleaded that the Court before which the suit had been instituted had no jurisdiction to try it by virtue of section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. The trial court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. It held that since the question involved in the suit was merely one of title to the suit land and it was not necessary to decide whether the suit property belonged to the Panchayat or not and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the petitioners. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A civil court has jurisdiction (a) to entertain or adjudicate upon any question whether any property or any right to or interest in any property is shamlat deh vested or deemed to have been vested in a Panchayat under the Act; or (b) to question the legality of any action taken by the Commissioner or the Collector or the Panchayat under this Act. [835B] 1.2 A civil suit is maintainable only when the defendant has claimed that the property in question was shamlat land and not shamlat Deh. The jurisdiction of civil court is limited to the question whether a particular property or a right to any interest in such property or is not shamil deh vested in it. [ 836A] 1:3 A civil Court has jurisdiction to entertain, adjudicate upon an issue whether any person claiming right, title or interest has been vested or declared to have vested in Panchayat under section 13 of the Act. The Collector and the Panchayat before the trial court had no power to decide such question whether the property was shamil land or not. [820B] 2.1 In the instant case, the plaintiffs who claimed to be the owners along with some others of the suit lands had avoided to seek a 836 declaration that the suit is not maintainable before the civil court. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration that they were shamlatted deh or not nor whether it belonged to them or that it belonged exclusively to the Gram Panchayat. [821C] 2:2 A Civil Court has no jurisdiction (as in the instant matter) to try any suit, application or execution proceedings. The civil court had not been taken away by virtue Of section 13(1)(g) of the Land Act which had been inserted by the Haryana Legislature into the Act by the Punjab Amending Act, 1976. [822C] 3:3 In the circumstances for the civil Court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question as whether the properties in question were shamil lands or not, it has jurisdiction under section 11 read with section 13B and not by the Civil court. [823D] 4:4 A civil civil suit can be filed only by a person claiming that any land has not been vested to a Panchayat. If the plaintiffs had claimed that he was the owner along with others of such suit land, they cannot by raising their plaint flied cleverryly by filing a suit for declaration that it is shamil property deh or otherwise and whether it belongs to the village Panchayat or the not. The Civil Court had no authority to decide the question in dispute between the parties. [825C] 4. In the present case, there was no finding of fact recorded by the trial Court that the land in question belonged to a Gram Panchayat and it did not belong to the same Gram Panchayat nor was it vested in them. The findings of the High Court are based on evidence and cannot be interfered with by this Court.

The appellant Board, in exercise of its powers under Section 49 of the Electricity Act, 1948, issued a notification on 27th May, 1988 to the effect that the Board had no power to demand additional security but the average consumption of three months should be taken as the basis for calculating the amount of such security. The appellant Board filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said notification and enhanced the rate of simple interest to 5 per cent per annum. The High Court held that the appellant Board had power to adjust its charges accordingly from time to time. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court erred in holding that the demand equal to the energy bill of two months or a little more is not unreasonable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board has power to make regulation. [782G] 1.2 The Board pays interest on the loans borrowed by the Board. Has this Court decided the question of rate of interest in jagdamba Paper Industries (Pvt.) Ltd. vs Haryana State Electricity Board ; , followed. 1.3 In order to maintain a balance between the interests of the consumers, it is necessary that the consumer should be given an opportunity to show cause why he should not pay the amount so demanded. [758E] 1:4 The Board is entitled, apart from framing uniform tariff, to insist upon such terms and conditions as the Board thinks fit. In one such case a man promised to give a 20 percent interest in all property that he might later acquire in Alaska in return for the Promisee 's payment of $1,000 and his cancellation of an $11,225 debt of questionable collectability. [759G] 2:5 The Board paid interest on loans borrowed from the State Government. The Board also pays interest at 6% per annum on the loan borrowed by it. The security deposit does not remain in tact like a fixed deposit but gets depleted day after day depending on the extent of consumption More often than not, the consumption charges and other dues exceed the security deposit.
