[761G] 3:6 In the instant case, the Board has framed uniform tariff to insist on such terms as the board thinks fit and proper. The rate of compound interest is fixed at 6 per cent. The respondent Board pays the interest on loan borrowed from State Government and not at 6%. The appellant company has no power or authority to demand any additional security deposit but the Board pays Interest on the advances borrowed by them. [765F] 3 :7 In the process 2 1/2 months elapse. The consumption security deposit is variable as per clause 28.2 (iv) If therefore, the object of consumption deposit is to ensure proper payment with reference to electricity supply, there is nothing arbitrary or unjustifiable. [764G] 4:8 The Board pay interest on all property which he might subsequently acquire in return For the Promi ty amount of security deposit before actual disconnection. No reason whatever has been assigned for such an increase of security deposited.

The appellant was employed as a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara. The charge sheet was not proper, that the Head Office of the appellant had no authority to deal with his case under the Standing Orders, that no evidence was allowed or filed on behalf of the employer and that the finding was based only on his statement and in particular his cross examination. Held, that there is nothing in the Act which warrants such a conclusion. Paragraph D of section 78(1) (D) of the Act gives the Labour Court the power to try offenses punishable under the Act and cognizance of such offenses .in respect of an industrial matter specified in Schedule III of the , and under sub section (2) every application under sub s.(1) has to be made in the prescribed form and manner. Reading section 78 as a whole, there is no doubt left in our minds that the legislature wanted the provision to be a comprehensive one. It can only exercise such jurisdiction as the statute confers on it : if there are certain pre conditions to the exercise of its jurisdiction, it must refuse to entertain any such application unless such pre conditions are first complied with. In the present case, the Labour court was not right in holding that the third respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application under section 42(4) of Act which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Courts and prayed for setting aside the order of the Labour Commissioner. The Legislature never intended to make a complete departure from the procedure to be adopted when powers under section 78 (1)D were to be exercised. A Labour Court is a creature of the statute and it can only exercises such jurisdiction, as the statutes conferring on it ; if there is some pre conditions for the exercise Of its jurisdiction , it must decline to entertain an application unless the pre conditions were first complied therewith. In other words, the legislature felt it unnecessary to make any mention of an order under paragraph D in section 84. The legislature did not intend to make such a complete deviation from the procedures to be followed when powers were conferred on it .in the circumstances of the case, there was nothing in section 78 which warrants the conclusion.

The appellants were inducted as sub tenants in the town of Ranchi. The respondents filed a suit for eviction on the ground that they had been occupying the property under a registered lease for 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971. The appellants did not accept the claim and filed before Munsif, Ranchi a case purporting to be an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Evic tion) Control Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The respondents contested the application and raised several points in defence which were rejected by the trial court. The company had granted the lease in favour of one S.M. Ganguli who on his death was succeeded by his legal representatives. The trial court held that the appellants ' application under Section 12 of Bihar Buildings Control Act 1947 (Act No. IX of 1947) before the Munsif was not maintainable as they were not bona fide and that the suit was barred by limitation. The High Court in revision set aside the order of eviction passed by the first appellate court and remanded the case to the trial Court for fresh disposal. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the application under s 12 of Act before the Sub Judge was not a plaint and the same was barred as the suit filed by the appellants as an application in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeal was barred. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question is whether the petition which was filed by appellants as a plaint or the impugned proceeding before the court below was not in the form of a plaint specially when the necessary verification was also there at the foot of the petition. [975G] 2.1 In a case dealing with compulsory retirement this Court may pass such decree or make such order as is necessary for doing complete justice in any cause or matter pending before it, and the present case is a most appropriate one for exercise of such power. The questions do not affect the substantive right of the parties as the controversy was concluded by the second appellate court in favour o the appellants. [ 975G H] 2:2 In the instant case, the question does not affect that the appellant 's application under Order XXI, Rule 58, C.P.C. is barred. The suit filed against the respondents as an objection to an attachment order under Order 21, Rule 59, C P.C., was to be treated as a suit and the impugned proceedings as the one in a Suit followed by a second appellate Court in favour thereof. [936B] 2 :3 In the circumstances, it is wholly immaterial as to whether the application original ly filed by appellant before the sub court was not at all maintainable. The appeal is allowed but the parties are directed to bear their own costs throughout throughout.

The appellant Society was elected as the Secretary of the Society. The suit was later transferred to the court of Additional Dis trict Judge No. 1, Jaipur City where it was renumbered as Suit No. 116 of 1974. After the institution of the suit, an election of the office bearers of the society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected. The appellant Society challenged the order before the High Court by a petition under section 1 15 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was also dismissed by the impugned judgment. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the exercise of inherent power under section 15 1 of the code of Civil Proce dure, a court can vacate an order obtained by fraud on it. If the appellant had consented to it, the court has the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set aside the decree if it is satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree on a fraudulent repre sentation made to it that the party had actually consented to the same. [237E] 1.2 In the instant case, the trial court failed to satisfy itself that Hari Narain Swami was not the elected Secretary of appellant Society with authority to withdraw the suit. The High Court while confirming the order, said that in the exercise Of inherent power, a Court can vacate any order obtained on it and set aside that decree if the court is ultimately satisfied that it is likely to be satisfied that such consent as fact was wanting and the Court was induced by fraud practised upon the party having actually consented. [238G H] 1:3 In the present case, there is no dispute about the election of Sri Laxman Dass Swami. The trial court did not satisfy itself on the merits of the case. It had committed several serious errors in deciding the question as to who was the elected secretary and was, therefore, not entitled to withdraw it. [236F G] 1 :4 In the facts and circumstances of this case, it is clear that Hari Narayan Swami was neither its elected Secretary nor had any locus standi to withdraw his suit. It was, however, not authorised to withdraw a suit on the basis of a prayer purported to have been made on behalf of the appellant Society at all and the impugned order was passed as a result of the court being misled. So far the finding of the trial Court that Hari Shankar Swami was no elected secretary or was, hence, not competent to withdraw is concerned, the same suffers from several errors and requires a recon sideration. [239G H; 239A] 1.:5 In the absence of any specific provision in the Code for withdrawal of the plaint under section 13(1) of the Act, the High court has rightly held that the trial courts have jurisdiction to recall its order permitting the withdrawal of suit under its inherent power and the High Courts have rightly held. [240B] 2:6 The High court while confirming that in exercise of the inherent power of the High ourt a Court cannot vacate an Order obtained by fraudulent repres sentation, made to itself that the parties had actually agreed to it. In the circumstances of the present appeal, the impugned judg ments of the courts below and the trial ci ture are set aside. The matter is remanded to the trial judge for reconsideration of the matter on merits. [243C D] 2.7 The trial judge shall decide the question afresh in accordance with law after taking into consideration all the relevant facts and material placed before him.

The appellant was sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 10,000 and in default six months ' rigorous imprisonment which had been awarded by the Presidency Magistrate to the appellant. The appellant took an appeal to the High Court which agreed with the learned Presidency Magistrate that the appellant had transferred by sale 10 High Denomination Bank Notes of the Denomination bank Notes of Rs 8,000 to the respondent. The High Court agreed with this view and held that the Ordinance lapsed or ceased to be in operation on the date of its promulgation. Held, that the words " for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation" were omitted from section 72 during the period specified in section 3 of the Act as they stood before the amendment of 1946. The words "for the space for not morethan six months" in section 72 of the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution Act, 1940, were not intended to include a temporary Act and the Ordinance was therefore not limited to the space which was actually used by the legislature for the purpose of making it effective. The fact that the Court cannot go behind a declaration of emergency made by the Ordinance making authority cannot affect this question. The Ordinance lapsed and ceased to operate at the expiration of six months after its repeal. It was not intended that the period of duration of the Ordinance in question should be determined having regard to the provisions of section 72 as they existed before the Act came into force. The effect of the deletion of these words from section 73 of the Constitution (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1939, was that the emergency had ended and if by operation of section 1(3) of the India and Burma (Ermergency Provision) Act 1940, the words ' for the time being in force" were substituted. The word "initiated" in the definition of "intimacies" in s. 2(2)(a) of that Act was not used to include an emergency which had already been completed before the Ordinance came into operation. The expression "inactivation" in cl. (b) of section 2(3)(a), means "to make a law". It is not necessary that the intention of Parliament was to extend the period for which the Ordinance should have been passed and it was not possible to say that the Act had lapsed or continued to be operative on the day when the Ordinance ceased to exist. The object of the saving clause in section 2 (3)(b) was to provide a special period of emergency. It is true that the word "shall" in sub s.(2)(b), means the period beginning with the date on which the Act was passed and ending with such date as His Majesty may by Order in Council declare to be the end of the emergency which was the occasion of passing of this Act. The intention of the Legislature was not to extend a period of time for making an Ordinance under section 72 but to provide that the provisions contained in section 73 shall cease to operate on the expiration Of six months and thereafter it would be deemed to have been extended by the Governor General 's Acts, thus enacted and the Ordinances thus promulgated were equated with the Acts of the Federal Legislature assented to by the President General. The Act was therefore a temporary one and could not be said to have lapsed or cease to be effective on the expiry of six month from the re assembly of the legislature.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge, who confirmed their conviction and sentence. The High Court upheld the conviction of the appellants but reduced the sentence to life imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the death penalty should be awarded only in rarest of rare cases; (2) the sentence should not be awarded unless there is a clear indication that the offence was committed with the intention or knowledge of the offender and (3) the punishment should not have been inflicted without any proper reason. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The death penalty is unmerited. It is a well settled principle of law that every decision contains three basic ingredients: (i) findings of material facts, direct and inferential. [1072C] 2.1 In a minority opinion, I emphasise the need for judicial restraint and the duty to avoid encroachment on the powers conferred upon Parliament. But the professed view does not stem from a firm belief in dignity of human life for them themselves advocate the death sentence penalty for certain classes of offenders, (ii) findings in criminal cases are not liable to be quashed merely because they are based on some evidence or direct or inferential; and (iii) the duty of care and caution is an integral part of the judicial process. [ 1072D] 2:2 The law of punishment under section302 I. P.C., has been largely settled by this Court and the High Courts are bound thereby. One thing is clear. But, after Ediga Annama 's case (l), the law of sentence under section 304 I.A. has been severely settled by a patchwork mediation which did not finally extinguish the fires of fury earlier ignited. [975E] 2 :3. The law does not refraite on the narrow survival of death sentence in our Code confined to its lethal aspect. But it is a mechanistic art which courts the cadavers to sharpen the sentence oblivious of other important criteria shaping a dynamic, realistic policy of punishment. That decision, it may incidentally be pointed out, has adverted to the "well settled principles" which have all these years governed the exercise of proper judicial discretion. But this does not preclude the courts below from falling into such fatal error. [0975F G] 2(a) The question whether death sentence should be granted or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances obtaining in such case. [1176G] 3:1 In the instant case, the law does provide for judicial intervention. But there has been antecedent irrigation irrigation between them. It was a mechanised art which Courts the creaters to slow down their sentences save by judges like Douglas and Thurgod Marshall, is that the gallows swallow, in most cases, the social dissenter, the political (1 ) Indian Penal Code, read with section 354(3) of the Code merely requires 'special reasons ' to the indicated for imposing the death Penalty. That view does neither stem from any firm belief nor jurist M.M. Singh 's Case. [1015G H] 2.(b) The law is that death penalty can be awarded or not should, in my view, be awarded if there is no clear indication to the contrary. [1007C D] 3.2 In a majority opinion, it is difficult to agree with the view expressed by this court in Rajendra Prasad 's cases (1).

The appellant was a Income tax Inspector. He was promoted to the post of Income Tax Officer in 1945. He had been confirmed early in 1952 as an Income tax Officer. The Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., by his order dated 2nd April, 1956 reduced the appellant 's rank from the post to that of an Income Tax Inspector. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the order passed by the Commissioner of Incometax was void and inoperative. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that no charge was framed as a result of any previous enquiry. The High Court held that the charges were not proved, but it was only after the appellant had been acquitted of charges involving corruption in the discharge of his duties that he was given the lesser punishment of demotion and neither dismissed nor removed from service. In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court did not deal with a number of submissions made because they had, apparently, been forgotten. HELD: (1) The question whether regular proceedings should be drawn up or started is a matter which must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [319D] (2) It does not exceed its jurisdiction by basing its decision upon an incorrect determination of any question that it is empowered or required to be raised in the course of a civil suit. Such bodies are deemed to have been invested with power to err within the limits of their jurisdiction; and provided that they keep within those limits, their decisions must be accepted as valid unless set aside on appeal. [519D E] (3) The High Courts had given its judgment eight months after it had heerad argumenst. It was probably because the appellant was absolved of charges involved involving corruption and violation of service rules that no chargesheet was framed against him. But, what is more important is the litigants must have complete confidence in the results of litigation. Justice, as we have often observed, must not only be done but must manifestly appear to be done. [619E F] (4) The appellant had a right to appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner against the order of the Commissioner. He could not say anything about the particular instances which formed the subject matter of the charges against the appellant. Unless the exclusion of evidence is of a kind which amounts to a denial of natural justice or would have affected the final decision it could not be material.

The appellants and the M.M.T.C. entered into direct contract with their foreign buyers for export of manga nese ore out of India. The contracts were inter se linked and connected and the sales effected were held to be sales in the course of export. The appellants contended before the Sales Tax authorities that these contracts were intrinsically linked and related and the sale effected was held to have been sales in their course of exports. The High Court held that the contracts between the M/s. S.T.,C. and their foreign buyer on F.O.B. basis were inter connected with the contract entered into by the M..M. T.C., and that the contract of sale was integrally connected with and connected with export of goods. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal held that these agreements were intrinsally linked and the contracts were held not to be integrated activities in the way of export of the country. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in holding that the Contracts between the appellants and M. M.T..C. were interconnected with the contracts entered into between them and their Foreign buyers on F.,O. B. basis. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The contracts between M/S. S T. C. and its foreign buyer are distinct contracts and it is the S. T.,C., which entered into a direct contract between the Corporation and their Indian buyers onF.O B.D. basis that the export or export of any goods under a separate contract with the foreign buyer to the latter will not make the two contracts either inte grated or the contract between them are different. The mere mention of F.o.B., price or F. O.B, delivery in contract between a merchant and the S T C. is not enough to establish that the transactions were inter interconnected. [466C D] 1.2 In the instant case, the contracts with M/ s. T C., and their Eo B.F.C.. are inter se connected and they are distinct and independent con tract of sale. The contract between M and its Foreign buyers is one between the corporation and their export and it has been the case of the appellant that the sales were effected in the progress or process of export, because the export was an independent one between them. [467D] 1:3 In the present case, there was no privity of contract between both the parties. The agreements between the S,T. C., & their foreign sellers on F,O B basis. The sales effected by M/ S.S. T,C. are interconnected and they have been held to constitute sale in the process of exports or export. There is no room for two or more sales in any the course o f export. [468G H] 1 :4 In the special leave petition the appellants challenged the assumption made by the High court to the effect that all contracts between them were linked and allied and the Sales effected were hold ted to be sale in their favour. The contention of the State was that there should be examination of five other contracts. It may be stated here that counsel for the State did not dispute that the decision in Serajuddin 's case (supra) applied to one of the six contracts but he disputed the application of the ruling in Serjuddin 'S case to the other five contracts. Only one contract was referred to in the High Courts. The S.D.,C, and their M.S.,C were the last purchasers of goods within the State of Andhra Pradesh because the exports were made by them to the S C.T,C, on F basis basis.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi 521 Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. Consequent upon this termination, an industrial dispute was raised and the Delhi Administration, by its order dated 24th April, 1976 referred the following dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication: "Whether the termination of services of Shri Mohan Lal is illegal and/or unjustified and if so, to what relief is he entitled and what directions are necessary in this respect?" The respondent management contested the reference on the ground that the appellant was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of the initial period, his service was terminated by letter dated December 19, 1974 with effect from October 19, 1975. The Labour Court held that the termination was illegal and unjustified and directed reinstatement of the appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs.. per month. The respondent challenged the award on the grounds (1) that the order terminating his services was not a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action; (2) that there was an inner indication that it was likely to be made permanent; and (3) that he had put in continuous service for not less than one year, his case would not be governed by section 25F. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the respondent management was a Salesman appointed under order dated July 21, 1973. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The termination of service of the workman is ab initio void and inoperative. [529G] 1.2 In Hariprasad Shivshankar Shukla vs A.D. Reverting to the facts of this case, admittedly the appellant had been on leave with full wages, earned in the previous years; ended on the expiration of nine days automatically may be, but cessation all the same. The termination was not by way Of disciplinary action. [525A B] 1:3 In Hari Prasad Shivs Shankar Shukla vs State Bank of Patiala, ; , relied upon. 2.1 There is no dispute that the services of the respondent were terminated during the extended period of probation and there was no inner indication in the letter dated July 10, 1974 that it would be likely to become permanent. The appellant had put into continuous service of 240 days for not more than one years. [500B] 2.2 There is also no dispute about the fact that the appointment was temporary in the first instance and there were an outer indication that this was likelyto be made Permanent. The question whether termination in the instant case was a punishment imposed by way or disciplinary action does not arise under any of the excepted categories. [511C] 2:3 There is nothing on record to show that the service of Shri was terminated during his period of temporary employment. In fact, there is no evidence to show the intention of the employer to terminate the services. The order terminating the services is ab legally void and invalid. [550D] 2 :4 The termination in this case was by way o disciplinary action and not by any disciplinary action or. The finding of the Labour court that the period of service was extended beyond September 8, 1974 cannot be sustained.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. The appointment was on temporary basis and terminable with one month 's notice. On February 5, 1955 the appellant was served with a "charge sheet" by the Settlement Officer, Bhatinda. The Deputy Commissioner by his order dated March 17, 1955 ordered that the services of the appellant be terminated forthwith and that in lieu of notice he will get one month's pay as required by the Rules. The appellant challenged the authority of the Settlement officer to hold the enquiry and submitted a memorial to the Minister for Revenue affairs. The High Court held that the order of termination was in contravention of article 311(2) of the Constitution as no reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order was given to the appellant, and quashed the order on the ground inter alia that the appellant had been served with the charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the settlement Officer with 719 which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) The order of dismissal from service was not in accordance with article 311 of the constitution as it did not comply with the requirements of article311(2). [721 B] (ii) The appellant had a right to hold an enquiry into his alleged misconduct, or inefficiency, or for some similar reason. The fact that he was a temporary employee and had no right to the post he occupied and under the terms of his appointment he was liable to be discharged at any time during the period of probation. [722 C] (iii) The question whether the appellant could hold an inquiry into his purported misconduct was not decisive of the question. It will make no difference whether the person who is a temporary servant, but, in principle it will make any difference whether he was appointed to hold such enquiry into His alleged misconduct. [758 D F] State of Bihar vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, ; , referred to.

The respondents Nos. 1 to 46 and others were in agreement that as the constitutional point which arises for consideration in this case relates to the interpretation of section 133(2)(b) of the Constitution, it will be enough to consider whether that section has been correctly interpreted and whether the Public Service Commission for the State of Jammu and Kashmir, hereinafter referred to as the Commission, had been consulted in accordance with its requirement. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government 's Order No. 643 HTE dated July 25, 1969, in regard to the appointments of respondents Nos 3 to 46. In appeal by certificate, HELD: (1) The Commission was consulted on the suitability of the candidates for promotion as Professors and the second requirement of clause (b) was also complied with. It is not provided by section 133 that all the members of the Commission should have interviewed all or any of the candidate, or that it was not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee consisting of only one of its members, so long as the commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the Committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. [873 H; 874 A B] (2) The High court erred in holding that the Commission was not consulted in regardto the principles to be followed in making the promotions in question, or on the merits. [820 E F] (3) The interpretation put by learned Attorney General is quite correct and we have no hesitation in approving it as in our opinion no other interpretation is really permissible on the plain language of the clause.

The petitioner was a Congress mem ber of that Assembly. One Shri Karpuri Thakur, who had remarked that he could express no view without knowing what had been printed and what had not been printed, delivered what has been printed in the Bihar Legislative Assembly on May 30, 1957. The Speaker read out the text of the notice sent in by Shri Nawal Kishore Sinha set out therein which referred to the issue of the Searchlight in question. He also stated that he would express no opinion without knowing whether any speech was printed or what had already been directed not to be printed. The petitioner contended that the Committee did not do anything for one year and then woke up one morning and then pressed the matter. Held, that article 194(3) of the Constitution is not attracted to the case on hand. The right to publish fair and accurate reports of Parliamentary debates, but actually the traditional privilege of Parliament continues in conflict with judicial opinion. It was not necessary for the House to make any law defining the powers, privileges and immunities of a House of the Legislature of a State, which was considered in Sankari Prasad Singh Deo vs Union of India, [1951] Mad. I. R. 880, referred to. The question whether a law made by Parliament in pursuance of the earlier part of article 194 (3) or by the State Legislatures in pursuance thereof could be declared void under article 19(1)(a) of Constitution must depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. It is true that a law which takes away or abridges any of the fundamental rights, it will not be a law passed in exercise of constituent power like the law which was consider in Sankri Prasad Singh 's case, but will be one made in exercise Of ordinary legislative powers under article 246 read with the entries referred to above and that consequently if such a law takes away, or abridges some of the rights it will contravene the peremptory provisions of article 13(2) and will be void to the extent of such contravention and it may well be that that is precisely the reason why our Parliament and the State Legislature have not made any law define the powers privileges, privileges, and immunities just as the Australian Parliament had not made a under section 49 of their Constitution corresponding to article 194. The fact that cl. (3), which was in force at the commencement of the present case, provided for the publication of the report of the Committee of Privileges and in the absence of such extension, the reference not being reported, the Committee became functus officio.

The respondents were appointed as Readers after the College had been taken over by the Government in pursuance of the unanimous resolution of the managing committee of February 18, 1970. The College was taken over on March 9, 1971 and the transfer to the Government was of all assets of the college but without any liability. The college was administered as a Government College. The management had to meet with financial crisis in the past and obtained financial help in the shape of liberal endowment under a trust deed from the then zamindar of Khallikote. The Colleges were taken over as a private college. The colleges were taken on the basis of unanimous resolution by the managing Committee of February, 18, 1971. The Government prescribed qualifica tion for appointment as a Reader by a Circular dated March 23, 1971 addressed to the Director of Public Instructions (Higher Education) Orissa, which appears to supersede the earlier circulars on the subject. The Director of public Instructions ( Higher Education), Orissa, issued a circular dated July 19, 1971, addressed to all the employees similarly situated on an absolutely artificial and irrele vant consideration results in denial of equal opportunity to the Respondents in the matter of employment under the Government under Article 16 of the Constitution. The respondents filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said circular. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the respondents were denied equal opportunity under Article 14 of the Consti tution and that they were not entitled to be appointed as Professors after the college had been transferred to the University. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the respondents are not entitled for equal opportunity; (ii) the High Courts have erred in holding that they are not eligible for appointment under Article 15 of the Constitu tion and that the High court has failed to take into consideration the fact that the college was taken as a going educational concern and it goes without saying that it must be administered on sound lines having regard to quality, efficiency and progress in all respects; (iii) the respondent institution had been given equal opportunity by the State Government under the circular of March 23. 1971, which is consistent with implementation of a correct educational policy and will not incur the frown of Article Article 16; (iv) the decision of the High Cou tions of the Managing Committee of the College dated March 9 1971, alone were relied upon by the state in connection with the appointment of the Respondents as Readers under the government circular of February 23,1971, and that it goes beyond saying that they will be suitable for appointment to the post of Reader; (v) the letter dated July 30, 1970 addressed to each of the employees of the private college, first time presented before the Government, was not a valid document because it was not signed by the Director or by any other officer. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were right in holding on the facts and circumstances of the case that the respondent institutions were denied equality under Article 19(1)(f) of the constitution in the matters of appointment as Readers. [782G H] 1.2 The High courts have erred by holding that there was no violation of Article 16 inasmuch as the respondents had been denied equal opportunities under Article 21 of the Con stitution and that their appointments were made on a purely temporary basis without any legal justification. [788A B] 1:3 It is well settled that in the case of appointment to a post, the initial appointment must be by consent, as long as the appointment is made on the recommendation of the Selection Committee. The appointment of such employees cannot be countenanced. [789B C] 2.1 In the instant case, the respondents have been denied equality of opportunity under article 16 of th e Constitution in the field of employment.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 A) for plying their vehicles on the route. The State Transport Authority granted them temporary permits to ply their vehicles in the route, but the application of the Corporation for three permits was rejected on the ground that once a scheme has been published in view of the provision contained in section 68 C of Chapter IV A of . 68 F (1 A). the Corporation alone will have to grant permit to the exclusion of any other applicant. The appellants applied to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and writ petition to the High Court for quashing the order of the State Government rejecting their applications, but that was dismissed on the grounds that once an application is made under section68 F(I A) by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled to obtain a temporary permit. The High Court held that since the scheme has already been published, it would be obligatory upon the State transport Authority or the Regional Transport Authority as the case may be to grant such temporary permits. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of Chapter III A of the Act are not relevant for the present purpose. [984 F] 1.2 The Corporation enjoys a preferential treatment in the matter of obtaining permits. While interpreting the provisions of section 68F (1A) and section 68 G(1C), it is undoubtedly true that the competing claims between the Corporation, and the other private operators may be examined with reference to the provisions contained in the Act. But if the Corporation does not apply for all the permits but only for some, the inevitable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation has made no application for the temporary permit and section68F(1A), would be squarely attracted. [1084 B C] 1:3 The State transport Appellate Tribunal as well as the High court were right in holding that the Corporation enjoys preferential treatment In interpreting the provision of Chapter V A of it is certainly true that while construing the provisions Of Chapter IVA of the it is not possible to gain said that there are 7 vacancies for temporary permit because the scheme had been published by the State. But, if the corporation does not applied for all these permits but merely for some reason the inevitable inference is that the corporation has made an application for grant only one permit, according to the Corporation. [986 C D] 1 :4 The Corporation has not recorded finding that in public interest remaining 4 permits were not required to be issued. Therefore, section 68 E F(l A) would be attracted. That is why power to increase strength of fleet operating on the routes is conferred and has to be exercised in public interests meaning transport facility to travelling public.

The appellant executed a registered mortgage deed in respect of the properties in dispute. The property in suit was ancestral qua the appellant 1101 and that the impugned alienations were not effected for consideration or for legal necessity. The trial judge held that the property in dispute was ancestral property and he was entitled to challenge its alienation by his father respondent 10. In appeal, the High Court set aside the decree and remanded the case for re substituting the legal representatives of the deceased defendant Ram Kala. The appellant then applied for and obtained a certificate from the High court under the first part of section 110 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit property was ancestral in nature and he had been given a declaration that the sale in dispute did not bind the appellant 's reversionary rights in the property after the death of respondent 10, and that even so it did not ask respondents 1 to 9 to go back to the District Court, but condoned the delay made by the said respondents in the presentation of the appeal before itself and proceeded to deal with the appeal on merits. Held: (i) The test laid down in Attar Singh 's case was clearly erroneous. (ii) It is true that in Mohammad Husain Khan vs Babu Kishva Nandan Sahai, A.I.R. 1950 P.C. 1105, the Privy Council held that under Hindu law a son does not acquire by birth an interest jointly with his father in the estate which the latter inherits from his maternal grandfather. But in Muhammad Husain Khan 's Digest which is regarded as an authority on the subject, does not support the appellant's case. (iii) The rule laid down by this Court in Mohammad Hussain Khan vs Mohammad Babu Kishwa Nandan Sahai and others, [1908] 30 P.R., 1105 case, would apply to Hindu law as well as to Hindu Law. (iv) It cannot be said that any pending actions would be disturbed because this right has already been taken away by the Full Bench in 1950. (v) The decision of the High Courts of Punjab as early as 1895 was not correctly decided by the community since 1895.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum on charges under section 449 and section 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of the 14th November 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on his Verandah of his hut, these appellants came there and while one of them Abdul Odud pressed his knees and Ekram and Habibullah pressed his chest and hands with Matiullah inflicted an injury on his neck with a dagger. The defence case was accepted by the Sessions Judge and convicted all the four under sections 449 and 307 readwith section 34. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for two years under section 307/34 of the Penal Code, and awarded the sentences to run concurrently. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there can be no conviction under section 450 of the Code unless murder has actually been committed. HELD : (1) The words "in order to" have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 but also in section 457 of the Evidence Act. [882 F] (2) There can be a presumption that an act is done by several persons, in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. [889 G H] (3) The fact that the murder was not actually committed will not affect the applicability of section 449 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The appellant, a Sarswat Brahmin, resident of Pathankot in the district of Gurdaspur, was a Sarmi Brahmin. He was a sarswatrahmin, who was a member of the family of Gurdial Singh and was a son of his father. The respondent 's case was that he had been excluded from inheritance by the collaterals up to the fourth degree with respect to ancestral as well as self acquired property of the last male holder excluded the daughter. The Subordinate Judge held that the lands in suit being in possession of tenants, the suit for a declaration of title thereto was maintainable but the suit was not maintainable. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court modified the decree of the Subordinate Judge to the extent that the declaration in favour of the male kindred up to certain specified degrees was made to relate only to the land in Khata No. 1 and not to ancestral property of her father. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was a custom according to which daughter was excluded from succession by the other members of the community, and that there were no such custom in the Gurdaspur district governing the parties under which a collateral within the fourth degrees excludes the daughter of the first male holder. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the evidence as to the succession to the property of Harnam Singh was of no assistance to the appellant for the reason that the Riwaj i ams of the Gurdasapur district and indeed a member thereof had no opportunity whatever of appearing before the Revenue authorities, the presumption will be weaker still and only a few instances would be sufficient to rebut it. [153 D E] (2) The evidence as regards the succession of the properties of Harnam singh was of little assistance to him for the reasons that the custom governing the party under which the collateral is excluded from the inheritance by her father, could not be said to have been established. [155 F G] (3) The appellant had fully discharged the onus that was on him by producing in evidence the Rwiwaji i am of the fact that the collateral was included in the joint family property of Gurdial singh and that the properties left by him were of no substantial value at all as would have made it worth while for the daughter to claim the same in addition to the properties gifted to her by her husband during his lifetime. [156 F G; 157 A B] (4) The presumption arising on these Riwazi i m ams was not accepted as correct in not less than six cases, namely, Bawa Singh vs Mt. (I.L.R. , Lah. (12) A.I.R., 1936 Lah. 252 and 1893 for those answers limit the exclusion in favour Of the male typered up upto certain specified degree. [157 D E].

The appellant, a Managing Director of Messrs Bird and Co. W. Bowen, applied to the Collector for adjudication of duty payable on a power of attorney, marked as Exhibit A in the proceedings, which he proposed to execute. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) of the Stamp Act to the High Court. The High Court held that the proper duty payable was Rs. 1,000 and that the appropriate duty payable thereon was Rs., 1,500. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the proper stamp duty payable under the instrument was Rs, 1,200; (2) the Collector had no power to determine the amount of stamp duty in respect of the instrument, and (3) the appropriate authority had no jurisdiction to decide the question as to whether the stamp duty was payable on the instrument. HELD: (1)(a) The expression "distinct matters" would mean something different from distinct "categories". [855 C] (b) The words "distferent matters" in section 5 and "descriptions" in Section 6 have different connotations. In its popular sense, the expression "Distinct matters", would connote something different than distinct matters. [856 D E] (2)(a). The expression 'distinct matter" would imply something more than a mere licensee; but whatever interest be enjoys in that property will be the subject matter of the power which he executes in favour of the donee. [ 855 C D] (3)(b) In the present case, the instrument under consideration was a deed of settlement which comprised certain Government securities as also other investments and under the Stamp law, it was chargeable with a single duty ad valorem on the value of all the properties settled. The instrument in question cannot be split up into separate instruments each comprising or relating to a distinct matter in so far as the different capacities of the donor are concerned. [820 E] In the instant case, there is no community of interest between the personal estate belonging to the executant and the trust estate vested in him, but whatever be enjoys, he could exercise all the powers as full owner qua whatever right, title and interest be enjoyed in the property, whether it be an absolute interest or a limited one.

The assessee, a company carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was formerly an Indian State. Later the name Kathiawar was changed to Saurashtra. In assessing the profits of the assessee for the year 1949 50 the Income tax Officer had therefore to proceed in accordance with the provisions of this Ordinance. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that no deduction should have been made on the basis of the words which would have been allowed to him if the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 was in force in the past as in fact no claim had been made or could be made for such allowance, and disallowed the claim of the appellant company. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the words "which would have got allo wed to him" were used in the Ordinance and not in the Act; (2) the depreciation which the assessee availed of under the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance was a deductible amount in computing the written down value of the assets. HELD: The words "such law shall have been allow to him". when they are used, they must be construed as having been allowed if proper claim had not been made and substantiated; (3) the word "or" is used in a sense which would mean that it should have got the effect of extending the Indian income tax Act. [231 B] The words 'which would otherwise have been granted to him " were used to mean "which shall have got to be allowed if a proper claim has been made, and so, depreciation actually allowed under a law relating to tax on profits of business which was law of a Part B State would come within the first portion of the clause.

The petitioner, a contractor, was awarded the contract by the respondent Corporation for construction of a Main Station Building of a Power House at the Raichur Thermal Power Plant at an estimated cost of about Rs. Paragraph I of the N.I.T. The petitioner submitted his tender books in view of the fact that M.C.C., had adequate experience in the construction of R.C, works and they were capable of mobilising the work force required for the work. The principal argument advanced on behalf of the peti tioner was that paragraphs I and V of the NIT specified certain pre qualifying requirements. It was further contended that paragraph I of N. I.T., which provided for prequalifying conditions, did not contain any condition precedent for the supply of forms of tender. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner 's contention that paragraphs 1 and V were not applicable to the case, was clearly untenable. [239D] 2.2 The respondent Corporation had relaxed its N.l.T standards in favour of the M. C.C.. works and had also furnished certain prequalification conditions. It is clear from para I of this N.i.T that only three prequal ent conditions were prescribed for information and are such they could be met before consideration of the tenders. The minutes relied upon show that after getting a clarification from the General Manager (Technical), the conclusion was reached that "the use of cement hollow block masonry may not be required at all and instead the brick masonry may be used". [239F] 3.1 In the instant case, the petitioner ' s contention that paragraph 1 of N I. T., which excluded other persons similarly situate from tendering for the contract and it was clearly arbitrary and without reason. The action of the respondent in accepting the tender of the 4th respondents even though they did not satisfy the pre scribed condition of eligibility, was plainly discriminato ry, since it excluded other person similarly situated from tendering the tender. [240F] 2:2 In the present case, there is no dispute that paragraph l of NI. T. which provided that only 3 prequalify conditions were to be fulfilled before acceptance of the successful tender. The fact that the petitioner had already supplied all the documents in time and sought no extension at all was clearly discriminat ous, since they excluded other parties similarly situate, from tendering, for the contracts all along. [241B] 4.2 In view of this clear position, it is not possible to accept the contention that the respondent corporation had relaxed the N I.,T. which excluded others similarly situated, from tender. It may not, however, be correct to read para I in isolation and treat it as the only condition precedent. [243C] 5.3 The second was that the party issuing the tender has the right to punc tiliously and rigidly enforce them. This is because, after getting clarification from a General Manager, the conclusion reached by the K.P.C.; the conclusion is reached that the use of Cement hollow blocks may not have been required at any stage. The second is that the parties issuing the tenders had the right, to punba tiliously or rigidly enforced them. [245D] 5:4 In the same way, changes or relaxations in other directions would be unobjectionable unless the benefit of those changes or relaxation were extended to some but denied to others. The third is that, as against the second requirement of para I(1) and (2), the prequalifica tion conditions contained in the brief tender notification, certain general requirements as described above will also be looked into.

The appellant was the owner of a house. At Lahore known as 5, Danepur Road. The appellant was put in possession of the said agricultural lands in Punjab Khore presumably by way of attornment 1120 of tenants who were in actual cultivating possession of these lands. The Custodian General rejected his application for confirmation on the ground that the Custodian General had no revisional power which he purported to exercise, and (2) was the order of the CustodianGeneral on its merits such as to call for interference by this Court. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the exercise of revisional powers in this case by the Custodian was without jurisdiction or is illegal. The contention of the appellant that the power of revision conferred by section 58(3) of the East Punjab Act XIV of 1947 which has been specifically made retrospective from the 15th August, 1947, operates in respect of the present transaction also cannot be accepted. Section 58(2) of 1949 which was specifically made prospective from the 14th August 1947, operated in respect to the case of a right of appeal against an order passed or to be passed in a pending action. The legislature by an amendment of the Income tax Act, which came into force on the 1st April, 1926, introduced section 66A and gave a right to appeal against such orders as provided therein. Section 55(3), however, did not apply to cases where the order was passed under the new Act a provision for appeal or revision had been made in respect thereof. The power of review conferred by the Act was not confined merely to appellate orders and there was no power given thereunder for revision by the Central Government.

The appellant, a small number of workmen in the neighbourhood of 5,000, was employed by the respondent. The dispute arose between the parties on the question whether bonus should be claimed as customary or traditional bonus. The Tribunal held that the conditions of service under all these employers should be governed by one standard and one criteria is, not tenable. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the Bonus Act did not provide for those categories of bonus demanded in 1965, (ii) the bonus Act did no provide for such other classes of bonus; (iii) the Tribunal had erred in holding that the bonus was customary or ordinary bonus and did not apply to customary bonus. HELD: (1) The Bonus Act does not provide that there should be contractual bonus or other species of bonus. [602 B] (2) The bonus Act speaks, and speaks as a whole Code, on the sole subject of profit based bonus, and does not govern customary, traditional or contractual bonus. It is not possible to accept the contention that it leaves untouched customary bonus; traditional or statutory bonus. Bonus has varying conceptual contents in different branches of law and life. The main object of the Act is to provide for payment of bonus based on profits and to recommend principles for computation of such bonus and methods of payment . [603 C D] (3) The Tribunal had not yet enquired into the merits. It was not even asked whether any evidence was produced before it or whether any other evidence was adduced before it, nor was it called upon to consider the relevant factors.

The Punjab Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1963 were amended from time to time by a notification dated September 2, 1977 rescinding the amendment introduced in rule 12 of the Punjab Superior judicial Service Rules. The petitioners who were directly recruited for recruitment to the Punjab Civil Service (Judicial Branch) after qualifying in a competitive examination held by the High Court, filed writ petitions in the High Courts challenging the validity of the amended rules and contending that the power to confirm a District and Sessions Judge resides in the Governor or in the State and not in the Chief Judicial Magistrate. The High Court set aside his reversion on certain other grounds but it held that the control over the subordinate judiciary vested in the high Court by Article 235 must necessarily override Article 309 wherever the two happen to conflict at all. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The control over subordinate judiciary is vested in a High Court by article 235. [1048C] 1.2 The control of the subordinate courts is vested with the High court in order to safeguard the independence of the judiciary. It is legislative power. As the High 'Court has been persistently refusing to follow, in the exercise of its administrative functions, the decision which was rendered by it in the exercising of its judicial powers cannot be challenged on the ground that it is arbitrary or unreasonable. [ 1049D] 1:3 The control vested in High Court over the district courts and subordinate courts, is exclusive in nature, comprehensive in extent and effective in operation. In the first place, in exercise of his administrative control over district courts, it is not open to the HighCourt to deny to a member of the Subordinate judicial service of the State the right of appeal given to him by the law which regulates the conditions of his service. The control is exclusive with the Governor beyond the period of two years. [1005E] 1 :4. The mere power to pass a law or to make rules having the force of law regulating seniority does not impinge upon the control vested by the high court over the District courts and the courts subordinate thereto by Article235 wherever the three happen to conflicts at all,. They are: (1) whether the power is exercised in accordance with the law governing the conditions governing their service; (2) whether such a power is justified on a proper interpretation of the relevant rules; (3) whether it is justified in applying the rule of rotation at the time of confirmation; and (4) whether, the High' Court based itself on the rule Of quota, is justified. [1015E F] 1.:5. The power to frame rules having force of Law regulating seniority do not impinge on the control of subordinate judiciary over the districts courts and Subordinate thereto by article235.[1049G] 2:6. The question for determination is whether the method of confirmation adopted by theHigh Court by rotation of promotees and direct recruits in the ratio of 2:1 is justified or not.

The petitioners, who were working as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of G.O.Ms. No. 1900 dated December 22, 1981 issued by the State Government and the order passed by the Tribunal directing that the zonal seniority be determined on the basis of the criteria laid down in paragraph 3(1)(e) of the Order. The Division Bench allowed the writ petition holding that the Zonal seniority is the criteria. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioners that (i) the zonal cadre is the criterion; (ii) the Zonal Seniority is the sole criteria and not the criteria; (iii) the order dated February 18, 1986 issued by G.0.Ms., which was published through G. O.Ms No. 1265 dated December 23, 1981, was in violation of the provisions of article 371D annulled that order; and (iv) the State Govt. had no power to bifurcate or reorganise a zone within a zone, cadre or cadres therein. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The word 'local cadre ' is used in the definition of local cadre in paragraph 2(e) read with paragraph 3 (7) of GO. Ms. No 1265, dated December 24, 1975, which was notified through GOMMs. A.) Deptt. dated January 24, 1981. [529G] 1.2 The word "local cadre" is used to mean the local area as a whole and not all the posts in the civil services of the State. Therefore, the phrase 'or constituted otherwise ' cannot be understood dehorse the scheme of the Presidential order. [630C D] 1:3 The words 'or formed otherwise ' in paragraph 4(7) are also not necessary. In fact, the word "or" used in paragraph 5(e)(i) is not used to describe the local cadre as a cadre but to describe it as a separate cadre. Therefore the phrase "or constitutedotherwise" cannot be construed dehor se the scheme Of the Presidential Order. [643E F] 1 :4 The words "or formed or otherwise" in paragraph 7 of the order refer ing to the local cadres within a specified part of the cadre and class or classes of civil posts, under the State as local cadres, and class and classes of Civil posts, and that too subject to the conditions precedent laid therein. [525E F; 526A] 1.:5 The word is used only to indicate the local areas which are regarded as a local area. It does not mean that the expression 'or" in the order should be understood as meaning "or forming otherwise". In fact the phrase used in paragraphs 5(7)(i), 5(2) and 7 of GOMMMs. referred to hereinbefore, is not intended to refer to the cadre or class or category of civil post under the state. [429G H; 526B C] 1):5 The words used in para 7 of order dated December 21, 1975 are also indicative of the fact that once the State Govern ment has orgaised the class or class of posts in a department and located within a particular zone, it ceases to have any power to alter or reorganize a zone. [ 526A B] 1.(6) The word used in clause (i)(e), means "or created otherwise" by act of parties or by operation of law or by eviction by the land lord or by assignment or transfer of the tenant 's interest. The phrase 'and constituted otherwise' cannot be interpreted dehorSe the scheme othe Presidential order.[529F] 1(7).

The appellant, a mortgagee in possession of certain lands mortgaged to the Bank by his own name and in the name of his son Chohan Ram. The mortgage was granted by the Court on the condition that the mortgagor would pay the dues of the Bank within six months from the date of the grant. The plaintiff obtained leave to appeal to Privy Council from this decision of the High Court. The appellant contended that he was subrogated to the position of the bank, that the decree which had been passed in the mortgage suit was binding on the defendants and that the defendant 2 was fully represented in the mortgaged suit, that he had no power to grant the permanent lease in question to the defendants, that since the plaintiff 's mortgage was subsisting, the decree in the suit was not binding on him, that as the mortgagor had in good faith granted the lease for a limited term a fair and reasonable rent, the mortgagee or the purchaser in execution of his decree could not repudiate it, specially as the mortgage deed did not prohibit the grant of temporary leases to middlemen or cultivators. Held, that section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act has nothing to do with the mortgagor 's power to lease the mortgaged property. The mortgagor is not normally bound by the acts of the mortgagor with reference to the mortgaged properties. It does not mean that a lease of this character is always operative against the mortgagee. The mortgagee is not ordinarily bound by his acts of his mortgagor with respect to the mortgage property. He is not usually bound by acts of parties with reference thereto, but he has no power whatever in the property demised to him. In such cases, the mortgagor acquires no interest whatever in it demised to the mortgagee, and the mortgagee is entitled to recover possession from the defendants. The lessee 's right of redemption does not necessarily mean that the lease in his favour was always operative upon the mortgagee 's security. The lessor is not generally bound by those acts of a mortgagor with regard to the property mortgaged. It is only when he has granted the (1) at p. 91, 92. 92. 93. 92, 93. 93 and 94. 94. 95. 96. 96, 97. 98. 98 and 99. 98 that the mortgagee in his possession had power to make a permanent lease of the mortgaged land. The right of the redemption does neither mean nor can it be said that a lessee from the mortgagor has power to create a lease in favour of the mortgagee to establish that the tenancy in his behalf was granted the usual terms in the ordinary course of management. The fact that there was no allegation in the plaint that the defendants had any power to execute the sale deed did make no difference between the plaintiff and the defendant, that there were no allegations in the pleadings that the plaintiff was sub mortgagee with possession of the four villages of which the defendants were in wrongful possession. The High Court was right in holding that the suit filed by the appellant was not maintainable as the appellant had failed to prove that he did not have such power to sell the mortgaged lands.

The petitioner, a retired employee of the respondent, filed an arbitration suits in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5 and 12 at 330 of the Act. The respondent filed an application for appointment of an arbitrator. The learned Single Judge dismissed the applications holding that Clause 68 of the Contract provides for appointment by the court where Arbitrator is removed or his authority revoked. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that Clause 67 of the contract provided for appointment and when the respondent had already made the claim for payment for the first time in July 12, 1979, the respondent was duty bound to appoint an arbitrator and on its failure it is open to him to approach the Court for appropriate remedy under section 8 of the Indian Limitation Act for appointment. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court HELD: 1.1 The claims of one party or the other might be put forward long after the persons who could give useful evidence had died and the most relevant documents had been destroyed if the legal defence were to be excluded, it would seem that the claims of either party or both may be put up long after they have died and in this case, as found by the High Court that though the petitioner was said to have made the claims for payment of the first two years in July, 12,1979, he issued notice to the respondent to refer the matter for arbitration. The question is when the cause of arbitration arises in the absence of issuance of a notice or omits to issue for long time or contract to the contrary? It would seem from the language used in section 3 of the Limitation Act that it is not a condition precedent that there should in the first instance be an order appointing an arbitrator or he should enter upon reference for adjudication. [368C D] 1.2 The words "any arbitration under it must be commenced when one party to the arbitration agreement serves on the other party thereto a notice requiring the appointment of such an arbitrator, or where the arbitration is not so commenced the claim concerned shall be barred. [369D E] 1:3 In the instant case, the petitioner had made the payment for more than 10 years after the respondent filed his application for reference under section 12 at 33 of the for short the Act and the Court exercised the jurisdiction in permitting the respondent 's revocation. The contention that Clause 66 of the agreement provided for arbitration was not to be deemed to have been commenced when another party to a dispute or differences had died, is clearly untenable. [370E] 1 :4 In the concluding findings it is said that there was an implied agreement between the parties to exclude any defence under any Statute of Limitations. The matter does not rest cause we have to consider how far the suggested elimination of defences available at law or in equity must logically be held to extent in other arbitrations. [371B] 1.:5 In the circumstances of this case as found, it is difficult to come to the conclusion that there had been an implied contract between the petitioner and the respondent by his conduct slept over his right for more years than 10 year from the date when the claim accrues. [372C D].

The appellants were the mortgagees of certain lands in Bihar. The decree holders filed a petition under section 47, Civil Procedure Code for passing a final decree on September 19, 1955. A final decree was passed in the mortgage suit on October 1, 1956. The judgment debtors resisted that execution by filing an application under section47, Civil. Procedure Code (Misc. A third application raising the same ground of objection (Misc.) No. 91 of 1960) was filed by the judgment debtors on September 12, 1960. The executing court came to the conclusion that the objection raised by the decree debtors is barred by principles of res judicata and further that the same has no merits. In second appeal by the appellants it was contended that the execution court had no jurisdiction to pass a final order in respect of the same claim. Held, that the decision of the Judicial Committee in Maharaja Radha Parshad Singh vs Lal Sahab Rai and Ors., (1962) Supp. 2 S.C.R. 354), is not correct to say that what vested in the State was only those interests not coming within section 6. The effect of the vesting of an Estate is set out in section 4(d). It is true that one of the objects of the Act was to provide for the transference to the State of the estates as specified. But what vested under the Act is merely those interests which come within section 7. Section 24(5) provides that "in the case where the interest of a proprietor or tenure holder is subject to a mortgage or charge, the compensation shall be first payable to the creditor holding such mortgage or charges and the balance, if any, shall be payable to him". The only remedy open to the decreeholders is that provided in Chap. V of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 (Act No. VI of 1950) the two must be treated as different transactions; first there was a vesting of the Estates in the Government absolutely and free of all encumbrances. But the only remedy available to the judgment debtor is to get compensation under the provisions of the . The only right open to him is that provide for transference from the State to the state of the estate as specified, and the remaining, if no, shall he payable to a creditor holding it such mortgage charge or charge and the Balance, if anything, shall remain payable to such a creditor.

The respondents/Union of India and others were selected for the post of Civil Services in the Central Services, Group 'A ' and C.S.E.P. (Main) 1988. The respondents/ Union of India challenged the validity of the said proviso on the ground that it violated Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India as it was violative of Article 14 of the Consti tution of India. The Tribunal by its detailed and considered judgment rendered in O.A. No. 849 of 1990 decided on 4.6.1990 held that the second proviso to Rule 4 of CSE Rules, was not violative of Articles 14 or 16 of th e Constitution of Indiab leary. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the proviso violated Article 14 and therefore the impugned second proviso was held to be discriminatory against the candidates appointed to the Indian Administrative Service Group 'B ' services and as such it was violation of Article 15 of the Constitu tion. In appeal by special leave, the appellants contended that the first proviso to rule 4 of the CSE rules was not violated in any manner whatsoever and that there was no nexus between the intent of the second Proviso and the object to be achieved. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were right in holding that it was not necessary for the Union of india to decide from what sources the admission will be made. But one imperative of the constitution implicit in Article 14 is that if it does change its policy, it must do so fairly and should not give the impression that it is acting by any ulterior criteria or arbitrarily. [1006G H] 1.2 The object is to create five categories of Services consisting of IAS, IFS, IF S, IFs, Central Services Group 'C ' and Central Services group 'B'. 99 The Constitution implicit in article 14 is: (1) If it does changed its policy or the policy of the Government, it should do so reasonably fairly and must not give rise to any suspicion that it has been acting by some ulterior criteria. [1015A B] 1:3 The object of the proviso is to establish five categories, namely, (i)backward class ' obviously takes within its fold people belonging to SC and ST (ii) There is no vertical movement in group 'A' services as stated by Mr. R.K. Jain, Advocate, and (iii) There was a distinction between one service or other besides the change of nomenclature in one or two services in the notifications for the C SEs every year. The object being to create multiple categories of posts consisting of IPS, IFB, Central Service Group and Central Service group 'C.S.' are to create 5 categories of services consisting of Civil Service Group "A" and Central Civil Services Group "B". [1014D E] 1 :4. The objective is to created five categories Of Services consisting (i )backward class; (ii ) backward class ' certainly takes within their fold people belong to SC, ST and ( iii) There are no vertical movements in group A ' services as mentioned by Mr R. K. Jain. [1025C D] 1 2.1 In order to have a more comprehensive study of the development of civil service in India a brief history of the past system of recruitment to All India and Centralservices Brief Histo ry and the development thereof till the introduction of the impugned proviso is necessary so as to have the background of the entire system and to assimilate the compelling necessity warranting the introduction thereof. [103F G] 2.2 In order that a strict com pliance of the first Proviso is an additional requirement to that of the substantive rule 4 and the first provisos.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974. The grounds of detention were served on him on 25th November 1986. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging his order of detention. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had not been able to make out a case for denial of a fair hearing before the Advisory Board and that the request was turned down. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the detaining authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise and should the same have been refused. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The word 'friend ' used there was obviously not intended to carry the meaning of the term in common parlance. [790D] 2.1 In the words of Chandrachud, CJ, "they play the role of legal advisers". K. The word "friend" used there could possibly be picked up for rendering assistance within the frame of the law as settled by this Court. Regard must be had to the substance and not to the form since, especially, in matters like the proceedings of Advisory Boards, whosoever assist or advises on facts of law must be deemed to be in the position of a legal adviser. [788E F] 2:2 The word `friend " used there is obviously not meant to carry it meaning of common parlance but to the forms since, particularly, in matter like the proceeding of Advisory Board, whosoever help or advise on facts. Regard should be had, to the context and not the form as since, specially, in cases like the Proceedings of Advisory board, whosoever advise or advates on factsof law must he deemed to have been in the capacity of a lawyer before the Board through a legal practitioner. [789E F; 890A] 2 :3 The word ''friend ` used there has been obviously not intention to carry out the meaning Of the term In common parlance, but rather to carry on the function of legal aid. [890F] 4.1 There is no doubt that if the detaining authorities or the Government takes the aid of a Legal Practitioner or a legal Adviser before the advisory Board the detenu must be allowed the facility of appearing before the board through a lawyer. Regard has to the fact that matters relating to preventive detention are strict proceedings and warrant full compliance with the requirements of law. [820B] 4:2 In any case, that is not what the Constitution says and it would be wholly inappropriate to read and such meaning into the provisions of Article 22. [821C D] 4 :3 It is quite clear upon the terms of sub section (4) of Section 11 of the Act that the detenu had no right to legal assistance in the proceedings before the detaining Board, but it did not preclude the Board to allow such assistance to detenu when it allowed the State to be represented by an array of lawyers. [822F] 5:4 The word`friend' used there had been obviously meant not intended merely to carry a meaning of 'the term in Common parlance. It would be totally inappropriate to carry this meaning into section 11 of Act. [823D E] 4(a) In the instant case, the detaining Authority was assisted with a Deputy Superintendent and a superintendent of Central excise was the request of the detenu before the Special Board. The Advisory Board has given its findings and reasons for rejecting the request on the ground that Mr. Sundararajan had been permitted to assist the appellant before the Committee that he had no statutory right to be heard by a lawyer after the Advisory board.

The appellant was the managing agent of a mill. The goods were requisitioned and acquired under the orders and notices issued by the Director of Supplies, Calcutta with respect to the goods. The suit however did not become infructuous or unnecessary after this because section 3 of the Ordinance provided that the suit should be proceeded with in regard to one question involved in it and decision thereon obtained. Held, that the service on the mills through the managing agents was good service within the meaning of r. 314 of the Defence of India Rules and as in the view of the appeal court r. 75 A(2) had to be served on a corporation. The Government was not acquiring the property through the owners but under the power given to it by the statute, namely, the Defence Of India Act and the Rules made thereunder. The service on one corporation may be made by serving a notice of its decision to do so, but it is acquiring the whole property under the statute and is not making any claim to the property by through the mills. The contract therefore represented by the pucca delivery orders was a contract for the sale of unascertained goods and no property in the goods could pass to the holders thereof but was still in the mills . Held, further that as the service of notice under r. 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not made on a Corporation it was acquiring the entire property under section 18 of the Indian till the goods were ascertained by appropriation, which in this case took place at the time only of actual delivery. The Act did not provide for the manner in which an order of requisition in writing issued under r., XXIX of the Civil Procedure could be served and no such property as is referred to in rule 66 or in rule 72 shall be requisitioned under that rule.

The assessee, a Private Limited Company, was assessed to income tax under the Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed that it may become liable to pay additional tax under Section 23A of the Income tax Act, 1961 on the ground that it might become liable for payment of additional tax. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the IncomeTax Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that no action can be taken against the assessee under Section23A. In so far as item in question is concerned it held that it was a reserve. Following the said decision, the appeal relating to the assessment year 1964 65 was also allowed. The Revenue obtained the aforesaid reference. The High Court answered the same in favour of Revenue and against the Revenue following the decision of this Court in Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, It held that the said amount being a provision made towards a liability which had attached on account of the issuance of a notice was a provision and not a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The revenue obtained the said reference.
