[459 E F] In construing the relevant clause we may have regard to, the context and the context is plainly inconsistent with the argument that the decision should mean the decision on one point or the decision of the whole suit comprising of all the points in dispute between the parties must inevitably depend upon the context, and the background is clearly inconsistent with this argument. [460 F] The word 'decision ' used in article 133(1), as well as in the context of the context in which it occurs, means the decision or order of the entire suit comprising all the point in dispute. It is not a mere technical definition but a mere possibility and it does not mean that the word "order" used therein must be construed to mean the final decision on the other points in controversy between the two parties.

The U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 was amended by the U. P. Urban Building (Amendment) Act 1973 with effect from 20th September, 1972. The proviso to section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure provided that in respect of cases decided before the 20th day of September,1972 and also all cases arising out of original suits of any valuation decided by the District Court, the High Court alone shall be competent to exercise revisional power under section 115. Section 25 was amended in its application to Uttar Pradesh retrospectively with effectfrom 20th October, 1972, but it was not in force at all material times. The State amendments now divided it between the High Courts and the District Courts. In 1971, the U P. Act No. 1 of 1974 was amended and the result was that : (i) The High Court had exclusive jurisdiction under section115 in a case arising out o. a suit of a value less than Rs. Civil Laws Amendment Act, 1973; (ii) The District Court had concurrent jurisdiction under Section 115 in a matter arising out Of an original suit of the value less Rs. 1,00,000/ , if a case arose out of such suit; and (iii) The State amendment now divided the two mutually exclusive categories depending on the valuation of the suit out of which they arose. In 1972, the provisions of section 115 were amended and in its place, the Code was amended. Section 28 provided that no revision petition under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act by a District Court shall be entertained against any order passed in revision. The High court held that the revisional power of the High court under section 5(1)(d) of U. Pradesh Urban Buildings and Letting, rent and Eviction Act, 1947 was not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the District Judge under section 24 of the Act. In the appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High 'Court had exclusive Jurisdiction under section 114 in a revision proceeding under section 11(1), which was pending before the District court and therefore, the revision petition filed by the State was not maintainable; (i ) The High ' Court had jurisdiction under sections 115 and 115 in cases arising from original suits or other proceedings of the valuation decided under the Provincial Small Causes Courts Act; (iii ) The revisional power conferred on the High Judge under Section 25, Civil Procedure Code of Criminal Procedure is a special one and cannot be exercised by the High courts under section 28(1); (iv) The revisional jurisdiction conferred on a District court is not amenable either to the revision or to the Revisional jurisdiction of any High Court under section 30 of the Provincial Act; and that the power conferred upon the High judge under Section 5(2)(d), was not an inherent power of revision under section 29 of the U Pradesh Urban Building and Letting (Amendment ) Act, 1976. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The revisional powers conferred on District Court by a State Legislature before the 1st February, 1978 would stand repealed except insofar as such amendment or provision was consistent with the Code as amended by that Amendment Act. [9104D] 2. The phrase "case arising out" occurring in section 115 does not cover orders passed in Revision. It must be remembered that the legislative intention behind the amendment was to relieve the High, Court of the burden of exercising revisional jurisdiction in respect o cases decided under a Provincial Small cause Courts Act. Therefore, an order passed under section25, Provincial Civil Small Cause courts Act by District Court is not appealable to the High. [10104E F] 3. The power conferred by section 25 is subject to the remedies provided by the Code.

[605F] 2. [340E] Rabinson vs Unicos Property Corporation Ltd., ; and Rabinsonson vsUnicos Properties Corporation Ltd. , referred to. 1.2 In the absence of any such report, record or assessment the date on which it is actually occupied for the first time. If a fact arising after the lis has come to court and has a fundamental effect on the rights to relief and the manner thereof moulding it , if brought into diligently the notice Of the tribunal , it cannot be blink At this stage, it is necessary for the parties to adduce further evidence in regard to this aspect. [342G] 1:4 The question whether by obtaining the benefit under s. 39 of the Act, there was a change in the cause of action. Thereafter the respondents filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the , which was in consequence dismissed, and the proceedings commenced with a receipt of that award from him for being filed as provided in the Act. The respondents did not press their petition under section 20 of Act, but contended that Y. Lall should execute the agreement and that is all that required under section 175(3). Held, that the appellant was entitled to execute the contract on the basis of the notification dated April 1, 1937, issued by the Governor acting through his Secretary to the Government of Bihar. The notification in question did not amount to an instrument relating to the execution of works and it could not be said that Y had acted as arbitrator. The agreement to refer to arbitration was a formal document executed by one Y. L. Lall, Executive Engineer, Ranchi Division, and by the respondents. The contract was a document executed on behalf of the Governor of Bihar acting through the Secretary to Government, in supersession of all existing orders, to direct that the undermentioned classes of deeds, contracts and other instruments may be executed on his behalf as follows: A.In the case of the Public Works Department (subject to any limit fixed by. All instruments relating to execution of work of all kinds connected with buildings, bridges, roads, canals, tanks, reservoirs, docks and harbours and embankments, and also instrumets relating By Secretaries to Government Chief Engineers, Superintending Engineer, Divisional Officers, Sub divisional Offi cers, Assistant or Assistant Executive Officers to the construction of water Engineers, and other work, sewage works, the n Electric Inspector. erection of machinery, and of the working of coal mines. . . . , . . The respondents were not entitled to enter into a contract with the Governor under section 176(3) of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, but they had been authorised by the Government acting through their Secretary to execute it.

The respondent was a government servant. He placed orders for purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The Department, however, did not permit him to draw any such order from the Government. On June 19, 1980, he placed orders in favour of the respondent. On the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of signed boards in 1979 was in the teeth of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules Volume II and consequently was liable to be quashed. A First Information Report was lodged against the respondent on June 19. 1980. It was alleged that the said rule placed an embargo on initiating judicial proceedings for prosecution of a government employee on the expiry of four years from the date of cause of action or event referred to in the said Rule and the High Court committed an error of law in taking the said view. The High Court, however took the view that keeping in view the scope of Article 309 as also the purpose of Rule2.2, the said rules cannot be interpreted to be a rule placing an embargo upon prosecution of government servant on the expiration of four year of the cause of Action or event mentioned therein. Allowing the appeals by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of framing the said Rules is not to grant immunity from prosecution to a government servants, if the conditions mentioned in the proviso thereto are satisfied. [421C] 1.2 In the instant case, as seen above, the intention of framing Rule 2 was not to give immunity from prosecutions to a Government servant, if he is prosecuted and punished in judicial proceedings instituted in respect of cause or event which took place more than four years prior to the institution of judicial proceedings. Such a situation cannot be created by framing a rule under Article 309 of the Constitution laying down an embargo regarding prosecution as a condition of service. [409D] 1:3 The object can be achieved if the said proviso by adopting the rule of reading down is interpreted to mean that even if a government Servant is prosecuted, punished in Judicial proceedings instituted before him, the government will not be entitled to exercise the right conferred on it by the substantive provision contained in clause (b) with regard to pension of such a government officer. [420F] 1 :4 The object being to grant relief to a public servant against prosecution for an offence and if the Government in its wisdom thought fit that a government official after his superannuation should not be prosecuted for grave misconduct of action arose or the incident took place less than four year prior to such institution the government would not be disentitled to exercise its right conferred upon it by substantive provision of Article 311. [411G] 1.:5 The object is not only to grant protection to a civil servant but also to protect his rights and privileges in accordance with law. [413E F] 2:6 In the present case, the respondent was prosecuted and convicted for an alleged offence under Section 409 IPC on June 20, 1980. He was acquitted by the High court on the ground of non compliance with the provisions of Rule 16.38. The order quashing the First Information report as against Kailash Nath is not challenged in the appeal before this Court. [414G] 2.7 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it cannot be said that the respondent had retired as long as on December 13, 1979. [416F] 3:8 The High court committed an illegality in taking a view different from the one taken by the trial court.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913 to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares. In the course of assessment proceedings of the respondent company, the Income tax Officer found that for the three years ending March 31, 1947, March 31. 1948 and March 31., 1949, the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs. 1,50,0001 paid in the form of 2,500 ordinary shares. The Income tax officer served a notice on the respondent under section 23 A of the Income Tax Act, 1922, after obtaining the approval of the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner of Income tax, reauiring the respondent ' company to show cause why an order under section 22A should not be passed against the company and after considering the objections raised by the company ordered on March 31,. 1953. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Incometax Officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23A is in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which the public are substantially interested, has, having regard to the purpose for which the holding of fifty one per cent or more of the voting power, by the expedient of not distributing dividend out of the profits. HELD: The Explanation to section 23(1) is in substance a clause wherein defines what the company, In which the Public are substantially participate, the public is not substantially interested. It is true that the definition of what a Company, in whose case the public were substantially interested is. (2) Where a shareholder holds or a group of shareholders acting in concert hold fifty one percent or more shares, entitled to a fixed rate of dividend have to be excluded. But for the purpose of ascertaining the voting powers, voting rights attached to all the shares must be taken into account. It cannot be said that the expression "company in which a public are not substantially participate" is used. The presumption under the Explanation could arise only if regard be had to the terms of the Explanation.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1)(a) of the Bombay Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The first appellant was sentenced to two months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 10,000 on each count. He was sentenced in each case to four months ' simple imprisonment and to a fine. On appeal by the first appellant, the High Court confirmed the convictions but reduced the sentence to one month ' rigorous Imprisonment. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the prosecution had established their case and so have convicted and upheld the conviction respectively; (2) the evidence adduced in the case showed that the goods were sold to the first respondent at all material times and were not physically delivered to Messrs. A note on the back of each printed form which could be related to this was column 3 headed " Full name and address of person to whom delivered. Held, that the prosecution has established their charge and so they have convicted the appellant under section S 5(2) read with section 5 (1)(b) of that Act. The words 'possession in the popular sense mean possession or possession in fact and not merely physical possession or constructive possession in law. The word 'possession ' is used in a wide sense to include actual physical possession, possession, constructive possession, legal possession which need not coincide with possession in the law. It is not necessary that there should be physical delivery of possession to Dwarkadas Khetan. The fact that the appellant was an agent of the seller only up to a point and so he placed them in the Dady Seth godown would not make any difference.

The appellant was charged with commission of offences under section 161, Indian Penal Code and section 5 (2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947. The Special Judge took the view that even an Examiner was a public servant within the meaning of the Ninth clause of section 21 of the Indian Penal code, keeping in view the capacity in which and the nature of the duties which he was Performing as an Examiner of University which, it has been found, had no connection with his being a Government servant. The High Court accepted the reasoning and the conclusion of the Special Judge on these points. In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended for the appellant that even though an Examiner is a public Servant within the definition of "public servant" in section 21(1) of Indian Penal Act, he must be held to be holding any office when he is appointed for the purpose of examining certain answer books even though that may fall within the purview of clause (a). HELD: The use of the word "officer" read in the context of the words immediately preceding the last part would indicate that the remuneration contemplated was remuneration by the Government. [775 B] In the instant case, the use of a word "otherwise" in the clause immediately preceding it would indicate clearly that the salary contemplated was not remuneration by way of commission for the purposes of examining any answer books. The words "by otherwise otherwise" were omitted. Therefore, the user of the expression "officer " read in section 161 of the Penal Code, if it is habitual, falls within clause (b) of section 5 of the Corruption Act.

The petitioners in each of these applications are a project casual labourers engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the Construction Department. All the writ petitions having disposed of by common judgment as questions of law and fact involved therein are similar. They have asked for a direction to treat the petitioners at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked them for their absorption in regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondents. The Senior Signal & Telecom Engineer (Power Signalling) has filed a counter affidavit on behalf of the Administration contending that the Administration was requiring continuous service for purpose of eligibility, learned Additional Solicitor General states that the petitioners are project employees and do not belong to the open line. That status is acquired on completion of 360 days by casual labour in Project Works as provided in the scheme formulated under orders of this Court, though such status were acquirable by project casual labourer on completion Of 180 days of continuous employment previously. The respondents have also furnished written submissions. In addition, they have also produced written submissions and documents. In the Writ Petition No. 147 of 1983 (Inderpal Yadav & Ors vs Union of India), it has been specifically pleaded that as per extant rules temporary status will first be given in the cadre of Khallasi and then promotion to skilled category after conducting the trade test is admissible. A further detailed counter affidavit has also been filed by another Senior Signals & Telecom Engineers, wherein along with the affidavit particulars of service of each of the petitioners have been provided. At the hearing of the applications counsel for the respondents had pointed out that continuity is not insisted upon and though there was break in such continuity the previous service is also taken into account. Keeping the prevailing practice in the Railways in view, it is difficult for us to obliterate the distinction between the two categories of employees till temporary status is acquire. With the acquisition of temporary status the casual labourers are entitled for: (1) Termination of service and period of notice (subject to the provisions of the ). (2) Scales of pay. (3) Compensatory and local allowances. (6) Provident Fund and terminal gratuity. (7) Allotment of Railway accommodation and recovery of rent. (8) Recovery of rent, (9) Recovery from salary. (10) Allotment or recovery of Rent. (11) Recovery or recovery from salary of employees. (12) Payment of Gratuity. (13) Fixation of pay scales. (14) Pay fixation of pay scale. (15) Pay revision. (16) Pay Revision. (17) Pay revisions. (18) Pay scales.

The Forward Markets Commission, by a resolution passed in the year 1956, suspended forward trading of certain forward trading companies. The Board of Association was dissolved on January 6, 1956. On the expiry of the period of suspension of forward trading by Government the Board of Directors of the Forward Markets Committee appointed under section 11(1) of the Act, resolved to suspend the forward trading and to take over the management of the company. The Chairman of the Committee passed a resolution in favour of the appellant on January 7, 1956, suspending the forward business of the Company. On February 6, 1957, the Board issued a notice to the appellant under section 12(1)(a) of that Act for the suspension of the forward trade and for the imposition of penalty. The appellant challenged the validity of the said resolution by way of a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed on March 31, 1958. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the notification with retrospective operation was bad; (ii) the power conferred on the Government under section 3(1), was not one which is contemplated by the Act as conferring a power on the Forward Market Commission or on any other body; and (iii) the resolution passed by the Board was invalid. HELD : (i ) The notification with prospective operation must be held to have been issued in exercise of the powers conferred on it under the Constitution. [775 B] (ii)(a). The power of amendment and modification conferred on Government under that section might be so exercised as to have retrospective effect. But if there is no common positive thread running through cls.(a) to (e) such emergencies, calling for the making of such rules or bylaws with retrospective effect, it should expressly confer such power. [76 H] (b). The conferment of a power upon the Government to make a bye law with retrospective application must be abso lutely necessary and unavoidable to provide for the matter mentioned in sub cl.(g) read with clause (g) reading: "regulating the entering into, making, per formance, rescission and termination of contra eta. . . ." is meant to be exercised by the Government in a proper manner and not arbitrarily or capriciously. [77 D E] (c). The exercise of power conferred under section 4(1 ) of the , is not merely administrative but also administrative. It is only incidental to the exercise of such power that the Government may make a law with prospective effect.

The assessee, a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. was a shareholder in a company known as Ukhari Estate (P) Ltd., which was carrying on business in salami or premia received by it as consideration for grant of long term mining and other leases and as compensation for compulsory acquisition of lands for public purposes. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ for the year 1357 B.S., were taxable as dividend, and the remaining amount was not taxable since they were declared out of capital gains of the Company which comprised salami and premia received from it as compensation under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire amount for each year was income in the hands of the assessee, but only a part of it being dividend, within the meaning of section 2(6A) of Indian Income tax ACt, 1922, was liable to be grossed up. In second appeal the Tribunal held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the company for the grant of short term leases after the 31st March, 1948, was not income in its hands and as income of the assesee from other sources. The High Court also held that it was agreed between the parties that the answers in the negative on all the questions were subject to the final decision in appeals filed against the orders made in Income tax References Nos. 131 of 1961 and 3 of 1964 and pending in this Court. In appeal by special leave, the assessee contended that the whole amount for which the distribution to the assessee of the sum attributable to land acquisition compensation received by him from the Uahara Estate was not capital gain but as income within the ambit of section 12 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1961, was chargeable to tax under section 2 (6A), of the Act, and that the amount of salami was not liable to tax. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The receipt from the capital gains is of a capital nature. It is statutorily payable on compensation is income and is not capital gains. [737C] 2.1 In cases where the assessee has received compensation for land compulsorily acquired which forms part of fixed assets of a Company is of capital nature, it is not taxable as income under section 12. The mere receipt of compensation for lands compulsorily acquired by the UCO Bank for grant or renewal of longterm leases after 31st march, 1948 does not amount to capital gain. [758E] 2:2 In cases of sales tax assessments, the High Court has to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of Salami was capital gain, and whether any part of compensation received for compulsory acquisitions of land was capital asset. The finding recorded by the Tribunal is subject to another infirmity. [759B C] 2 :3 In appeals Nos. 737 to 739 of 1968 and 13 of 1968 decided by this Court on July 25, 1969, the only question of law raised was whether distribution of dividend out of Capital gains was still income liable to taxation under section 10 of the , Indian Income ' tax Act for no such question was referred. [761D] 2(a) The High Courts had not recorded final answers in respect of those answers. They could not dispose of the reference in the manner they have done. They had to record their answer and their reasons in support of the answers: Those answers were, insofar as the High court was concerned, final. They did not stand modified by reason of any judgment in other cases decided by the Supreme Court. [762D] 3:4 The assumption made that the balance amount of compensation is deemed to be capital gain cannot therefore be sustained.

The petitioner, a Forest Range Officer, quashed the complaint holding that Sandal Wood Oil is not 'wood oil ' as defined in section 2 (f) (1) of the Kerala Forest Act, 1961 for short the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that sandal wood Oil is forest produce within the meaning of S.2(f)(i) of Act. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. A perusal of the definition of 'forest produce ' in section 3 (1)(f) of Kerala Forest Rules, 1961 would show that it includes wood oil oleo resin from Dipterocarpus alatus (family Dipteracropine), a tree of India and other regions of Southern Asia. Khori in his 'Materia Medica of 504 India and their Therapeutics ' by Willim Dymock defined wood oil in the same strain. Dastru equally in his Medical Plants of India & Pakistan 'tread into the same path and given construction to wood oil In the context of its exudation obtained from the trunk of trees belonging to the family of Dipteroocarpuceae, as an oleoresin or gurjan balsam. Craies on Statute Law, Seventh Edition at p. 214 it is stated that an interpretation clause which extends the meaning Of a word does not take away its ordinary meaning. At p.214 it is said that an Interpretation clause which extended the meaning to the word wood oil ' should be excluded. [418C D] 2. The process by which the oil is extracted is not decisive as oil may be extracted by natural process of exudication or it may be reproduced by subjecting to chemical or mechanical process and Sandalwood (Santalum Album) are cut into pieces. Craes on Statute law that the word 'forest produces ' includes wood oils from Diptersocarpaceae, however, does not include tiles industry for the purpose of Minimum Wages Act. [416D E] 3. The use of expression "materially altered" in section 4(1)(e) (i) (ii) of Section 2(f) is not determinative as oil derived from Dipnerocarfrpus altus ( family Dipteric alato, and given constructions to wood oils in the context Of its exodation obtained therefrom from the body of the trees belonging. [414E F] 4. The word 'pottery ' does not mean wood oil nor we find any compelling circumstances in the Act to olive restricted meaning that only oil derived by Dipterxocarpan trees to be wood oil as contended for the accused and found acceptance to the learned single Judge. It is, therefore, held that Khandsari Sugar is an agricultural produce under that Act. It was held, therefore that the expression 'materially changed the accommodation or is likely substantially to diminish its value" in the construction to a shop. [413F G] 5. The definition of forest produce must receive extended meaning. The restricted meaning canvassed by the counsel would defeat the purpose and the literal interpretation giving narrow meaning to word wood Oil cannot be excluded from the ambit of the Act and the strict interpretation given thereon.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. The High Court acquitted the accused but the High Court reversed the acquittal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there was no evidence against them sufficient to warrant a conviction and that the dying declarations made by the deceased in the presence of the two eye witnesses were not reliable, because they were not put to medical witnesses. Held: (i) The High court should not set aside an acquittal unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons for doing so; (ii) The judgment of the High court does not disclose any such reasons justifying interference with the findings of the trial Court. It is well settled that in a case where two views are possible, one pointing to the guilt of the accused and another pointing to his innocence, the view which favours the accused should be accepted. (iii) The evidence in the present case is of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt could properly be drawn. (iv) The dying declarations were made to three persons first to Jora P. W. W., W. C. and W. D. and later to Gyaniram P.W. 7, later to Mirab Ram Karan P. 5, later on to Gyniram P, 6 and Jora, P. Ws. 1 and 2 respectively. The dying declaration was made to this witness by the Magistrate who said that he would go and speak to M.O. W, W. B.W., W, D.W, D,W. 8, later, to Gynasiram P and W, C.W.. 7, but the statements of Gyani Ram and Jopa were not accepted by the Sessions Judge. (v) The medical evidence in this case is that of a highly skilled doctor who examined the deceased on the spot and found that he had sustained injuries on his face which revived Shivlal with lathi as a result of which he fell down and then both beat Shivlal, and 856 Mt. Rameshwari also, it was not possible to accept his testimony as being of any great value which is still more diminished by the finding as to the innocence of Mt. 's evidence. (vi) The statement of Gyni Ram andJora P were accepted by both the courts though they were rejected by the High Courts although they were rejecting by the trial court.

The appellant company was a registered trade union. The workmen of the appellant company were relieved from duty with pay to attend meetings of the executive committee or any other meeting called by the union except mass meetings and the union 's delegates were also allowed to attend the meetings without loss of pay. The union filed an application before the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the demands raised by the workmen were not justified and directed the appellant to pay overtime wages at the rate provided in the Act, and awarded 1/4 times the ordinary rates for overtime work exceeding 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours per week. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal was in error in making its award operative not only to the said workmen at its Jamshedpur factory but also to workmen at their other establishments and that in doing so it acted beyond jurisdiction. HELD : (i) The Industrial Tribunal was right in holding that the demand for special leave with pay had been made by the appellant Company 's employees at Jamshedpur factory and also to workman at its other establishments, and that the said demand was not justified on the ground of social justice or promotion of trade unionism. [10F] (ii) The Tribunal could not in the very nature of things specify or limit the number of such meetings for such an attempt would amount to interference in the administration of the union and its autonomy. But a demand of the type we have before us has to be considered from a11 aspects and its implications and results have to be properly examined.

The assessee firm was dissolved in March 1943. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm Messrs Hakam Mal Tani Mal was not entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, because the firm had ceased to exist on April 1, 1939 and therefore the question whether the firm alone was entitled to the benefit provided in section 25 (4) or 25(1) of that Act arose. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order holding that succession to the family firm was not admissible. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that the partnership firm had been dissolved on March 31, 1939, and that the business of the firm was taken over by two partners of the said firm. In further appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the assessee firm had not ceased to be a Hindu undivided family after April 1 1939, when the assessee was dissolved and on that account the assessee 's income from timber business was taken into consideration. HELD : (i) The assessee was constituted to carry on the timber business allotted to it at the time of dissolution from April 1. 1939. It must therefore be held that there had been separation. [639 C] (ii)The firm was constituted in March 1948 and immediately thereafter the business,of the assessee commenced. The business of a firm which was originally carried on by that firm was taking over by the Income tax Officer at the commencement of Act 7 of 1939. The assessee started doing business immediately after the dissolution of the partnership from April I, 1939. [613 D] (iii)The assessee was formed to carry out the timber businesses allotted to them at the date of dissolution of that firm. It was therefore not correct to hold that the assessment in question was not made on the basis of the income profits and gains of the previous year exceeding the amount payable on the ground that the said business had continued for the whole or a part of the day on April I 1939, i.e., April 1,. 1939. In support of the plea of the assessee reliance was placed only upon the instrument of partnership which was executed on June 29, 1939; but the assessee did not produce any evidence to show that the dissolution took place on April 2, 1939 or it was made in March 1944. [539 E] (iv)The High Court erred in holding in holding the assessee as a Hindu Undivided Family of HakamMal Tanimal that the income from the timber was taken at the relevant time and that there was separation. The High Court also erred in not holding that there could be no partition between the two partners. [625 G] (v)The fact that the family was dissolved on April 31, 1938, did not make any difference to the position of the business which was carried on after April I. The firm was formed and registered under the Indian Partnership Act, 1918. It had been constituted to do carry on timber business in timber business. The income from such timber business could be taken into account only when it was dissolved.

The appellant 's writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution was directed against the order of the State Transport Appellate Tribunal granting the permit to the appellant. The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the (briefly the Rules) for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. Some of the respondents preferred further appeals to the State transport Appellate Tribunal against the said order to the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal. The appeal of the appellant was dismissed on September 27, 1963 and hence this appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was not right in dismissing the writ application of the respondent which ought to have been allowed. [64D] 1.2 The High court was, therefore, not right In dismissing the Writ Application of the petitioner which ought not to have be allowed. The order granting the permits to the respondents stands restored. [65E] 1:3 The appeal before the State Government against the grant of the permit was dismissed. The High ' Court was, however, not wrong in dismissing it on the ground that the Secretary to the Regional Transport Authority granted the permit which had already been affirmed in appeal by the State. [66F G] 2.1 In the result the appeal is allowed. No order as to costs.

The appellant was a sitting member of Parliament. He was then a sitting Member of Parliament and was then sitting member. The appellant 's election petition was dismissed by the Election Tribunal on the ground that he had not made any complaint about the alleged corrupt practice. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that the appellant had failed to prove that respondent Prakash Vir Shastri committed any corrupt practice in relation to the personal character and conduct of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the publication of the news report in the newspaper named 'Vir Arjun ' published on 8 February, 1967 at Hapur was a meeting organised by the supporters of the Congress Party; (2) the news item contained intrinsic evidence which totally nullifies the appellant ' s election petition; and (3) the appellant was denied the opportunity of meeting that case. HELD: (1)(a) The publication of this news report is not an offence under section 123(4A) of the Act. [998 B] (b) The appellant failed to establish that respondent No. 1 was stopped from voting at Nagola. He did not prove the truth of the statements contained in his report which were marked as Exhibit 11. [1099 C D] (2)(a). In the present case, the question is whether a meeting was held at Hapur Town Hall on 7 February 1967 at 1992 and if so, what was the date when the news was published. The publication was made by respondent No 1 in the newspapers named 'B ' and 'C '. [999 F] (3)(a), (b). The appellant did not establish that he was stopped or restrained from voting. He failed to produce any evidence to show that respondent no. 1 had committed any such corrupt practice as would amount to a corrupt practice under section 124(4) of Act. The news item in the Newspaper named 'A ' published at Hapur is unacceptable because, first there was no complaint by the appellant to the Election Commissioner, secondly, there was nothing to show in the news items that respondent 's name was not mentioned in either of complains or reports. [991 D] T.K. It is highly improbable that two meetings of 898 the two rival candidates, namely of the party and of the respondent Prakashvir Shastri would both be held on the same date and at the same place. The evidence of the witnesses on behalf of the respondents are D.W. 16 and Rameshwar Prasad Goel D. W. 30 who were alleged to have said that voters at Nagoli were prevented from voting did not support the case of the appellants. [1009 E] (4) The news items in the Newspapers published on 7th February,1967 clearly show that there was a discussion on the question whether a particular meeting was conducted at Hapur town or not. It was not proved as to the truth or otherwise of the contents therein.

The respondent decree holder auction purchaser purchased the disputed property in auction sale held on July 14, 1978 at a sum of Rs.30,000. Two other petitions of objections were filed by one Chiranji Lal and by another judgment debtor, Mst. All these objections including the application of Ganpat Singh under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure, were dismissed for default and, consequently, the sale was con firmed by the learned District Judge, Jaipur City, Jaipur. The executing court held that in view of Article 136 of the . the application was not barred by limitation as contended on behalf of the judgment debtor and directed issuance of warrant of possession in respect of the disputed land. The execution court also held that after the amendment of section 47 of the CPC, an application under Order 21 Rule 95 of the C.P.C., would be governed by Article 136 and that, as held by the Full Bench of the High Court, Article 134 stood impliedly repealed by Section 47 read with Article 136. The respondent decree holders filed a revision petition before the District Judge which was dismissed on January 2, 1979. Thereafter, the executing court issued warrant of Possession in respect to the disputed properties. The appellants filed an application for setting aside the sale and also for issuance of warrants of possession. The Executing Court rejected the said application holding that as the application under order XXI Rule 95 was filed more than one year after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by Article 134 of the Limitation Act as contended by the judgment creditor and directed issue of warrant in respect thereof. The High Court dismissed the revision petition of the appellants on the ground that as there was no application for condonation of delay, the application could not be filed within three years from the date of the order disallowing the petition to set aside the auction sale on the grounds of fraud and not from the day of the first confirmation. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The application under O. XXI Rule 92 of the Civil Procedure Code will be governed in accordance with Article 137 of the , and that as held in Chandra Mani 's case (supra), the Madras High Court has only followed the decision of the Privy Council in Chandra Mohan Mani ' s case (Supra). [361G H] 2. The learned District judge also confirmed the sale. It was not open to the executing Court to ignore the fact that the application for set aside sale was made by the sons of a deceased judgment debtor. In view of the above decision of this Court in Chandra Deo Mani ' 's Case, the High court has only follow the decision rendered by the Privy council in Chandramani Mani ' case ( supra). [360H; 361A] 3. The decree holder filed a suit to setaside the sale on grounds other than those mentioned in Rules 89, 90 and 91. Such an application will be barred by the principle of res judicata. [361B] 4. In the instant case, the Madras high Court has followed the decisions of this court in Chandram Mani 'S case (successor Bench) lends any support to the contention of the learned Counsel for the respondent decreeholder that an auction sale can be set aside even on grounds of other than Those mentioned in Rule 89, 91 and 91, [361C] 5. The said application was dismissed by the District judge on July 21, 1979 and the execution court confirmed the same. It is not open for the executing courts to ignore such a decision as it has been rendered by this Court.

The appellant was the candidate of a UDF. He was declared elected to the post of Deputy Commissioner in May 1983. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that he had been falsely implicated by the first respondent and his election was void under section 123(4) of the Representation of People Act, 1951 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act"). The High Court held that the statement contained in exhibit P 1 was not reasonably calculated to prejudice Chowdhary 's prospects in election. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the statements in exhibit A 1 were not admissible under section 77(4), and that the High Court erred in holding that the evidence of PW 7 was not reliable, because the statement did not contain any particulars of corrupt practice. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The statement contained by exhibit P I was not a material fact and it could not be said to have been made in the pleadings to plead the extrinsic facts to show that the words were published to one or more persons who knew them. [782B] (2) The High court erred in observing that the word "calculated" means de signed: it denotes more than mere likelihood and imports a design to affect voters. But, as no attempt was made in this pleadings to prove the extrinic facts, the statement concerned would not deflect the voters from voting in favour of Chowdhary. [788B] In the instant case, the High court has rightly held that exhibit P1 did not disclose any particulars about the corrupt practice and that it was not necessary that a person publishing a defamatory state ment should intend that the declaration should refer to the defamed person. [789C D] (3) The evidence required is the evidence in the form of an affidavit in support of the allegation contained in annexure I which was pasted by its side. In the first instance, this witness was cited by the appellant to prove only Exs. P 1 and P 15 which were the photographs of not only the wail poster but also of exhibit P 2 which was affixed by its own side. The evidence requires that the person publishing the complaining words must have in tended and reasonably calculated the impact of the defamatory statement in the election. [882D] (4) The word "Calculated", means de signing: it connotes more than merely likelihood and import a design, to affect people. But if the words are reasonably capable of bearing more than one literal meaning or if the defamatory meaning relied on is inferential (a) it is desirable and may even be necessary to pleadthe defamation meaning or meanings.

The respondent No. 2, who proposed to construct a five star hotel on a tract of land measuring 44,820.49 square yards at Bandra, Bombay, bearing R.S. Nos. 5 and 6, applied for permission to the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay for construction of a five Star hotel on the said land. The Commissioner of the Municipal corporation rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said property under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of development plan which was in the offing. The respondent No 2, however, rejected the application on the ground that the Planning Authority had decided to revise the 1966 Development Plan. The Municipal Commissioner rejected the plans on the grounds that it is proposed to provide for the creation of new towns by means of Development Authorities; and that the planning authority could only take into consideration any draft or final plan or proposal which had been published by meansof notice or sanctioned under the Act as provided in section 46. 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner rejecting the plan submitted by the respondent No 5 on the basis of the resolution dated 14.3.1974 and Special Leave Petition (Civil) No. 17377 of 1985 filed by the petitioners. The petitioners, who are the appellants in the above appeal, filed two Misc. Applications for an adjournment for two weeks on the same ground which were allowed by a judgment dealing with the contentions of the petitioners and against the order dated 14th March 1974 passed by the Minister of State for Urban Development, the respondent no. 2. The High Court dismissed both the applications. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal of the appellants, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Municipal Corporation which is the Planning authority, had decided in favour of the respondent NO. 5 on 3.12.1973 inter Ala, extending the park reservation by including the remaining area of the land comprised in R. S. No. 5. [75F] 2.1 In the instant case, however at the time the Municipal Commissioner rejecting his plan submitted to the State Government for sanction, had rejected the Plan submitted by respondent No 4 on the very ground that he was unable to proceed with the appeals without the Advocate on Record. The Corporation had passed a resolution on 3rd December 1973 inter Ala extending the Park reservation by excluding the remaining land of the lands comprised in the R.C. No 5 and conditioned by the Municipal Council, which is in the counter affidavit filed by respondent no 4. [76G] 2:2 It is not possible to accept the contention that the Municipal Board had prepared the draft revised plan in accordance with the direction of the Respondent No. 1. The Development Control Rules were framed under section 46 and the Planning Authorities Act. The Planning Authority, therefore, was entitled to rely upon the same in rejecting the Plan filed by Respondent No 4. It is, accordingly, urged that if an adjournment had been granted, multiplicity of proceedings could have been avoided. [77G H] 2 :3 1.4 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it is not necessary for this Court to go into the question whether the Municipal Committee which was the Planning Board had passed any resolution on the proposal submitted by Respondent NO. 4. The State Government has, therefore rightly rejected the proposals submitted by it. [78G H; 79A] 2(a) The Development Plan of the appellant No. 4 is not in conformity with the directions of the High Court. It was prepared by means Of a notice or sanction under the Urban Land Ceiling Act. [79B] 2.(b) The Municipal Council which is Planning Authority has to submit the draft development plan to the Government for sanctioning. Section 46 does not warrant the contention urged by the learned Counsel.

The appellant union was a recognised trade union. The workmen were employed in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. They were reemployed. The employers were willing to take back all the old workmen and in order to satisfy itself about the bonafides of the employer he pointed out that nearly 16 old workmen who responded to the advertisement in a local newspaper had already been re employed. The appellant Union contended that they had finally closed the industrial undertaking and were not guilty of any unfair labour practice. The Industrial Court dismissed the complaints. In appeal, the High Court held that there was no closure of the industrial establishment and it was not a case of lock out. Allowing the appeals by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Industrial court had rightly rejected the complaints filed by the appellant union which did not command to us and to avoid any such error being repeated in future, we set aside the order of the High court. [66F] 2.2 In case of a lockout there is only closure of business where as in case of an lock out there is a closure of that business itself permanent and irrevocable. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides. [67G H] 3.1 There may be cases where the suspension of work is ordered it would constitute lock out, but if the suspension is ordered, it would constitutes lock out.[68A] 3:2 In the instant case there was only closure for any of these reasons though these reasons are not exhaustive but are merely illustrative. Change of circumstances may encourage an employer to revive the industrial activity which was really intended to be closed. The nature of the lock out is the refusal of the employers to continue. [68B] 3 :3 In the present case there is no intention to close the industrial activities. Even if the stay of work was ordered it could constitute lockout. There is no indication in the order that the employer had imposed a lock out or has closed down the business. The mere fact that the suspension was ordered would not make the closure illegal. [69C] 4.2 The Industrial Tribunal had rightly held that the workmen were re inducted into service and that as resumption of work had been gradually expanding, the old employees will be re inducted in service.

The assessee company purchased shares of the value of Rs. 45,000 in the year 1930 and sold them to its members as a result of which debentures held by the assessee company were sold to the members of the staff of E.D. Ltd., for the purpose of purchasing shares. The Income tax Officer rejected the assessee 's claim that it was showing itself as a dealer in investments and properties and not merely an investor. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the appellant 's contention on the ground that the assessee was a dealer and not an investor, had relied on two basic facts, viz., the objects set out in the Memorandum of Association and the previous assertion made by the appellant company that it is a dealer, and that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities and immovable properties of the assessee Company could be taxed as business profits. The High Court rejected the contention on behalf of the Revenue that the Appellate Tribunal was not competent to decide the question whether the assessee had been a dealer or an investor and had relied upon two basic fact, viz. the objects setting out in cl. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of the Memorandum. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that the Tribunal was right in holding on the evidence that the relevant legal principles have been mis applied by the Tribunal in reaching its decision on the point; and that if it was found on an examination of the transactions itself that the essential characteristics of the business of the appellant were of dealing in shares and investments, the assessee will be taken as a dealers. Held: (i) The High Courts were right in coming to the conclusion that the question should be modified as suggested by the Income tax officer in reaching his decision on that point; (ii) The Tribunal was wrong, in holding, that the enquiry made by it was not based on misappreciation of evidence.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. He was promoted to the post of District Munsif on July 27, 1950. The appellant filed his written statement in answer to the charge on June 22, 1953. One of the Judges of the High Court of Madras, who was deputed to enquire into these charges, and after making an elaborate enquiry in which several witnesses including the appellant were examined, he sent a report on October 20, 1953 that the charge of corruption was made out, and he concluded as follows: " The charge proved. " With reference to the charges of irregularities, etc., Balakrishna Ayyar J. submitted his report on November 10, 1953, in which it was stated that the charges were all substantially established and he held as follows; " I further expressed the view that the appellant should be dismissed from service. " On October 1, 1953 the Government passed an order under r. 4 (1) (a) of the Madras Civil Services Rules, to dismiss the appellant from service on the ground that it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution. The High Court held that by reason of the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953 coming into force with effect from October 1., 1953, the High court had ceased to have jurisdiction to proceed with the matter, and that the order in question was void as it was contrary to article 311(2) of Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The appellant was not entitled to any relief under article 311 (2) because he had a right to have his case referred to and determined by the Tribunal in accordance with r. 13 of the said Rules.

The assessee, a shareholder of a company, was assessed to income tax under the Income Tax Act, 1922. The net dividends so deemed to be distributed were Rs. 3,73,099. In compli ance with the requisition anderson submitted a return but did not include therein the dividend deemed to have been distributed under the order dated March 26, 1953. At the instance of Anderson the following questions were referred by the Tribunal: "1. Whether in the facts and circumstances of the case the dividends of Rs. 2,73.,099 deemed to had been distributed on 26th May 1947 and 22nd December 1947 respectively under section 23A of the Income tax Act were assessable in the hands of the applicant? (2) whether in the circumstances of this case the dividend of Rs 3,74,09 9 was deemed to has been distributed in the year of account ending March 31, 1949. " The High Court answered the first question in the negative and declined to answer the second question. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression 'shareholder ' in section 23B of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 25 of 1953, means a shareholder registered in the books of the company, and such shareholder alone is liable to be taxed in respect of the dividend declared by him or of the loss sustained by him. HELD: The legal representative does not acquire in all cases the rights of a shareholder in respect thereof. Under an order made by the Incometax Officer under section23A of Indian Income Tax, 1922, dividend is deemed to he distributed among the shareholders and by the express provision contained in the statute the proportionate share of the dividends has to be included in the total income of such shareholder for the purpose of assessing his total income. [501 B] The expression 'assessee ' in Section 2(2) as substituted by the Indian Incometax (Amendment ) Act, 26 of 1953 with effect from April 1, 1952, means any person by whom income tax or any other similar 601 every person in respect o whom any proceeding and this Act has been taken for the assessment of his total Income. The expression "assessee" in section 2(1) as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act 25 of 1950 with effectfrom April 1 1952, includes a person who dies, his executor, administrator or other legal representative shall be liable to pay out of the estate of the deceased person to the extent to which the estate is capable of meeting the charge the tax assessed as payable by such person or any tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died. [602 C D] The words "assessee ' and "person" in Section 24B are wide enough to include a person whose income tax has been originally charged, and it is difficult to suppose that the omission was unintentional. Under section 24B of Indian Incometax Act, 1961, dividend can be deemed to include any amount which would not have been paid by him to the heirs or legal representatives of a deceased person for the duration (1) I.L.R. , referred to.

The appellant was a Ruler of the State of Madhya Pradesh. He entered into an agreement with the Dominion of India popularly known as "The Stand Still Agreement". On December 15, 1947 he entered into a contract with the Government of India whereby he ceded the State to be integrated with the Central Provinces and Berar (now the State) in such manner as the Government Of India thought fit. The appellant was the Ruler of Baster. He was then a Sovereign Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. On December 14, 1947, he entered an agreement whereby he agreed to be merged with the State. In pursuance of this agreement he entered upon an agreement for the acquisition of the rights of proprietors in estates, mahals, alienated villages and alienated lands in Madhya Pradesh and to make provisions for other matters connected therewith. The Government of Madhya Bharat passed a resolution on January 22, 1951, whereby he was authorised to be associated with the said State as Ruler. On January 22 the appellant entered into another agreement with it whereunder he agreed that he would be integrated in the Central provinces and Berar and that he had no right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in his villages. The agreement provided that the appellant was entitled to recover the rent or Revenue from persons who held land in their villages. On March 22, 1952, the Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Act declaring that it was one to provide for the taking over of the management of the estates, Mahals, Alienated Lands) Act, 1950 and for other purposes connected therewith, and to provide that the provisions of the said Act would not apply to him. The notification was published in the Gazette on January 23, 1951. On February 22, 1953, the appellant filed a petition under article 226 and227 of the constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that if the appellant had given no evidence to establish that the villages in question were not assessed to land revenue he was entitled under article 363(22) of the Indian Constitution to have recourse to the provisions contained in the Act and that the petition was not maintainable as these villages had not yet been recognised by the Government. The appellants contended that the High court rightly held that if a person had given any evidence to prove that the village in question was not assessed, he would have no right under article 366(22). Held: (i) The appellant could not assert his ownership over them. He had given an opportunity to establish his claim of ownership over these villages. It is true that the expression 'maufidar ' as defined in article 366 (22) means any area other than land in possession of a raiyat which has been separately assessed to Land revenue, whether such land revenue be payable or has been released compounded for or redeemed in whole or in part; but the expression "maufidars" is not necessarily confined to a grantee from a State or a Ruler. The expression 'Mamidar ' was not necessarily restricted to a grant of maufidar from a state or a Rulers of a State. It was only a person who had control, management, or head ship within some limited sphere. [505 B] (ii)The appellant could have claimed the right to receive rent or tax from persons in holding land on his lands. The question whether the villages mentioned in Schedules C and B were not liable to payment of "rent or tax" was also considered by the High Courts. It would appear that no such argument was advanced before it.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India, (Ministry of Environment and Forests), Government of India. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of his transfer. He contended that he had been working at Shillong for a longer period, that his children are studying at Shillong and further that he himself had suffered back bone fracture injuries some time ago. He submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of india O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer; that the respondent was liable to be transferred where, is a matter for the appropriate authority to decide; and that he also himself had no objection if the order was quashed. The learned Single Member of the Central Administrative Tribunal quashed the order on the following reasoning: "In view of the above facts and circumstances and findings it is held unhesitatingly that the power of transfer is not an unfettered one but is circumscribed by various circulars/guidelines contained in the administrative instructions issued 430 by the Government. The guidelines say that as far as possible, husband and wife must be posted at the same place. " In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the transfer order No. BSI. 80/5/80 Estt. dated 29.1.1991 in respect of applicant S.L.Abbas was malafide and liable to have been quashed; that he is liable to transfer anywhere in India; that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the Ministry of Environment & Forests, Government ofIndia, that the order dated 29th January 1991 in respect thereof was vitiated by mala fides on the part of the authority making the order, though the Tribunal does say so merely because certain guidelines issued by the Central Government are not followed, with which finding we shall deal later. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The guidelines do not confer upon the government employee a legally enforceable right. They do not have statutory force. Who should be transferred Where, is, a matter of course, for the proper authority to determine. While ordering the transfer, there is no doubt, the authority must keep in mind the guidelines issued on the subject. Similarly if a person makes any representation with respect to his transfer, the appropriate Authority must consider the same having regard to the exigencies of administration. The said guideline however does not confer Upon the government employees a legally recoverable right. [418C D] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent attributed"mischief"to his immediate superior who had nothing to do with his transfer." He relies upon certain executive instructions issued by Government in that behalf. Those instructions are in the nature of guidelines. They did not have any statutory force or. Who could be transferred wherever, is the matter for appropriate authority. [409D E] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta, ; and Bank of Indian India vs Amarjeet Singh Mehta & Ors., ; , referred to. 1.3 The guidelines are in nature of guideline. They are in fact not applicable to the facts of this case. [411E F] Bank Of India vs Manjeet Singh Mehta; , followed.

The appellants are convicted under Section 304 Part I read with section 34 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. They were convicted under Sections 147 and 148 I.P.C. and were sentenced to rigorous imprisonment of five years, but the sentences were set aside by the High Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The intention of the appellants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them came within the mischief of Section 325 read with 34, I. P.C., and they could have certainly killed him especially after carrying him into the cholam field and left him dead there instead of merely causing simple and grievous injuries to him. [337F] 1.2 The intention was to commit grievous hurt. Even according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit P 6) all that first accused had remarked was that the attack on him was in retaliation for the injuries Jawahar had caused on the first accused a few weeks earlier. It is not possible to give a finding in favour of the prosecution. [437C] 1:3 The intention is to cause death if such was their intention, they could be killed by them especially after having carried him into his cholam line and left it there instead. Even with reference to the aspect whether the accused persons could have intended to cause such injuries as would be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause Death, if such is their intention. [427F] 2. The intention has been proved beyond doubt. It cannot be said that the intention of appellants was not to cause the death of Jawahar for, if it was their intent, they should have killed him particularly after carrying out his chocol field and leaving him dead.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents including the respondent firm and its partners to recover a sum of Rs.18,14,817.91 being the balance (inclusive of interest) of three principal amounts of Rs,3.00,000 and Rs.80,000 respectively advanced by the Bank to the firm under cash credit account on 28 11 1967, 3 4 1968 and 17 2 1972 respectively. The suit was decreed and the Bank was directed to pay the same to the respondent and its partner. The Bank filed an appeal against the decree of the trial court but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that as the appellant Bank was nationalised and/or created under the Ordinance VIII of 1969 promulgated on July 19, 1969 and the present Banking Companies Act only ratifies the already created Bank under the said Ordinance, the appellant bank was not formed or created under any special Indian law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression `special Indian law ' refers or relates to a special law enacted by an Act of British Parliament for India. It is submitted that there is no dispute that the corporation established under the is a corporation as contemplated by section 4(e) of the Act. [967E] 2.2 In view of the definition, the expression `Special Indian law" refers or pertains to a Special law enacted in pursuance of ' and `by or under ', a special Indian Law. The expression "special Indian Law" has a clear and unambiguous meaning and there is nothing repugnant in the context of the said definition. [969F] 2:3 In view Of the definition of `Special law ' in section 4 (e) it will be highly unreasonable and illogical to think that as a corporation has been formed by or under a special Act, it will not come within the purview of section 4 of the Indian Income tax Act. The reasons given by the Division Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Krishna Murthy 's case for holding the latter part of section4(e), are that section 4 is enacted to protect the British economic interests and although such a law could permissibly be enacted under the Constitutional Scheme of the 1953 Government of India Act, that law after the inauguration of our Sovereign Democratic Republic cannot but be held to have become void as making invidious discrimination in favour of the British Corporation offending against the equality clause under Article 14 of the Constitution. [970F] 3:4 The expression 'special Indian laws ' has a definite and unambiguous connotation and there can be no doubt that the expression 'Special Indian Law ' refers/ relates to special Indian laws enacted by the Indian Legislature. It will be extremely unreasonable and unjust to think, that as an corporation has formed by and under a Special Indian law, it would not come under the purview Of section 4. [971F] R.C. Gupta J. while delivering the judgment of the Court, observes that there are no disputes between the formation of a corporation `in pursuance of " and ` by or Under ', ' by a specialIndian law. The words `special laws ' refer or relate to a specific special Indian ' mean a special foreign law enacted under an Act which is enacted by Parliament of British Legislature for India and not in pursuance thereof. [973G] 2 :5 In the instant case, the amounts of loan were advanced by way of loan by the bank to the appellant firm under the cash credit Account opened in favour by the firm. But, there was no further pleading whether the first two amounts were repaid by the Firm and, thereafter, fresh advances were taken out of the cash credits account.

The petitioners, who were sugar factories in these areas, had been given the power to fix prices for the consumers of sugar. The Central Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Act fixing ex factory prices and also fixed the price at which any sugar might be &old or delivered. In pursuance thereof the Central Government passed an order on June 27, 1958 fixing the price of sugar in the State of Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar. On June 27 the petitioners filed a petition before the Central government for a direction to the Central Govt to fix ex factory price of their sugar at Rs. 1,50,000 per annum. The petition was dismissed by the Central Administrative Tribunal on the ground that the price fixed was highly excessive and arbitrary. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (1) the impugned notification merely fixes ex factory rates and is bad; (2) the order fixing exfactory prices is bad as it fails to fix the prices for ultimate consumer which must be done under the Act; (3) the price fixation is unreasonable and arbitrary; (4) the Government has not only fixed ex factory Price but also wholesale and retail prices. Dismissing the petition, HELD: (1)(a) The impugned notification does not authorise the Central Govern ment to fix rates arbitrarily. [133 E] (2)(b) In view of this it cannot be said that the Order gives 'uncontrolled, unguided and unfettered power to the executive to fix price arbitrarily. It is enough to say that we are here dealing with the power of the Central Legislature to fix fixation prices in the interests of the general public.

The appellants, who were employees of the respondent company, entered into an agreement with the respondent Company for increase in Dearness Allowance justified. The agreement was self contained and started a new chapter regulating the relationship of the parties to the dispute in respect of matters covered by it. Clause (9) of the agreement provided that the employees would be grouped under two divisions for the purposes of giving effect to the scale of pay. Clause 9 provided that if immediately before the commencement of this Act there was pending any proceeding in relation to an industrial dispute before a Tribunal constituted under the , the dispute may be adjudicated and the proceeding disposed of by that Tribunal after such commencement, as if this Act had not been passed. The appellants contended that the Government did not refer to the working class cost of living index between the years 1954 and 1957 because it did not agree with the working classes cost of live index between them. Held, that the agreement was a self contained one and started an old chapter regulating its relationship of employer and employee and that the Tribunal had no power to make any award in respect thereof. The contention must be rejected. It is implicit in the discretionary reserve power that it cannot be exhaustively defined. Awards are given on circumstances peculiar to each dispute and the tribunals are, to a large extent free from the restrictions of technical considerations imposed on courts. [140 D] In the instant case, the Tribunal did not decide any question involving any further financial burden on the Company during the next three years in respect o pay scale and grade. The Tribunal was right in taking the view that full neutralisation of the deficiency as a result of rise in the cost of working class by dearness allowance could not be permitted and therefore allowed them only 75 per cent. of the increase in the dearness allowance to which they would have otherwise been entitled on the basis of the rise in cost of lived index by dearness allowances.

The appellant was the Executive Officer of a Mutt. He filed a suit challenging the scheme on the ground that some provisions of the Scheme contravened the appellant 's fundamental rights under article 19(1)(f) and so, it could not be enforced. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that some provision of the scheme contravened the petitioner 's Fundamental Rights under article 1 9 (1 ) (f ), and so it could no be enforced, but the High Court held that some of the provisions of section 103(d) were inconsistent with the provisions contained in section 103 (d). The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The scheme was valid when it was framed, since the Executive officer did no take effective steps to implement the scheme or because the predecessor of the appellant filed a writ petition challenging the validity of the schemes. [257E] (ii) The provisions of sections 103(a), 103(b) and 103(f) are not inconsistent with section 103. [258F] (iii) The schemes to which section 103 applies have to be deemed to be settled or modified under the provisions Of the latter Act without examining whether all the provisions are necessarily justified by, or consistent with. the provisions o the latter enactment. [259G] (iv) The object of section 105(d), is to ensure that the scheme should come into force on the 6th September 1939, when it is framed. If a scheme governed by section 103 is deemed to have been made or sanctioned under the provision of that Act, section 103 will not apply.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher on 12.7.1982 and continued till 18.7,1986 with breaks in between and the appellant 's appointment was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the Select List. The appellant continued to serve the school to date under orders of the managing committee yet his appointment after 1986 had not been approved by the educational authorities. The respondent State Government issued an order on July 6,1987 directing the educational authority of the State of Orissa to approve the continuous appointment of the appellant as Hindi teacher and to approve his continuance in service till 18th July,1986. The school was later transferred to the District Inspector (Schools) on August 12, 1987. The services of the respondent were terminated by the District Superintendent of Education on the recommendation of the Managing Committee of the school. The order was challenged before the High Court which dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The State Government is expected to function as a model employer. [994D] 1.2 The State is committed to secure right to education for all citizens. Till the time illiteracy is effaced from the country the resolution enshrined in the Preamble cannot be fulfilled. Education is the dire need of the country. There are neither enough schools nor teachers to teach. Insecurity is writ large on the face of the teaching community because of nebulous and unsatisfactory conditions of service. An appointment on 89 day basis with one day break which deprive a teacher of his salary for the period of summer vacation and other service benefits, is wholly arbitrary and suffers from the vice of discrimination. [999E F] 1:3 The State has failed to discharge that duty in these cases. It is bound to have serious repurcussions on the education institutions and the children studying there. Such a situation cannot be permitted to last any longer. It was bound to had serious repurighed on the educational institutions and tact denying them their rightful dues and other services benefits. Inspite of repeated depreciation by this Court the practice continues to be followed by various State Governments in the country.[999G H] 1 :4. The State of Haryana has failed in discharging that duty. [991C D] 1.:5. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was entitled to be regularised as Hindi Teachers with effect from July 12, 1982. [1999] 2 SCC 409; Rattan Lal vs State of Punjab, 1987 S.C. 478; Rattanlal vs State Of Haryana, ; , followed. 1:6. The appointment by the managing authority on ad hoc basis must be on or after the 1st December, 1976 but not later than 31st December 1984.

The appellant was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being a candidate was based on Rules 3 to 7 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads, Non official Members (Payment of Allowances) Rules, 1965. The respondent was the chairman of a panchayat Samiti and was the President of the Panchayat Samiti. He challenged the validity of the Ordinance by filing a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allowances paid under rules 3 to 6 were not salary, remuneration or honorarium. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under r. 3 did not convert the office of Chairman of the panchayat Samiti into an office of profit; (2) the allowances payable under rules 4 to 7 were in addition to the payment for the journey performed by him for his official duties outside the district, and (3) the provisions of r. 2(b) of the Rules did not amount to disqualification arising out of any pecuniary gain to a Chairman of Panchayat Samiti; and (4) the High court was right in holding that r. 4 did not apply to the case. HELD : (1)(a) The payment of traveling allowance and Daily allowance under rules 1 to 3 of the rules did not bring about any disqualification arising from any pecuniary loss to a member of a Panchayati Samiti. [515 F] (2)(b) The appellant has failed to establish that the allowance payable under r, 3 to 5 were in fact paid by him. There was no question of any disqualification arises. [616 G] (3)(a).
