The payment to a Member, Panchayat Samiti under r., 3 to 8 was in addition not to the salary, emoluments or allowances attached to his office for official duties within the district. [613 A B] (4)(b). The appellant had failed to prove that the amount payable under rule 3 to 9 were in any way connected with the office or that it was not a remuneration, remuneration and allowance.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damages to it. The trial court decreed the suit. On appeal by the respondent, the first appellate court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court. In second appeal, the High Court set aside that order. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The construction of a Chabutra, Almirah, opening a window or closing a verandah by temporary structure or replacing of a damaged roof which may be leaking or placing partition in a room or making similar minor alterations for the convenient use of the accommoda tion do not materially alter 'the building as in spite of such constructions the front and structure of the tenanted shop may remain unaffected. [972G] 1.2 The construction whether permanent or tempo rary is not relevant for the purpose of determining the 'material alteration '. In Words and Phrases (Permanent Edition) one of the meanings of the word 'alter ' is 'to make change, to modify, to change, alter, change, change of a thing from one form and set to another. In words and Phrases, (Per Permanent Edition) One of the meaning of the expression 'materially altered" occurring in sec. 3(1)(c) of U.P. Act does not include the word "altered" or the word `altered". [975G H] 1:3 The Legislature intended that only those constructions which bring about substantial change in the front or structure of a building should provide a ground for tenant 's eviction, it took care to use the word ''materially alter the ceiling, instead; it took note of the fact that the construction had been made without digging any foundation of the floor of the room nor it touched the ceiling. The Legislature meant that only such constructions which brought about substantial changes in the rear and structure should provide ground for tenants ' eviction, they were permanent or temporary, is a relevant consideration in determining the question of "material alteration" [976H] 1 :4. In order to determine whether the construction whether temporary or tempo dary is of such a nature that make material alterations in the accommodation. [936B C] 2:5 The High Court in second appeal interfered with the findings of fact recorded by the lower courts on the question whether tin shed and the partition wail constituted material alterations. The High court in second appeals interfered with those findings of facts recorded by both the Courts below on the questions whether tin sheds and the family wall did not change the front, structure of that building, it being temporary in nature, did not constitute material alteration as the constructions were temporary in character which could be removed at any time without causing any damage to the accommodation; and it interfered with that findings. [963C] 2 :6. The observations made in Babu Manmo han Das Shah 's case do not justify inference that the nature of construction whetherpermanent or tempo arary is relevant for determining the "material alterations" made by a tenant. In Babu Man Mohton & Ors. vs Bishun Das, ; , relied on.

The appellant company filed a suit for setting aside an ex parte decree against the respondent firm on 22 4 1975 against the appellant. The Trial Court held that handing over of summons to Navlakha was not valid service of summons on the respondent company and, therefore, set aside the ex parte order. The High Court allowed the revision, setaside the judgment of the Trial Court and upheld the passing of the exparte decree. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that since Navlakkakha was an employee of the company sitting in its registered office in Calcutta the summons could be left anywhere uncared for in the registered office of the Company, and that the High Court committed error in interfering with it. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. [1033C] 2. The meaning of clause (b) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the Code in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summon on natural persons. In Rule 17 of Order 5 it has been provided: "Where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or where the serving officer, after using all due and reasonable diligence, cannot find the defendant, and there is no agent empowered to accept service of the summons on his behalf, nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving Officer shall affix a copy of the notice on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain, 1032 and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued, with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the copy, the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed. " [1034D] 3. The words "Principal officer" in Clause (a), of Rule 17 would include Managing agents and the word "principal Officer" has got a wider connotation than the word 'principal '. In the instant case, nothing of the kind was done. In paragraph 9 of the rejoinder it is stated: "Inspection of record of this Hon 'ble Court relating to the service of notice on Shri Nawlakha shall be deemed to have been duly served as stated in this para." [1035C D] 4. The expression "Principal" in Rule 2 has got significance in the context of the provision of the code in Order 6 which is intended for issue, and service or summons on natural person would include management and control of affairs of the defendant company. In order to bring about a situation where the suit is against a corporation, the summons may be served (a). on the secretary, or on any director, or other principal officer of the corporation, or (b). by leaving it or sending it by post addressed to the corporation at the registered Office of the Corporation if it is literally interpreted to say that the summons can be left elsewhere uncared.

The respondents filed a complaint against the respondents on the basis of a police report. After passing preliminary order on the 29th July, 1976 (wherein the Magistrate had recorded reasons for his being satisfied that a breach of the peace existed at the time when the order was passed. The Magistrate passed the final order in favour of the appellant. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. for quashing the order of the Magistrate. The High Court allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate for fresh enquiry as provided by section 145(5) Cr.P.C., but in the circumstances it could be safely presumed that apprehension of breach of peace existed and such a finding was implicit in the final decision passed by the Magistrate so it was not necessary for the Magistrate to repeat what he had said in the preliminary order in the provisional order also. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order passed by High Court is legally erroneous and cannot be allowed to stand. [952 F] 2. A finding of existence of breach on the part of the magistrate to mention in his final order that there was an apprehension of violation of the law existed even in 94 the final orders. Once a preliminary order drawn up by the magistrate sets out the reasons for holding that a dispute likely to cause a breach exists, it is not necessary that the breach of such peace should continue at every stage of the proceedings unless there is clear evidence to show that the dispute has ceased to exist so as to bring the case within the ambit of sub section (5) of section 145. [962 F G] 3. The enquiry under section 145 is limited to the extent to which the fact of actual possession is not sufficient to vitiate the order passed in favour by the Court. Once an preliminary order is drawn up, it becomes not necessary to repeat What he has said in his preliminary order that a complaint regarding an immovable property exists and such dispute is likely to causing breach of it. [972 F H] 4. The inquiry under section 146 is limited only to the question whether there was apprehension of the breach or not. Once the Magistrate has given a finding to the effect that there is apprehension of contravention of the laws, he can continue the proceedings. If the Magistrate did not mention in the order that it was an error of procedure would clearly fall within the domain of a curable irregularity which is not enough to vitiate his order passed under sub section(5). [973 F] 5. The question whether a breach or breach of a peace exists, depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. If there is no evidence to indicate that the disputed property has ceased or ceased to be so as not to bring it within the purview of sub Section (5), he can still continue the proceeding. [992 F; 9. The fact that the Magistrate was satisfied that there exists an imminent apprehension of a breach in the peace, that being an error apparent on the face of the record, it was open to him to proceed under section 144 Cr.PC. for the purpose of taking proceedings under section145 Cr. PC.

The appellant was a partnership firm. The partners belonged to the Nattukkottai Chetti caste which was a trading community. The appellant sold it in turn to C, which ultimately sold it to the usual customers of the appellant. The sales were not bonafide but were made with the object of defrauding the shareholders by purchasing goods themselves at low valuation for their own benefit and that the intermediaries were benamidars for the appellant and on this ground the Tribunal held that the intermediary was benamidar for the company, and on that assumption were grounded several contentions which were pressed on behalf of the assessee. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the Tribunal had no power to substitute its own judgment in a second appeal but it did not consider the evidence as correct in law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the appellant that (1) the Tribunal was wrong in holding that it was immaterial whether these conclusions were of fact or (2) the finding on questions of fact based on inference from other facts should be regarded as questions of law open to review by court, and (3) the decision of the Tribunal is final even though the court might not, on the materials, have come to the same conclusion if it had the power to substituting its own judgments. Held: (i) The finding of the Commissioner was that it did. not involve the application of legal principles to facts established in the evidence. It was a question of law which could be decided only by the court of first instance and not by the High Court. The decision in the American Thread Company Ltd. vs Stanley, (1923) L.R. 55 I.A. 178, relied on. (ii)The Tribunal had held that it had jurisdiction to substitute a own judgment for the decision in second appeal. It could not be said that the finding of fact was open to challenge as erroneous in law merely because it was not supported by any evidence or if it was unreasonable and perverse but that where there is evidence to consider, I the decision does not involve any question of fact. The Tribunal had found certain basic facts and stated its conclusions thereon ,in the accounts. It did not say that the tribunal had actually found some basic facts in support of the final conclusion a position which did not arise here. The finding was open by the Tribunal to review its own decisions. The Court could not substitute its judgment for that decision merely because there was no evidence before it on which he, as a reasonable man, could find as he has found. The true legal effect of a proved fact is essentially a question Of law, but the question whether a fact has been proved when and against has been properly admitted is necessarily a pure question of facts. [183 D E] (iii)The finding on the question of "whether the intermediaries are benamidars" for the purpose of defraud the shareholders was not open to attack as erroneous. The question whether the intermediaries had been benamidars or for the benefit of the shareholders, could be determined only by a court of appeal and not in an appeal against that decision. [184 D E].

The assessee, a public charitable trust, was appointed as an agent of the Government of India. The assessee claimed deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to the General Manager Shri J.P. Vaish in excess of tiffs amount. The Income Tax Officer determined a sum of Rs, 5,000 and disallowed the claim of deduction of the said amount from the assessable income. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount of Rs 75,464 paid to Shri Vaish was an amount laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of carrying on business. The Tribunal also rejected the view of the Income Tax officer that the rate of commission was reasonable and the allowance was therefore restricted to half of the amount claimed by the assesee. On reference the High Court held that in the circumstances of the case, the amount was not sufficient and it was reasonable to allow the payment of commission at the rate Of 121/2% and allowed the appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the entire amount of commission paid by Shri Vaish had been taken over by the Income tax Officer and so the Commissioner should have increased the commission payable from Rs. 37,733 in that year. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The principle of commercial expediency for determining whether an expenditure was wholly or exclusively laid out for the purposes of the business is not applicable to the present case. [501B] 1.2 In the instant case, both the Appellate and the Incometax Officer rejected the contention of the assesees that the whole amount of the commission paid was an income laid out entirely and exclusively laid down for the business of the appellant within the meaning of section 10(2)(xv) of the Act. [602C] 1:3 The question referred by the Tribunal and answered by the High court only deals with the claim for deduction of expenditure of the year in question. But, as observed by this Court in Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd., (supra), neither the High Courts nor the Appellate Tribunal has applied the proper legal test in this case. The principle that commercial expediency is not a matter of commercial concern for determining what should be paid to an employee of the company. [643D] 1 :4 In the present cases, both these Appellate Assistant Commissioners and the Appellate Tribunals rejected the claim on the ground that the rates of commission were reasonable and they were therefore restricted only to half the amount sought by the appellant. The case of the respondent assessee was that a higher rate of Commission of 25% was fixed for Shri J P Vaish in the running of the mill which was "old and unbalanced" and had never worked continuously or satisfactorily before it was taken over. Vaish had a special aptitude to show in his work so far as the marketability of the goods was concerned. Vaish was paid nothing beyond the salary and car allowance. The succeeding year he was able to secure an order from the account of ,which the mill made some profit. The previous year he succeeded in securing an order for Lohis from Government and so he was unable to secure a order from that account. [525E F] Swadeshy Cotton Mills Ltd., vs Commissioner of Income Tax, ; Swadeshani Cotton Mills Company Ltd. vs Commissioner Of Income tax, , referred to.

The appellant was a member of a trade union. He was actually represented in the proceedings before the Tribunal by an officer of that Union, its Secretary, Fateh Singh. The Union made an application praying for an issue of an appropriate writ or direction quashing the Tribunal 's order of February 26, 1957, by which the Tribunal had rejected his prayer for representation by a person of his own choice in place of Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union and that he did not want his case to be represented by Fateh Singh as he had no faith in him. The appellant contended that the Secretary had no authority to compromise on behalf of the union and that the Tribunal erred in rejecting his application for separate representation. Held, that the appellant was entitled to a separate representation in spite of the fact that the Union which had espoused his cause was being repre sented by its Secretary Fateh Singh and that it was not necessary to make the award. The Secretary of Union had no power to compromise with the representative of workmen. The question whether the Secretary has any authority to enter into a compromise on the behalf of Union is undoubtedly of some importance. It will be unwise and indeed impossible to try to lay down a general rule in the matter, the ordinary rule should in our opinion be that such representation by an Officer of the trade union should continue throughout the proceedings in the absence of excep tional circumstances which may justify the Tribunal to permit other representation of the workman concerned. The principle that the party to a dispute should have a fair hearing is not applicable to industrial disputes and it is only desirable that such representations by an employee of the Trade Union should be considered at this stage. In deciding this question, the normal rule should be that Such representation by the officer of the industry should continue during the proceedings of the Tribunal in the presence of expec tional conditions which may warrant the Tribunal not to make a award. It is only when such representations are made and so there can be no direction as prayed for on the Tribunal. The ordinary rule would apply where the party concerned has a fair opportunity to deal with the representatives of workmen, instead of individual workmen, not only for the making or modification of contracts but in the matters of taking disciplinary action against one or more workmen and as regards all other disputes. In the present case, the appellant had no right to represent the Union. The appeal is accordingly dismissed.

The appellants were the tenants inchief who had sub let the premises to defendant No. 2. The suit was filed by the respondents for eviction of the tenant on the ground that the appellants were not members of the joint Hindu family and that they were, therefore, competent to continue the appeal even after the death of Kedar Nath and the abatement of the appeal so far as he was concerned. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the surviving appellants could have instituted the appeal against the entire decree in view of r. 4 of O. IV of the Code of Civil Procedure. In appeal, the High Court held that the provisions of rs. 4 and 5 of O., XLI had not been correctly construed in Baij Nath vs Ram Bharose, ; , and that the abatement was not a case of such a kind. The appellants then filed an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of delay in filing the appeal. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that r.4 of O,. XLI did not apply to the facts of the case. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the appeals could be treated to have abated in the particular circumstances and that therefore the provisions Of 0. XLI, r. 5 of C.P.C. were not correctly construed. Held, that the High court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving appellant when the appeal had been filed by all the plaintiffs. The provisions of O . XLI would apply to cases where an appeal has been filed against a decree and not at its institution. There is nothing common in their provisions which make the provisions o one interfere in any way with those of the other.

The appellant was the tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent landlord under a lease deed dated May 19, 1954. The respondent landlord filed an application for eviction under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on the ground that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) and no notice terminating the tenancy under section 108 was needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111 (g). The Rent Controller held that the appellant had failed to prove that the tenant had lost all alone the way. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the tenancy was not terminated by efflux Of time limited under section111(g), because the TP Act did not apply proprio vigore to such demises and their determination, could be taken into consideration only in May 1975 so much so the freshness of counsel 's submissions might have faded somewhat and so the newness of the appellant 's arguments might have been advanced by the tenant provided this Court permits it, having regard to the circumstances. The appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The right to possession under the lease deed is a statutory right and not a contractual tenancy. [912G] 1.2 In the instant case, the landlord has by a volta face, switched to the TP act as against the rules of equity, justice and good conscience. The obligation for the weighty reason that the formality is merely statutory and it cannot trace its origin to any rule of equity. [ 913A B] 1:3 In the present case, there was no dispute that in view of this only such of the principles embodied in section 111 of the TPAct would regulate the matter as could be held to be consistent with the rules Of equity, equity and good justice. The plea based on section 111 is writ large in the Tribunal 's order and the High Court 's judgment. [964D] 1 :4 In the absence thereof, the ejectment proceeding must be rebuffed. [969B] 2:5 The appellant has not established that he had lost any more or less the way of legal proceedings for eviction fulfils the requirement of law for determination of the lease.

The appellants were dismissed from service by the Governor of Assam. The Governor made an order under proviso (c) to article 311(2) of the Constitution, imposing a penalty on them for misconduct which was found proved against them. The appellants challenged the validity of the said orders before the High Court in a writ petition filed by them challenging the validity and legality of the orders passed by the Government. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Governor had no power to pass an order imposing a punishment on the appellant, as he was not given reasonable opportunity of making representation against the proposed action. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Governor 's satisfaction was recorded by him in his discretion and that the Government servant should have the opportunity, to show cause against his guilt; (2) the order passed by him was not mala fide or based on no evidence; (3) the Government had no authority to pass the order under article 311 of the constitution; (4) the power conferred on the Governor under proviso(c) was a discretionary one and it could not be exercised arbitrarily, without any application of mind; (5) the High court was in error in holding that there was no justification for imposing a lesser penalty than the one imposed by the State Government. HELD : (1)(a) The order passed under proviso to article 309(2), is an administrative order and it does not contain any provision in the Constitution which empowers the Governor to pass orders on the question of punishment; nor does it contain any such provision in that behalf. [487 E] (b) The power conferred by proviso (C) to this sub article must be exercised reasonably, fairly and reasonably, and there is nothing in the language used in the order impugned. It is not necessary that the government servant should be given an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him as stated above. [488 F] (c)(i) The Governor ' s satisfaction was not recorded by the authority empowered to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank on the ground of conduct alleged against him and given a reasonable opportunity to show that he has not been guilty of any misconduct to merit any punishment at all and also that the particular punishment proposed tobe given is much more drastic and severe than he deserves. [489 G H] (2)(a). The Governor was therefore entitled to make an order of dismissal or removal from service under proviso, (c), (d) and (e) of article 311. [490 B C] (3)(b) In the instant case, the Governor intended to record his satisfaction on the questions of inexpediency of holding the inquiry as required by the amended article 311 (2). The order was not based upon any evidence adduced during such inquiry. It did not contain a provision in regard thereto which authorised the Governor or the Governor, as the case may be, to pass such orders.

The petitioners, who were the Shia community of Shias and Sunnis, filed a suit for declaration that the Notification dated 26th February, 1944 issued under section 5(1) of the 1936 Act by the Sunni Board was ultra vires and void. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the notification dated 26rd February, 1945 issued under rule 54(vii), was not of avail to the Sunnis for the purpose of defeating the customary rights of Shia to perform their religious ceremonies and functions on the concerned nine plots and structures thereon which had already been adjudicated, determined and declared in their favour by decisions of competent Civil Courts in the earlier litigations and that the declaration sought in the prayer clause was really incidental. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that all that the Shias community is seeking by this Petition is enforcement of their customary rights to perform religious rites, practices observances and functions thereon which have already been determined, determined, and declared by decisions rendered in earlier litigations, and that no such order could be passed under section 144 Cr. P.C., as it was not a case of infringement or violation of any fundamental right. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the petitioners it was contended that (1) the Notification issued under Rule 54(viii) was not in accordance with law and therefore, the order made by the Shian Board was without jurisdiction; (2) the declaration claimed in the plaint was merely incidental; and (3) the notification issued under sec. 5(i) of 1936 Act was published for the first time by the Gaon Sabha on 19th August, 1934, which runs thus "All Magistrates should 1130 make it an invariable condition that music shall cease playing while the procession is passing any recognised place of worship, to whatever denomination belonging, except of course the places of worship appertaining to the processionaries themselves. The Shia Board was therefore not competent to issue the Notification under section J 18/108 and therefore the order passed by the Deputy Commissioner was without authority. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1)(a) The notification dated 9th May, 1874 issued under Section 5(I) of Act No. VII of 1936 by the District authorities is of no avail to them as it violates or infringes any fundamental rights. [245C] (b) The Notification dated 9rd May, 1873 issued under sub section (1), of section 5 of the Act was not published in Urdu language in the issue of Oudh Panch dated 19th Aug., 1874 which ran thus " All Magistrates should have made it an expectable condition for music shall ceased playing while processions would be passing or repassing the mosque is passed any recognisedplace of worship". [245D] (c) The Shian Act was enacted to consolidate and amend the law relating to the maintenance of religious ceremonies, practices, observances etc. and for matters connected therewith. It was not possible to accept this contention for the reasons which we shall presently indicate. [246E F] (2)(a). The Notification issued by the State Government under section 3 of the U.P. Act No, VII of 1938 is of a very wide import and it does not cover any particular religious denomination or sects. It only covers the Shiana community as defined in the 1936 Acts. [247C D] (3)(a), The Notification was published in Hindi language in Urdu script in the Issue of Oudh Panama by the Jamadar Board, which is a part of the record of rights and possession of Shian Boards. The notification issued by Sunni Board under section 4(1), therefore, was not one of availment to the Shians for the purposes of defeating customary rights. It did not cover the Shiena community as contemplated in the 1965 Act.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58 and the same should be set off against the capital gains in the assessment years in question. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee on the ground that loss had not been determined as required under section 24(3) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the provisions in Section 24(1)(b) and (2A) were equally applicable to the loss falling under the head 'capital gains '. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Tribunal and reiterated its claim. The High Court found against the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. In view of the language used in sub section (1), where the loss sustained is a loss arising out of or in connection with any business carried on by the assessee, such loss shall be set Off only against profits and gains falling under that head. [1164C] 2. The expression "capital gains" in Section 80(2) means any loss which has not been computed in pursuance of a return filed under section 139. [1064D] 3. In the instant case, the assessee had made the claim and he took note of it. his failure to comply strictly with the requirement of sub section(3), of section 24 should not be permitted to be taken advantage of by the Revenue nor should it be used to the prejudice of the assesse d. [ 1064E] 4. The provisions of Section 74(1) (b) & (2 A) are equally applicable in the instant cases also. [1005B] 5. In order to bring about a loss, the Income Tax officer must have regard to the nature and extent of the loss suffered by the assesee. If the assessee has made the claims and he takes note of them, his failure in complying with the requirements of sub sections (1) and(2A), the amount thereof not so set off shall be carried forward to the following assessment year and so on.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P). The recruitment was made always to the Defence Scientific and Technical personnel (gazetted) of DTD &P. at the relevant time, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the said three units. All, the service conditions of the persons working in the three units including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. were the same and were regulated by the same set of Rules, viz. Defence Science Services Rules. In the year 1979, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) was reconstituted as Defence Scientific Quality Assurance Service (DAQAS), and after that recruitment, recruits were transferred according to exigency of service, and thereafter sent to different units. The respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal, who held that respondent K.T. Shastry was entitled to remain in service upto the superannuation age of 60 years and was not liable to be retired at the alleged superannuation age. The Tribunal held that the re spondent was not entitled to continue in service beyond the age of 58 years his superannuation age being deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of the OM dated 24.12.85 read with OM dated 10.2.86 referred to above. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that respondent was not eligible for being re sorted at the age o f 60 years, his superannuation date being deemed as increased to 58 years in terms of OM dated 9.2,86 and that he was entitled only to remain till the superannuation period of 60 year provided they had been promoted to the grades they were holding at the time of attaining the age Of 58 years within the preced ing five years. The appellants contended that respondent could not be retired on the ground that he had not been retired at any time before the expiry of his five years ' service, as if he had never been retired. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The respondent was entitled for the benefit of the aforesaid OM dated 7.3.86 read with letter dated 10th February 1986 and letter dated 11th February 1987. [22D] 2.1 In spite of the decision of the Tribunal and even pending this appeal when no stay was granted, the appellant Union of India retired the respondent at the fag end of his service as if they had not already been retired on attaining the said age of superannuation within the meaning of OM No. 7(3)/85 D (R & D) dated 10/2.1986 read with O.M. dated 10 2 1986. [23F] 3.1 It is not correct to say that in spite of decision of Tribunal and also pending this Appeal when no stayed was granted by the Tribunal, the respondent retired at his age of 55 years. [24G H] 4.2 The respondent could have been retired only on the basis of an unilateral action.

The appellant was elected as a member of the Sangli City Municipality. The first respondent, who was the election petitioner, was declared elected to the Sangli city Municipality on June 15, 1967. On June 24, 1968 the appellant filed an application before the Judge for issuing summons on these two persons as his witnesses and prayed that he should be allowed to cross examine them in respect of whom an application had been made by the election petition on the previous day. The Judge rejected the application holding that the election was held under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965 (Act No. 1 of 1966) and as such it was not maintainable. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The High Court 's power of superintendence is confined to seeing that the trial court had not transgressed the limits imposed by the Act. If the Court was satisfied that a corrupt practice has in fact been perpetrated, may be by one side or the other, it was absolutely necessary to find out who was responsible for the distribution of the first pamphlet and as Such found him guilty of a corrupt practices and made an order disqualifying him under the Act from taking part in municipal elections for the next. [982 G] (2) The trial court 's order is set aside on the ground that there was no evidence to show that the appellant had been personally responsible for distribution of first pamphlet or that he had distributed it. [ 983 A B] (3) The question whether the election Petition was filed beyond the period prescribed by the statute and as a matter of fact, it does not appear that there is any difference between the two Gazettes with regard to the names of the successful councillors. Neither could the High Court have set aside the order of the trial Court under article 227 of the Constitution under which the High court ' s power of supervision is confined only to seeing see that the Trial Court had not exceeded its limits imposed in the Act, and not to call as a witness by a party to the suit but of its own motion to give evidence therein. [969 B C] (4) The order of dismissal passed against the appellant was set aside by the High Courts under article 226 of the constitution under which it was given powers wider than those given by the Code of Civil Procedure under 0. 21, r. 1, of the Code. If there is no evidence as to where it was printed or who got it printed and who got the backing of Muslim community, the Court may examine any person other than a party thereto and not called as a ' witness by the party to suit but only of its authorised agent. [970 C D] (5) The appellant would have had a real cause for grievance if he had asked for an opportunity to rebut the evidence of these two witnesses and had been denied the same but this has nowhere been alleged.

The appellant State of U. P., was a dealer in motor vehicles including motor cars, motor cycles and cycle combinations, motor scooters, motorettes, motorbi drivers, motor lorries, motor car drivers, etc. The appellant State issued a notification under section 3A of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, which came into force on May 28, 1956, and published in the Official Gazette on August 1, 1956. In the meantime, the State Government published the following notification No. P. P Sales Tax (Amendment) Act XIX of 1956, namely: "No. P dated August 1. 1956, under section 4A of U .P. Act XV of 1948, the tax on sales effected between April 1, 1957 and July 31, 1956 was to be and deemed to have always been substituted in respect of such sales, as if the sale relates to goods specified below: (i) Motor vehicles including Motor cars, Motor cycles and motor scooter combinations; motor scooiles, motasorettes and motor lors. (ii) Motor Vehicles including motor car bodies and motor car combinations. (iii) Motor cars including motor cycle combinders, motor cycle scales and motor cycles combinations." The appellant contended that the notification was invalid because it was issued before section 3 A was in operation, that objection could not be raised as that section would now operate from a point of time anterior to the issue of the notification. Held: (1) The Validation Act is not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54, for the reason that it operates retrospectively. It operates retrospectively and does not affect the validity of the impugned notification. (2) The validation Act is therefore not ultra within the saving of the Validation Act. (3) The validating Act is invalid because the State Legislature has no authority to enact a law with reference to a topic entrusted to it, and it is not a law which the State legislature was competent to enact and it was therefore a nullity. (4) The impugned notification must be held to be within the saved of the validation Act.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Court and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court affirmed it in appeal. In this appeal, the appellant contended that the conviction of the appellant under section 376(2)(i) of the Indian Penal Code is bad because he has been convicted only on the basis of his own statement made before the police officer and not on the ground that he had given a false statement to the police. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The courts below have rightly held that the appellant was not a 'habitual ' and had no vicious antecedents except this fugitive, Shivalingappavation molestation which is bad enough in a society where women are often socially weak and sexually victimised. [591D] 2.1 In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation apart from being deterrent. The functional failure of our pachydermic prison projects, exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, deserves judicial cognizance. [592E] 2:2. In prison Treatment must, however, be enlightened than the blind strategy of prison severity where all that happens is sex starvation, brutalisation, criminal companionship, versatile vices through bio environmental pollution, dehumanised cell drill under 'zoological ' conditions and emergence, at the time of release, of an embittered enemy of society and its values with an indelible stigma as convict stamped on him a potentially good person 'successfully ' processed into a hardened delinquent, thanks to the penal illiteracy of the Prison System. The Court must restore the man. A hyper sexed homo sapiens cannot be habilitated by humiliating or harsh treatment, but that is precisely the perversion of unreformed Jail Justice which some criminologists have described as the crime of punishment. This Court has held in Sunil Batra 's case and later that, constitutionally viewed, punitive deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative, apart frombeing deterrent. [593B C] 2 :3. The appellant is not a "habitual" and has no semious antecedents excepting this fuagitive,uttable mental trauma, etc. [595A B] 4.1 There is no evidence to show that the two families being close cousins are ready to take a lenient view of the situation. Of course, this does not bind the Court in any manner. But that is exactly what has been done by the courts below. The present case is one of circumstantial evidence and the circumstances of this case do not warrant sentencing sentencing sentencing. [590C D] 4:2 In prison custody treatment must be more enlightening than the speed of prison life, apart with being deterrent.[591D E] 4 :3 The Court should restore the person 's man. a hyper sexised homo tutorens cannot possibly be hablleditated by moliating or sentencing harsh treatment but that too is precisely what has happened in prison custody. [589E F] 5:4 In prison treat must, as part of the sentencing package, design a curative course for this prisoner to rid him of his aphrodisiac overflow and restore him into safe citizenship. The human dignity of the individual is not so much that it would be difficult to maintain a conviction on the sole ground that the accused may procure such condonation from unwilling victim, the fact remains that the three families being clos cousins were ready to come a lenient action of their release.

The assessee was a dealer in land acquisition proceedings. The Income tax Officer fixed the amount of compensation at Rs.30,10,873 on account of permanent acquisition of the land, thus enhancing the original amount of the compensation by Rs.5,13,624 on which he directed interest at 5 per cent per annum from January 8, 1953, the date of acquisition to the date when the amount was actually determined and had become payable. The Arbitrator also directed that further recurring compensation at the rate of Rs.6272/10/4 per mensem should be paid to assessee from the date it was due till the date the amount became payable. On receipt of the amount the assessee credited it in its suspense account on the same date. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the first contention and held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and therefore a receipt of revenue nature liable to tax. In second appeal by the Revenue before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, two contentions were raised by it. It was urged on behalf of the appellant that the amount received by it related to acquisition of property which was not the stock of trade of its business carried on by the appellant and was, therefore, a trading receipt of a revenue nature. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The legal position is explained in further detail by the Gujarat High Court in Topandas Kundanmal vs Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat, [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 393. In the present case, though the award was made by the Arbitrator on July 29, 1955 enhancing the amount, the entire amount was in dispute in the appeal filed by the State Government. The liability to pay compensation arose immediately on a dealer affecting sales which were subject to sales tax and what remained to be done was a mere quantification of that liability. [395B] 2.1 In the instant case, although the award had been made by an Arbitrator on August 29, 1956 enhancing the compensation, it was only that amount which had accrued or deemed to accrue, whether in fact paid or not. The entire amount of Rs,737,190 payable to the assessee was in controversy in the appeals filed by State Government and therefore, no income could accrue to him. [397C] 2:2 In the circumstances, it is only that part of the sum which had been received by an assessee after taking possession of the property, at a particular rate or for a certain sum is not compensation. The amount actually awarded by the Collector or the court accrue on the respective dates on which the award or the decree was passed. [398D] 2 :3 In the facts and circumstances of the case, it safeguards the assessee and prevents harassment. [399F] 3.1 The legal fiction created by section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act accrued or arose to the appellant when he sought 396 a reference under section 18 Of the Act or when the award is made by Civil Judge though an appeal was pending against that award. It is sufficient to point out that there is a clear distinction between cases 397 such as the present one, where the right to receive payment is in dispute and it is not a question of merely quantifying the amount to be received, and cases where the rights to receive payments are admitted and the quantification only of the amounts payable is left to be determined in accordance with settled or accepted principles. There is no doubt a liability to make payment as offered by the Land acquisition Officer. But there is further right of appeal to the Supreme Court. [400F] 4.2 The legal principle was explained in detail by Gujarat High Courts in Topsandas Kundan Mal vs Commissioner Of Income tax (Central), Calcutta, ; , and Topadas Kundanmal & Sons.

The appellants landlord filed a suit for eviction against the respondents on the ground that he was entitled to possession of the shop in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit and dismissed the execution case. A miscellaneous appeal filed by the respondents was dismissed by the Third Additional District Judge Gwalior. A Letters Patent Appeal filed by them was dismissed. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the decree was not a 880 nullity; (ii) the compromise decree was a nullity in the case of Kaushalya Devi & Ors. vs Shri K. L. The High Court held that the decree did not fall within clause (f) of sub section (1) of Section 12 of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 and (iii) the suit was not maintainable; (iv) the order of eviction was a non est in the eye of law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The language of Section 13(1)(f) is somewhat different from many similar State Statutes. On a superficial reading of the provision aforesaid it would appear that the inhibition related to the filing of the suit only. In other words, parties cannot be permitted to have a tenant 's eviction merely by agreement without anything more. [881B] 2. The protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 23, Rule 3 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise". The protection under the section is inherent In the language used in sub sections (2) to (11) of section 12 certain conditions have been engrafted to show under what circumstances an order for the eviction of a tenant can be passed. [820G H] 3. Section 12(1) provides that where at the time of passing of the decree, there was some material before the Court, on the basis of which, the Court could be prima facie satisfied about the existence of a statutory ground for eviction, it will be presumed that the Court was so satisfied and the decree for eviction is valid. [821C] 4. The section does not say that the compromise is in violation of the requirement of law or any other provision which prevents the tenant in vacating the accommodation in spite of the fact that none of the grounds mentioned in Section 12 exists. It says further in paragraph 10 "Merely enumeration of grounds on which relief can be claimed" does not either expressly or impliedly exclude the operation of Order23, Rule3 because grounds for claiming relief are always limited whether the relief be claimed under the general law or a statute. [822D] 5. The words "where it is established to the conclusion that a decree for the ejectment of a person from any accommodation can be made except on one or more of the ground mentioned in section 12(2). Reading the section as a whole and remembering the beneficial object of the Act for the protection of a tenants based upon public policy, we do not find much difficulty in bringing the section at par with other similar State statutes and holding as a matter of construction that no decree for ejectment can be granted except on two or more grounds mentioned therein. [823D] 6. The provisions of Section 11(1), 12(3) and 13(4) are quite different from those of Order 21, Rule 4 when it states "Where the Court is satisfied that a tenant has been evicted by any unlawful agreement or settlement. the Court shall order such compromise, either express or implied, to be recorded, and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit". [823F] 7. The expression "where the Court finds that a case has been settled by any legal agreement or otherwise." is not different.

The assessee company was doing business as selling agents of a Textile Mill. The Income tax Officer disallowed an amount of Rs. 11,88,COO/was a loss relating to shares held by the company in Elphinstone Mill Ltd. of Bombay. In appeal, the Asstt. But all the same as there was no commercial profits in the relevant accounting years it was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividend in respect of those years in view of the capital loss incurred and he. therefore cancelled the orders of the Income tax officer under section 23A (1). The Tribunal held that the amount of depreciation had been a loss of Rs, 11,87,COo/was not reasonable. In further appeal, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the High Court erred in holding that the payment of a dividend or a larger dividend than that declared by a company would be unreasonable within the meaning of section 23 A (1) (Consolidation) Ordinance, 1950 of Tanganyika Mills Ltd., and that the Tribunal had not taken into consideration the depreciation in the value of the shares in the matter of declaration of dividends. Held, that the assessee had suffered a capital loss of about Rs. 10 lakhs during the relevant assessment years. The High Court was right in holding on the facts found by the Tribunal that the sum of Rs 11,86,CO0O/is a loss related to shares owned by the assessee in El Phinstone Mills Ltd. was not unreasonable within section 23 (1)(Consolidation) Act, 1950. Commissioner of Income tax vs Williamson Diamonds Ltd., ; , referred to.

The appellants filed objections before the Civil Judge, Aligarh, under section 12(4) of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954, against an award made by the Civil Court. The District Judge overruled the objection and set aside the order of the Civil judge modifying the award. On appeal to the High Court, it was contended that the provisions of section 15 of the Act apply only where there is a dispute between the parties and the arbitrator has no jurisdiction to modify the award in his favour. Held, that the effect of section 37 of the . is inter alia to apply sections 15 and 39 of the to the proceedings under the Act. The effect of s.37 of the , is that all the provisions Of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations referred to in section 37. Section 37 of ' the Act does not make any distinction between provisions like section 39 and section 15. It is true that at p. the stage of making an award under section 11(4), the arbitrator will be appointed by the State Government from amongst Civil Judicial Officers or Assistant Collector of the I class of not less than five years standing and in all other respects the matter shall be determined in accordance with the provisions contained in the . Section 37 does not apply to arbitration proceedings referred to under section 37, but only to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holding Act. It cannot be held as providing anything inconsistent with this. The object of section 36 is that the arbitrator should have been appointed by a competent Court and he should have given his award on the basis of the provisions in the Act and if it was so read it would not make no difference between provisions of sections 15, 16 and 39.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the Corporation without making any rules or regulation in that behalf. The corporation made regulations by passing a resolution and continued the same practice. In 1988, the corporation passed a resolution for the first time making 75 per cent of the posts of superintading Engineers available to the executive Engineers holding degrees and 25 per cent to the Executive Engineers who were diploma holders. This resolution was also subsequently not a regulation made under section 64 of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961. But for this resolution, the petitioner who was senior to respondent No. 2 would have been promoted to the post on that date. The Corporation passed a Resolution, for the second time making 50 per cent posts of attending Engineers available in the executive Engineer holding degrees or 25 per percent to the Assistant Engineers. This Resolution was also not a Regulation made under the said section 64. But, for this Resolution, the Petitioner who was junior to respondent NO. 2 could have been considered as senior to him. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineer on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the posts in question on a basis other than that in the case before the them, the classified for purpose of promotions on a scale higher than that was in the category of junior Engineers. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The classification is permissible and does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [75B] 1.2 In view of the above, the petition stands dismissed. [76D] 1:3 The principle that in a given case, a valid classification can be made amongst the members holding the same post on the ground that they belong to the same cadre on the date when they were promoted to that cadre on a consideration other than the one in the cases before them the classified person for promotion on a particular basis. [77E] 1 :4 The principle of equality is applicable only where there is a discrimination which is permissible, it could be said that such a classification is impermissible and does neither violate Articles14 and 16. [78G] 1.:5 In the instant case, the classification was already made which was challenged before the Court. It is not a case where no separate quota for promotion to post of Assistant Engineer was kept for degree holder Junior Engineers and diploma holder Junior Engineer. Hence, the observation are per incuriam as regards the next contention, admittedly neither the practice adopted till 1988 nor the resolution passed in accordance with section 64 was not challenged before any Court. [79G] 2:6 The very Bench which decided Roshan Lal Tandon vs Union of India, ; , relied on Roshan Lal 's case [supra] and H.C.R.S. Kholi vs State of Mysore & Ors., ; , distinguished.

The petitioner, an advocate practising in this Court, was appointed as a Judge of the High Court. He was promoted to the post of Chief Justice of the Bombay Bar Association. The first petition was filed by an advocate practicing in this court. The second petition was by an Advocate practising in the High Courts. The third petition was directed against the appointment of the petitioner as a permanent judge of the Supreme Court. The petitioner contended that the constitutional obligation of the Union of India to provide the sanctioned Judge strength in the superior courts and the default, if any, was a matter of public interest and the writ petitions requiring a direction to the Union Of India to fill up the vacancies within specified dates. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that it was the constitutional duty of the State to provide for the sanctioned judge strength in superior courts subordinate to the High court and seek the views of the Chief Justice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Petitioner that (1) the constitutional mandate of the Constitution is a basic feature of the judiciary; (2) the Chief Judge of a High Court, the Chief Minister of the Government of India, the District Judges subordinate to him are merely Constitutional functionaries having a consultative role and the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Government ; (3) the President of India is not an officer of the Central Govern ment; (4) the Governor of the States is not a person who has been appointed as Chief Justice or the Chief Secretary of the concerned State; (5) the High courts are not independent constitutional functionaries having any consultative capacity and the powers of appointment are vested in the President under Article 239(1)(a); (6) the power to appoint Judges of the high Courts is a part of the executive function of the Governor. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The constitutional philosophy of separation of powers to the extent recognised and adumbrated and the cherished values of judicial independence cannot be divorced from the process of appointments. [121B] 2.1 The Constitution envisages Rule of Law and inde pendence of the Judiciary. The State executive initiating the proposal must first forward it to the ChiefJustice of the Court who would be better informed about the practising advocates as well as the District Judge subordinate to that High Court and seek views of his Chief Justice; and there can be a fresh look at the matter only if the Chief Justices of the two Courts, in the order of preference, to which they would prefer to be so appointed as permanent judges. [122C D] 2:2 The constitutional phraseology would require to be read and expounded in the context of the constitutional philosophy that the Chief Judges of a high Court and such other Judges of this Court as the Central Gover ment may deem it neces sary to consult, are merely constitutional functionaries who have a consult ence and the Power of appointment resided solely and mainly in the State. [123D] 3:3 The constitutional language would require that to be interpreted in the light of the Constitutional philosophy of equality enshrined in Article 14 of the Consti tution of India. The power of appoint ment resides solely or exclusively in th e Central Government. It is clear on a plain reading of these two Articles that the Governor, the State executive initiate the proposal for filling up of vacancies within stipulated dates. [124D] 4:4 The constitutional concept postulates Rule of law and indes sion of the justice of the people. The Constitution provides that every functionary associated with the process remains cognisant of the legal obligation involved in the matter we see no justification as to why for selection of the incumbent more than 3 to 4 months should be necessary. [125E] 5:5 The constitutional provi sions are essentially meant for the executive and not for the judiciary.

The respondent was a Relieving Head Cashier in the K.G. He submitted a bill for Rs.2,800 on May 5, 1978 along with a stamped cash receipt purported to have been issued by M/s. The said bill was passed by the bank on May 15, 1978 but subsequent investigations revealed that the firm of M/S. Thereupon the respondent was served with a Memo dated August 1, 1978 by the Divisional Office of the Bank calling for his expla nation. The Enquiry Officer conducted the departmental enquiry against the respondent and held the re spondent guilty by the end of 1979. The respondent 's departmental appeal was also dis missed on June 17, 1980. Thereafter the respondent filed an application before the Chief Executive Officer to hold and conduct departmental enquiries against the members of the staff governed by the provisions of Chapter 19 of the Bi partices Settlement dated 19th October, 1966. The Chief Executive officer dismissed the said application. The High Court allowed the writ petition quashed the order of discharge and directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The acts of an officer de facto performed within the sphere of their assumed official authority, in the interest of the public or third parties and not for his own benefit are generally as valid and binding as if they were performed by a de jure Committee. [201B] 1.2 In all other cases, the acts done by an officer whose appointment is found to be defective are valid and effec tary, while he is suffered to retain the office, as though he were an officer by right and the same legal consequences will flow from them for the protection of the Public and of the third parties. [202G] 1:3 The acts done in the present case do not attribute any bias or mala fides to the Enquiry Officer nor did he com plain that he was in any manner prejudiced on account of the said Enquiry Officer conducting him domestic enquiry but that will not cure the defect as to his compensat ion. [203F G] 1 :4 The respondent had not denied any bias, mala fides or mala fide to the enquiry officer nor did it lead to any inference that he had been in any way prejudiced on the account of his alleged misconduct. The acts were done by a person whose appointment was found to have be defective and the official acts done were valid and invalid and effac tive, while the respondent is suffered from retain ing the office as though they were an Officer by right. [204A] 1.:5 In the instant case, the respondent did not attribute anything bias or malafide to the Enquiring Officer nor does he com pany that he is in any position to perform his duties as a de facto Committee. The allegations made against him are clearly vague and do not constitute any malice or mala rea on account thereof demand but because the technical plea of incompetence suc ceeds. [205B] 2:6 In the circumstances, the High Court was right in quashing the order passed by it. [206C D] 1:-7 The respondent will be paid 50% of the consequential benefits and not all the consequential bene fits.

The appellant Corporation, by a letter dated February 4, 1966 informed the respondents that their application for execution of construction work in respect of house Nos. Attempts made by the respondents to satisfy the Commissioner that their applications were quite legal and that there was no violation of any law or rules having failed, they filed Civil Writ Petition No. 169 of 1967 before the High Court challenging the validity of the Master Plan. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that the Master plan prepared under the Delhi Development Act 1957 was not in contravention of the master plan and that the Zonal Development Plan had been prepared under section 7 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 (Act LXVI of 1957) (hereinafter referred to as the Development Act). The appellant Corporation filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the order of rejection passed by the Commissioner. The Division Bench dismissed the Writ Petition on the view that the master Plan prepared under s.7 of the Act was not a zonal development plan and, therefore, the Zonal Planning Plan had no force. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant Corporation that the building in question was constructed by the appellant under the Master Plans and the Zonal Master Plan had not been prepared for the area in question. HELD: (1) The Master Plan is prepared under sections 7 and 9 of the Development act, 1957. [3766 C] (2) The Zonal Master plan has been prepared simultaneously with the preparation of the Zonal development Plan simultaneously with preparation of a Master Plan simultaneously alongwith the preparation thereof. Section 14 provides for the preparation by the Authority of a zonal Development plan for each of the zones into which Delhi may be divided and also refers to the various matters which are to be indicated in the same. [38A] (3) The master plan is prepared simultaneously along with the proposal sent for sanction. If such an indication is made available by the Zonal Authority, then section 14 will quite naturally stand attracted, because any user of a land or building otherwise than in conformity with the Zonal Plan will be hit by that section. [39B] (4) The reasonable interpretation to be placed on section 14 would be that if any particular and definite use of land is indicated in a Master plan, a different use of that land cannot be permitted.

The appellant No. 1 was charged with having committed offences under sections 120 B, 161, 465 and 466 of the Indian Penal Code and the appellant No 2 was charged for having committed an honest mistake when narrating the events that had happened on that night. The Special Judge acquitted both the appellants of the various offences with which they were charged. He did not award any separate sentence to him. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The statement made by the appellant no. 1 before them was also attacked on the ground that it was intended to be made to the police and was represented as having been made to a third person merely as a colourable pretence in order to avoid the bar of section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code or by way of greater caution particularly having regard to the fact that the appellant had brought about Rs. 1,000 from his home. [1111B C] (2) The statements made by him before them were not read over to them and therefore could not have the value which otherwise they would have had. [1211D E] (3) The circumstances under which the numbers of currency notes were recorded in the Panchnama, the statement made on oath by the appellants before them being a colourable device was not admissible. [1311B] (4) The evidence of these witnesses therefore was not such as to inspire confidence in the mind of the court. [1412C D] (5) The circumstance under which they might have committed an offence of taking bribe or illegal gratification by the accused persons was not a relevant factor for determining whether the appellant was guilty of the offence charged against him.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971 which led to the prosecution of the plaintiff along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the appellant was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh, who was also con tinued with the plaintiff 's service because of his being in jail. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that the plain tiff was not served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. The High Court held that the suit was barred by limitation and that the order of dismissal was illegal on the grounds that the clear tiff had to be re instated in service for a short time in pursuance of the decision in the suit as the order was not passed by an authority not compe tent in this regard, and that there fore, the bar of limitation would not apply. The State appealed against the judgment of the High Court which was dismissed at the admission stage by merely saving: "HEARD. DISMISSED" It has been further contended on behalf of the appellants that the impugned orders of dis missal were void on the basis of the ground of limitation and, therefore, the order passed by the first appellate court was illegal in the eye of law inasmuch as the plaintififf was given the 825 benefit of probation by the criminal court and his case, therefore was distinguishable. It has also been contended that the High Courts erred in dismissing the second appeal in limine. The respondent filed a regular second appeal before the High court against the decree of the first appel lant which was allowed by the High Curt. In this appeal it was contended on his behalf that the other accused constable Kahan singh had also filed a separate suit against his dismissal from service, which was decreed with an observation that it was open to the competent authorities to pass fresh order of punishment in accordance with law, but while no further punishment was awarded to Kahan SINGH, the respondent 's services stood terminated. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question involved in this suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the courts below permitting the competent authority to inflict only minor punishment on the plaintiff in certain conditions, and the direction about the payment of salary and other emoluments. [724C D] 2.1 In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the High cir tions shall permit the plaintiff to file relevant rebutting evidence. The operation of the decree o f the first appeal court shall remain stayed till the final disposal of the second appeals by the trial Court by the order dated 8th December, 1982. [761D] 2:2 In the instant case, the question involved is whether the suit should be barred by Limitation and whether the order awarding the salary and the other emoluments was illegal or not. The authority was also permitted to take a decision in regard to the pay and allowance for the period the plaintiff remained out of service because he being in prison. [758E] 3:3 In the case of admission, fresh evidence is required to be filed before the competent court 's decree in his favour, and to argue before the Civil Court that the case was an old one. The order of dismis sion is patently illegal inasmuch as it assumes that no law of limitation is applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void.

The assessee was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites. The assessee entered into a contract with M/s. The Income tax officer held that the transactions were speculative and consequently the losses suffered by the assessee in these transactions could not be set off against the profits made by the appellant 's non speculative business. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner on reference held that there was no actual or physical delivery of possession of the goods sold and that the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh (1) and Duni Chand Rataria vs Bhuwalke Brothers Ltd., M. 24 (2) read with explanation 2 to section 24(1). Justice Ayyangar speaking for the Court relied on an English decision in D. V. Ramanna Bhimayya & sukhdevi Rathi 's case (supra) and duni Chand vs Bhuawalke Brothers, Ltd., ; , referred to. Held:(i) The transactions described above entered into by the respondents were mere sales of delivery order or sales of any commodity so as not to bring it within the meaning of explanation 2 thereto. The transaction was a speculative one and the assessee had taken actual delivery of the possession of goods sold. It was not a mere sale but a mere delivery of physical possession which was obtained by the intermediate parties was thus translated into a physical or manual delivery of Possession in the ultimate analysis eliminating the unnecessary process of each of the intermediate Parties taking and in his turn giving actual delivery thereof possession of their goods in the narrow sense of physical or electronic delivery thereof. The intention of the legislature was that "actual delivery of actual delivery" was actual delivery as also symbolic or constructive delivery, and having regard to the mischief which was sought to be averted by the promulgation of the ordinance to prevent persons who dealt in differences only and never intended to take delivery under any circumstances it was held that a transaction of sale wherein the goods were not physically delivered by the seller to the buyer but only laid down that if there was actual or actual delivery, the loss, if any, would be a loss in a speculative transaction which could be allowed to be set aside only against a profit in a transaction. (ii) The intention was that the ultimate purchaser of the P.D.Os. had taken physical delivery and had no control over the goods. It is not correct to think that if any transfer of the R.D., were followed up by actual delivery or transfer of possession, that transaction was to be considered as speculative. (iii) The definition of "delivery" in section 2(2) of the Indian it was clear that the expression "actual deliver" occurring in sec. 2(1) of Indian it would include actual delivery and having respect to the object which was intended to be achieved by the enactment of the Ordinance, the legislature did not intend to affect any transaction of transfer wherein the property was not physically or physically delivered. (iv) The word "actual" occurring therein in section 24 of the Act is only designed at segregating for 187 income tax purposes loss sustained in transactions of a certain kind. It would include physical delivery as well symbolic or actual deliver, and had regard to all mischief which were sought to been averted by virtue of the enactment. (v) The expression "

The appellant was elected to the Legislative Assembly of Punjab from the constituency. The first respondent was declared elected by the Returning Officer on the ground that he had not attested the nomination paper and that he was entitled to be declared elected. The appellant challenged the election of the first respondent on the grounds (1) that the nomination papers were invalid, (2) that there was no failure to comply with section 33 unless he could and should have had recourse to section 36(4). Held, that the word " subscribe" is used in Chapter I of Part V dealing with the Nomination of Candidates while in every other place the word ' sign " is used. It imports assent to his nomination. The Returning Officer was therefore bound to reject any nomination paper on the view that there had been a failure to do so and the omission formally to record the satisfaction could probably, in a case like that, be regarded as an unsubstantial technicality. The words " signs" and "subscribe" are not used in the same sense in the Act because a special meaning has been given to the word I sign " plus something else, namely a particular assent, the element of " signing" has to be present; the omission merely formally to make the attestation is not an essential part of the process of signing. The word " subscribing" is only used in section 36 and not in the ordinary sense. It does not mean that the words "sign" and 'subscribe", therefore, must be construed as having been used in it.

The appellants were employees of the Company. During the pendency of the reference No. 336 of 1972, the Company put up a notice stating that their names had been struck off from the rolls of the company from that date and that they would report for work the moment the strike was called off by their union. On September 19, 1972, certain proposals for settlements were made on behalf of the employees whose services were terminated by the Company and requesting the Company to re instatement of the appellants and 10 other workmen. The Company sent a cheque to each one of the appellant for the amount due to him on account of gratuity leave salary and one month 's salary. On October 2, 1972 the Company sent separate communications to the appellants stating that since "by not reporting for duty they had confirmed their presumption that they were no longer interested to continue in service of theCompany and had totally abandoned the Company 's service" their names have been struckoff from the roll of the said company from the register of the Labour Department. On November 23, 1972 certain proposals were made by the employees' union for settlement of disputes between the appellants, 10 other employees and 10 others informing them that since they had already been replied by letter dated September 26, 1972 they would come to a conclusion that they had abandoned the service of Company and had thereby abandoned the services of the workmen. On December 2, 1973, the appellants wrote to the Company returning the cheques sent by the company and stating therein that their letters dated September 7, 1972 were received by them on September 20, 1972 and not earlier was never denied or refuted by the appellant in the correspondence that passed between the parties. The Assistant Commissioner thereupon summoned the parties for discussion on July 19, 1973 but his attempts to conciliation did not bear fruit. Thereafter, the respondents made the aforesaid complaints before the Industrial Tribunal with the result as stated above. On May 19,1973, certain demands were made from the appellants. On August 30, 1972 a notice was sent by one of them for the payment of gratuity, leave salary, and one months 's wages. The appellants filed their replies to the said notices on September 26. 1972 but did not give any reply thereto. Thereafter the appellants made the aforementioned complaints before Industrial Tribunal. The Industrial Tribunal summoned the appellants for discussion as stated in the letter dated October 23,1972 but his attempt was unsuccessful. On July 19 1973, certain applications were made before the Company Law Board and the Company was allowed to be withdrawn by the appellants on September 21, 1972. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Industrial tribunal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the action of the respondent in removing the names of the petitioners from its rolls was illegal and arbitrary and that the appellants had not abandoned the company 's services and that since the standing orders did not provide for treating the workmen as having abandoned service in case they were absent in connection with the notified strike, the action was manifestly illegal and invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf the appellants that the High court committed an error of law in holding that there was no abandonment of employment by the respondent and that therefore the action taken by the respondents was not justified.
