Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The letter dated August 7,1972 is received by the workmen on September 10, 1972 which is on all fours with the present case, it is held that if the employees absent themselves from the work because of strike in enforcement of their demands, there can be no question of abandonment of service by them. [606B] 1.2 The failure to perform the duties pertaining to the office must be with actual or imputed intention, on the part of the officer to abandon and relinquish the office. Temporary absence is not ordinarily sufficient to constitute an abandonment of office '.

The appellant, a public trust, styled as "Shri Tricumraiji" was created by the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. The trustees applied under 0. 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale and deposited Rs. 6 for payment to the mortgagee, claiming that in consideration o the latter amount the mortgagee had agreed to give six months ' time for payment of the mortgage amount. The appellant was not given any notice as required by r. 21 of the Bombay Land Revenue Rules, 1959. The respondent filed a suit against the trustees and the appellant was impleaded as defendant No. 1. The trial court held that since the trustees bad failed to comply with the requirements of r.21 Code of Criminal Procedure, the executing Court had no jurisdiction to set aside the auction sale. On appeal by the appellant, the District Judge reversed the order holding that since a trustee had agreed in the meantime to abandon the application for execution, the execution court had no power to set it aside and remanded the case to the District Court for decision on all the points correctly arising out of the matter. The High Court held that the sale was invalid as the trustees had failed to complied with the requirement of r 21 Code of civil Procedure. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The expression 'sale ' in section 36(a) includes a sale of the property of a public Trust in execution of a decree of a civil court for recovery of a debt due by the trust, and on that account a sale in execution was invalid. [459 E] (2) The High Courts were not justified in holding that the executing court had jurisdiction to decide the question until after notice had been given to the Charity Commissioner. [460 F] (3) The Court sale was valid as the trustee had failed in complying with the provisions of r, 21 Code Of Civil Procedure.

The appellant, a Government servant, joined the Post and Telegraph Department as a clerk on June 4, 1935. He was served with a notice dated June 4. 1935 to retire him at the age of 58 years. The order of retirement was challenged by him before the High Court. The Division Bench dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no in firmity in Rule 2(2) of the Pension Rules and that there is no vice of arbitrariness in the Rule. The Union of India has come up in appeal by special leave against the judgment of the Division Bench of the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The instructions are supplementary to the Rule, according to which the appropriate authority shall give a notice of not less than three months before the date on which he is required to retire, or three months ' pay and allowances in lieu of such notice, whichever is earlier. [608B C] 1.2 The instructions can only supplement and not supplant the rule. The relevant part of the memorandum is as under: "It has now been decided and the President is pleased to direct that the age Of compulsory retirement of Central Government servants should be 58 years subject to the following exception: 6. This will be in addition to the provisions already contained in Rule 1(2)(a) only on the ground of 'Public Interest '. [613D E] Union of lndia and others vs R. Mr. Anil Der Singh, ; , referred to.

The assessee firm, a partnership firm, was carrying on the business of manufacturing and sale of various kinds of goods. The assessee firm did not maintain any books of account and the entire record of the business transaction was maintained in the books of M/s Biharilal Balkishan in the account styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". The Income Tax Officer allowed such deficiency of Rs.5,600 only. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the assessee had suffered no deficiency of profits during the period 28th October, 1940 to 31st March, 1943 and was entitled to be given the benefit of such deficiency. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court set aside the order of the Income Tax officer and allowed the assessee 's claim for deduction under section 10(1) of the Act. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High court fell in error in holding that upon the principle of apportionment of profits to which it had adverted to, the profits earned upon sales effected during the chargeable accounting period ending 31st December, 1941 should be set off in computing the excess profits for the chargeable year ending 31 st March, 1944 and that the said amount was not liable to be treated as the profits of that charge able accounting period. HELD: (1) The High Court fell in an error in coming to the conclusion that upon a principle of apportion ing profits to Which it had referred to,the profits earned on sales effected after the chargeable date ending 31 March, 1946 and the deficiency of the profits worked out on that basis in respect of the chargeable period ending 3rd March, 1945 must be set aside. [608 B] (2) The question must be answered in the negative and in favour of the Revenue. [613 C D] (3) The assessee was entitled under section 4(1)(a) to claim deduction for the loss sustained by it during the relevant accounting period and not on the basis of any profits earned or arisen during that period.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department, as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May, 1978. The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after in an interview held by it. There was a common question paper which contained, in category I, questions in Mechanical Engineering and in Category II, questions In Mechanical Engineering. After the written examination and the interview, but before a common rank list was prepared by the Public Service commission, the Government and the Public Services Commission of Kerala proceeded to prepare separate lists. The petitioners had to be appointed when his turn comes. There were directions to the K PSC to prepare two separate rank lists for Civil Engineering graduates and the other for Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted. The Government and Public Service Commissions of Kerala, however, did not find any valid ground to reverse the judgments of the High Court. On receipt of information from the Government on the above lines, the Public Commission was directed to prepare a separate list for Civil Engineer and Mechanical Engineering prepared on the strength of the directions given by the learned Single Judge in his judgment dated 23rd March, 1979. The Public Service Commissioner, Kerala issued an order dated 28th April, 1980 dismissing all the S.L.P. with observations referred to above. On receiving information from Government on these lines, it was directed that the two separate lists should be prepared and published separately. On publication of the two lists the Government can request the service Commission to advise the candidates for appointment to these branches on the ground that they have already been appointed. The KP SC filed appeals before the Division Bench of the Kerala High Court which allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government to prepare "two separate rank list, one for the Civil Bench and the others for the Mechanical Branch. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Government had advised the candidates according to the separate lists for civil Engineering graduates prepared on their basis and that these candidates had already been recruited. It was further submitted that in pursuance of the direction given by this Court in its order dated 11th November, 1980, the K.PSC had advised 239 candidates according according to separate lists, one from the Civil and Mechanical Engineers prepared on behalf the basis that the petitioners had already be appointed. It is contended that the expression "the common list prepared by Public Service" contained in clause 4 of the Government order No. G.O.MS. It reads thus: "Government also order that all those who have submitted unconditional options and who possess the required qualifications prescribed in the rules will be appointed by transfer to the respective service". The K P.SC, therefore had made the Misc. Petition before the High court for clarifications and directions. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioner will be entitled to exercise his option and then take his turn according to his rank in the common list. [775G H] 2. The expression "in pursuance of" in clause (4) of the order dated 23 rd March, 1980 has been subsequently recalled by this court by its order on 7th April. 1981 and we do not find that any valid reason has been given to reverse these judgments of High Court.[776B C] 3. The High Court was right in holding that there were directions for preparation of separate list of selected applicants holding Civil and Electrical Engineering diploma and the two other for Civil Engineers and Mechanical Engineer candidates as stated above. [771D] 4. The order dated 7th March, 1981 is obviously an inadvertent mistake. It refers to a common list though no common list was directed.

The plaintiff respondent No. 1, a partner of a partnership firm, filed a suit for dissolution of the partnership firm and for accounts. The defendant No. 2, besides denying the plaint allegations made by the plaintiff, challenged the valuation given by the defendant as grossly undervalued and arbitrary. The trial court decreed the suit on the ground that the correct value of the suit is beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the relief to the tune of lacs of rupees has been claimed by the appellant in the suit. In this appeal, it was contended for the appellant that the plaintiff requested for and was allowed a larger share 'in the well established and reputed business of auctioneer known as "Russell Exchange" and its assets and goodwill as well as the amount lying in the Habib Bank, Karachi Branch, solely and absolutely '. The respondent No 1 has challenged the said valuation given on behalf of the plaintiff as grossly inadequate and arbitrary, and that the court is bound to accept that ' made on behalf o the plaintiff before the Allahabad High Court in Aizaz Ahmad vs Nazirul Hasan, AIR 1935 Allahabad 849, was rejected after observing that there was some authority for the extreme view as urged in two Calcutta decisions but later a different view was taken by the said Court as also by the Allahabad Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. [501F] 1.2 In a suit under section 7(iv)(f) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, the plaintiff is entitled to give his own tentative valuation. The plaintiff has not been given the absolute right or option to place any valuation whatever on such relief and where the plaintiff manifestly and deliberately under estimates the relief the court was entitled to examine the correctness of the valuation made by him. [525A B] 1:3 In a case for accounts the plaintiff can give an arbitrary valuation in the plaint, and if he does so put a quantified valuation upon his suit but he cannot do so, he is entitled not to ask for an unreasonable or arbitrary figure. The court is entitled, therefore, to examine correctness of such valuation. [500C] 1 :4 In a proceeding under section 8(iv) of Income Tax, the Court has to consider whether the valuation put by the assessee on the relief claimed in the application is patently arbitrary or unreasonable. If it is patently illegal and unreasonable, the court would be entitled to examined the correctness and to revise the same if it is manifestly arbitrary or irrational. [511F] 2.1 In a petition under section 9 of the Act, the petitioner has not challenged the value given by him on behalf or in any other manner. The question whether the Court was powerless to challenge the valuation fixed by the Income tax officer on the basis that the valuation was erroneous is a matter which can be examined by the trial court and it cannot be said that the Court is bound, to accept the valuation so fixed. [506B] 2:2 In the instant case, the defendant No 1, in his plaint, has not disputed the value of Rs. 50 for the purpose of court fees. The suit was governed for the purposes of court fee by section 7 (iv)(a) of Act, 1961 and the plaintiff had no absolute right to put on the plaint any value he wishes to and the court has no jurisdiction to examine such a valuation. It is not only open to the Court but its duty to reject such a valued.

The appellant, a small scale industrial unit, was granted exemption from excise duty under the notification dated 23.10.81 and thereafter, on the basis of an agreement entered into with it, the appellant was required to pay sales tax at the rate applicable to the new industrial units including pioneer units going into production after 1 4 1981 not only under the earlier schemes but also under other notifications dated 1 5 82 and 29 6 82. The appellant 's case was that the notification did not authorise him to say that, though the applicant fulfills the terms of the notification, he will not grant the eligibility certificate because, under the previously prevalent schemes, he could not issue an eligibility certificate to "tradition al industries". The Assistant Director of Industries, by his order dated 12.1.1983, rejected the appellant ' s claim for exemption on the ground that the earlier scheme and procedure were different in nature and did not cover the case of the appellant. The appel lant filed a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant had failed to satisfy the conditions laid down in the notification and that the Director of Industry was not competent to issue an Eligibility certificate to new industrial unit for the purpose of this concession. In appeal, the Division Bench held that the exemption granted by the Government under the notifications dated 23 10 1981 and 29 4 82 was valid and that there was no violation of any provisions of the Act or the Rules made thereunder. The High Court also held that since the notification does not authorise the appellant to say in respect of cotton fabrics which had been got manufactured by him on powerlooms belonging to a cooperative society in pursuance of an earlier scheme, he would not be entitled to the exemption under the said notifications. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the High Courts were wrong in holding that since there was a notification issued separately, the Government had decided to issue the eligibility cer tain certificate to the appellant and that, therefore, the Director could have granted the same. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The notification does neither authorise him nor to say whether, though he fulfills the conditions of the earlier notifications, he can not issue any eligibility certificate for "training industries". [418C] 2.1 In the first place, the earlier Schemes spe cifically provided that "traditional industries" were out side their purview. The notification did neither authorise the Director to say anything more than what was required by the notification. It only authorised him to issue eligibility certificate. It does not authorize him to state that, although the applicant fulfill the terms Of the notification he will be entitled for exemption under it. [419D] 2:2 In the second place, there is no indication that the Government has decided to grant the exemption certificate because under the previous prevalent schemes he could have issued an eligibility certain to new units claiming exemption from/deferment of payment of sales tax. The option once exercised shall be irrevocable. [420G] 3:1 In cases where the plea is that, despite the earlier orders, he was not entitled to exemption under notification and the procedure in accordance with which the Director had issued the eligibility Certificate, that earlier scheme was out side his purview. [416D] 4:2 The Government has announced "conces sions" regarding the payment of Sales Tax by new industrial Units including ptioneer units gone into production before 1 41981 not only on 12. 1 1983 but also on 29 682. In other words, registered dealers selling raw materials to a new industrial Unit are not required to charge any sales tax from the new Industrial unit on sales made by them to such unit. They travel beyond and counter to the notification issued. [413E] 4.

The appellant was appointed as Additional District and Sessions Judges on an ad hoc basis in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service. The post of Additional District & Sessions Judge was a temporary post. The appellant was promoted to the post of District and Session Judges on ad hoc appointment. On the basis of the recommendations made by the High Court, the appellant was placed at serial No. 1 in the seniority list. In the seniority lists, the name of the appellant figured at serial Nos. 2 and 3. The respondent 's name was not included in the said list. The High Court held that the appellant had been appointed as a District and sessions Judge for an unbroken period of anything between 8 to 12 years were regarded as juniors to the direct recruits who were also working in the same capacity. In appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) Rule 16(2) requires that at any given point of time, 1/3rd of substantive posts shall be reserved for direct recruits or does it only stipulate that the posts held by direct recruits shall not be more than 1/4th of the total number of substantive vacancies in the Service. [529G] (2) The rule making authority must have regard to officiating service and count only regular service when claims of seniority arise before it, provided the rules in that regard are clear and categoric and do not admit of any ambiguity and an arbitrary cut of long years of service does not take place. All incumbents holding either substantive posts or temporary posts in substantive capacities are members of the service, in the context of the present rule. [629G H] (3) The seniority list has to be quashed. It is only when they are appointed in a substantive capacity to a post in the service that they become members of service, that they became members of Service. In other words, does the proviso require that at no given point or time,1/3 rd of the substantive posts in the Services shall be filled in by direct recruitment. [525A B] (4) The principle which has received the sanction of this Court 's pronouncements is that officiating service in a post is for all practical purposes of seniority as good as service on a regular basis. It may even be that in the process of consultation, the High court exercises greater vigilance in regard to appointments proposed under Rule 16 than in regard thereto. But if they are selected in accordance with rules and regulations, they would be entitled to count only officiating service for purpose of seniority. [500B C] (5) The expression "Cadre Post" is used in a wide sense so as to include substantive vacancies which may arise in the course of time. It does not mean that the rule making power must be exercised with due regard to the exigencies of administration and the need for maintaining efficiency in the services. [429G G] (6) The word "C Cadre Post" means a post specified in the Schedule. The inclusive clause contained in the second part of Rule 2(b) has to take its meaning from what precedes it. It cannot be said that the principle which had received the approval of this court 's decisions is that substantive vacancies should not be filled by making temporary appointments. [504B C; 504A] (7) The contention that the seniority of promotees ought not to be disturbed on the ground that they have derived quite some benefits from the operation of Rules 16 and 17, is misconceived. It was urged that the High Courts had exercised greater vigilance while considering the cases of direct recruits and promotees who were working as temporary Additional District Judges for an over aged period of time and had been serving since then with ability.

The appellant was a partner in a firm carrying on business of manufacturing and selling cotton. The partnership business was carried on by an association of persons and the income from the business was liable to be brought to tax on that footing. For the assessment year 1951 52, Debi Parshad filed a return in the status of a Hindu Undivided Family. In appeal to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal, the appellant contended that the Appellate Assistant Commissioner had no jurisdiction to direct after setting aside the order of assessment that Debi Parishan was a stranger in respect of the income tax proceedings against Ambala Flour Mills 3. The High Court allowed the appeals and remanded the case to the Appellate Tribunal for fresh assessment. In further appeal by certificate, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Income Tax Officer had no power to direct the Incometax Officer to make fresh assessment after setting out the reasons for his order. HELD: (1) The Appellate Assistant Com missioner had directed that the income in the three assessment years be assessed in the hands of the family of Debi Parathan and he was liable, to be assessed personally in respect thereof. [439 F] (2) The Income tax Officer had directed the IncomeTax Officer to assess the income of the Ambala Flour Mill on the view that by the order dated September 26, 1951, the income belonged to Debi Parker. The Appellate Tribunal had directed him to give directions with regard to the assessment of the Income. Tax Officer to the effect that the assessee may be personally assessed in respect o the income. [539 F G] (3) The High court was right in holding that the order passed by the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner was not and could not be referred to the High Court.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was the widow of the undivided paternal uncle of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for partition of the joint family properties in suit at Rs. 15,00,000 under section 7(iv)(f) of the Madras Fees Act, 1933. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court held that the plaint was governed by article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act and that the proper court fee to be paid was determined by article 5 B of schedule II of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appellant should have paid court fees under section 5 of the , in respect of his claim for partition as the respondent had not accepted the said view and that he was not bound to set aside the prior compromise decree between his father and the respondent and that, therefore, the suit was governed under article 17B of Schedule 11. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that the suit filed by the appellant was governed only by article 13 B of the Schedule II and that it was a claim for recovery of possession based on title within the meaning of section 7 (v) of Act. The question whether the property in respect Of which a share is claimed is joint family property or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is true that the question of court fees must be considered in the light of the allegations made in the plaint and its decision cannot be influenced either by the pleas in the 131 1032 written statement or by the final decision of the suit on the merits. The appellant was not entitled to set up a claim based on his title within article 17 A of Schedule I of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

The respondent No. 1, a high rise building on plot No. 2, was granted permission to construct a building on the ground that it had been constructed by the NDMC and that the construction of the building would be contrary to bye laws. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi, in its counter affidavit filed before this Court, denied the claim of the respondent No 1 and contended that the clearance of the Chief Fire Officer did not prevent the NDMC from enforcing the applicable bye laws and submitted that the approval given by the Chief fire officer was without jurisdiction as it had no power to sanction the revised plans. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the permission granted by the Municipal Corporation on 27.10.1987 was without authority of law and that, therefore, the NDMC could not take any steps for enforcing the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the NDMC had no jurisdiction to sanction a revised plan in respect of the construction work undertaken by it and that since the approval granted by it did not preclude the NDMC to enforce the applicable byelaws in any particular case, the clearance given to the plan by the D.D.A. was without any authority of power and that therefore, there was no question of the NDMC being empowered to sanction revised plans in respect thereof. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The NDMC has to bestow serious re consideration on its insistence to have such a pedestrian walk way for the building, if such walk ways do not already obtain in other buildings on the Road. Indeed at no stage of the proceedings before the High Court or even in important 613 communications bearing on the question of sanction, did the NDMC refer to specific objection based on the lacuna that Refuge Areas were not located on the "external" walls. [601B] 1.2 The purpose of refuge areas include that in the event of an out break of fire in the building the persons exposed to the hazard should be able to have immediate access to a place of safety which by its access to fresh air insulates them from heat and smoke and further that those persons could conveniently be extricated and rescued to safety by rescue operations. [0601C] 1:3 The purpose for Bye law 16.4.8 is intended to serve "Refuge Areas" must be located on walls which open into vacant space from which rescue operations are possible. In the event the Statesman Limited wish to provide only 0.3 sq. metre per person in accordance with the resolution of August 4, 1988, the MCD would have no objection to the same and the States man Limited in this regard be directed to amend their building plans in accordance With their desires . [602D] 1 :4 The purpose behind the Bye law is intended not to promote safety in building designs. While the clearance by theChief Fire Officer is an indispensable condition for eligibility for sanction, however, such clear ance, by itself, is not conclusive of the matter nor binding on the NDMC. [613B C] 1.:5.1 In the instant case, it was urged that the permissions granted by Municipal Corporation were without jurisdiction and that there was violation of Bye law16.4 which required the approval of the plans in question. The contents of Bye laws 16. 4.8 are borrowed from Part IV dealing with "Fire Precaution" in the National Building Code of India, 1983. [501C D] 1;602A] 2:7 In the light of the fact that the plans provide for refuge areas including that in case of an Out break of Fire in the buildings, persons exposed thereto to the risk should be unable to have adequate access to such a place.

The appellant, a joint Hindu family, was running the liquor shops. The parties tried to have partition effected between them through arbitrators but the attempt failed. The suit was numbered 39 of 1945 and the trial court decreed the suit on June 30, 1951. In appeal the High Court held that though the motor business carried on after the partition had ceased to be a joint family business yet as it was carried on by some members of a family their position was analogous to that of a partner carrying on partnership after dissolution and applying the principle underlying section 37 of the Partnership Act, he held that the two brothers carrying on the motor businesses were liable to account. In further appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the suit was barred by res judicata as the motor licence for the liquor shop carried on before the partition having ceased to exist and not up to March 31, 1946, and that the plaintiff 's conduct in going back upon that arrangement by filing a fresh suit in regard to the motor tenancy only was an afterthought. Held: (i) The compromise arrived at between the parties in the circumstances of the present case was binding on the parties thereto as a decree passed by invitum. (ii)The compromise was not a decree for partition but it was a decree and it was not binding upon the parties to the suit as a result of which the plaintiff could claim the benefit of section 90 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. (iii)The plaintiff ' s conduct in coming back upon the agreement of compromise arrived between the two parties in regard thereto was not precluded from reaping the fruits of that business.

The Salt Works extend over an area of about two hundred and fifty acres. At a few places, pucca platforms exist for fixing the water pump when required to pump water from the sea. (k) of section 2, read with the relevant rules framed in that connection, does not mean that every factory must have a building and that necessary permission for its construction or extension is to be obtained. The Salt Works extended over an Area of about three hundred and twenty acres. In respect of these areas, the salt works were carried on by the laborers engaged in the manufacture. The salt works did not come within the definition of the word " factory" under cl. (d) of s. 2 of the Act. The appellant firm was carrying on a manufacturing process in a building which was covered by the Factory Act of 1833. The respondent, who was the owner of the Salt Works, applied to the Salt Commissioner for permission to carry out the work and the application was rejected. The appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Salt works were not within the meaning of the expression " factory " under cl.(d) Of section 2 of that Act, and that the word ' premises " in cl.(d) meant only a building or a place where certain type of work is carried on. Held, that the definition was wide enough to include sheds erected in the quarry merely as a protection against the weather; they were only accessories to the quarry and the quarrying processes; and the legislature had not yet declared that open air works would be within the scope of the Factory Acts. The word " premises" is not restricted in scope to buildings alone, but includes buildings which are used for carrying sea water from a sea to the reservoirs, thence to the tapavanis and from there to the crystallizing pans which are specially prepared by thumping the mud and making the layer of tile ground hard and water tight. The definition of " factory ' in cl.(c) Of s.2 is carried out in the Salt Department only with a view to bringing about the change in its quality, and becomes salt, a marketable article. If that finished article was only put into the condition of a finished article by the processes to which it has been subjected in the hereditament, then the process will fall within the expression altering or adaptation for sale ". The words " premises " are not restricted to buildings only. They are only accessories of the quarry, and the definition is carried with reference to the word used in cl (d). The word 'premises" is wide enough so as to include buildings which have been used for building purposes. The term " premises ' is not confined to buildings which were used for a building but also includes buildings erected in such conversion. It merely means buildings which do not come under the definition, and are only incidental to the manufacture of salt. The expression " premises ", is not limited to buildings erected by way of trade or for purposes of gain. The mere sorting of rags will not amount to adapting for sale. The question whether a factory must be having a building, and if that constructed was only incidental, it would have fallen within the purview of cl.(b) Of sub section (1) of Section 151 of the Factories Act, is not relevant in this case.

The respondent was appointed as Instructor in Tailoring in the Department of Public Instructions. In 1949, he was absorbed with effect from December 1, 1949, but no order was passed in the case of the respondent despite repeated representations made by him. The respondent continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were taken on deputation from other Departments, he should also be absorbed in the department of Technical Education with effectfrom November 28, 1949. On June 11, 1956, the respondent was again posted as Instructor under Tailoring and recommended for his absorption with effect effect from November 28. 1949, which was the date on which he initially came on deputation. The intervening period between his reversion and reposting to the Polytechnic establishment subsequently was treated as leave. The case of Sri Srinivasamurthy is on all fours with that of Sri Narayanaswamy Chetty and he was deserving of similar treatment. D ' In view of the above, and since Sri Srinivasa Murthy, who was junior to him in the parent Department, came on Deputation to the polytechnic establishment later, he could not claim such promotions as of right. The State Government by a notification dated December 12, 1949 directed that the promotions of 63 petitioners therein from the post of Surveyors as Assistant Engineers were to take effect from that date irrespective of the dates on which they were put in charge of sub divisions. On April 21, 1965, the Government ordered the absorption of the respondents in the Departments of Technical education with effect form November 28 1949, and to give them benefits of revision of scales of pay. The Government by order dated February 19, 1964 directed that all the 63 petitioners who were similarly situated, should also stand absorbed in Department of Technical Affairs with effect on November 28 , 1949, as such they would be given the benefit of revision in scales of Pay. On May 21, 1966, the State Government ordered that the promotion of 63 petitioner therein from November 1, 1950, to November 28 was to take affect from that day irrespective of dates on where he was initially sent. The respondents filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the State to absorb the respondent with effect retrospectively from November 27, 1949 and to grant him all consequential benefits including weightage benefit. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the absorption was not ordered owing to any fault of the Respondent. Hence this appeal by the State. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The absorption of K. N. N., who was admittedly junior to the respondent and was identically situated, was accorded the same treatment as that of Narayanaswamy Naidu because the order of Chetty 's absorption was passed on March 19, 1965. [260F] 2.1 In making the impugned order, contrary to the recommendations of the State Public Service Commission, the state Government had acted arbitrarily and in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. The question whether the absorption is made by way of increments or weightage or benefit accruing depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [261F] 3.2 In making a wrongful order contrary to any rule of policy or service rule on the basis of which they could claim such promotion as of rights, it has not been shown that the absorbee was deputed to the Department. The absorption is not ordered due to any mistake of the employer. It has not come out from the record that the absorbed employee with effect to which he could claim those promotions as his right.

The appellant, a child of the Indian Council of Social Welfare and S.O.S., was appointed as a guardian of a minor appointed by the court in terms of section 26 of the . The appellant made an application to the High Court for a direction that the appellant be allowed to take a child in adoption. The High Court directed the appellant to make proper provision by way of deposit or bond or otherwise in accordance with the rules made under this Act to enable the child to be repatriated to India, and directed the respondent to permit him to remove his child from the limits of its jurisdiction, except for such purposes as may be prescribed and the leave to be granted by the 826 court may be special or general. The appellant contended that (i) the High Courts were in error in directing the appellant not to make a provision by which he was appointed; (ii) the appellant had made proper provision in the rules for the grant of permission to take child in the adoption, and (iii) the respondent had no authority to make such a provision. The respondent contended that the High court was in error when it directed the petitioner not to remove the child from its jurisdiction except for certain purposes as were prescribed under section 26(1)(a). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant has made proper provisions by way o deposit or bonds or otherwise, in accordance therewith and the rules framed thereunder to enable him to take such child in a particular State. [849E] 2.1 In order to make an order appointing a foreigner as guardian of the person of a child, it is necessary that the biological parents are known, they should be properly assisted in making a decision about relinquishing the child for adoption, by the Institution or centre or Home for Child Care or social or child welfare agency to which the child is being surrendered. [ 849E F] 2:2 The Indian Council for Social Welfare & the Indian Councils for Child Welfare are clearly two social and child welfare agencies operating at the national level and recognised by the Government of India as appears from the letter dated 23rd August, 1980 addressed by the Deputy Secretary to the Government, of Kerela. [820B] 2 :3 The appellant is a child under the care of a social or Child Welfare agency operating at a national level. He has made adequate provision in his rules for making a child for being given in adoption and an application for appointment of a guardian was made in the court of the latter State. Comparatively it may be some what difficult for a grown up child to get acclimatized to new surroundings in a different land and some times a problem may arise whether foreign adoptive parents would be able to win the love and affection of such grown up children. If after attaining the age of maturity, the child wants to know about its biological parents, there may not be any serious objection to the giving of such information to the child because after the child attains maturity, it was not likely to be easily affected by such information and in such a case the foreign adoptive parent may furnish such information as he thought fit. [821F H] 2(a) The appellant had no right to take the child in question in adoption except for those purposes as are prescribed under the rules. [822G] 3:1 In the instant case, the appellant has not made any proper provision for the giving or taking of a particular child in his adoption and nor has he made any application for the appointment of the foreigner as a guardianship of the child.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of dustrials and other items. The workmen were paid bonus at the rate of 13.51% on the basis of the formula adopted by the Tribunal. In consequence they raised a dispute with the Company. The Com pany denied the allegations of the Unions that enormous expenditure had been shown with a view to reduce the quantum of bonus. On the other hand, the Unions required various items to be added back. The Tribunal directed the payment of the balance 6.49% within the period mentioned 109 in the Award. D. Mukherjee, relates to three items (1) the method of calculation of direct tax and alternatively rebate for bonus found payable has to be calculated and 60% of the rebate has to he added back as allocable surplus. The Company challenged the award on other grounds without filing an appeal by it. The High Court rejected this contention of the Union. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1)(a) The claim of the union that enormous expenses had been paid with a direction to reduce its quantum of Bonus found payable is justified. [746C] (b) The Tribunal was not justified in allowing deduction of certain items from the gross profits for purposes of computing the available and allocable. [758E] (c) The third item objected to by the Unions related to the ex penditure shown by the Company for repairs and renewals. The Unions had furnished interrogatories requiring the Company to furnish certain particulars. They had also given details as to how the amount of Rs. 35,44,830 was paid to all such officers totalling Rs. 750 per mensem. [759E] Metal Box Co. of India Ltd. vs Their Workmen ; , followed. (d) The evidence of Mr. No evidence contra has been adduced by the Union and it has later corrected this figure by adding a sum of Rs, Rs. 20,000 as awarded by the Com poration. [761F G] (e) The Company had furnished an interrogatories asking the Company not to pay bonus to its workmen. It had also furnished interrogatory requiring the company to furnish particulars. The evidence adduced by it was clear that over and above this sum of money Rs. 25,44 ,830/- was paid as bonus at a rate of Rs.. 750 per month. [762B] (f) The contention of Union that the Tribunal was wrong in allowing deductions of certain item from the net profits for computation of the available surplus is not justified. It has later on corrected this figures by adding an amount of RS. 1, written by the company, is justified and accordingly it is obligatory on an employer to pay the minimum bonus and also the maximum bonus upto 20% respectively. [763D] (g) The award of the Tribunal is set aside.

The appellant was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes in 1954, and thereafter as a Joint Commercial Tax officer in 1962, he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On promotion as Deputy Commissioners of Commercial taxes he was transferred to the said cadre. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of his transfer from one of the respondents, and the High court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government had accepted the views of the Full Board and dropped the charges made against him in respect of allegations proved, obtained his explanation and sent its report thereon. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The order of November 29, 1974 of the Government was not a bona fide order but it was based on an adverse entry in the confidential file of the respondent. [80G] 1.2 In the present case, the appellant had been promoted as Assistant Commercial Tax Officer in 1954 and thereafter he was promoted to a Selection post. The Government accepted the view of the High Courts that all the charges framed against Thiru D. Ramaswami were not substantiated in the enquiry made by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption. [81B] 1:3 In the instant case, there was no ambiguity about the effect of the order dated November 29. 1974 of Government. The reason for the order was that the appellant was a very intelligent and capable officer who kept the entire district under his control in perfect discipline. There was an adverse entries in the personal file of respondent to find something adverse to the appellant apart from the 1969 entry. All that we could find was some stray mildly deprecating entries such as the one in 1964 which said: "He is sincere and hardworking. He maintains a cordial relationship with public. With a little more tact he will be an asset to the Department". One curious feature of the case is that while the 1969 Entry noted that an enquiry was pending with the Vigilance and anti Corruption Department in regard to the allegations against. the appellant, the ultimate result of the enquiry which was that of the charges could not be pursued and proved. The basis of the entry was knocked out by the order passed dated November 30, 1974. [82C D] 1 :4. In the absence of any doubt about the correctness of the entries in personal file, it is difficult to hold that the previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored, once he is promoted. The fact that the 1969 entries noted that the enquiry was under investigation by the Vigilance Department in respect to the allegation against.the appellant, and that there was an entry in his confidential file to his discredit or hinting even remotely that he had outlived his utility as a Govt. servant, would not make any difference. [83D] 1.:5. The order dated October 29, 1975 of the government is based on the adverse entries recorded in the Personal file of appellant in 1969. The effect of this order was to grant absolution to the petitioner from the repercussions of, the note of the Deputy Commissioner, Commercial Taxes and posted as member, Sales Tax appellate Tribunal, a prestigious post. [84E F] 1.(a) In the facts and circumstances of the present cases, it cannot be said that the earlier history of the Govt. servants should be totally ignored, when he is promotion. The previous history was that while he was working as Commercial Tax officers he was senior to the respondent and that his juniors were promoted to the Selection post, and in the meantime, as an Assistant Commercial Taxes officer in 1966, later as a Commercial Tax Inspector in 1962 and finally as Deputy commissioner of Commercial Tax on 7 S 1975. The High Court rightly held that all charges framed by the Director of Vigilance & Anti Corruption were not proved.

The appellants and some others filed writ petitions under article 226 of the Constitution praying for quashing of the schemes. The High Court dismissed them on the ground that the scheme was not in conformity with the requirements of section 68 C of the Act so long as the choice of the "area" in which and the routes in it to be run by the Corporation was made by them alone, and that therefore the approval by the Transport Minister must be held to be vitiated by mala fides. The appellants contended that the decision by the State Minister overruling the objections raised by several road transport operators to the schemes was also mala fide, in that they too acted in pursuance of the mala fide intentions of the Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh; and (2) that the approval of the Transport Commissioner must be upheld on the grounds: (1) that there was no mala fides of the State Government in approving or modifying the scheme; (2 ) that the order by the transport Minister was also not vitiated by any mala fides; (3) that even assuming the Chief Secretary directed the order in which districts were to be taken up for nationalisation, still the scheme framed by the corporation could not be challenged as not in accordance with the provisions of section68 C of Act so far as the option of the Government to make a scheme was concerned; and, (4) that since the State Transport Minister had merely carried out the wishes of the Prime Minister and that he too acted on behalf of the Corporation alone, the approval could not have been challenged as mala fides or mala fide. HELD: (i) The scheme framed under section 68C requires draft schemes and approved schemes to contain inter alia "the number of vehicles proposed to be operated on each route and the total number of trips to be performed daily on each occasion; and", that speci fication carries with it and obviously implies that the ope ration of transport between two terminii is intended to be nationalised. [657 D] (ii) The variation in the number was not a mere irregularity but a mere error. It must be remembered that the point most strenuously contended related to an illegality which was alleged to have occurred in the implementation of the scheme. Where, in pursuance, an approved scheme any State transport undertaking applies in the manner specified in Chapter IV for a stage carriage permit or a contract carriage permit in respect of a notified area or notified route, the Regional Transport Authority shall issue such permit to the State transport Undertaking, notwithstanding anything contained in Chapter V. [643 E] (iii) The expression "area", in section 68D requires draft scheme and approved scheme to contain interalia "the total number and number of motor vehicles proposed for operating on each routes; and" that specio fication carry with it "and obviously implies the variation in number. The variation is intended only to be notified by the Regional transport Authority, notwithstanding any anything to the contrary contained in section68C. [557 F] (iv) The distinction between an illegality and a mala fide exercise of power must be borne in mind while considering whether the order was vitiated by malafides or mala fides, because it is not merely the proportion but the variation of the number. It is only the terminal points that are specified and that specii fication carried with it. [525 G H] (v) The difference between an irregularity and a bona fide exercise cannot be said to have been caused in the execution of the order, because the variation is not a bona fides or a mala fides but a material fact which has no bearing on the question whether the variation was made in accordance therewith.

The appellant company, a registered dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, claimed exemption from sales tax on the ground that it was not able to furnish the duplicate forms of declaration forms received by it. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected the claim and levied on it additional tax of Rs. 2246,006 0 6 on the said amount in the treasury. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the Department was responsible for preventing the appellant from furnishing duplicate forms for all the declarations that were lost. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The proviso to section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act is not applicable to a case where the declaration forms issued by the purchasing dealer are found to have been lost or on the question whether the department went wrong in not summoning the dealers to produce the relevant documents to establish that the declarations were lost were in fact issued. [638 B] (2) The words "on demand" and "ondemand" are used in the proviso to sub section (1). But the said expression does not mean that a dealer who wishes to claim the said exemption must furnish the declaration in the prescribed form. It only empowers the Commissioner or any person appointed to assist him under sub section(1) of section 3 to take evidence on oath etc. [613 B C] (3) The substantive part of section 5 of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1940, provides for the exemption in respect of certain sales to a dealer if the sales are made to a registered dealers for the purposes mentioned therein. Under that proviso, in the case of such sales a declaration form duly filled up and signed by the registered dealer to whom the goods are sold and containing the prescribed particulars on a prescribed form obtainable from the prescribed authority has to be furnished in the specified manner by the dealer who sells the goods. [625 G H] (4) The expression "on demands" only fixes the point of time when the declaration Forms are to be produced; otherwise the rule would be inconsistent with the section.

The State of Bihar has assured us in the affidavit that necessary steps for transferring women under "protective custody" in jails to the institutions run by the welfare department have been taken and directions to that effect are issued by the Government. This averment does not at all constitute compliance with the direction given by the Court. The State has assured him in the affidavits of Mrinmaya Choudhri, Assistant Inspector General of Prisons that necessary action for transferring Women under " Protective custody ' in jails should be taken and directed to that extent. The High Court of Patna also furnishes the above particulars to us within three weeks from today since the High Court on its administrative side must be having records from which these particulars can be easily gathered. The Government of Bihar, however, assured us that necessary step for transferring woman under " protection" in prisons to the institution run by welfare department has been taken. This unfortunate situation cries aloud for introduction of an adequate and comprehensive legal service programme, but so far, these cries do not seem to have evoked any response. The poor in their contract with the legal system have always been on the wrong side of the law. They are unfamiliar with the rules of evidence. Without it, though he is not guilty, he faces the danger of conviction because he does not know how to establish his innocence. This noble ideal cannot be realized if the poor man charged with crime has to face his accusers without a lawyer to assist him. The right of one charged with criminal to counsel may not be deemed fundamental and essential to fair trials in some countries, but is in ours. It is an essential principle of "reasonable, fair and just procedure" to a prispenseman who is to seek his liberation through the court 's process that he should have legal services available to him. This ideal cannot also be realized when the poor can enjoy the law, as a doubtful luxury, and the poor, who need it most, cannot have it because its expense puts it beyond their reach, the threat to continued existence of free democracy is not imaginary but very real, because 542 democracy 's very life depends upon making the machinery of justice so effective that every citizen shall believe in an benefit by his impartiality and fairness. The Court in the last mentioned case asserted that it "has the duty of fashioning a decree that will require defendants to eliminate the conditions and practices at Parchman here in above found to be violative of the United State 's constitution" and in discharge of this duty gave various directions for improvement of the conditions of those confined in the State Penithambi. The court in the first mentioned case stated that it was "has been the dutyof fashioning the decree that would require defendants should eliminate the condition and practices put up beyond their reached, the threats to continued detention of free life are not imaginary and very real. But so far as women under trial prisoners whose names were set out in the chart filed before us on behalf of the State ofBihar also cannot escape its share of blame because it could not have been unware of the fact that thousands of under trial prisoner were languishing in jail awaiting trial which never seems to commence. The rich in their Contract with the Legal system has always been On the wrong part of law. [542A B] In the last cited case, the poor in the contract with legal system had always been at par with the poor who need them it most. But this unfortunate situation cry alouds for introduction by an adequate lawyer to help him. It was an essential indegredient of reasonable, fair, and just " procedure to a judicial pris grower who is not to seek its liberation by his ability and fairness, compel the collaboration of lawyer power for steering the wheels of equal justice under the law".

The appellant landlord gave notice of termination to the respondent on December 31, 1951 under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The notice was for one year as required by section 34 (2 A). The tenancy was to terminate from after March 31, 1953. In the meantime, an amendment was made to the Act by the Amending Act No. XXXIII of 1952 which came into force on January 12, 1953, whereby certain restrictions were placed on the right of the landlord to terminate the tenancy of a protected tenant. The appellant objected and claimed the benefit of the third clause of subs. (2A) to section 34. The respondent thereupon appealed but his appeal was dismissed. In revision, the Revenue Tribunal held that sub section (2) of section 34 did not apply to the present proceedings. On reference, the High Court held that the amendment made by the amending Act would not affect any vested right of a landlord till the tenancy actually stood terminated after the expiry of the notice. The Revenue Tribunal also rejected the contention on behalf of the appellant that the provisions of section 29(2 A) were applicable to the facts of the case and that the revenue courts were wrong in holding that sub s.(2A), was not applicable to a notice given before the Amending act came into effect. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Amending Act did not affect vested right which had accrued to the landlord till he came into existence after the commencement of the Amending Acts. [570 E] (2)(a) The amendment made in section 34 by the Amendment Act would be applicable only where a notice of one year was given before or at the date on which the notice expires. It is not open to the tenant not to carry out his intention. It does not speak of any notice at all. [571 G] (b) The words "if the landlord at the time of giving notice has been cultivating personally" in section 29 (2), are wide enough to cover cases where notices might have been given but where the tenancy had not actually terminated before the coming into force of the amending Acts. In other words, the Amending Ordinance did not operate to affect any right of landlords till the tenant actually stood termination after the expiration of the period of notice. [572 D] (3) The word "shall" in sub section(2A)(a), means "the landlord shall have no right to terminate" and it is always open to a landlord not to do so. It was only when the tenancy expired that the court has to enforce the right arising out of the notices and therefore the court had to see whether the termination was in accordance with the restrictions imposed by subs.(2 A), on the date the right was to be enforced.

The petitioners are his other son and two of their daughters.The petitioners, who had been declared an evacuee and had died on or about October 1, 1950 leaving three sons and five daughters, who thereupon became entitled to them in certain shares. No notice under section 7 had at any time been issued to them nor were they ever declared to be evacuees. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification by a writ petition in the High Court which was rejected on the sole ground that it bad been filed beyond the time prescribed for it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The petitioners have no longer any claim to them. They are not entitled to their rights in the houses concerned. Their interest in the house could not be affected by the order made under section 6 of the Act. [775 B] (2) The properties had already been acquired under the , and therefore the petitioners had no longer, any claim against them. [761 C] (3) The petitioner Zafar Ali was not a patty to the proceeding in which the order in dispute had been made. It only affects the rights of an evacuee which the petitioners, on the admitted facts, are not. [76 H] (4) The Act does not affect the petitioners ' right. It merely affects the right of an " evacuee" which the petitioner, on his admitted facts is not entitled. [77 G] (5) The provisions of section 12 of the , do not affect any rights of a person to be declared to have been evacueies and their properties cannot be upheld.

The assessee company was engaged in the business of spinning and weaving yarn from imported wool tops. The selling agents agreed to pay 6% interest on advances to be made by the agents and further agreed to accept 2% commission on the net proceeds of sales of goods in India. The assessee Company entered into an agreement with M/s. 8,71,873/ and received Rs. 37,157/ and Rs. 190 The assessee company paid a sum of Rs. 40,157/- as advance on the advances to the agents. The sale agents agreed that the payment was a permissible deduction as it was incurred for the purpose of the assessee 's trade in order to facilitate the business ' of the assesse. The sales agents received Rs 37, 157, and Rs 190/ were received by the selling agents. On the question whether the amount paid to the agent could be claimed as a deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Act, HELD: (1) The High Court was not right in holding that the agreement dated October 20, 1955 read as a whole amounts to a joint venture for the purposes of division of profits. [192D] (2) The assessee had no control over the expenses incurred by it in the character of trader or it is not laid out wholly and exclusively for the business. It was open to the Appellate Tribunal to come to a conclusion either that the alleged payment was not real or that it is made by a partner in the nature of trader, it is laid out entirely and exclusively as a result of his own profits. The High court was right in coming to a finding either that there was no agreement between the assessee and the selling agent. [191E F] (3) The Tribunal was not entitled to go behind the statement of the case. That, in our opinion, would only amount to apportionment or distribution of the profits after they have been earned. [193F G] (4) The expenditure incurred by the assessee company for the purchase of machinery and buildings and commencing from the date on which manufacturing actually started under this agreement is not a capital expenditure but it is a revenue expenditure. It is claimed for the company that when it makes over to the Colonial Government their half of the net profits it is making an expenditure wholly for the benefit of the business or for earning profits. In these circumstances, if we construe the agreement as a sort of a joint Venture or a transaction like a partnership which has been given the form and appearance of a contract of agency, the law must have its course. [194F G; 194A] (5) The amount paid by the agent to the selling Agents is not capital expenditure. The expenditure merely serves to promote or increase the commercial activity they may amount to an expenditure which is incurred for that purpose of business. [195C D] (6) The expenses incurred on tops, manufacturing bank charges, transport, insurance and octroi will be debited to the account of the company. [196F G].

The assessee company maintained an account pertaining to him in its books. In January 1959 for the first time he became indebted to the company in the sum of Rs. 18,950. The total amount due by him stood at Rs.18,905. The Income Tax Officer rejected the contention of the assessee and determined a sum of RS. 18090 as "dividend" under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal filed by the assessee. In an appeal to the Tribunal, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the expression "accumulated profits" in section 2 (6A) (c) of Income Tax, 1961 includes current profits in the expression 'accumulation ' and that the present definition of "accciment" in Explanation 2 to section 2 of the Act is not applicable. The Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to include current profits under section 1(6 A)(e). In appeal to this Court it was urged on behalf Of the Revenue: (1) that the High Court was right in answering the first question in favour of the appellant and against the Revenue; (2) that in view of the provisions contained in section 254 of the Income Tax Rules, 1962, the Appellate Tribunal was right. HELD : (i) The expression " Accumulation" occurs in section 1 (6 A) (e) and that it is only the party applying for a reference who is entitled to specify the questions of law which should be referred to the High court. [950 E] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs M. V. Valliammai Achi & Others, ; , followed. (ii) The word "accident" occurs within section 2 and that in every case it is open to the non applicant, in the event of the Appellate tribunal agreeing to refer the case to the Supreme Court, to ask for a Reference of those questions of Law also which arise on its submissions negatived in appeal by the Appellate Tribunals. [ 951 E] (iii) The words "accrue profits" occurring in section 3(6) (a) of Indian Income tax Act, 1922 clearly indicate that the profits must in the first place be accumulated in queueinc 948 tion to the profits being current. [969 A B] Commissioner Of Income Tax vs M/s. K. H. V Vallimaiahi A.I.R. , referred to. (iv) The High Court had rightly answered the first point in favour o the assessee because no reference application was made by the appellant. [970 E F] (v) The question whether the provision of Rs, In the Twelfth Report of the Law Commission of India, the authors of the report consider that the intention of the Legislature was to include Current profits in accumulated profits is a matter which has been decided by this Court in Commissioner of Wealth Tax vs Arundhati 952 Balkrishna but the point raised before us does not appeal to have been taken there. [971 E F G] (vi) The Explanation 2 of section 2 makes it clear that the words " Accciment", occurring in sub section (6) are not intended to take in current profits. But on a reference being filed by an aggrieved party it is permissible for the non applicants, in case of the appellate Tribunal agreeing to referred the case, to refer to the Income tax Officer who is competent to decide the question of law arising out of the order made by him under section 254. [974 A B C] Commissionerof Wealth Tax, Madras & Anr. vs M S.

The plaintiff was the proprietor of a joint family. The suit lands were comprised in Mouza Nala forming part of the permanently settled estate of Burdwan, and were Mal lands assessed to revenue, and that more than 200 years previously there had been a permanent Mokarrari grant of those lands by the Maharaja of Burdwan to the Rajgunj Asthal, and the plaintiff was entitled to assessment of fair and equitable rent. The defendants claimed that they held them under a Lakheraj grant made prior to 1931, and as they and their predecessors had been in possession for over 200 years under assertion of an adverse title, the claim of the plaintiff being barred by limitation. Held, that on the facts found no presumption could be made in favour of the defendants, and it was not a presumption juris et de jure, and, the Courts were not bound to raise it, if the facts in evidence went against them. The High Court was right in holding that there was no proof that the defendants claimed to hold under a rent free grant to the knowledge of the plaintiffs prior to 1932, and they must therefore be excluded. The presumption of lost grant could be raised only when there is no person competent to be the recipient of such a grant as where the right is claimed by a fluctuating body of persons. There was no evidence that the defendant claimed to have held under a lease free grant for a considerable length of time, but it had not been established precisely for how long. The plaintiff was not entitled to assess fair and reasonable rent on the holdings in their possession.

The appellant was the owner of a land in dispute. The respondent filed a suit for possession of the land on the ground that he had been cultivating the land since 1960 and that he was not an agriculturist, but was ineligible to purchase agricultural land and enforcement of such a contract would be violative of statute and, therefore, opposed to public policy. The trial Court decreed the suit but in first appeal the District Judge reversed the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit as in his view under the proviso to section 43C incorporated in the Tenancy Act by Bombay Act XIII of 1956 the respondent continued to enjoy the protection of the Tenancy Acts and the civil Court had no jurisdiction to decide it treating it as a subsidiary or incidental issue. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the judgment of the District Court and dismissed that suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 85A comprehends civil suits which civil Courts are competent to decide but takes note of the situation where upon a contest an issue may arise therein which would be required to be settled, decided or dealt with by the competent authority under the Tenancy act and, consequently, it is made obligatory for the civil court not only to arrogate jurisdiction to itself to decide the same treating it himself as a Subsidiary or incidental Issue but also to refer the same to the competent authorities under the Bombay Tenancy Act. [593D] (2) The expression 'land ' is defined in section 2(8) to mean; For the purposes of this Act, the following shall be the duties and functions to be performed by the Mamlatdar: (a) to decide whether a person is an agriculturist; (b) to determine whether a land is an agricultural land; (c) to settle whether a transfer or acquisition of land is invalid and to dispose of land as provided in section 84C. [592E] (3) The word 'land" is defined by section 2 (8) as meaning "land ' means any land which is capable of being used for agricultural purposes, whether such use is made with the object of making it suitable for the purpose of agriculture; (d) to include within its ambit any land in the nature of a building or other structure or any land appurtenant thereto and includes any land belonging to the Government or any local authority; (e) to confer on a person any right, title or interest therein; (f) to transfer by way of sale, mortgage, lease or otherwise any land held by him under a contract or otherwise; (g) to dispose off any land acquired by him in pursuance of an agreement with the Government for the purposes for which it was acquired; and (h) to sell or exchange any land or building belonging to such person.

The assessee was a heavy engineer ing concern manufacturing boilers, machinery parts, wagons etc. and for that purpose the assessee started the Jute Mill Division where the parts made out of the raw material supplied by the Boiler Division by machining and forging them were given to the Boiler division of the assessee. The assessee started its jute mill division where the part made out from the raw materials supplied by it by machising and forging their own machinery, but they were purchased from outside and this purchase was replaced by produc tion or manufacture from within the asses see 's own business. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner on the above facts held that the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 15C of the Act. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal held that in view of the provisions contained in section 15 C of the , it was not necessary for the assessee to establish a new industrial undertaking which is already running one industrial unit and set up. The High Court on reference held that though the new industrial units were covered by licences, they were entitled to the benefit under section15C of that Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Tribunal was right in answering the two questions in the affirmative and against the Department. [776 D] (2) The assessee was entitled to a partial benefit so far as the quantum of the exempted profits of the new Industrial undertaking under taking as also for a limited period or periods as specified in the section. [77 E F] (3) The benefit grant ed under this section is a partial relief so far that the quantum is of the exemption so faras the quantum are concerned. It is not possible to exclude any new indus trial undertaking other than the three categories mentioned above.

The appellant Corporation was a charitable trust. The Municipal Council levied the house tax on the basis of gross annual letting value at the rate of 7% of such value for the financial years 1953 54 and 1954 55. The difference came to Rs. 1,50,000/ . The Trial Court decreed the suit and the appeals filed by the Corporation in the District Court were dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the Corporation could do so because the rules made under the Indore Act are saved by sec. 79(1) of the 1954 Act, the Corporation need not prepare a fresh assessment list every year, that the Municipality may adopt the valuation and assessment contained in the list for any year with such alterations as may be necessary for the year immediately following. HELD: (i) The Municipal Corporation had to prepare a new assessment list once in every 4 years, that it has to prepare an assessment list only once in each 4 years. That fact however does not entitle the appellantCorporation to impose the housetax on the ground of the gross annual rent as such imposition is inconsistent with sec. 74(2) of The 1954 Act and the rules framed thereunder on the footing of the value of the property assessed on the valuation or annual letting values. [775 B] (ii) The tax imposed under the old Act and rules framed under the repealed Acts and added a fiction that so far as they are not inconsistent with the new Act they shall be deemed to have been made, issued, passed or imposed as the case may be under this Act. [76 H] (iii) The word "if" standing by itself makes no sense at all. That is the position of the Municipal Corporation in respect of the assessment and levy of tax leviable on buildings or lands or both.

The assessee Company entered into an agreement with one Rao Sahib Natesa Iyer for the sale of the lands, buildings, plant and machinery of its match factory for Rs. 7 12 0. The purchaser made a default in payment, and on August 9, 1943, a fresh agreement was entered into between the parties, this time for a consideration of Rs. 1,15,259. 1.15, 259. 1 15,259, 1.16,259 and 1.17,259 The assessee Company started to manufacture plywood chests for tea, paints and lemon grass oil. On May 9, 1944, the assessee Company sold its assets to a third party. In a confidential report made on August 1, 1944 to the shareholders, the 963 Directors stated that the price obtained had shown a capital appreciation of about six times the cost price and the sale was also resulted in a substantial profit. The Deputy Commissioner of Income tax then issued a notice under section 25 of the Travancore Income tax Act to the Company 's Liquidator on the ground that the profits from the sale were escaped assessment. The assessee company filed an appeal before the Tribunal, but the Tribunal referred two questions to the High Court for its decision, and held that the amount of Rs 1, 15, 259 was not a capital holding, but a profit of Rs 2,15259. The High Court answered both the questions in favour of the assessee. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant Company that (1) the transaction of sale of raw materials along with the business, including machinery, plant, and premises is a revenue sale; (2) the amount received as an appreciation of capital and not as assessable profit; (3) the High court was in error in holding that the assessee company was liable to income tax on a profit derived from Rs. 2, 15259, and therefore the sum of Rs 3,15 259 should be treated as a revenue receipt; (4) the sale by the assessee was a capital asset and not a trading transaction; and (5) the assessee had no right to sell its properties. HELD: (1)(a) The High court has rightly held that there was a sale of chemicals on July 24, 1943 to an educational institution for Rs 7 12 1,16, 259, and that the sum received as a consideration for the purchase of raw material along with its business,including machinery, Plant and premises was not trading. [966 D] (b) The assessee had the power to sell his properties. It is difficult to infer that the chemicals and raw materials were sold in the ordinary way of business or that the appellant company was carrying on a trading busi ness. [969 E F] (2)(a). In the instant case, there was evidence. There was no evidence. The mere realisation of assets was not trade; but the completion of outstanding contracts after the dissolution of a firm, the commencement of liquidation of a company, or the winding up of the affairs of a trader, has been held to be trading. It was only when the assessee received the consideration that it represented profit assessable to income Tax, that the excess obtained over the book value was treated as assessable profits, but in the Australian case, it was not. [970 G H] (3)(a), In the present case, the High Courts have rightly held against the appellant.
